Chapter 1 — Page Seven

[Quiet, observant narration; keep the domestic warmth and approaching dread restrained]

Nobody described Kindling the same way twice.

Cael had collected eleven. They were on page seven of his notebook, the current one, in the order people had given them to him. He had started the list in spring without meaning to start anything, because it turned out that when you asked people a question they liked answering, they told you, and if you wrote down what they told you, you had a list.

Sunlight, the fruit woman told him, from behind her trays of dates in the Outer Market. She had carried an Ember Path for eleven years and had never once doubted it, and she said it while weighing his dates, without looking up.

A door opening, the Merchant Row gate guard offered. He was Copper-tier, Shield Path, and he had a great deal of time between carts. He said it twice, the second time slower, in case Cael had missed it.

Like remembering something you never knew, announced the girl from three streets over. She was two years past her own Kindling and explained it with the confidence of someone to whom a thing has happened exactly once.

Like a wheel seating on its bearing, so you feel it go home, said Garrik, who fixed carts.

Warm, said Ressa at the bakery. Then she thought about it and added, Like the oven catching.

Like every timetable you own being right at once, said the man who sold hand-copied transit schedules, and when Cael laughed, it turned out the man had not been joking.

Cold water, and then not cold, said the lock-keeper at the canal gate.

Like a bell you feel in your teeth, said the boot-mender.

Brief, said the woman who ran the reference room at the community hall, and went back to her ledger. Cael had thought it the most honest answer on the page, until the last one.

Heavy, good heavy, said Joren, two days ago, on his way home from Weaver's Row. He had said it too fast, as if handing over something hot.

I don't know how to describe it, Hesk had said, and nothing more.

Cael had starred that one. Only that one.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

This was the morning before his Kindling.

There was no way to skip it and no way to ask for more time. In the year you turned fourteen, you stood in the circle at a certification office, and your Path woke there whether you wanted it to or not. The only thing anyone could choose was the day, and the city chose that for you, a year ahead, because the district made so many fourteen-year-olds that the offices would drown otherwise. Cael had turned fourteen five days ago. His appointment was at eight tomorrow, on Weaver's Row, and he had spent most of the past year not thinking about it, which had not worked.

He ate breakfast at the kitchen table while Hesk read the city notice sheet. The east window let in light at a low angle for about twenty minutes each morning, clear and sideways, so that it lay across the table like a ruler. The bread was from Ressa's bakery on the corner, where she kept the side door open while the ovens were going. The smell carried half a block in every direction, and walking home in the morning was mostly a matter of following your nose. Under the bread was the workshop smell of solder flux and machine oil and brass filings, which did not really have a smell, except that they did.

"Weather's turning," Hesk said, from behind the notice sheet.

"It says that?"

"No, it says the canal authority is raising the lock fees." He folded the sheet. "I can tell about the weather myself."

Hesk was fifty-four, with a square, weathered face and hands that looked too big for the fine work he did with them. He was Iron-tier, retired from active practice for longer than Cael had been alive. He made instruments now: pressure gauges for the canal authority, level meters for the survey office, and once, memorably, a very small clock for a man who wanted it hidden inside a walking stick.

He looked at Cael over the folded sheet. "You're not eating."

"I'm eating."

"You're holding a piece of bread, which isn't the same thing."

Cael took a bite to prove something. Hesk watched him chew it with the patience of a man who had raised a boy and knew exactly how much a single bite proved.

"Workshop, when you're done," Hesk said. "I want your numbers on the lock gauge housing before we test it."

Cael knew it was a kindness, and he took it anyway.

The workshop was the back half of the house, with a long bench under two windows, a stove, racks of brass stock sorted by gauge, and a wall of small drawers labelled in Hesk's square hand. Springs, fine. Springs, coarse. Springs, do not use. Cael had asked about that last drawer when he was six, and Hesk had said, "Those are the ones that taught me something," which Cael had not understood then and did now.

The housing sat in the test rig. It was a brass case for a canal pressure gauge, about the size of two fists, and it would bolt to a lock wall and hold its dial steady while tons of water leaned on the gate beside it. Hesk had built the case. Cael had done the bracket calculations three days ago, at this bench, with the city's appointment letter tucked into the back of his notebook so that he would not have to see it.

He opened the notebook to the page.

"Walk me through it," Hesk said.

"Wall bracket, four bolts, and the load is the housing's weight, plus vibration from the gate, plus a margin for when somebody bumps it with a boat hook." He ran his finger down the column. "The allowed load on each bolt comes from the stock sheet. I used the supplier's figure for the bracket alloy, and with the margin you like, it holds at three times working load."

"Three times, good, let's see."

The rig was simple: a lever arm, a hanging tray, iron weights stacked in fives, and a dial gauge touching the bracket at its weakest point, so that if the bracket bent the needle would move, and if it bent too far and did not come back, it had failed.

Hesk added the first stack, then the second, and the needle stayed near zero. At the third stack, which was working load, the needle twitched and settled, and Cael, who had been holding his breath, let it out. Hesk added a fourth stack, slowly, and then a fifth, and Cael leaned in over the dial so close that he could see his own eye in the glass. At five and a half stacks the bracket made a small sound, not loud, a tick like a knuckle cracking, and the needle swung across the dial and hung there and did not come back.

Hesk lifted the weights off one stack at a time. The needle stayed where it was. The bracket had a slight new curve to it, as if it were thinking about bending. It had failed at less than twice working load.

Cael felt his face go hot, which was ridiculous, because it was a bracket and nobody had been standing under it.

"Well," said Hesk, with interest. "That's a lie somewhere."

"My numbers were right."

"Then find out what was wrong."

Cael went back down the column twice. The arithmetic held. He had weighed the housing himself; the bolt spacing was right; the margin was right. Then he came to the one number on the page that he had not made.

Allowed load, bracket alloy, per supplier stock sheet.

He had copied it, and he had not tested it, and he had not even looked at where the supplier had got it from.

"The alloy," he said.

Hesk said nothing, which meant go on.

So Cael took the bent bracket to the bench, clamped a scrap off-cut of the same stock in the vice, and spent the next forty minutes doing the small, boring test that would have taken forty minutes three days ago. File a sample, measure it, load it, read the needle, and do it all again. The real figure, when he had it twice, was about two-thirds of the supplier's.

"They printed the number for a different temper," Hesk said, when Cael showed him. "Softer stock with the same name, and it happens." He turned the off-cut over in his fingers. "It's a good calculation, Cael. Everything you made yourself was right."

"But I used their number."

"You did."

"Because it was printed."

"Because it was printed, and it looked like a number. Never trust a number you can't trace back to where it came from," Hesk said, and set the off-cut down on the bench between them.

Cael had heard him say it before, at eight, over another failed bracket, and had filed it away with everything else Hesk said, without any idea yet how many things the sentence would turn out to be about. He wrote it down anyway, at the top of a fresh page, with the alloy figure he had measured underneath it, and the date.

"Redo the bracket in thicker stock. You know the number now."

"I know a number."

Hesk looked at him for a moment. Then he smiled, which he did not do often, and which changed his whole face.

"That," he said, "is the right answer."

The new bracket went into the rig an hour later and held at three times working load, and at three and a half, and Hesk stopped there because there was no reason to break a good part to prove a point. Cael watched the needle sit still at the top of the stack. He had made something, and it held, and he knew exactly why, and for nearly a whole minute he did not think about tomorrow at all.

[Steady, observant narration; let place, distance, and social position register]

He went out afterward, because the house had begun to feel small.

Denvash's Outer District was a long ring pressed against the inside of the interior wall: wide up here in the north, where the transit depots stood, and squeezed thin in the east, where the lanes knotted up against the Inner District. The northern quadrant was where Cael had grown up. He knew its depots and its market, its community hall, and the canal gate that sighed when the locks let water through. He knew which streets flooded and which dogs bit. He walked north toward the market with nowhere particular to go, his breath showing in the cold. He counted things, because his own thoughts were too loud: fourteen carts between Fen Street and the market road, six stalls open and three still setting up, and one man disputing a delivery's weight with his supplier in the tone of a quarrel both of them had enjoyed every week for years.

At the end of Tallow Lane, the Inner District wall came into view over the rooftops.

It was higher than any wall had a reason to be. Cael had five pages in his notebook about that wall, covering its height, the grade of the road on each side of it, how many street lamps stood per hundred paces on each side, and the gate. The gate mattered most, because every city in Valdris was built in rings, and the rings were built on rank. The Registry kept your classification, and your classification decided where you could go. Copper-tier got the outer districts and part of the markets. Iron-tier got the whole city in general, and the guild districts if you carried the right papers. Bronze opened the administrative core, Silver opened every district and the roads between cities, and Gold opened whatever was left, which was mostly the kind of thing people put on posters.

Hesk was Iron-tier, so he went through the Inner gate twice a month to deliver gauges, showed his registration, and was waved on, and he never talked about it, as people never talk about the doors that open for them.

Below Copper was Unranked, and Unranked could not legally pass that gate at all.

Most of the people Cael knew were Copper, because about six in ten practitioners settled there for life, according to the Registry's public summary; another quarter reached Iron, perhaps one in ten reached Bronze, and Silver was rarer still. Each tier had ten ranks, which you climbed by use, by doing what your Path did again and again until a registered Arbiter station evaluated you and agreed that you had climbed. Rank 10 was the doorway to the next tier, which most people never went through and some went through once.

He had read the public summary three times at the long table under the community hall's window. He had read the sections on tiers and ranks, on declarations, on district access and guild enrollment, and the part near the end, under a heading called Non-standard designations and legacy classifications, which was four lines long and which he had needed to read only once.

SHATTERED: Classification indicating fractured Path architecture, historically associated with unstable practice and practitioner safety risk. Currently deprecated. Four (4) instances recorded in the history of the Compact registry.

Four.

Not a percentage, and not one in a hundred thousand: four people, in the whole history of the Registry, and Cael, who wrote down everything, had not written this down.

His preliminary assessment had been in the spring. Every child in the district had one. You sat in a chair at the district office while an assessor laid two fingers on your wrist and her other hand flat on your chest and frowned at nothing for a minute, and then she wrote something down. Most children got standard coupling, but Cael's assessor had looked at him a moment longer than she had looked at the boy before him, and written irregular coupling patterns, and under it, kindly, uncommon variation, no action required. He had looked up irregular coupling patterns that afternoon, and there had not been much, except those four lines a page further on in the same summary.

He turned off Tallow Lane before the wall could fill the whole sky, and let his feet take him toward Weaver's Row.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The certification office on Weaver's Row had been a dye-house once, and you could still smell it when the wind was wrong. Now it had grey stone facing, the Compact Registry seal over the door, and tall windows that let in light without seeming to want it.

Alis Trent was standing outside it with her mother.

Alis lived two streets over, had turned fourteen early in the autumn and Kindled three days ago, and was holding her certificate in both hands and reading it as though it were in a language she was still learning. Her mother was crying quietly into a handkerchief. Cael looked at the mother once and then not again, because people's crying was their own.

Alis looked up when his boots scuffed the step. "Tide Path. Copper, Rank 1."

"Tide's good for healing," Cael said. It was true, so he said it.

"That's what everyone says."

"Everyone's right."

"My brother got Blade Path."

"Also good."

"He's Silver Rank 3 now."

There was a space after that, and Cael tried several things in it, and none of them fit. Tide was a real Path with steady guild demand, and in ten years Alis could be an Iron-tier healer with her own rooms and a waiting list. But Copper Rank 1 at fourteen was not the same as a Silver-tier brother with travel papers and a guild sword, and Alis was clever enough to know it. Pretending otherwise would have been an insult.

"In two years you'll have more choices than it feels like you have today," he said.

"You sound like a pamphlet," she told him.

"I'm quoting my grandfather."

"Is he right?"

Cael thought about the needle sitting still at three and a half times working load. "Usually."

Her mother had gone inside to ask the clerk about the guild enrollment inquiry. Cael knew the order of it from the procedural summary in the community hall: certificate, family notification, the residential registry updated, and then a visit to the guild of your Path to ask whether they had room.

"What does it feel like?" he asked. "Having one."

Alis considered the question properly, which he liked her for, because most people answered before they thought.

"Like being able to hear my own pulse in my hands, all the time," she said. "I touched my mother's arm yesterday and I could tell she had a headache." She frowned at the certificate. "It's not very dramatic."

"You didn't want dramatic."

"I wanted it over." She looked at him squarely. "And tomorrow it's yours."

"Yes."

"Are you worried?"

It was a direct question, and he gave it a direct answer. "Yes."

She nodded once, as if he had confirmed something she already knew. "Me too. Before. Three days ago." She looked down at the paper again. "It's—I can't explain it. Better when it's done. Even if it's not what you wanted."

Cael took out his notebook, turned to page seven, and wrote it below the eleven descriptions, standing on the office step with the cold coming up through his boots.

Better when it's done. Even if it's not what you wanted.

He starred it.

"Are you writing me down?"

"Yes."

"Is that a compliment?"

"It's the second star on the page."

She almost smiled, a tired, real almost-smile. "Who's the first?"

"Hesk."

"Then I'll take it." She folded her certificate in half, and then, after a moment, unfolded it and held it flat again, as though folding it had been the wrong thing to do to it. "Good luck tomorrow, Cael."

"Congratulations," he said. "On the Path."

He meant it, and he hoped she could tell.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Everyone in the northern quadrant knew Joren's result, so Cael did too. Joren had spent a year predicting his Kindling, starting with something fast and narrowing it week by week until, by midsummer, he was telling people at the market Blade Path, Silver-track, probably Rank 3 by sixteen. He had told Garrik, and Ressa, and even the guard on the Merchant Row gate, who had said a door opening and then good luck, son in a voice that made Cael wince. The whole quadrant had followed his certainty with the close attention people give to certainty they suspect is wrong.

The certainty had been wrong. He had come out Stone Path, Copper Rank 1.

It was not a bad Path. Cael had looked it up the day Joren Kindled, because he looked everything up, and Stone rewarded patience; it built slowly and held well, and at the higher tiers it did things with ground and weight that the guilds paid good money for. Joren had patience underneath the noise, and in ten years, if he worked, he could be Bronze, which was more of the city than most of the Outer District ever saw. But it was a place to start from, not a place to have got to, and Joren had spent a year promising everybody he would get there.

Cael found him at the low wall.

It stood at the corner where Fen Street met the canal path, waist-high, made of old grey blocks, and it held nothing up. It had been part of a building once, and the building was gone, and the wall had stayed because nobody could think of a reason to take it down. When they were seven, Cael and Joren had sat on it every afternoon arguing about which Paths they would get. Joren had always wanted Blade, while Cael had wanted whichever Path would let him make things that held up for years, had never worked out which Path that was, and had at some point stopped wanting anything in particular.

Joren was standing in front of the wall with his feet planted wide and his arms folded, wearing the fierce, private look of someone concentrating on something nobody else could see.

"You look like you're waiting for a cart to hit you," Cael said.

Joren turned only his head. His feet stayed exactly where they were. "Cael, good, good timing." He grinned, remembered not to grin too much, and grinned anyway. "Come here and push me."

"No."

"Push me as hard as you can, and I'll tell you why after."

"You'll tell me why before, or I'm going home."

Joren sighed the long, wounded sigh of a person whose friend had always been like this. "I got my declaration, my first one, Rank 1. It came with the word, the same morning." He glanced up the street and lowered his voice. "You're not supposed to show anybody."

Declarations were private; the Registry summary said so, and everybody knew it anyway. When your Path gave you an ability, your Arbiter showed it to you and only you, and sharing one was allowed. But it was the kind of thing you did with family, or with someone you would trust with a door key.

"Give me your notebook," Joren said, holding out his hand.

Cael hesitated for one heartbeat. Then he gave it over, open to a clean page near the back, and Joren took the pencil from the spine and wrote slowly, his tongue at the corner of his mouth, as he had written everything since they were small. When he handed it back, the page said:

PATH DECLARATION — COPPER RANK 1
Rooted Stance — Passive. While both feet are planted flat, your stance resists displacement by force. The effect ends when either foot lifts.

Cael read it twice. "That's the exact wording?"

"Exact, because I've read it about four hundred times." Joren tapped his own temple. "It shows up right there. Not in your eyes, sort of behind them, like words written on the inside of your eyelids, except they aren't really words, and your eyelids are open." He scowled. "That's a terrible description."

"It's better than Brief."

"Who said Brief?"

"The reference room."

"Of course she did." Joren set his hands on his hips without moving his feet. "Passive means it's always on. I don't do anything. I just stand, and it's there. You know what that means?"

"It means you're hard to push over."

"It means I'm impossible to push over." He lifted his chin. "Go on, before it gets dark."

"It's ten in the morning."

"Before it gets dark, Cael."

So Cael put the notebook on the wall, set both hands flat on Joren's chest, and pushed.

It was like pushing a doorframe. He had expected it to be hard, but he had not expected it to feel like that. Joren's body still felt like Joren's body under his hands, warm and thin, a boy's shoulders under a wool coat, and yet behind it there was something else, as if the push went into Joren and kept on going, down through his legs and into the paving stones, and the paving stones were not interested. Cael leaned and put his weight into it and dug in his heels. Joren did not move. Around his boots, the loose grit on the paving shivered once and lay flat, every grain of it, as though the ground had settled itself like a dog that has decided it is staying.

"Huh," said Cael.

"Right? Right?" Joren was beaming, his face a little red. "I've been out here both mornings since. You have to use it to rank, that's what the Stone Guild woman said. An hour a day, feet down, let people push." His voice dropped. "Nobody else wants to push me, and my mother won't, because she says it feels like pushing the house."

Cael stepped back and looked at him. Not at his face; at his whole shape.

Joren's weight was low and wide, his knees a little bent, and everything about him was set. It was a stillness Cael had never once seen in him, because Joren had never in his life stood still for longer than it took him to think of the next thing to say. But he was talking now, about the Stone Guild woman and the hour a day and the Rank 2 threshold, which was nowhere close. She had told him, he said, that Copper Rank 1 to Rank 2 could take a year for Stone and that this was normal, and normal was a word he was going to have to get used to—

And as he talked, his left heel came up.

Only a little, and only at the end of each sentence, when he wanted the sentence to land. It was the bounce he had always had. At seven, telling Cael he would be a Blade Path champion, he had bounced on his toes so hard he had fallen off this exact wall.

The effect ends when either foot lifts.

Cael did not decide anything. He simply waited for the end of the next sentence.

"—so it's not the Path I wanted, but I'm going to be the best Rooted Stance in the whole—"

The heel came up. Cael put two fingers on Joren's shoulder and pushed, gently, as you would close a door that was nearly shut already.

Joren sat down in the street.

He sat down hard, with his mouth still open around the word he had been saying, and for a second he looked so astonished that a cold flash of worry went through Cael that he had hurt him. Then Joren began to laugh. It was not his market laugh, the loud one he used when people were listening. It was the old laugh, from the wall, from when they were seven, and it came out of him in a rush and kept coming until he was lying flat on his back in the grit with his arms flung out, wheezing at the sky.

"You—how did you—"

"Your heel."

"My what?"

"It comes up when you talk, at the end of a sentence, and you've always done it." Cael sat down on the wall. "The declaration says either foot lifts. A heel is part of a foot."

Joren stopped laughing. He raised his head off the ground and looked at his own boots as if they had betrayed him personally.

"That's not fair."

"It's in the wording."

"You read my declaration once."

"Twice."

Joren let his head fall back on the paving and lay there looking at the sky, with some of the laugh still in his face and something else coming in underneath it.

"So that's the whole Path," he said at last, very lightly, very carefully. "I'm very hard to move, as long as I don't move. Great, good, I can be a door."

Cael did not say anything clever, because there was nothing clever that would not have been worse. He got down off the wall and held out a hand, and after a moment Joren took it. Cael pulled him up easily, because Joren weighed what a fourteen-year-old weighed and the ground did not hold him at all when he did not ask it to.

"It's Rank 1," Cael said. "It's the first thing it does, not all it does. Higher ranks build on the stance, in the Stone section—ground reading, weight transfer, things that make other people's footing go bad." He brushed grit off Joren's sleeve. "And the heel's fixable. You only have to stop being you for an hour a day."

Joren snorted. Then he looked at Cael, and the carefulness went out of his face, and what was left was only Joren.

"Nobody else would have seen that," he said. "The heel."

"You'd have seen it eventually."

"Not for about a year, and not before somebody at the guild sat me down on my backside in front of everyone." He shook his head. "You notice stuff, you've always noticed stuff, and it's really annoying."

"Thank you."

"It's not a compliment." He grinned. "It's a little bit a compliment."

He set his feet again, flat, and Cael watched the grit shiver and settle around his boots.

"Again," Joren said. "And this time I won't talk."

"You're always going to talk."

"Then I'll talk without my heel. Push me."

They did it six more times. Joren talked through four of them and kept his heels down for three. On the fourth, Cael waited him out, and Joren began a sentence about the Stone Guild woman's terrible tea, and you could see what it cost him to finish that sentence flat-footed, but the heel stayed down and he stayed up, and he crowed about it as if he had won a tournament. The sixth time, Cael pushed until his arms shook. Joren did not move, though his face went red and sweat came out at his temples, until at last he said, "Stop, stop, it's on all the time but holding it isn't free, it's like holding your breath in your legs," and Cael stopped, and Joren let go of whatever he had been holding and nearly fell over anyway, from relief.

They sat on the wall afterward, side by side, as they used to, and Joren rubbed his trembling calves and pretended they were not trembling.

"So," Joren said. "Tomorrow."

"Tomorrow."

"What do you think you'll get?"

"I don't know."

"You'll get something good, Cael." He said it with all the old certainty, as though his certainty had never once been wrong. "Something smart. You notice things, so they have to give you something that goes with that."

Down the canal path, the lock-keeper was opening the upper gate. The water leaned, and the gate sighed, and the sound went out across the rooftops like a long breath. Cael thought about four lines in a summary at the community hall.

"Maybe."

Joren looked at him sideways, and for once he did not fill the silence. He sat in it with his trembling calves and let it be there, and it was the most patient thing Cael had ever seen him do.

"Come by after," Joren said finally, "tomorrow, whatever it is, and I'll show you how to fall down properly; I've had a lot of practice these two days."

"I'll come by."

Joren slid off the wall, set his feet on the paving, and stood there, flat-footed and stubborn, in front of a wall that did not hold anything up. Cael could see in his shoulders that he meant to stand there for the whole hour.

Cael picked up his notebook and looked once more at the page near the back, at the declaration in Joren's round, careful hand. Then he closed the book over it gently, as you close a door on someone's room, and walked home the long way, and did not count anything at all.

Chapter 2 — Tuesdays

[Quiet, observant narration; keep the domestic warmth and approaching dread restrained]

There was a line in the back of Cael's notebook with a pencil stroke through it, and he had been looking at it on and off for most of the afternoon.

He had copied it a month ago from the foot of the registry summary page, under the four-line entry he already knew by heart. It was a footnote, and it told anyone whose Kindling came out non-standard to present themselves at a Compact district office inside two days for something it called standard compliance processing. He had gone and found out what that processing involved, written it underneath, and struck both lines through. He never struck anything through. A wrong figure stayed on the page with the right one beside it, because Hesk said an erased mistake was a mistake you got to make again. This one he had crossed out anyway, and he still could not have said whether he had done it to be rid of it or so that he would always know where it was.

They both called this going up for the sight lines, which spared either of them saying anything truer. A ladder in the back hall ended at a hatch. Past the hatch there was tar and gravel, the chimney stack, the water tank on its iron legs, and a low lip of brick along the southern edge where you could sit with your legs on the safe side and see most of the northern quadrant at once.

Below him a cooper was rolling a barrel along the gutter with a stick. Two practitioners in Copper armbands carried a bundle of planks between them, the man holding his end as if it were a loaf, the woman holding hers with the set jaw of someone who would sooner drop it on her foot than be offered help. Children ran between the houses, shouting about nothing.

Then the grey dog came round the corner by the chandler's.

Nobody on the block owned it, or everybody did. It was big and shaggy, with one ear standing up and the other folded flat as if it had lost an argument, and it turned up several times a day to bark at things only it could see. Cael had once given a whole week to following it home, and every evening it had beaten him at the same corner by the canal; he had written the corner down and never solved it. Now it trotted across the crossing, stopped, and barked twice at a drainpipe.

The hatch creaked behind him, and he heard china touch china. Two cups on one saucer meant Hesk had come up the ladder one-handed, and Hesk only did that when he had brought something up with him besides tea.

Cael had known that since he was nine and had never said so, on the theory that a thing like that would stop working once both of them knew it.

Hesk lowered himself onto the brick lip, passed him a cup, and looked at the street rather than at him.

"Joren seems better."

"He's working at it." Cael wrapped both hands round the cup. "He made me sit him down in the street this morning. Rank 1 Stone, a stance declaration, and you really can't shift him while his feet are set. But when he wants a sentence to land, his heel comes up at the end of it."

"His heel," Hesk said.

"He fixed it twice before we stopped. He's built for Stone, honestly. He's patient, and he doesn't mind being shoved."

Hesk made a small noise in his throat. He had at least four, and Cael had grown up reading all of them; this one meant a job had been set on the bench and Hesk was choosing which side to begin from.

"You're not Joren," Hesk said.

"No."

"Whatever happens tomorrow—"

"Hesk."

Hesk broke off to watch the dog trot over the crossing. When he went on, his voice had dropped. "—we'll figure it out."

He kept his eyes on the street, either to give Cael room or out of plain care, and with Hesk those usually came to the same place.

"I know," Cael said.

"I've been down to the record office," Hesk said, "the district one, asking about non-standard classifications. What the procedure is. What comes after."

Cael kept his face exactly where it was and turned the notebook over on his knee, so that the crossed-out line lay against the tar. "And?"

"It can be managed, whatever comes. There are provisions."

He did not know what a provision was, in that sense. He turned the book face up again and wrote the words in the margin, there are provisions, because Hesk did not say things he did not mean, and nobody walked into a record office to ask about something he was sure would never happen.

"How long have you been carrying this?"

"A while."

"Since my preliminary assessment."

"Before."

The dog came back across the crossing the other way, slower now, as if it had forgotten what it went out for. Cael watched it rather than his grandfather.

"You should have told me." He was not angry. It was only true, as a measurement is true.

"I had a feeling, not a fact. You don't hand somebody a feeling."

"So I've been worried about it on my own."

For a while there was only the street. Then Hesk said, "Yes. I know. I'm sorry for that," and gave his cup a quarter turn on the brick. "Saying it out loud at the kitchen table would have put it in the house with us, and I didn't want to make a thing real before it was."

Cael held that up to the light and found that, with the two of them turned round, it was exactly what he would have done himself. That ought to have been a comfort. It mostly wasn't.

"What do you actually know about my assessment? Not what you think. What you know."

Hesk took longer this time. "Irregular coupling patterns. You read the sheet. The assessor wrote it up as uncommon variation, which is true as far as it goes, but there's more than one kind of uncommon." He breathed out through his nose. "I've seen one like yours. Once, years ago."

Cael had the pencil ready and wrote nothing. "Who?"

Hesk shook his head. It was not a refusal; it was not that story, and not today. "Tomorrow will make it clearer, one way or the other."

"And if it's—"

"Then we figure it out." He said it the way he seated a part in a rig, not hoping it would fit but having measured. "I mean it, Cael. Whatever it is."

Cael found he believed it. He believed it for the reason he trusted the load tables chalked up on the workshop wall, where every figure had a line drawn back to the figure it came out of.

They stayed while the light went long and yellow and then thin. The carts dwindled, the children were called in one name at a time, and the dog made a last circuit and did not come round again. The noise of the district softened into the hour before supper, when every sound seems to come from one street further off than it really is.

Hesk looked down into his cup with the face of a man let down by an old friend. "This has gone cold."

"You let it."

"I did." He made no move to fetch more, only got up, knees cracking. "Come down when you're ready. I'll see about supper."

He went down the ladder, and the hatch settled shut over him. Cael stayed where he was. He was being let off having to look ready, and he knew it, and he was grateful as you can only be grateful to someone who will never make you say so.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Dinner was rice and the last of the week's leftovers. Hesk had kept house alone for years before Cael came, and he still cooked a meal as he would solve a problem, so it was always adequate, and tonight Cael barely tasted it.

Hesk put the radio on, the small brown set on the shelf by the stove, with its cracked dial and the one knob that only worked if you pressed it in while you turned it. Most evenings it gave them the weekly Path athletics programme from the regional service. Tonight two men with large voices were discussing the sanctioned regional season at length, with strong opinions and no power to change anything.

"—and of course the Ardenmere quarter-final is the one everyone's still talking about," said the first. "Third exchange. If you weren't there, I can't describe it to you."

"You've described it to me four times," said the second.

Cael put his fork down. "The Wind Path practitioner from Ardenmere. They've been on about her all month."

"Third exchange," Hesk said, without looking up from his rice.

"She did something you can't follow on the radio."

"She dropped her stance before the commitment. It looks wrong, and it bought her the angle."

Cael stared at him. "How do you know that?"

Hesk ate a forkful of rice, chewed it, and swallowed. "I watched the community hall broadcast. On Tuesday."

There was a pause, in which Cael learned that he had no idea how his grandfather spent his Tuesdays. He had thought Hesk went to the guild house on Tuesday evenings to look over the trade notices, and he had never asked, because it had never occurred to him there was anything to ask. The notebook came open beside his plate, and ask Hesk about Tuesdays went into the margin with two lines under it.

Hesk watched him do it. "You could just ask."

"I'm asking."

"You're writing."

"Writing is how I ask."

Hesk set down his fork and looked at the clock over the stove, a plain round face with the hours marked in brass dots, which he had made himself, and whose hands said ten past seven.

"What day is it?"

Cael looked at him, then at the clock, then back at him. "Tuesday."

"The reel starts at half past," said Hesk, pushing back his chair. "Get your coat."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The community hall stood at the end of Chandler Street, two blocks from the canal, a long brick building with a slate roof patched so many times that it looked like a quilt. By day it held the reference room, the district notice board, a small kitchen, and a hall with a wooden floor where people held weddings, funerals and the occasional meeting about drains. Cael knew the reference room better than his own bedroom, but he had never once been in the building after dark.

Hesk did not go to the front but down the side of the building, to a narrow green door with a brass handle worn bright, where he knocked twice, paused, and knocked once.

"You have a knock," Cael said.

"Everyone has a knock."

"You have a secret knock, though."

"It isn't secret. It's polite." Hesk did not look at him. "Garrik's hearing isn't what it was, and two and one means somebody who knows to come in."

The door opened, and Garrik looked out.

Garrik was seventy or near it, with arms like a bargeman's and a white beard trimmed square, a retired Copper-tier who had fixed carts on Fen Street since before Hesk moved there. When Cael was eight, Garrik had spent a whole afternoon explaining wheel bearings to him, because Cael had asked and Garrik loved being asked, and Cael still remembered every word of it. Several things went across Garrik's face at once when he saw who was with Hesk.

"Well, well," he said. "Finally."

"He found out," Hesk said.

"Took him long enough, clever boy like that." Garrik stepped back to let them in. "Come in, come in, you're letting the warm out. The reel's threaded, and the good biscuits came."

The back of the hall had been made into a small room with a curtain, and inside it stood perhaps a dozen folding chairs, eight of them occupied, all by old people. All of them looked up when Cael came in, and looked at Hesk, and then back at Cael. It was the look of a club that had been waiting a little impatiently for a new member to be old enough.

At the front hung a white sheet pinned flat to a wooden frame, and at the back, on a little iron cart, stood a projector, tall and black and covered in brass fittings, with two big reels mounted on arms above it like ears.

"The regional athletics office films the main bouts and sends the reels round the district halls," Garrik said, patting the machine as if it were a horse. "We get them a week behind, and we're the only hall in the quadrant that still runs a projector." He said this with enormous pride. "I keep her going. I've rebuilt the lamp housing twice, and your grandfather made me the gauge for the tension arm."

Cael looked at Hesk. "How long have you been coming here?"

Hesk took off his coat, hung it on the back of a chair, and sat down before he answered. "A while."

It was the same answer he had given on the roof, and Cael heard it and filed it without yet knowing where it went.

A tiny old woman in a knitted hat held out a tin of biscuits. Cael took one, and it was very good, and she watched him eat it with great satisfaction.

"Sit by your grandfather," she said. "He's the best watcher in the room. Don't tell Garrik."

"I can hear you, you know."

"You can't, actually. That's rather the point of you."

Garrik turned off the lamps, and the projector clattered and woke, a beam of white light leaned across the room full of turning dust, and the sheet lit up.

The reel was the Ardenmere semi-final.

The picture was grey and flickered at the edges, and there was no sound but the clatter of the projector. It showed a square of packed sand under a high roof, with a crowd around it so thick that it looked like a dark wall, and two figures walking out onto the sand from opposite sides. One was a woman in a pale sleeveless tunic, lean and light on her feet.

"The Wind Path," Garrik said from the back. "The one from the quarter-final."

The other was a man nearly twice her size, broad and heavy, with his hair tied back.

"Iron Path," said Hesk quietly, "and Iron-tier as well, by his sanctioned rating. Rank 6 or so."

"How can you tell?"

"Watch the way he walks."

Cael watched him walk, and the man walked like a man, and that was all Cael could see.

"Not his body," Hesk said. "His feet, and where they land."

The man's feet landed heel first and then rolled flat, every step the same length, with no hurry in them, as though they had walked across a thousand floors exactly like this one.

"He's measuring the sand," Cael said slowly.

Hesk turned his head a little, and in the flicker from the screen Cael saw the edge of a smile.

The fighters touched hands and stepped back, and the bout began, and it was nothing like the radio. On the radio everything happened in sentences; here, almost nothing happened for what felt like a very long time. The two of them circled, the woman staying out of reach and the man following, slow and patient, and now and then one of them moved a hand and the other answered it.

"Nothing's happening," Cael said under his breath.

"Everything's happening, if you watch his hips."

"His hips?"

"Hands lie. Shoulders lie. A good fighter lies with everything above the belt." Hesk kept his eyes on the screen. "But the hips have to go where the weight goes, and the weight has to go where the strike goes, so you watch the hips and the feet under them, and you'll see the strike before the hand does."

Cael watched the man's hips, and on the screen the man's shoulders dipped right and his hand flicked out right, and the woman leaned away to the left, but his hips had not moved at all.

"That was a fake."

"It was a question, really. He wanted to see which way she leans, and now he knows."

The first exchange ended with nobody touched, and the fighters went back to their marks.

"The first exchange is a handshake," Hesk said. "You learn the other person's distance, their reach, how they stand. You give away as little as you can and take as much as they'll let you."

"And the second?"

"Watch and see."

The second exchange was faster. The man pressed forward and the woman gave ground, and gave ground again, and then suddenly did not give ground at all but stepped across him, quick as a bird, her hand coming up toward his ribs. He turned, so that her hand found only his forearm, and swept her away with it, not hard, almost gently, and she skidded back across the sand on her feet. A murmur went through the folding chairs, and somebody said, "Oh, nicely."

"The second exchange is questions," Hesk said. "Real ones this time. Each of them tries something they think will work. Not the best thing they have, but something they can afford to lose."

"Why not the best thing?"

"Because then the other one's seen it."

Cael sat back while on the screen the two figures stood at their marks again, breathing, watching each other.

"So the third—"

"The third exchange," said Hesk, "is where they tell you the truth."

The third exchange began. The man came forward with the same pressure as before, his hips square and his feet rolling heel to flat, heel to flat. Cael could feel him getting ready to commit.

"There," Cael said. "There, he's going to—"

On the screen, the woman began to drop.

It was the move from the quarter-final; Cael knew it the moment he saw it. She let her stance fall away from under her all at once, as if her knees had forgotten their job, so that it looked like a mistake, as if she were falling, while her weight went low and sideways under the line of his strike.

And the man did not commit.

His hips stayed back, and his front foot, which should have landed, did not. He let his own strike die halfway and stepped, not forward, but down and across, so that when the woman came up out of her drop in exactly the place she had come up in the quarter-final, he was already there. His forearm met her shoulder, not as a blow but as a wall, and she came up into it with all her own speed, and it spun her, and she went down on the sand on one knee with her hand flat to keep from falling further.

The bout official stepped in, and the woman stayed on one knee a moment before she stood, touched her fist to her chest, and bowed her head to the man.

The old people in the folding chairs let out their breath together. The woman in the knitted hat said, "Oh, poor thing," and Garrik said, "Knew it. Knew he'd seen it."

Cael sat very still. "He watched the quarter-final."

"Everyone watched the quarter-final. Everyone in this room did, and so did he, more carefully than we did, I expect." Hesk leaned back in his folding chair. "A trick works once. After that it's a habit, and a habit is something somebody can plan for."

"But she must have known he'd seen it."

"She did. I think she believed she was faster than his knowing." Hesk shrugged. "Sometimes you are. That night, she wasn't."

The reel ran on into a little footage of the crowd and some officials, and then the sheet went white, and the loose end of the film began to flap round and round on its reel with a noise like a trapped bird, until Garrik switched the machine off and the lamps came on and everyone blinked.

"Well," said the woman in the knitted hat, turning to Cael, "what did you think?"

Cael opened his mouth and found he did not know what to say. He had been to the community hall perhaps five hundred times and had read every summary in its reference room. He had read about Paths and tiers and ranks and guilds and districts, and he had believed he understood them, and he had understood nothing, because he had been reading the hands.

"I think," he said slowly, "that I've been watching people wrong my whole life."

There was a short silence, and then all the old people laughed together, a warm, crackling laugh that filled the little room.

"Oh, he's one of us," said the biscuit woman. "Garrik, he's one of us. Give him another biscuit."

The second reel did not start.

Garrik threaded it, muttering, and switched on the lamp. The projector clattered for four seconds and then gave a long, grinding shriek, and the picture on the sheet stuttered, froze, and went brown at the centre, where the film had stopped in front of the hot lamp. Garrik hit the switch with the flat of his hand, and the room filled with a smell like burnt sugar.

"It's the tension arm," said Garrik, in the voice of a man naming an old enemy.

"The tension arm," Hesk agreed, already on his feet.

What followed took twenty minutes, and Cael would remember it longer than he remembered either bout. Garrik held the lamp hood open with a rag around his fingers. Hesk knelt on the floor with the side plate off the machine, and Cael held the hand lamp. Between the three of them they found the trouble. The little gauge Hesk had made, which told Garrik how tightly the film was being pulled, was reading true, but the spring behind the arm had tired, so that the arm sat a hair too low and let the film ride up off its sprocket. Hesk did not have a spring with him. Garrik did not have a spring anywhere.

"I could bend it back," Garrik said.

"You could bend it back, and in a month it'll do this again."

"In a month I'll bend it back again."

Cael, holding the lamp, looked at the arm, and at the spring, and at the little brass stop the arm came to rest against, and said, "If you shim the stop, the arm sits higher and the spring doesn't have to do as much."

Both old men looked at him.

"Shim it with what?" said Garrik.

Cael felt in his coat pocket, where he kept the things that ended up in coat pockets, and brought out a thin brass washer he had filed for nothing in particular a week ago. Hesk took it, held it up to the hand lamp, and turned it over.

"That'll do," he said, which from Hesk was a medal, and he slid it in behind the stop, and Garrik threaded the film again, and the second reel ran clean from first frame to last.

It was two Bronze-tier Blade fighters, very fast, and Cael could not follow it at all, and did not mind in the least. He watched the hips, and twice he saw a strike come before it came, and once he said "there" out loud, half a second early, and Hesk said nothing and did not need to.

They walked home after nine through empty, cold streets, where the lamps on Chandler Street made long yellow pools with darkness between them and their breath went up white.

"How long?" Cael said again.

Hesk walked three lamps before he answered. "Some years."

"Why?"

"Because I like it." That was true; Cael could hear that it was true. Hesk walked one more lamp. "And because I wanted to understand how people move when they have a Path in them. How a body changes, once it's carrying something."

"Why?"

Hesk did not answer that, and Cael did not ask again. He had the feeling of a door he had not known was there, standing slightly open, and he did not want to push it, because he was afraid of what it would weigh.

They turned onto Fen Street, where their house stood dark and the workshop windows were black.

"Hesk."

"Yes."

"The one you saw. The coupling like mine." Cael stopped walking. "The person. How did it go for them?"

Hesk stopped too, under the last lamp before their door, with his hands in his coat pockets. He looked down at the cobbles and said nothing for so long that Cael began, privately, to put the question away.

"It was a tangle. I know how it started. I don't know how it ended." He lifted his head. "I've gone without the rest of it for longer than you've been alive."

He went in and lit the lamp in the kitchen, and after a moment Cael followed him in.

The water stain on the ceiling was shaped like a boot, and had been since the winter four years ago when the gutter froze and the melt came in at the northeast corner. Cael was looking at it in the pitch dark without being able to see it, which meant he was awake, and something had woken him.

He listened for what. Nothing in the house owned up to it. Hesk's reading lamp had clicked off through the wall an hour after Cael went up. Outside lay the heavy quiet of a quarter that started work before light, and far off the canal's night gate let its water through with one long sigh. It was two in the morning, or near it.

Tomorrow the Arbiter would wake in him, and nobody could tell you beforehand what that was like; the people it had come to could only describe it from the far side. A door opening. Sunlight. Brief. Heavy. Like remembering something you never knew. Eleven of those were on page seven, and the starred one, Hesk's, said only that he could not say.

His mind went down the day without his asking it to, as it would run a column of figures to see whether they summed. Alis on the step at Weaver's Row, folding her certificate in half and pressing it flat again. Joren on his back in the grit, laughing up at the sky until he wasn't. The woman on the grey sheet, dropping under a strike that never came, rising into a forearm, touching her fist to her chest. And Hesk: at the record office asking about provisions; a man who had seen this once, long ago; a man who had sat in a folding chair in the dark every Tuesday for years, learning how a body moves when there is a Path in it, and never once said why.

I know how it started. I don't know how it ended.

He reached for the shelf by the bed without looking and found the notebook by its corner. There was no light to write by. It did not matter; he had put this down before, in other words and other notebooks, and his hand knew its shape better than his eyes would have.

He put it back and lay down. The night noises came one at a time once he was listening for them: a beam in the old frame ticking as it gave up the day's warmth, the stove below cooling, the window glass shifting when the wind leaned on it. He began to count them, because he counted things, and lost count, and somewhere after losing it he slept without having decided to.

Chapter 3 — Eleven Seconds

[Quiet, observant narration; keep the domestic warmth and approaching dread restrained]

The certification office opened at eight, and Cael arrived at a quarter to, because he had never been able to stop himself being early. He had tried once, at eleven, for a whole week, arriving everywhere at the exact minute, and it had made him so anxious that Hesk had asked whether he was ill.

Hesk had offered to walk with him this morning. They had stood in the kitchen with the low sideways light lying across the table between them, and Hesk had said, "I'll get my coat," and Cael had said, "No," before he knew he was going to say it.

"I want to walk there by myself, like Alis did, and like Joren did." He had felt his face going hot. "I want it to be ordinary. Until it isn't."

Hesk had held his eyes a while, then given one nod. "I'll be in the workshop. They'll send for me if they need me."

He had not said if anything happens. He had said if they need me, and Cael had noticed the difference and was not sure Hesk knew he had.

So he walked to Weaver's Row alone, past Ressa's side door with the ovens going and Garrik's shop, which never opened before nine, and past the low wall at the corner of Fen Street and the canal path, where Joren was not standing yet. Along the canal the water lay flat and brown, and the lock-keeper was drinking tea in his little hut with the window steamed over. His breath smoked in the cold, and he did not count anything.

The waiting room had a long bench, and a counter with a window in it, behind which an official was doing paperwork beside a small brass machine that gave out numbered tickets, and Cael took one and was seven.

Three people were there already. At the far end of the bench sat two girls, twins, his age, with the same dark hair tied back the same way, not talking. One of them was turning a thin bracelet on her wrist, three turns and a pause, three turns and a pause, and Cael did not think she knew she was doing it.

At the near end sat a boy of about fourteen, very upright, holding his registration slip in both hands and reading it without really reading it. His eyes had the glazed look of someone who has imagined a thing so many times that the real thing has become hard to get to. The twins had numbers five and six, and the glazed boy had eight.

Cael sat between them, opened his notebook to a clean page, and put the date and the hour at the top, and then sat with the pencil over the paper and wrote nothing else, which was not like him.

There was a clock above the counter with a big white face meant to be read from across the room, and he found himself watching it more than anything else, not because he needed the time but because it was the only thing in the room behaving predictably. It moved forward, had no opinions, and was the calmest thing there.

At two minutes past eight, the official called five, and both twins stood up.

"Same week?" the official asked, looking at them over her glasses.

"Same day," said one twin. "We were born nine minutes apart."

"Together, then. It's allowed. Second door."

They went in together, the bracelet still turning, and the door shut behind them.

"Do you know what you'll get?" Cael asked the glazed boy.

The boy blinked slowly, as if he had been very far away. "Force. My father's Force, and my grandmother, and my aunt." He looked down at his slip. "It's always Force."

"That's good, if you want it."

The boy thought about this as though it were a new question. "I don't know," he said, and went back to looking at nothing.

The twins came out twelve minutes later, each with a certificate, their faces almost identical in their stunned, loosened relief, like people who have been holding something heavy for hours and have just been allowed to put it down. One of them was crying a little, quietly, not as though anything was wrong. Their mother was waiting by the outer door, and when she saw their faces, something in her own face answered a question Cael had not known he was asking.

This is what it looks like, he thought, when it goes the way you hoped.

The glazed boy went in when eight was called. Eight minutes later he was out again with a Force certificate in his hand and the face of someone who had always known it would be Force and was now trying to have a feeling about it. At the door he paused and glanced back toward the examination room, as if to make sure it was still there, and then he left without looking at anyone.

Cael was alone in the waiting room, and he looked at the clock and at the brass ticket machine, and then at his own hands, which were not quite steady, and he decided to stop looking at his hands.

"Seven," said the official.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The examination room was smaller than he had expected. It held a desk, two chairs, a grey filing cabinet, a shelf of identical grey folders, the Compact Registry's charter in a frame, and one tall window.

In the middle of the floor, set into the boards, was a circle of pale wood about as wide as his outstretched arms, worn smooth in two places side by side, where years of feet had stood. Under the paper and ink, the room smelled bitter and mineral, like the inside of a stone jar, a smell that had been in the walls longer than the Registry had.

A woman of about fifty sat at the desk, writing. She had short grey hair, a grey wool jacket and reading glasses on a cord, and the nameplate on her desk said WARDEN-ADJUNCT PELLIN. She finished her line before she looked up, and Cael understood that this was not rudeness; she was giving him a few seconds to arrive in the room before she needed anything from him.

"Name and registration."

"Caelen Hesk-ward. Registration 41-7843-V."

He had learned the number the week before and said it three times in the dark, so it would come out right.

Pellin found the file, checked a line with her pen, and made a small mark. "Kindling assessment, the usual way. Your Arbiter wakes here, and the result goes straight to the registry ledger." She laid two fingers on a flat brass plate let into the desktop at her elbow, dull and unremarkable, about the size of a book. "When your result reaches the Registry, this lights, and I record what it shows. The resolution itself is usually done before you've finished a breath; with the paperwork, the whole appointment runs from three minutes to fifteen. Do you have questions first?"

"What happens after fifteen minutes?"

She looked at him over her glasses. "It doesn't take fifteen minutes."

"But if it did."

"Extended evaluations are rare," she said, smoothly, in the voice of somebody who had been taught that sentence and nothing to go with it. "It only means we're being thorough."

"How rare?"

"Extremely." She lifted her hand toward the circle. "When you're ready."

A year of being ready, and he was not ready, and it turned out you could be both. He knew the procedural summary by heart: The practitioner stands within the marked circle. No external device is required. Every practitioner's Arbiter is their own, dormant since birth, and Kindling is the moment it wakes. What the waking felt like, nobody had managed to tell him; only that it came.

He stepped into the circle and put his feet where the wood was worn.

Something woke.

It did not come from outside him; that was the first thing, and none of the eleven descriptions on page seven had told him so. He had imagined something arriving, as light arrives through a window; instead it gathered from inside him, from somewhere behind his breastbone, as though it had always been there and had only now decided to be noticed.

It was small, a point of light he felt rather than saw, and it climbed through him slowly until it reached the edge of his sight and stayed there, just off to one side. When he turned his eyes toward it, it was still just off to one side, like the place a held breath sits in your chest, which you can feel exactly and never point to.

He glanced at Pellin, who was three feet away watching the brass plate, and her face showed nothing, because she could not see it and nobody could; it was his, and it had always been his, and nobody else would ever see it. It was his Arbiter.

It made a sound that was less a sound than the memory of one, a single low note he felt at the bottom of his breastbone and not in his ears.

Then it was quiet.

The count started in him on its own.

One. Two. Three.

By now, he understood, the plate should have lit; Pellin had said it was usually done before you finished a breath, and he had finished one. He kept her face at the edge of his eye; her face was information. She was not looking at him but at the brass plate.

He could feel his heart, and the worn wood under his boots, and the sigil at the edge of everything, very still and very attentive. It was looking at him, and he did not know how he knew that, but he knew it as surely as you know someone is standing behind you in an empty room. He thought of page seven, a door opening, sunlight, like remembering something you never knew, and before the count was finished, he knew that none of them was going to be his.

Four. Five.

Pellin's face had the pleasant, patient blankness of a professional doing something routine who does not want to look bored in front of the person she is doing it to.

Six. Seven.

The patience shifted, not much, only a little way toward something that was not quite attention. The plate at her elbow had not lit.

Eight.

She sat up straighter. Half an inch, perhaps less; it was small and it was real, and he saw it because small real things were what he saw.

Nine.

Her hand left the desk, went to the filing cabinet beside her, and rested on the handle of the bottom drawer without opening it.

Ten.

The sigil did not move. It hung at the edge of his sight, steady as a nail.

Eleven.

Eleven seconds. He was sure of the number. He had counted every one.

Then the Arbiter spoke.

It was not a word, exactly, but the shape of a word with everything warm taken out of it. Joren had called his classification heavy, good heavy, arriving like something set down on him. What Cael heard was very far away and very close at the same time, clear and complete, and certain.

SHATTERED.

The brass plate at Pellin's elbow lit, eleven seconds late. Text rose up in it, pale and even, and settled into the same word he had just heard.

At the edge of his sight, the sigil went out.

It did not dim. It went out like a lamp when the wick is pinched, and where it had been there was nothing. He turned his eyes after it, left and then right, and there was nothing to find. It had arrived from inside him and spoken one word, and then it had gone somewhere he could not follow, and it did not come back when he looked.

Pellin's face did not change.

That was the first thing Cael thought, in the half-second before he could think anything else: her face did not change, and that was extraordinarily professional of her. Her hand on the drawer handle opened the drawer, and her fingers went past the thick front files to the very back and brought out a single form with a coloured tab, clean and stiff, as though it had not been handled much. She uncapped her pen and began to fill it in, with the same small, quick strokes she had used for everything else.

"Your classification has resolved," she said, and her voice was perfectly level. "Please wait a moment."

She did not say the word. Cael understood why, even then, standing in the circle with eleven seconds of silence still sitting in his chest. It was not unkindness. The word had already arrived and they both knew it, and saying it aloud would only have been for form, and she was not a person who did things for form.

He stepped out of the circle. His legs worked.

Pellin finished the form, and then she took his registration card from the file, set it on the desk, pressed a stamp onto the classification line, which had been empty for fourteen years, and slid the card back to him. He did not look at it. He knew what it said.

She lifted the telephone receiver on her desk, dialled three numbers, and waited. "Weaver's Row, Pellin speaking. I have a non-standard result." She listened. "Understood. Proceeding."

She hung up, and for the first time since he had stepped into the circle, she really looked at him. Her eyes were grey and tired and gave nothing away, but she looked at him for a full second longer than she needed to, and in that second he thought there was something in them that was not on the form.

"There's a secondary consultation room," she said. "I'll need you to wait there. Someone will come for you. It won't be long."

[Steady, observant narration; let place, distance, and social position register]

She walked him down a corridor lined with shelves of the same grey folders, and he wondered as he walked how many of them held mornings like his, and then made himself stop wondering. The room at the end held two chairs and a window, and that was all.

The window looked out on a small courtyard of grey flagstones and had been left open an inch, so that cold air came through the gap. In the middle of the courtyard a tree grew at a slant. Its trunk came up out of the flagstones leaning hard to the left, as though it had started out in one direction and thought better of it. Then, about halfway up, it bent and grew straight again, like a question that had changed its mind partway through being asked.

Pellin left, and the door closed, and he heard her footsteps go back up the corridor at the same unhurried pace she had used coming down.

He sat and counted the tree's branches: the ones growing up toward the light, and the ones that had stopped reaching and gone off sideways. Eleven reaching up, he made it, though he was not sure and did not count again to check. There was no clock in this room, nothing to measure the minutes by except his own attention, and his attention had never felt so untrustworthy.

He was fourteen. A minute ago, perhaps, he had been given a classification the Registry's own summary called deprecated and a safety risk to the practitioner, held by four people in its whole history. He tried to feel something about that and could not find the place where the feeling should go. Instead he looked at the tree and thought, that's what it is. Not the word. The tree. Something that had set off one way and was now testing whether there was another way to go.

He opened his notebook to the page with the date and the hour, and under them he wrote Eleven seconds, and closed it again.

Twice he looked for the sigil, turning his eyes to the edge of his sight where it had hung, and found only the wall. The second time he tried to call it as the procedural summary said practitioners did, by attending to the place behind the breastbone. Nothing came. It was not silence; silence would have been something there, keeping quiet. It was just absence.

He waited thirty-seven minutes. He had counted those too, less carefully.

At the thirty-seventh minute the door opened, and Hesk came in.

He was wearing his good coat, the dark wool one he wore to the Inner gate, not the workshop coat with the burn on the sleeve, and his boots were clean and his hair was combed. In his left hand he held a flat leather folder, and Cael knew without being told that it held his registration papers and Cael's, and that it had been waiting by the front door. Possibly for days. Possibly for years.

His face was completely still. It was not closed; Hesk never pulled anything down over his face like a shutter. It had the stillness of water just before something surfaces through it, and Cael could see, even in that first moment, that the stillness had been prepared, and practised, and kept ready for years.

Hesk sat down in the other chair like a man who was not going anywhere until this was done.

He looked at Cael. "All right."

"All right," Cael said.

"You're not hurt."

"No."

Hesk nodded slowly, studying Cael as he studied a housing he had just opened on the bench, checking for cracks, testing where the load went, with care that came out as attention.

"The officer told you."

"She didn't say it. She didn't have to."

"What did it say?"

Cael said the word. He had meant to lead up to it somehow, but it came out bare, the one word and nothing round it, and he watched Hesk receive it.

"Yes," Hesk said, very quietly. "You've read the registry entry."

"Yes."

"How much of it?"

"Enough."

Hesk was not surprised. Cael could see that he was not surprised. He had the look of a man whose long preparing had finally been called on, and had turned out to help less than he had hoped.

"I should have told you things," Hesk said. "Several things."

"Yes." Cael looked out at the crooked tree. "When did you know?"

"Before your preliminary assessment. There were signs, small ones, before that."

"How much before?"

Hesk did not answer at once. "A few years."

A few years. Something in the words tugged at Cael, as a word on the tip of the tongue tugs, as if he had heard that answer somewhere already and in another shape. Then Hesk spoke again, and the tug was gone before he could follow it.

"I'm sorry, Cael. I made a choice that seemed right. It may have been wrong."

Cael let that sit, watching the tree stir in some wind that did not reach into the room. "A few years. A few years of watching me, and not one word—"

"Not one word," Hesk said, before Cael could finish. "No. That's fair to be angry about, and I'd rather you were angry about it out loud than carried it quiet, if it's all the same to you."

"I'm not—" Cael stopped, because he could not have named what he was, beyond tired and too full to have room left for anger even if he had wanted some. "I can't tell what I am right now."

"That's a reasonable place to be. You don't have to sort it out today."

Cael could see the shape of the choice now, and he could build it as he built a calculation. Don't tell him it might be SHATTERED. If it turns out normal, he'll never have had to carry it. Keep the preparing quiet and the worry separate, and don't make a thing real before it is. The logic made sense to him; he did not like it, but it made sense.

"Tell me now," he said. "What you know."

Hesk told him.

He told him that he did not know for certain what SHATTERED meant, that nobody alive did, not really, and that anyone who claimed to be sure was claiming more than they had. Then he told him what he believed, and said plainly that a belief did not weigh much against a word like that.

The name was registry language, he said, chosen by people who were frightened of something they did not understand, and fear giving a thing a name did not make the fear right. Broken, perhaps. Or perhaps something the system had no better word for yet. He did not know which, and he was not going to pretend he did.

He told him that abilities would come, might already be starting, but would not come the way a standard Path's did, with declarations and ranks and clear markers of how far you had climbed. Cael would find out what he could do by trying things, not by being told. And there would be practical problems, registry problems, because the Compact kept records, and the record would follow Cael wherever he went, and what people in certain positions did when they read it would depend on who they were.

He said nothing at all about the other four, and Cael was too full to notice the gap.

At the end, Hesk leaned forward with his forearms on his knees and looked at Cael from very close.

"Don't let anyone see you move. Not until you know what you're doing."

Cael frowned. "I don't know what that means."

"You will." Hesk said it the way he read a needle: not drama, a measurement. "If it's what I think, one day you'll catch yourself doing something you never chose to do. When you do, keep it to yourself. Not yet."

"Has that already happened?"

Hesk held his eyes. "Has it?"

Cael thought about the notebooks, three of them, full of things he had never decided to start writing down. He thought about the hall last night, when he had said there, out loud, half a second before the strike, without knowing how he knew. He thought about Joren's heel coming up at the end of a sentence and his own two fingers already moving before he had finished thinking now. But that was only watching, and he had always watched.

"I don't know," he said. "Possibly."

Hesk nodded slowly, as though Cael had given him a number he could trace.

"Then start paying attention to what you don't decide."

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

They did not go back through the waiting room. Hesk opened the door and looked down the corridor, and then said, "This way," and led Cael not left, toward the examination room, but right, to a door at the other end with a bar across it.

"How do you know about this door?"

"I asked," said Hesk, "on the way in."

The bar was stiff, and Hesk lifted it, and the door opened onto the grey courtyard and the crooked tree. They crossed the flagstones, and Cael passed so close to the tree that he could have touched its bark, and almost did, and then didn't. On the far side was a wooden gate in the wall, and beyond it an alley, the back of a laundry, steam from its vents, and the smell of hot soap. Nobody saw them go, and Cael understood that this was the point.

They came out onto the canal path two streets east of Weaver's Row, and the walk home was the walk it had always been, north along the canal and left at the corner where the man sold transit schedules for cities Cael had never seen. The morning had warmed while he was inside, and the district was going about its errands with the perfect unconcern of a place where everybody had one.

Two blocks from home, they passed Alis.

She was across the street with a basket on her arm, and she looked up. She saw Cael, and she saw Hesk in his good coat with the leather folder, and something in her face shifted. It was not pity, which would have been worse. It was more like I see what happened, and that was harder to hold.

She did not cross the street or call out, only lifted one hand, not waving, just an open hand raised and held there for a moment. I see you.

Cael raised his in return.

He did not know how much she knew. Kindling results travelled through a neighbourhood like water through a ditch, so she probably knew that his had not gone well, and probably not the word. What she had given him was what he had given her on the step: notice, and nothing asked in return. That evening, under her starred line on page seven, he wrote in small letters: She was right that it's done. It doesn't feel done.
