Hesk made tea that night.

Somewhere in there they ate, out of the cold box, without either of them noticing what, but the tea was what mattered. Hesk made it the careful way, which Cael had seen him do perhaps four times a year: on the first frost, on Cael's birthday, and on the night Garrik's wife had died.

He warmed the pot first, measured the leaves with the little brass spoon instead of tipping them from the tin, set the clock, and waited the full time instead of the short time they used on ordinary nights, and he did not talk while it steeped.

They sat at the kitchen table with the lamp between them.

"There'll be a notice in two or three days, by registered post," Hesk said. "It's the standard procedure for a non-standard result. It'll say what you're allowed to live in and where, and it'll say that my standing is affected while you live here."

Cael had read the residential provisions in the Registry summary months ago, at the long table under the window, and he had not needed to be told. Being told was different from reading it.

"Your guild standing."

"I hold the residence, and they like the people who hold residences to be easy to file." Hesk drank his tea. "So. Ardenmere."

Cael looked up. "You've said that word before. Last spring, when I asked about other cities. You said it like it was a word you'd been carrying around."

"Did I." Hesk set the cup down. "You looked it up."

"Six months ago. The reference room has a section on the eastern cities." Cael had made notes and told himself it was ordinary curiosity. "It's a two-day walk east on the merchant road, and its Unranked District is huge."

"Big enough to get lost in, if you need to be."

"I don't want to disappear."

"No. That's not what I mean." Hesk turned the cup a quarter turn on the table. "I mean large enough that nobody checks your registration at the district gate, because there isn't one. Anywhere the Compact enforces properly, they pull your record when you come in, but Ardenmere's Unranked District is unofficial. They put up with it because they think it keeps certain kinds of practitioner contained."

"Or they think they do."

"Yes." Something like amusement crossed Hesk's face and did not stay. "It won't be safe like home is safe. But nobody there reads your classification off a card, and that gives you time to learn what you're carrying before anyone with power over you gets a say in it. Go there first. Find your feet."

"You've been there."

"Once. A long time ago."

"What was it like?"

Hesk took so long to answer that Cael thought the question had gone off somewhere without him. "Noisy," he said at last. "Bigger than I'd pictured. I was younger than you'd think, and most of what I saw went straight past me. I make more sense of it now, from here, than I did with it all round me. Places are like that. You only see the outline of one once you've walked far enough off."

He did not say more, and Cael did not push.

Cael opened his notebook and wrote Ardenmere, and under it Unranked District. Large. No gate, and under that Hesk knows things about this he hasn't said. He looked at the last line for a moment and then crossed it out, because it was not untrue, but written down it looked like an accusation, and he did not mean it as one. It was a note to himself: there was more to find out, and he could find some of it without Hesk.

When he looked up, Hesk was watching him write, with a look that was part pride and part worry, twisted so tightly together that there was no point trying to separate them.

"You're already cataloguing it," Hesk said. "Good. Write all of it, the things that look like nothing too. You can't tell which ones count until afterwards."

"Is that going in the notebook you keep not giving me?"

Hesk's eyebrows rose.

"Last week on the roof you said, I'll give you some things, if it comes to it," Cael said. "When you thought I was asleep against the chimney."

"You were asleep against the chimney."

"I was resting my eyes against the chimney."

Hesk shook his head slowly, and something in his face loosened for a moment, as it did on quiet mornings in the workshop when nothing was broken. "Some of it's in the notebook. I've spent years working out what I'd say to you if this day ever came, and it turns out it doesn't fill many pages. You'll have it before you go."

Before you go. It was the first time either of them had said it, and it sat on the table between them with the teapot.

"Hesk."

"Yes."

"Whatever you were preparing for, the provisions you asked about, the notes—" Cael said it because it was true, and the easier thing to say would have been less so. "It helped. I'm not saying you were right to do it that way. I'm saying it helped."

Hesk said nothing for so long that the evening found its way into the room between them: a cart on the stones outside, the grey dog somewhere announcing something to nobody, and the long mechanical sigh of the canal gate to the north.

"All right," Hesk said at last, and his voice was not quite steady, and he did not try to make it steady. "Drink your tea. I made it properly."

Cael drank his tea, which was very good, because it had been made properly. They sat with the lamp and the pot until both cups were empty, and then a while longer, and neither of them got up to make more.

Chapter 4 — The Record

[Quiet, observant narration; keep the domestic warmth and approaching dread restrained]

The day after Kindling was the strangest day of all, because nothing happened in it.

No notice came, and no officer knocked. The sun came up at the usual time and lay across the kitchen table for its usual twenty minutes, Ressa's ovens went on at the usual hour, and the canal gate sighed on schedule. It was as though the whole city had agreed to pretend that yesterday had not occurred and was waiting to see whether Cael would play along.

Hesk went into the workshop after breakfast, and all morning Cael heard him in there: the vice opening and closing, files on brass, the creak of the rig's lever. Near eleven he went to the workshop door and looked in, and Hesk was sitting at the bench with a gauge face in one hand and a jeweller's loupe in the other, perfectly still, not looking through the loupe at all. Cael went away again without saying anything. He was not sure Hesk had heard him come.

He spent the afternoon on the roof.

From the brick lip on the southern edge, if you leaned out a little, you could see the corner where Fen Street met the canal path, and the low wall. Joren was standing in front of it with his feet planted and his arms folded. Even from here Cael could see how still he was holding himself, flat-footed and stubborn in front of a wall that did not hold anything up. Every few minutes he unfolded his arms and looked up Fen Street, toward Cael's house, and then folded them again.

Come by after, Joren had said. Tomorrow. Whatever it is. And Cael had said he would.

He sat on the roof with his notebook on his knee and watched Joren wait, and tried several times to work out what he would say if he went down. Hello. I got SHATTERED. It means I have to leave. No, I don't know where. No, I don't know what it does. Show me how to fall down properly.

Every version he built fell apart under its own weight before it reached the end. The word was surely all over the quadrant by now, but he did not know whether Joren had heard it, and he could not stand the thought of watching Joren's face find out.

So he did not go down.

Joren stood for his hour, and then for a little longer than his hour, and then he unfolded his arms, looked up Fen Street one last time, and walked away along the canal with his hands in his pockets.

Cael sat on the roof until the light changed. He had broken a promise to his oldest friend. It was not a large promise, but it was the first one he could remember breaking, and he wrote that down, because a person who broke one and left it out of the book was a person he did not mean to become.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The notice came on the second morning.

It came with a courier wearing the city administration's grey and brass, who knocked once and waited exactly long enough to be polite. Hesk answered. From the kitchen table, through the open doorway to the front room, Cael watched the courier's satchel, worn pale along the strap from going out every morning and coming back every night. He watched Hesk's signature on the receipt slip, slow and square, neither hurried nor hesitating.

Over Hesk's shoulder the courier's eyes found Cael at the table and stayed for half a second before they slid away, with the look you give a thing you have been told about and do not know how to look at directly. When he left, his boots on the front step going down were quieter than they had been coming up.

Hesk brought the document into the kitchen and set it in the middle of the table, between the bread and the teapot, and stood looking down at it as he looked at a block of brass stock before deciding where the first cut went.

"It's addressed to you," he said. "You read it."

The seal was dark wax pressed with the Compact's mark, a hand holding a balance, so cleanly that a machine must have done it. Cael thought, for no good reason, of the brass plate on Pellin's desk, and all that care poured into the outside of things. He broke the seal and unfolded the paper.

The language was official, holding its own meaning at arm's length in long sentences and passive verbs, so that everything was true and nothing was felt. He read it twice, because the first time had been like reading through water.

By authority of the Denvash City Administration, acting under Compact Registry Statute 14, Section 9 (Non-Standard Classification, Residential Provisions):

The bearer of Registration 41-7843-V, classified SHATTERED as of this date, is hereby notified that residential access above Unranked District designation is revoked effective immediately. The bearer retains legal access to Unranked-designated residence.

Note: the registered residence at 14 Fen Street, Outer District, Denvash, is held under the standing of an Iron-tier practitioner (registration 22-1190-H). Continued cohabitation by a SHATTERED-classified individual may affect the standing-holder's guild status pending Compact review. The standing-holder is advised to consider residential arrangements accordingly.

This notice does not constitute a criminal or civil finding against the bearer. It constitutes a residential and administrative provision only.

He read the last part a third time. This notice does not constitute a criminal or civil finding against the bearer. It was a strange thing to put in writing, because nobody puts that in writing unless a good many readers would otherwise assume the opposite.

He set the paper on the table, and it was good paper, heavier than the certificate had been. When the light from the window caught it he could see a watermark in the corner, a little official flourish, as though someone somewhere had decided that this document deserved nice paper. He almost laughed, and it did not come out.

Then he read the note about the residence again, the line that told the standing-holder to think about where people slept, and understood, not the words, but the machine behind them.

He looked up at Hesk. "They're not expelling me. They're expelling you. From having me."

Hesk had come round to read it over his shoulder, and his face did what it had done in the side room two days ago, going still in the prepared way.

"That's the mechanism," he said. "It's built that way on purpose. A family that chooses looks better than a city that puts a fourteen-year-old out on the road."

"That's convenient."

"Very." Hesk set his hand flat on the table beside the notice. "It isn't a request, Cael. Don't spend yourself being angry at the choice. There isn't one."

"There's an Unranked quarter here," Cael said. "Down by the tanneries. The notice says I keep legal access to Unranked residence. I could live there and come to the workshop in the day."

"You could live there," Hesk agreed. "Inside the same walls, three streets from the Compact's district office, which checks that quarter every month, with every gate in this city pulling your record each time you pass it. And a review doesn't count houses, Cael. It counts people. A SHATTERED boy sleeping by the tanneries and working at his grandfather's bench all day is still a boy at 14 Fen Street, as far as the review is concerned." He shook his head. "In Denvash, the record is always waiting for you at the next gate. Ardenmere's Unranked District doesn't have one."

Cael looked at the line about guild status, pending Compact review. He thought about all the years Hesk had spent being precisely himself, an Iron-tier instrument-maker, quiet and able and dependable, with canal gauges and survey levels and a clock inside a walking stick, and a name on the guild roll that nobody had ever had reason to look at twice. Three lines of print could put all of that in question, over something Cael had not chosen and could not have stopped.

"You could refuse," he said.

It was not really a suggestion. He needed to hear how it sounded out loud, and it sounded exactly as impossible as he had known it would.

"I could. And in three months my registration gets reviewed, and in six I lose the workshop. In a year we're both living in some Unranked District with nothing coming in and nothing to stand on, and anything I could do for you then would be worse than this." Hesk said it without heat; it was a calculation, not an argument. "Saying no doesn't win this. What wins it is you landing somewhere with something in your hands."

"I don't want you losing anything because of me."

"I'm not losing anything because of you."

Hesk's voice did not rise. It went flatter and steadier, and that made it land harder than shouting would have.

"Years ago I made up my mind to do whatever it took," he said. "This is the whatever. Don't shrink it by saying sorry for it."

Cael did not have an answer.

They sat with the notice between them on the table, and neither of them moved it. Outside, the street went on making its usual noises without them: a cart, a vendor calling. Three doors down, Ressa's flour being unloaded off a wagon sack by sack while somebody counted the sacks in a loud, bored voice. At first Cael could hardly bear how ordinary it was. A moment later the same ordinariness steadied him. The sacks would keep coming off the wagon and the count would keep going up, and whatever else happened, somebody would bake bread tomorrow.

"What happens to the workshop," he said at last, "if they actually review you?"

"Nothing today, and possibly nothing for months. The Compact takes its time whenever taking it suits, and it nearly always suits." Hesk's voice had come back to its usual level, the one he used for load figures and hard truths alike. "There's risk, and I won't tell you otherwise. It's mine to carry. I settled that long before this morning."

"When?"

"When I took you in."

He said it simply, as if it were the least interesting fact in the room.

"You don't take on a child and hold back the right to rethink the price afterward," Hesk said. "That isn't raising. That's something else. I didn't do something else."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

He went to the district record office in the afternoon.

It was three streets from the house, and he had been there twice before, both times as a curious boy reading up on something he never expected to need. Now he needed it. The building was older than the certification office and did not care how it looked. Its stone had never been refaced, and its front steps had worn into a shallow dip in the middle from centuries of feet. Inside, it smelled of paper and dust and ink that had dried long ago and had no plans to fade.

The young woman at the front desk looked barely older than Alis's brother, and when Cael gave her his registration number, her pen stopped moving. It was only for a moment before she caught it and smoothed it away. But he saw it, and he saw something else cross her face just before she smoothed that away too, something that looked very much like sympathy.

She did not ask why he had come. She took a key from a hook and led him down a passage to a door at the back and unlocked it.

"Historical classification archive. The full summary's on the second shelf from the window, bound in green." She hesitated. "The reading table's by the window. The light's better there."

"Thank you."

She went back to her desk and left the door open behind her. So much for discretion, he thought; news ran through the system faster than he could walk. She had known his number without being told, when two mornings ago, before the circle, his number had meant nothing to anyone.

The archive was one long room, shelved from floor to ceiling, with a scarred reading table and a single chair under a window that faced north, as archive windows always seemed to, as though direct sunlight might hurt something. Dust turned slowly in the pale light, and he watched it for a moment before he made himself start. The full summary was where she had said, thick and green and heavy, and the spine gave a small dry crack as he opened it, a sound that seemed much too loud in the quiet room.

He worked back from the index and found the section, not where he expected it but near the very end, under a subheading he had never seen in the community hall's copy:

Deprecated and Non-Standard Designations, Pre-Compact Era Holdovers.

He read the subheading once. Then he turned the page.

The entry here was not four lines but several paragraphs, in the same tight, careful print.

SHATTERED: Designation assigned where Arbiter evaluation finds practitioner architecture that does not resolve to a single recognised Path. The coupling between practitioner and Path framework presents as broken or incomplete. Ability manifestation in such cases has historically been irregular and difficult to predict, and practitioner risk has been assessed as elevated.

Of the four (4) recorded instances, disposition is as follows: three (3) practitioners are recorded as deceased within weeks of classification, cause of death listed as "practice-related incident" in Compact records. One (1) practitioner's disposition is recorded as unknown, last registry update dated 32 years prior to the present record.

He read the last paragraph again, and then a third time, because it was doing something he needed time to take in.

He had known the number four as you know a fact you read once and set on a shelf, and until this moment he had never turned it into people. Now he did. Four people with names, who had each stepped out of a circle somewhere and heard what he had heard, and three of them had been dead within weeks. One was not accounted for.

This was not a rule or a caution. It was an account of what had really become of every other person who had ever stood where he had stood, feet in a worn circle, counting.

Practice-related incident.

He looked at the phrase again, because it was doing a great deal of work. It could mean that they had died trying to use something they did not understand, or it could mean that someone had made sure of it, and he did not have the information to know which. What he suspected, without any evidence yet, was that the person who wrote it down had cared which one was believed, and that this was the only part of the sentence he could trust.

He took out his notebook and copied the entry word for word, the subheading too, in handwriting far tidier than the job needed, and he knew what that gave away. Then he sat with the green volume closed under his hands and did not read anything. He thought about the clerk at the front, young and briefly sorry before she caught herself.

He thought about how many people had sat in this chair over however many years the archive had stood, reading something that applied to someone they loved, while the room kept no trace of a single one of them, having only its shelves and its dust and the patience of paper, which outlasts everyone who ever needs it.

He put the book back exactly as he had found it, its spine level with its neighbours. At the front desk the clerk looked up as he passed and opened her mouth as if to say something, and then closed it and nodded, and he nodded back.

The street outside looked exactly as it had two hours before, which was almost the worst part. The vendors were still calling, and a cart creaked past with a load of new-cut lumber that smelled of resin, and once again the world had not noticed that his had shifted under him. He did not decide on the walk home how he felt about any of it.

He decided something else instead: he was not going to be the fifth entry in that book, and it was so easy to decide that it worried him, because deciding things on a walk home was easy and staying alive long enough to make them true was going to be the hard part.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Hesk was in the workshop when he got back, with a half-built housing clamped in the vice and a tray of small tools beside it. He glanced up when Cael came in, saw whatever was written on Cael's face, and laid the tools aside.

"You went to the archive."

"Yes."

"You found the full entry."

"Yes." Cael sat on the stool across the bench from him, the stool he had sat on since his feet did not reach the floor; they reached now. "Three of them died. One, nobody knows."

Hesk was quiet a moment. "I know."

"You knew before, and you didn't tell me."

"No." Hesk met his eyes and did not look away from it. "I gave you what you needed to decide things. I kept back what would only have frightened you and given you nothing to do with the fear. That wasn't a neutral choice and I won't say it was. It was my judgement, and you can think it a bad one."

Cael found, a little to his surprise, that he did not think it was wrong, or not completely. It was the choice of a man trying to carry two loads in one pair of hands: the job of getting Cael ready for what was coming, and the instinct not to hand him more weight than the day required, and those two things did not fit together neatly. They hardly ever did.

Hesk's hands went back to the housing in the vice and moved through the work without hurry. They were a craftsman's hands, which had done this motion ten thousand times and could keep doing it, steady and exact, while the rest of him held a conversation that mattered far more than the instrument ever would. That steadiness had always been a comfort, and it was a comfort now, and it took him a moment to see that the comfort and the anger were both there at once, side by side, neither cancelling the other.

"From now on, tell me things," Cael said. "As they come. Not managed, and not saved for when you decide I'm ready."

"All right." Hesk set down the file. "Then there's something you should have now, while we're being plain."

"Okay."

Hesk looked at the housing, and then back at Cael. "The fourth record, the one with no disposition. Thirty-two years ago." He paused and picked the next words out one by one, like a man who had practised them for years without ever knowing which day he would need them. "I was twenty-two, serving two years in the Compact's regional logistics division. No fighting. I routed supplies, which is the work they hand to steady Iron-tiers who keep their questions to themselves. That file was opened while I was there. I watched it begin. I never saw how it finished."

Cael had gone very still. "What happened to them?"

"I don't know." He said it plainly, and Cael could hear what the plain answer cost him. "I'm not dodging. I mean it. Someone took the case away from regional oversight and moved it up, somewhere my clearance didn't reach, and after that the file went silent. Twice I asked about it, and twice I was told it was none of my business, in the voice that means stop asking."

He let out a long breath.

"I left the division eighteen months later," he said. "Thirty-two years I've wondered, and no answer. What I do have is a name I've never said to anyone, and a promise I made myself the day I mustered out. You ought to know that both of them exist, even if I can't give you the ending yet."

"Will you tell me the name?"

"When you're older."

Cael opened his mouth, and Hesk lifted a hand.

"It isn't that I don't trust you. A name like that is a thread. Pull it before you're strong enough, and it pulls you instead." He lowered his hand. "That isn't a managed timeline, Cael. It's a real condition, and you'll know it when you meet it."

He did not write any of it down, not yet, not with Hesk watching. He held on to it instead, and turned it over as he had turned over the third exchange on the sheet in the community hall. Right now the shape of it mattered more than what was inside: a name never told, a file opened and then taken somewhere higher, and a promise.

"Okay," he said at last. "I believe you."

Hesk nodded once and took up his tools again. They stayed in the workshop together a long while without a word, Hesk filing and Cael watching the brass dust pile into a small gold drift on the bench, and the quiet said more than either of them could have.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Cael packed that evening, once the window had gone dark and Hesk had settled into silence over a book in the front room.

It did not take long, because he did not own much: clothes, three notebooks, and a handful of small tools he had made himself in the workshop, more for remembering than for using. Among them were a file with a handle he had turned on Hesk's lathe at ten and a pair of fine tweezers ground from spring steel that closed a hair off true. He packed them anyway.

He held each notebook before he put it in the bag. The first was three years old, its spine cracked and its cover gone soft. It was full of a younger boy's observations so earnest that he could not be embarrassed by them: Garrik says a bearing is happiest when it is doing nothing. The grey dog does not like the colour blue. The second covered the year he had first seen how far apart the Outer District and the Inner one really were. The five pages about the wall had felt like an essay when he wrote them and felt now more like a warning he had written to himself without knowing who it was for.

The third was the current one, with eleven descriptions of Kindling and two stars and a Stone Path declaration in Joren's round hand near the back. Folded into its back pages was a copy of a registry entry about four people he had never met and was never going to stop thinking about. Into the bag they went in order, the oldest underneath, as you stack a thing you mean to keep adding to.

Then he sat on the bed with a single loose page from the back of the current notebook and wrote to Joren. It was slow work, and he tore up two versions before he kept the third, which was short.

Joren —

I didn't come by. I said I would and I didn't. That was wrong of me and I'm sorry. I couldn't work out what to say.

It was SHATTERED. You can look it up in the hall. Don't read the green book in the record office. It isn't worth it.

I have to leave Denvash. Hesk's standing depends on it. I'm going east. I'll write when I know where I am.

Keep your heels down.

— C.

He folded it in four and put it in his coat pocket.

Hesk came in as he was tying the bag. He was carrying three things, and he set them on the bed one at a time with the care of a man who had planned this for a long time and would not admit for how long.

The first was a cloth pouch, tied at the neck, heavier than Cael had expected. When he looked inside, the coins were all small ones, worn marks and half-marks, the kind that are put by one or two at a time rather than drawn out all at once.

The second was a book small enough to fit in a pocket, bound by hand in leather gone soft at the corners. A cord was wound round it to keep it shut, worn smooth in the place where it was always tied. Cael reached for it, and Hesk did not stop him, but Hesk did not let go of it right away either, and for a moment they both had a hand on it.

"Not tonight," Hesk said. "Save it for the road. It reads better with some miles between you and this house."

Cael nodded, and Hesk let go, and Cael put the book in the bag without opening it.

The third thing Hesk had brought was not a thing at all. He lowered himself onto the edge of the bed and waited, as if he knew something was coming and had decided to let it come.

"Joren's got a declaration," Cael said, to the bag. He had not meant to say it. "Alis can tell when her mother has a headache. The twins at the office came out holding certificates. Even the boy who didn't know if he wanted Force came out with Force." He pulled the strap tight. "Everyone I know is Rank 1 of something, and they've all started. I've got a word. I'm behind before I've begun."

"No," Hesk said.

It was not gentle. It was the voice he used when a measurement had been read wrong, and Cael looked up.

"Rank 1 of something means somebody already wrote down where it goes," Hesk said. "Joren's Path has a book. He'll follow it, and it's a good book, and in ten years he'll be wherever it says. Yours doesn't have a book. Nobody's ahead of you on it, because nobody's on it." He put a hand flat on the bag between them. "You're not behind, Cael. You're early. There's a difference."

Cael looked at the bag, with its money and notebooks and crooked tools and the leather book he was not allowed to open. It was complete in an odd way. Everything he owned that mattered was in there, and not one item of it could tell him what he would turn into.

"I'll write," he said.

"You'd better."

Hesk's voice caught on the second word, very slightly, and he covered it by getting up and going to the window and working the latch, which did not need working. He opened it and shut it twice. Then he stood with his back to the room and his hand on the frame.

"Long walk tomorrow," he said, to the window. "Get some sleep."

He went out and left the door open a hand's width, as he had left it when Cael was small and afraid of the dark, which he had not been for years.

Cael did not close it.

Chapter 5 — The Six O'Clock Light

[Quiet, observant narration; keep the domestic warmth and approaching dread restrained]

He woke before it was light and lay still, doing what he always did on days that mattered. He took inventory: the ceiling, the boot-shaped stain up in its corner, and his bag by the door, packed and tied and waiting with the patience of an object that knows what it is for, and the door to the hall, still open a hand's width.

From the kitchen came the sound of Hesk already up and filling the kettle. He set it on the stove rather than banging it down, like a man being careful not to hurry something he did not want to end. Cael stayed in bed a little longer than the inventory needed and listened to the house. The second floorboard from the kitchen door creaked when Hesk crossed it. The tap ran and stopped. A cupboard closed with a soft, deliberate click. It was the cupboard by the stove, whose latch had worked loose two winters ago, so that if you shut it firmly it rattled for a full minute afterward, and Hesk always closed it with two fingers.

Cael knew this house's sounds as he knew the streets outside it, completely, without ever having had to think about them, and he was thinking about them now. He supposed that was what leaving was. You noticed what you knew because you were about to stop being able to use it.

He got up, and getting dressed took him far longer than it should have. There was nothing to decide and everything else was packed, but his hands kept doing small unnecessary things, smoothing a sleeve, re-tying a lace that was already tied, and he let them. They seemed to know something he did not want to say out loud, which was that he would like this part to last.

The breakfast Hesk had made was not really about eating. There was bread from Ressa's, still warm, which meant he had been to the bakery before it was properly open, and the plum preserves from the jar on the high shelf that only came down for birthdays and first frosts, and tea made with the brass spoon and steeped the full time. It went unmentioned on both sides of the table, which was how they both wanted it.

"There's a waystation about a day out on the merchant road," Hesk said, over the tea. "South side, low timber building, lamp over the door. Sleep there."

"The waystation bars its door at full dark, and I'm not to be on the road after dark the first night," Cael said. "Page two of the record office's notes for the merchant road."

"I know. Now say it back in my voice."

"I could say it back before."

"Not in my voice. You did it in the record office's voice." Hesk pushed the preserves across the table with great care. "It's a dry voice. Nobody listens to it on a road at dusk."

Cael looked at him. "Is that going in the notebook too? Under things I told him that he knew already?"

"It might." Something in Hesk's face loosened, and he nearly smiled. "It's a long section."

Cael ate the bread, which tasted exactly as it always tasted, and that seemed wrong somehow, as though the bread ought to have noticed that everything else had changed. He chewed more slowly than usual and did not admit to himself why.

When they had finished, Hesk went into the workshop and came back with something small in his closed hand, which he put on the table in front of Cael before taking his hand away.

It was the lock gauge bracket, the first one, the one that had failed at less than twice working load with that small sound like a knuckle. It still had its faint new curve, as if it were considering a bend.

Cael looked at it and then up. "The drawer."

Springs, do not use. The ones that taught him something.

"Everyone needs one," Hesk said. "You'll have a bench of your own someday, and you'll want something in the drawer." He sat back down. "Start with that."

Cael picked it up. It was cold and small and slightly bent. He turned it over in his fingers and thought of the needle swinging and not coming back, that's a lie somewhere, and of forty minutes of filing and loading and reading a dial to find a number that had been printed and never traced. He put it in his coat pocket, next to the folded note for Joren.

"Thank you," he said, which did not seem like enough, though Hesk nodded as if it were.

Then Hesk got up and lifted something else off the workshop bench and set it beside the door. It was the finished lock gauge, in its brass housing, with the second bracket bolted to its back, the thick one that had held at three and a half times working load.

"It's due at the Fen Street lock this week," Hesk said. "It's on our way."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

Hesk carried the gauge in a canvas sling against his chest, with one hand under it. Cael had the bag on his shoulder and the satchel of tools on the other side to balance it. Neither of them had said they would walk to the depot together. Cael could have found the depot asleep; his feet had known the way there for as long as he had had feet. They walked anyway, and it was not discussed.

Six in the morning was its own district. He had lived inside it for fourteen years without once turning round to look at it, any more than you look at the inside of your own coat. He looked now. The street was blue in the shadows and pale where the sky reached down between the roofs, and the gutters were still wet from someone's bucket, and the first chimneys were putting up thin grey threads that leaned all one way.

The bread reached them before the bakery did. Ressa's side door stood open with the ovens roaring behind it, and the smell came half a block up Fen Street to meet them, as it had come every morning of his life. Ressa was out on the front step with a broom. She was broad and quiet and floured to the elbow, and she had been selling Hesk his bread since before Cael could see over her counter.

She stopped sweeping. Her eyes went from the bag on his shoulder to his face, and whatever she found there, she did not need it explained.

"Safe travels," she said.

She asked nothing else. She did not have to. By now everyone within four streets knew something, because news in the Outer District ran like water through the locks and found every low place, and Ressa had evidently decided on her own that two words were the right size. Cael said thank you. She nodded and went back to the broom.

They were past her step when she spoke again, to the paving rather than to him. "I put one by for the road, in with your grandfather's this morning."

Cael looked at Hesk. Hesk was studying the sky.

"It's in your bag," Hesk said. "She wouldn't take for it."

When Cael turned, the step was empty and the side door open, and the smell went on coming out of it. That was all the answer he was going to get, and he understood that it was a whole one.

He heard Garrik before he saw him: the slow tick of a hub going round on a stand, three doors down. Garrik did the first wheel of every day before his tea, turning it by hand with his head on one side, because he said a wheel told you everything if you kept quiet enough to let it. He was doing it now. His hand went round with the rim and his head kept its tilt, and he did not look up.

It was not the not-looking of a busy man. It was the kind that has to be held in place, and Cael could see what it cost him to hold it. Four nights ago this same man had opened a green door and said Well, well. Finally, and let a boy shim his tension arm, and called him one of us. Four nights ago Cael had not been anything yet. Now he was a word in a green book that four other people had owned.

It hurt more than he had braced for. He had thought there was none left to spend. So he did with it what he did with everything that would not hold still, and took it apart while he walked. Some people met a hard thing face on and some had to look past it, and which one they did said more about them than about the thing. Garrik's hand on the wheel was not saying I think less of you. It was saying I don't know how. Cael was almost certain those were different.

The ticking stopped behind them.

He did not turn. Perhaps Garrik had looked up once they were safely past, and perhaps that was as far as Garrik could get this morning. Cael decided to count it.

At the end of the street the community hall was still shuttered, the reference room dark behind its glass and the green door at the side pulled to. Somewhere on a shelf in there sat the summary with the four lines near the back that had started all of this. Denvash was taking a good deal from him today, but it had never hidden anything. It had left the truth on a public shelf for any boy stubborn enough to read that far, and he found he was grateful to the room for that.

"Will you keep going?" he said. "Tuesdays."

Hesk took several steps over it. "Someone has to tell Garrik when he's threaded it backward."

"He threads it backward?"

"One week in four, about. The biscuit woman says those are the only weeks the films make sense."

Cael laughed. It came out of him short and rough and startled them both, and it hurt a little on the way, and he was glad to have it.

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

At the corner of Fen Street and the canal path, the lock-keeper was waiting for them.

He was a long, thin man in an oilskin coat, the one who had told Cael, months ago, Cold water, and then not cold. He came out of his steamed-up hut with a mug in his hand and nodded to Hesk and then looked at Cael, and at Cael's bag, and nodded again in a slightly different way.

"You'll want the upper wall," he said. "I've dropped the level for you."

The old gauge was still bolted to the stone beside the upper gate, a cracked dial in a green brass case that had been reading the water since before Cael was born. Hesk had it off in four minutes and laid it on the coping like a retired friend.

Then he held the new housing up against the wall, and Cael, without being asked, set the thick bracket against the marks the old one had left, found that two of the old bolt holes were sound and two were crumbled, chose new holes a thumb's width to the left, and drilled them by hand with the brace from the satchel while Hesk held the housing steady and said nothing at all.

It took a quarter of an hour, and the stone dust got into Cael's sleeves, and the lock-keeper drank his tea and watched with the deep contentment of a man watching other people work on his wall.

When the last bolt was in, Hesk stepped back and looked at Cael. "Call it."

"Open the upper gate," Cael said to the lock-keeper.

The lock-keeper set his mug on the coping, put his shoulder to the long beam, and walked it round. The paddles opened, and the water from the upper canal came pouring into the chamber, brown and loud, rising fast up the stone. The needle on the new dial lifted with it, smooth and true.

The whole wall shuddered under the weight of the moving water, a deep vibration Cael could feel through his boots, and he watched the bracket, not the dial, because the bracket was his, and the bracket did not move by so much as the width of a hair while the water rose to its level and the gate sighed open and the needle came to rest at the mark.

It held. He knew exactly why it held.

"That'll do," said Hesk.

The lock-keeper looked at the dial and grunted, which seemed to be his highest form of praise, and then he looked at Cael for a long moment.

"It'll be here when you come back," he said.

Cael did not know what to say to that, so he said thank you, and the lock-keeper went back to his hut with his mug and the old gauge under his arm.

The low wall stood a dozen paces up the canal path, waist-high and grey and holding nothing up, and there was nobody in front of it, because Joren would not come for his hour until after breakfast. The grit on the paving lay loose and ordinary, as it lay when nobody was standing there asking it to settle.

"One minute," Cael said, and Hesk waited, and did not ask.

When they were eight, they had found a gap between two of the top blocks, at the end nearest the canal, where the mortar had crumbled out just wide enough to slide a folded paper into. They had used it for a whole summer to leave each other messages, most of them maps to places that did not exist. One of them, Cael remembered, had been a list of every word Joren knew that rhymed with canal, which had come to four, two of them made up.

The gap was still there. He took the folded note from his pocket and slid it in deep, until only a white corner showed. Joren would see it. Joren would stand right in front of it for an hour, flat-footed, with nothing to look at but the wall.

Cael put his hand flat on the cold top of the wall for a moment, and then went back to Hesk.

"Joren," Hesk said. It was not a question.

"I didn't go and see him the day after. I said I would."

Hesk nodded slowly. "And now you've written."

"It's not the same."

"No," Hesk said, "but it's honest, and honest lasts longer." He started walking again. "He'll be all right. He's got a stance declaration."

"He's got a heel problem."

"He'll fix it. You showed him where it was."

Two streets on, a woman Cael half knew, somebody's aunt whose face he knew from the market and whose name he had never learned, gave Hesk the ordinary nod of one neighbour to another. Then her eyes found Cael's bag, and whatever Hesk was carrying underneath his steady face, and her nod slowed and softened into something more like a held breath.

She did not say anything. Nobody, it seemed, had the right words for this. Cael was beginning to think that was not a failure on the street's part but an honest admission, because there were no right words, and people who said none were telling the truth about it.

Then they came out onto Lantern Street, which ran east toward the depot, and the light came in.

It was six o'clock, and the sun had just cleared the rooftops at the far end of the street and was coming down its whole length at a low, flat angle. It was gold, not yellow but the deep warm gold of brass that has just been polished, catching the dust from the bakeries and the smoke from the first chimneys and lighting them, so that the whole street seemed to be full of slow, bright, drifting specks.

It caught the edges of the cobbles, and the wet in a horse trough, and the side of Hesk's face, where it turned his grey beard briefly to the colour of wheat.

Cael stopped walking and looked at it, all of it, deliberately, as he would look at a page he meant to copy.

This, he thought. This exact colour. I am going to keep this.

He did not take out his notebook. Some things did not go in the notebook.

Hesk had stopped beside him, and did not ask what he was looking at, and after a moment Cael saw that he had turned to look down the street too, into the same light, with the same face. They stood there until the sun was clear of the rooftop and the gold had thinned to ordinary morning, and then they walked on.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The paving of the north transit depot did not end so much as give up. Somewhere past the last loading bay the cobbles thinned, went ragged, and stopped, and beyond them the merchant road ran east as packed pale earth between low field walls. Hesk stopped with the toes of his boots at the last stone, and Cael stopped beside him.

Behind them the depot was making all its usual noise. Carts were being loaded, and a family with a great deal too much luggage was having a low, furious argument about whether they had too much luggage. A driver stood feeding his steaming draught horses from a nosebag and telling them about his sister. At the toll booth a carter and the toll-taker were disputing a charge in the comfortable tones of two men who had had this exact dispute every week for years and would have missed it.

"You have the money," Hesk said.

It was not a question. It was the checklist being read aloud, because Hesk ran every load figure twice even when he knew it was right.

"Yes."

"The notebook. Not opened until the road."

"Yes."

"Ressa's loaf."

"Yes."

Two Bronze-tier practitioners in guild colours came across the yard behind them, and the crowd moved out of their way without anyone asking it to. Cael watched their feet go by, heel then flat, heel then flat, the same unhurried measuring walk as the Iron fighter's on Garrik's sheet. He thought, with something between dismay and delight, that he was going to be looking at people's feet for the rest of his life.

"Feet first," Hesk said. "Get your footing in the place before you go looking for anything else in it."

Cael almost laughed, and didn't. "I remember."

"The first person who's kind to you." Hesk was looking down the road, not at him. "Don't give them all of your trust. Don't give them none of it either. Watch them. You watch everyone anyway. Whichever way the watching tips, lean that way." His shoulders shifted, as they did at the bench when a repair turned out finer than it had looked. "I'm saying all of it twice. I know I am. I had two days, and two days turns out to be the wrong size."

"You could have two more."

"And two more after that, and I'd be standing on this same stone remembering the things I'd left out. It isn't the days." The smile he tried was worn thin with use. "At some point I hand it over. What you've got isn't finished. Nothing is. But you've spent your whole life building on things that weren't finished, and you're good at it."

Cael had nothing to say back, so he did not invent something. Hesk seemed to hear something in the silence anyway, and nodded at it.

Over at the booth, the carter and the toll-taker shook hands on the same figure as last week. The driver came to the end of his sister. The family with the luggage set one bag down by a post, deliberately, and walked off without it. For a moment it seemed to Cael almost an insult that none of these people knew this morning was different from the others. Then it seemed the opposite. The world would get on with its own errands whatever he did next, and there was a kind of generosity in being let off so lightly.

Hesk drew breath to say something else. Cael saw him take hold of it, something large, the size of the morning, and saw him weigh it and set it down again and pick up something smaller instead.

"Write to me," Hesk said. "When there's nothing to say, write anyway. Especially then."

"I will."

Hesk put his hand on Cael's shoulder.

It stopped a little short of a hug, and the little did not matter. The hand was hard, an instrument-maker's hand that had spent forty years closing on tools and had never been taught to close any more gently than the job required. Through it Cael learned what Hesk could never have told him in words and been believed: that the old man was holding on to him exactly as hard as he was holding on back.

"Whatever's out there," Hesk said, "and whatever it turns out you can manage. You were worth raising before any of it. Nothing you find will change that. I need you to believe it. Not just to have heard it."

"I believe you believe it."

"That's not the same."

"It's what I've got this morning."

His voice cracked on the last word. He let it crack. Hesk was the one person who had never once asked him to put on a face, and hiding it from him now would have wasted what little honest time they had left.

For a second Hesk's face came open. He did not cry; Cael had never seen him cry and did not now. But the cost of the morning showed in it plainly, more than his steadiness had been made to hide.

"It's enough." He said it quietly. "It's plenty. Go on, before I talk myself out of letting you."

Cael's voice would not hold for an answer to that, so he said, "I'll write," which was not one, and Hesk took it as one.

The hand lifted. Cael swung the bag up onto that same shoulder, still warm from the grip, and turned to the road before the turning could get any harder, and stepped down off the last stone onto the earth.

He went.

He let himself look back once. By then Hesk was too far off to have a face, only a dark upright shape in a good wool coat at the edge of the paving, not waving, not moving. Cael put up a hand, and the shape put one up in answer. After that he kept his eyes on the east, because a second look would cost more than the first, and he needed walking away to stay a thing he was able to do.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Five carts were queued at the district gate when he reached it, and the guard took a little under a minute over each. Cael timed the third and fourth without meaning to, by counting under his breath. The gate itself was a low stone arch where the Outer wall ran out into open country, and the guard post beside it was about the size of a garden shed. It mostly existed so that someone could look at merchant manifests, and the man in it looked at them with the speed of someone who had done it nine thousand times and expected nine thousand more.

He lifted a hand at Cael from habit. "Registration."

Cael gave him the card. The guard's eyes went across it in the order everyone's eyes went: name, number, classification. On the stamped line they stopped going.

Cael saw the half-second happen. It was the moment when a face doing routine work runs into something it has no routine for and has to pick, very fast, what to do instead. This face picked nothing loud. It did not narrow or harden. It simply withdrew, and settled into the look of a man who had decided the kindest thing for everyone was to have this be over.

"Go on," the guard said.

He held the card out with his eyes already on the next cart, and Cael was under the arch and out the far side in less time than the guard had given a load of onions.

He kept walking. He did not turn round, though part of him badly wanted to see the man's face and whether the boredom was back on it already. It would be. Cael was fairly sure that by the first milestone he would be the only person still carrying the arch about with him. That, he thought, was the real lesson of it. To himself he was going to matter a great deal, for a long time. To most other people he would last about the length of a sentence.

Twenty paces on, with the wall already shrinking behind him, he stopped in the road and got the notebook out. Information went in the book whether he liked the feel of it or not.

Gate guard, Denvash Outer gate. Saw SHATTERED. Didn't ask questions. Waved me through faster than routine.

People don't engage with what they're afraid of. They get you through the interaction as quickly as possible so they don't have to keep looking at it.

This is useful. Fear that wants to look away is fear that isn't paying close attention. Remember this.

He read it through and had the cover half shut before he opened it again.

Corollary, added a moment later, because it felt important enough to earn its own line: this will not always be true. Somewhere, eventually, I am going to meet the kind of fear that does the opposite — that looks harder, not away. I don't know yet what that looks like. I should.

Chapter 6 — The Rise

[Quiet, observant narration; keep the domestic warmth and approaching dread restrained]

The dog came out of a farm gateway in the second hour, as though it had been waiting there for him by arrangement. It was thin and brown, with a white bib on its chest and one ear torn at the tip, and it fell in at his left side without looking up, matched its trot to his walk, and asked for nothing at all.

"You're not the grey dog," Cael told it.

The dog did not argue the point.

He was glad of it, which surprised him. The first hours out of Denvash had been farmland: stubble and plough on both hands, low stone walls dividing it, a farmhouse every mile or so with its morning smoke going straight up. Carts had passed him going the other way into the city with cabbages and split wood. A family had gone by on foot, pulling a handcart with a baby asleep among the sacks, and two merchants on horseback had overtaken him at a trot without once looking down. None of it had felt like company. Every walk he had ever taken had been inside a city that answered him. Each street had a name, each distance stopped somewhere, and round every corner was a thing he already knew. Out here the road simply kept going and had no opinion about him. The only regular thing in the whole landscape was the sound of his own boots.

So he had looked at things, because looking was the one tool he could count on having brought. The mist had lain in the hollows between the fields and gone off unevenly as the sun got up, the high ground clearing first and the low places staying white long after, as if they were keeping hold of the night on purpose. A farmer two fields away, setting stones back on a broken wall, had lifted one hand to him between one stone and the next, and Cael had lifted his back. The road had felt less empty for as long as that lasted, and he had been surprised at how much less.

The dog stayed most of an hour. It went where he went, at the easy distance of an animal that belonged to the road and not to anybody walking it, and at a crossroads with a milestone it turned off toward a farmhouse without a backward look, exactly the way it had come. Cael watched it out of sight. He minded more than made sense.

By the middle of the morning his legs had started to speak up. It was not pain so much as a dull insistence on being noticed, which the city had never asked of them, because city distances were short and crowded with things to look at. The road notes advised a pace you could keep all day rather than one that felt bold. He let himself slow, and his breath came back. Hurrying would buy him nothing. Ardenmere was two days off, and it would wait for him whether he came in spent or only tired.

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

The cord round the leather book had a smooth place in it, worn almost to a shine, where it had been knotted and unknotted more times than Cael could estimate. He sat with the book on his knee and his thumb on that place for some while before he did anything about it.

He had made himself wait for a wall. Not until the road, Hesk had said, and a mile out of the gate had felt like a technicality, so he had walked on until late in the morning, when a low grey wall ran along the road's edge with a stubble field behind it, waist-high and good for sitting. It made him think of the other one, at the corner of Fen Street and the canal path, with a folded paper pushed into the gap between two blocks. Joren would have found it by now and stood there for his hour. Cael hoped he had kept his heels down.

He ate Ressa's loaf first. It was still faintly soft, and it tasted of the corner and the side door and every early morning he could remember, and he made it last. When it was gone he brushed the crumbs off his knees for the sparrows, who had been watching him from the wall with great attention, and untied the cord.

The book was smaller than it had looked in Hesk's hands. It sat in his palm. The leather had gone soft with handling, and the writing inside was Hesk's but not the square, careful hand that went up on the workshop slate. This one was rougher, and it changed from page to page: pale brown ink that had aged, black that had not, a hard-pressed line here and a light one there, the work of a man who had come back to the same few pages over a great many evenings.

On the first page there were only a few lines.

If this is in your hands, then I was right, and I'm sorry. I'd have given a good deal to be wrong. I can't take the word back off you. What I can give you is what I've managed to work out, most of it by watching, since there was nobody I could ask without being asked why I wanted to know.

None of it is sure. Read it anyway.

He turned over.

First: I don't know what SHATTERED actually means. I'm putting that at the top so you can't miss it, because everything under it is guesswork in advice's coat. Here is what I think, for what a thought is worth against a word with a registry behind it. Frightened people chose that word, and being frightened enough to name a thing is not the same as being right about it. Broken is one reading. Another is a country nobody has mapped yet, which is a different thing from no country at all. I can't tell you which. I've turned it over for years and I have nothing better, and anyone who sounds sure is spending money they haven't got.

Cael read it a second time. Only then did he notice what he had been waiting for. Somewhere below the parts of himself he kept an eye on, he had believed that a man who had spent years getting ready for this day would have come out the other end with an answer, and that the answer would be in here, in Hesk's hand, the way the answer to a load problem sat at the foot of the slate.

There was no answer. There was a grown man writing down that he did not have one.

Cael sat on the wall with that. It took a while, and it turned out to be more use than an answer would have been. Answers could be wrong. This was a figure taken by hand and written down honestly, and you could build on a figure like that, because you knew exactly what it would bear.

The next page.

Second: your body is going to learn before your mind does, and I mean that as plainly as I've ever meant a measurement, so don't go looking for poetry in it. Nobody is going to give you a card with a neat box on it saying what you can do, the way they gave Joren his. If anything comes, it'll come as your body doing a thing before you've chosen to, and you working out afterwards what happened. When it does, keep it to yourself. Watch it. Learn it the way you would learn a new tool, by using it where nobody can see, and only then try to say what it is, even to yourself.

Third: don't perform weakness, and don't perform strength. Perform competence. Look strong, and people start measuring you for a fight. Look helpless, and they start measuring you for something worse. Plain, quiet competence is the only face I know that buys you time, and time is what you'll want most. Let them find you dull until you know.

Joren's declaration was copied out at the back of Cael's own notebook. It had its heading, PATH DECLARATION — COPPER RANK 1, and its name in brackets, and one sentence that said exactly what Joren could do and exactly where it stopped. Joren must have read it four hundred times by now. He knew where his edges were, because his whole Path had been handed to him as a set of edges with the measurements written on.

There would be nothing like that for Cael. Not at Rank 1, not at Rank 10. No box, no line saying where the effect ran out. He would have to find his edges by walking into them, quietly, with nobody looking, and the two entries were telling him so from two directions at once.

The ink went paler on the next page, and the writing slower and more careful, as if the man holding the pen had put his weight down on each word.

Fourth: if the abilities do come, they will not come labeled. No notice, no box, no voice telling you what it is or how you came by it. Here I've the least to offer, because I've never seen it happen to anyone; this is reasoning, not watching. My guess, then. Mind what you can do when it's real, not what you can do when you're practising. I don't think whatever this is turns up because you've asked it nicely in a quiet yard. I think it turns up when it has to.

Fifth, and this one matters more than the others, so read it twice: you are allowed to be afraid and competent at the same time. I've watched good people talk themselves into believing those two can't share a room, that being scared means you aren't ready. That's wrong. Fear that keeps your eyes open is a tool like any other in the drawer. Worry about the other sort, the sort that shuts them. Yours won't. I've watched you for fourteen years, and you have never once known how to stop looking. Of everything about you, that's the part I'm least afraid will let you down.

He read the fifth twice, as instructed, and then a third time because he wanted to.

He had always thought of the watching as a kind of hiding: a way of standing a half-step outside things so they could not quite get hold of him, and something he would have to grow out of sooner or later. In the circle he had counted eleven seconds. On the morning of the notice he had named what his own hands were doing so that he would not have to feel it. In the archive he had copied the entry out in his best writing so that he would not have to just sit there and know it.

And Hesk did not call any of that hiding. Hesk called it the tool. Cael let that sink, and it did not sink all the way, but it went a long way down.

After the fifth there were many more pages. There were notes on the Registry, and lists of cities with most of them struck through, and single unnumbered sentences in fading ink. Near the middle, alone on its page, in ink so new it had hardly had time to dull, there was one more.

When you don't know what you can do yet, watch someone who does. Your body will learn before your mind does.

It had no number. It had been written lately, a few months ago at the most, perhaps only weeks.

He looked at it for a long time. Then the small snag he had felt in the side room at Weaver's Row, when Hesk said a few years, caught again, and this time he could follow the thread to its end.

A few years, in the side room. Some years, under the lamps on Chandler Street, about the folding chairs. They were the same span of time. For as long as Hesk had known what Cael's coupling looked like, he had been going to sit in the dark behind a curtain every Tuesday and learn how a body moves when it carries a Path, so that he would know what he was seeing if it ever happened to Cael's. Then, on the night before Kindling, with nothing left to learn and no time left to explain it, he had taken Cael along. He had sat him down and said watch his hips, and the third exchange is where they tell you the truth, and there, out loud, over and over, so that one day, with Hesk a week's post away and no chair beside him in the dark, Cael would be able to say there for himself.

It had not been a treat, or something to keep his mind off the morning. It had been the one lesson Hesk was sure enough of to give. He had given it at the last moment it could be given, and then gone home and written it down in new ink in case it did not take.

Cael tied the cord and sat holding the book against his knees with both hands.

This isn't nothing, he thought. I'm starting from this.

It helped. It did not help all the way. True things had always held more weight than comfortable ones; he had known that for years without ever having to lean on it, and it held now, even with I don't know written across the top. He put the book in the inside pocket of his coat beside the bracket, and stood up, because Ardenmere was still the best part of two days east and the afternoon would not wait for him.

The road dropped after midday into a long shallow valley with a stream at the bottom, and here the walls gave way to hedges, high and thick, so that the road ran between them like a corridor. It narrowed and bent, and you could not see more than fifty paces either way, and the air was still and close and smelled of wet leaves and turned earth.

Cael walked with his head down, counting milestones. He had passed nine since Denvash, and he was trying to work out his pace from them and from the sun, and getting different answers, and enjoying the problem as he had enjoyed the bracket.

He stepped sideways.

He did not decide to. One moment he was walking in the middle of the road with his eyes on the ruts. The next, his left foot had gone out onto the grass verge and his weight had followed it, and he was standing in the long grass at the bottom of the hedge.

The cart came round the bend behind him.

It came quickly: a high-sided farm cart heaped with turnips, pulled by one big dun mare going downhill at a trot that was not quite under control. Its wheels were rimmed with iron, but the road was soft dust here, and they made almost no sound at all. The driver was slumped on the bench with the reins slack in his lap and his hat over his eyes.

The cart went through the place where Cael had been walking. It went through it so closely that the near wheel hub brushed the strap of his bag where it hung at his hip, and he felt the brush, and the wind of it on his face, and a turnip bounced off the top of the heap and rolled into the grass at his feet.

Then the cart was past, and the driver came awake with a jerk and hauled on the reins, and the mare slowed, snorting, and the cart stopped twenty paces on, half across the road.

The driver twisted round on his bench, a red-faced man with a grey moustache, and stared back at Cael in the long grass with the turnip at his feet. "Lad!" His voice cracked. "Lad, are you hit?"

"No."

Cael looked down at himself. He was not hit. His bag strap had a pale scuff across it where the hub had touched, and his heart was going very fast, faster than it had in the circle; he could feel it in his throat.

The driver climbed down and came back up the road at a stiff old man's half-run, and stopped in front of Cael and looked him up and down as if counting his arms and legs. "I never saw you. You'd have been right under the wheel."

"I heard you coming," Cael said.

"You never."

"I must have. I stepped out of the way."

The driver looked at him with his mouth working, and then at the road, at the soft dust and the iron-rimmed wheels standing quiet as a pair of plates. He did not say anything. Cael could see him not saying it.

"Well," the man said at last. "Well. Thank the sky for good ears, then. Mine are no use to anybody."

He would not let it go after that. He was going as far as the waystation with his turnips, a few miles on, and he would not hear of Cael walking it. It was the least he could do, and a good deal less than the least, if you asked him. Get up, lad, get up on the bench, and here, have the turnip, it's yours, it's got your name on it now.

So Cael got up on the bench beside him with the turnip in his lap. The dun mare took them down the dip and up the other side at a walk this time, because the driver held the reins in both fists now and did not once close his eyes.

He was a talker. Before they were out of the valley, Cael had learned that he had four daughters and a son, and that the son was no good with turnips but very good with ledgers. He learned that the waystation woman's stew was better than it looked and her bread was worse, and that he did not hold with the new lock fees on the Denvash canal.

"Ah." The man nodded as though that explained a good deal. "The big one. Family there?"

"No."

"Work?"

"I'll find some."

The driver glanced at him sideways. "What Path are you, lad, if you don't mind my asking? You've got a look about you. Fresh. Kindled recent, I'd say."

Cael felt the question land and go all the way down.

He could lie. He could say Copper, Force and watch the man nod and move on. He found he did not want to, not because lying was hard, but because he had already watched Pellin's hand go to the back of a drawer, and the gate guard's face draw back, and he did not want to do that same thing to himself from the inside. "Still finding out," he said.

The driver considered this, and then laughed, a big comfortable laugh. "Aren't we all. Aren't we all. I'm sixty-one and Copper Rank 4 and I'm still finding out what Stone Path is for, besides knowing when the turnips want lifting." He shook his head. "Ardenmere's full of people like that. You'll fit right in."

Cael looked down at the turnip in his lap. He did not think about the bend in the road, because there was nothing to think about. The cart had made more noise than the driver thought, and he had heard the wheels without noticing that he heard them, as you hear a clock, and then he had moved.

Anyone would have. He was sure of that. He was nearly sure. He did not take out his notebook, because there was nothing to put in it; a cart went past close was not information. It was only a cart.

The waystation was where Hesk had said it would be, on the south side of the road: a low timber building with a mossy roof and a lamp over the door, already lit, though it was not yet dark. The driver dropped him at the gate and shook his hand very hard and told him twice more to thank the sky for his ears. Inside there was one long room with a stove at one end, a table with benches, and a row of cots along the far wall with blankets folded at their feet. Two were taken already, one by a drover asleep with his boots on and one by a thin woman knitting, with a small girl asleep against her side.

The keeper came in from the back, tall and bony, with her sleeves rolled up and her hair tied in a cloth, and named a price, and Cael counted it out of Hesk's pouch in the small worn coins. She counted them again herself, and then a third time. She did not once look at his face, not when he paid and not when she pointed him to the cot by the window and not when she said, "Stew's at dark. Bread's on the table. Don't eat the bread." It was not unkind. If anything it was the opposite, he thought. She did not want his face, only his coins to be right, and here that was all anyone needed to be.

He folded it and put it in the leather book between the pages to keep it flat.

These were not his sounds, and he did not know any of them, and he lay awake a while learning them, and then he slept, without meaning to, before he had learned them all.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The second day was longer than the first. His legs had stiffened in the night and took most of the morning to forgive him. The road climbed out of the farmland into rougher country with fewer walls and more sheep, and long slow hills that looked short until you were on them.

The sheep watched him go by with flat, unimpressed faces. There were no more turnip carts. He walked by himself and watched the milestones, and for nearly half an hour he watched a hawk working a field without ever seeing it catch anything, and by the end he was on its side.

He did not take the leather book out again. He did not need to, because he had read it often enough on the wall that its lines came up by themselves as he walked, like the old descriptions on page seven.

And the record came up by itself too, the green book and the four entries, and this time he made himself do something with it instead of just letting it come.

He did not know their names or how old they had been, or where they had come from, or what they had found themselves able to do before whatever happened to them happened. He did not know whether any of them had had a Hesk, or been given a book. But he knew the one word in the entry that he had read past in the archive, because the other words had been louder.

Weeks.

Not years. Not after a long life of trying and failing. Weeks. Whatever had happened to three of them had happened fast and early, before they could have found out what they were, before they could even have found their feet. He thought about the phrase practice-related, and about how little practice anyone could do in a few weeks, and about someone, thirty-two years ago, choosing which kind of true to write down.

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

Late in the afternoon, the road began to climb in earnest. It went up a long bare hill in a series of slow bends, with no hedges, only grass and stones and the wind, which had picked up out of the west and was pushing at his back. The sun was low, and his shadow went up the road ahead of him, long and thin, with a bag on its shoulder.

He came over the top and stopped.

Ardenmere lay below him in a wide river valley, and it was enormous.

He had read about it three times in the reference section on the eastern cities. He had known it was larger than Denvash, but he had not known what larger meant until he stood on the rise and looked. The river came in from the north, wide and slow and copper-coloured in the low sun, and bent through the middle of the valley like an arm.

On the far bank, in the crook of that arm, rose the Ranked core, walled and stepped, ring inside ring, each ring higher than the last. He could see the districts climbing toward the centre, Copper, he thought, and Iron, and Bronze, and at the very top something white with towers catching the last of the light. He had five pages in a notebook about one wall in Denvash. He could see six walls from here.

And around them, outside them, spilling past every one of them, was the rest.

The Unranked District was not a district. It was a city of its own, running along both banks of the river and up the slopes on either side and out across the flat land to the south. It had no walls at all, and no shape that he could find except the shape of a great many people deciding where to live one at a time.

There was old stone in it, solid and square. There were things that looked built and things that looked stacked, roofs going up on top of roofs, and three or four bridges crossing the river with movement on all of them.

The sun went down while he watched. The gold went out of the river, and the white towers on the Ranked hill held the light a little longer than everything else and then let it go too, and the sky turned grey-gold and then a deep, clear blue.

And the fires came out.

They came out one by one at first and then all at once, cookfires in yards and on roofs and in doorways and along the river, hundreds of them and then more than hundreds, little orange points of light across the whole Unranked District, each with a thin grey thread of smoke going up from it and leaning east in the wind, until the whole valley below him was lit like a field of embers that somebody had banked for the night and would come back to in the morning.

A thousand fires. He could not count them, and for once in his life he did not try. Each one was somebody's dinner, somebody not Ranked enough for the walls, making do.

He stood on the rise with the wind at his back. He was very tired, and his legs ached all the way down. He had a turnip in his bag and a bent bracket in his pocket and a book against his chest that said I don't know in his grandfather's handwriting.

He thought about the green book in the archive, with its four entries, three of which had ended in a few weeks and one in a line that said nobody knew. He was the fifth.

On the walk home from the record office he had promised himself there would be no fifth entry in that green book with his name at the top. It had been easy to promise, as things are easy on a walk home. He said it again now, to himself, and it was not easy anymore, because he could see how big the thing was that he would have to say it to.

He took out his notebook, opened it to a clean page, and wrote in the last of the light:

Three of them were dead within weeks. They didn't get time to find their feet. Whatever happened, it happened before they knew what they were.

So that's the first job. Not to find out what SHATTERED means. Not yet. First, get past the weeks.

Find somewhere to sleep. Find work. Watch everything. Show nobody anything. Be dull. Be competent. Be still here.

Then find out.

He looked at it, and underlined still here, once, firmly.

He did not know what was down there. He did not know where he would sleep tonight, or who the first person to be kind to him would be, or whether he would be right to trust them. He did not know what the Unranked District did to people like him. He did not know what he was.

He knew he was not going to be an entry somebody else wrote. He decided that, standing on the rise at the end of the second day with a thousand fires coming up out of the dark below him, and he decided it properly, the way you set a part into a rig and load it to see whether it holds.

He put the notebook away.

Down in the valley the road ran on toward the river, pale in the dusk, and where it met the first houses there was no gate at all, only a wide space in the dark with fires on either side of it, standing open.

Chapter 7 — The Open Gate

[Wary, grounded narration; let the unfamiliar district open a detail at a time]

The road came down off the rise in long, loose bends, and by the time Cael reached the bottom the last of the blue had drained out of the sky and left the valley to its fires. The nearest ones burned on either side of the road where it met the first houses, in iron baskets propped on stones, and the people who had lit them were selling things by their light.

There was no gate. He had known there would be none, because Hesk had said so at the kitchen table and the reference room had said so before that, but knowing a thing and walking through it were different. He found that his hand had gone into his coat on its own and closed round the registration card in the inside pocket, beside the bent bracket and the leather book.
