He let himself in by the front door and stood in the hall with his coat still on while the clock over the stove ticked. The second floorboard from the kitchen door creaked when he crossed it, as it always had, and he caught himself stepping on it on purpose, to hear it, and was annoyed with himself. The cupboard by the stove had to be closed with two fingers or it rattled for a minute, so he closed it with two fingers, and it did not rattle.

Cael's door was open a hand's width.

He had left it that way the night before, out of a habit that was ten years out of date, and in the morning Cael had not closed it either. Hesk stood in the hall and looked at the narrow dark gap between the door and the frame, and at the edge of the bare bed he could see through it, and he did not close it.

He took his coat off, hung it on the peg, and went through to the workshop, because the workshop was where he had always gone when the house was too quiet, and lit the lamp over the bench and sat down in front of a half-built level for the survey office. He picked up a file and put it down again.

On the bench, under the lamp, was the drawer marked Springs, do not use. He pulled it out an inch. Inside lay the springs that had taught him something, a little tangle of them in the corner, and beside them a space he had cleared that morning without thinking about why, a space about the size of a small bent bracket. He shut the drawer.

There were several things in his life he had prepared for over years and still not been ready for when they came. He had expected this to be one of them, and he had been right, and being right did not help as much as it should have.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

He went to Ressa's in the morning because he always went to Ressa's in the morning.

The side door was open with the ovens going, and the smell came half a block to meet him. He followed it as he had followed it for more than twenty years, since before there was a boy to follow it with him, and Ressa was behind the counter with her sleeves pushed up. Two loaves were already wrapped and waiting at the end of the counter, side by side, as they had been waiting every morning for as long as Cael had been old enough to eat one.

Ressa saw them at the same moment Hesk did, and her hands, which had been reaching for his coins, stopped.

Neither of them said anything for a moment; it was a small thing, two loaves in brown paper, and it stood on the counter between them like a third person.

"One," Hesk said.

"One." Ressa unwrapped the second loaf without a word and put it back on the rack, and the paper she folded and set under the counter to use again. Then she took his coins for the first loaf, and Hesk put down more, for the loaf she had put in Cael's bag on the morning he left.

She pushed the extra coins back across the counter with one floury finger.

"That one was his," she said.

"It came out of your oven."

"It went into his bag. That makes it his." She did not look up at him. She had a way of not looking up that was not at all like Garrik's; it was how a woman avoids looking at a man so that he can keep his face. "You'll want to know if he ate it."

"He'll have eaten it on a wall," said Hesk. "Somewhere about the first milestone. He won't have been able to wait."

Ressa nodded, and something eased at the corners of her mouth, and she gave him his loaf. He took it home and ate half of it standing at the kitchen table in the sideways light, which came in at its usual angle and lay across the table for its usual twenty minutes and did not seem to know that anything had changed.

At about ten there was a knock at the workshop door, the side door that opened onto the lane.

It was Joren, standing in the lane in his wool coat with his feet planted flat and his hands in his pockets. Hesk saw at once that he was keeping his heels down, and that he was keeping them down on purpose, because his whole body leaned very slightly forward with the effort of it. He had a folded paper in one hand, folded small and opened and folded again so many times that the creases had gone soft.

"Sir," Joren said. "Has he written?"

"Not yet. He'll get to Ardenmere tonight, if the road's kind. He'll need somewhere to live before he's got an address to write from." Hesk looked at the paper. "And then it's a week on the carrier, at least."

"A week." Joren took that in, and Hesk watched him decide to be patient about it. It was not something Joren had ever been good at, and Hesk watched him do it anyway, which was more than most people managed at fourteen or at fifty. "I found this in the wall. Our wall, by the canal. He put it in the gap."

"I know. I was there."

"He said he'd come by after." Joren's voice did not wobble, quite. "He didn't. He wrote that it was wrong of him. It wasn't—" He stopped. "I wasn't angry. I want him to know I wasn't angry. I just stood there. I stood there yesterday too, the whole hour, and he wasn't there either, because he'd gone, and I didn't know."

Hesk said nothing, because there was nothing he could say that would make Joren's two mornings in front of a wall any shorter.

"When you write to him," Joren said, "will you tell him I read it standing up? Flat-footed. The whole time." He lifted one boot an inch and put it down again, deliberately, flat. "Tell him I'm working on it."

"I'll tell him."

Joren nodded, and folded the paper once more along its soft creases, and put it inside his coat. Then he walked off along the lane toward the canal with his heels down, slowly, as if the ground had become something he had to think about, and Hesk stood in the doorway and watched him until he turned the corner.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The letter from the guild came on the second morning after the depot, by the same grey-and-brass courier, with the same satchel worn pale along the strap.

It was shorter than the registry notice and more polite, which made it worse. It said that the guild had received notification from the Compact Registry under Statute 14, Section 9, concerning the residence at 14 Fen Street, Outer District, held under the standing of registration 22-1190-H. It said that in accordance with the guild's obligations the standing of that member was now under review.

It asked the member to submit, within thirty days, a written account of present residential arrangements at that address, and it said that the reviewing officer would be in touch in due course regarding any further requirements. It was signed with a name Hesk did not know, above a title he did, and below the signature someone had written Routine in a different ink and a different hand, as if to be kind.

He read it twice at the kitchen table, and then he went into the workshop and took out a sheet of good paper and his steel pen, and wrote the account.

He had thought it would be easy, since it was one sentence of fact. He had written ten thousand sentences of fact in his life, load figures and tolerances and the readings of dials, and every one of them had been easier than this one.

The person named in the registry notice of the second day no longer resides at this address.

He sat looking at it, and it was true, and had been true for two days. It was exactly the sentence the review wanted, and it was exactly the sentence the notice had been built to make him write, and he had known that when he read the notice at this table with Cael beside him and had said so out loud: It's easier to make a family choose. He had chosen. He had walked Cael to the depot and watched him go down the merchant road until he was a shape, and this sentence was the receipt.

He added a second sentence, because the first one looked too much like an apology.

He left on the morning of the third day for another city, where he is lawfully resident, and he goes with my full support.

That was also true, and the review did not need it, and he left it in.

He sealed the account and set it by the door to go to the guild house, and then he put the guild's letter not in a drawer, where he would not have to look at it, but on the shelf above the bench, propped against the clock, where he would see it every time he lifted his head.

He did not know yet what the review would come to. He thought it would probably come to nothing, slowly, as the Compact made most things come to nothing, with a great many forms, though it might not. He had decided long ago that the risk was his, and he was not going to start pretending otherwise now just because the risk had arrived with a signature on it.

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

On Tuesday evening he very nearly did not go.

He stood in the hall with his coat half on and his hand on the door, and the clock over the stove said ten past seven. He thought about the narrow green door at the side of the hall, and the two-and-one knock, and Garrik's hand on a turning wheel three mornings ago, keeping its rhythm while Hesk and the boy walked past. He thought about sitting in a folding chair in the dark with Garrik four seats away and neither of them saying anything for two reels.

Then he thought about what Cael would say if he wrote to him and asked, Did you still go? And Hesk had to write back No.

He put the other arm in the coat.

The green door opened at the second knock of the two, before the third, as though Garrik had been standing just behind it. He was in his shirtsleeves with a rag in his hand, and his eyes went to Hesk's collar and stayed there, on the collar, an inch below the face.

"Hesk."

"Garrik."

"Reel's threaded." Garrik stood back from the door. "Biscuits came."

The back room was as it always was. The sheet on its frame, the projector on its iron cart with its two big reels like ears, the dozen folding chairs and the eight old people in them, who all looked up when Hesk came in, and looked past him at the empty doorway, and back at him. Nobody said anything about the empty doorway; the woman in the knitted hat held out the tin of biscuits, and Hesk took one, and sat in his usual chair.

Garrik turned down the lamps. The projector woke with its clatter, and the beam of light leaned across the room through the turning dust, and a bout came up on the sheet: two Copper-tier fighters from the sanctioned regional season, neither of them very good, a long cautious first exchange that went nowhere.

Hesk did not watch it; he watched the tension arm.

It sat a hair higher than it had a month ago, held up off its stop by a thin brass washer that a boy had filed for nothing in particular and carried in his coat pocket until it turned out to be for something. The film ran smooth over the sprocket and did not ride up, and Garrik had not taken the washer out. Hesk had half expected him to, and had not let himself think about why he expected it.

On the sheet, one of the Copper fighters dropped his guard in the third exchange and was put on the sand, and the woman in the knitted hat said, "Oh, he didn't see that coming at all," and somebody else said, "Nobody ever does, at that rank," and the ordinary talk of the room went on.

At the change of reels, while the lamps were up and Garrik was threading the second one with his back to the room, the woman in the knitted hat leaned across the empty chair beside Hesk.

"Where's he gone?" she said. She said it as she said everything, plainly, and she looked straight at him while she said it. "The boy. With the washer."

It was the first time since Wednesday that anyone in the quadrant had asked him a direct question about Cael, and it came to Hesk that he had been waiting for it for six days without knowing he was waiting.

"Ardenmere," he said.

"On his own?"

"On his own."

The woman nodded slowly. "That's a long way for a boy who watches like that," she said. "They'll not know what they've got." She took a biscuit out of the tin and put it into his hand, though he had one already. "You tell him we said so. Give him that."

At the projector, Garrik had stopped threading.

He did not turn round. He stood with the loose end of the film in one hand and the other hand on the reel, and he did not move, and Hesk could see from the set of his shoulders that he had heard every word.

The lamps went down, and the second reel ran clean from first frame to last.

Afterward, when the others had gone, Garrik stayed at the projector and wound the film back with the little crank, round and round, much more slowly than it needed. Hesk stood by the door with his coat on and waited.

"I didn't look up," Garrik said to the reel.

"I know."

"I meant to. I had the wheel up and I heard you coming down the street and I thought, I'll look up when they're level, and then you were level, and I didn't." The crank went round. "And then you were past, and I thought, well, that's done it. And I stopped the wheel. And I stood there with my hand on it like a fool."

Hesk said nothing.

"When my wife died," Garrik said, "I couldn't look at anybody for a month. Not at you. Not at the girl from the bakery. I used to cross the street. I thought I'd got past it." He stopped cranking. "Turns out I'd only got past it for things I'd already done once."

"He saw the wheel stop," said Hesk. He did not know that, though he thought it was probably true. "He didn't look back. But he'll have heard it. He hears everything."

Garrik looked round at last, and for the first time all evening he looked Hesk in the face, and his own face was red above the square white beard and not at all composed.

"When you write," he said. "Tell him the arm's running clean. Tell him it's his washer, and I've not touched it, and I'm not going to." He turned back to the reel. "That's all. Tell him that."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

Hesk sat down at the kitchen table at half past ten with the lamp lit and a clean sheet of paper and the steel pen.

He wrote Cael, and stopped, and looked at it.

He had no address, to begin with. He did not know where the boy was sleeping or whether he was sleeping at all, and any letter he wrote tonight would sit on this table for a week, at least, until the carrier's runner brought one up Fen Street with a return direction on it in a careful, slanting hand. He was writing to nowhere. He knew that perfectly well and he went on anyway, because Joren had stood in front of a wall for an hour with a folded paper and Garrik had wound a reel back twice as slowly as it needed to go. Hesk was not going to be the only one on Fen Street with nothing in his hands.

He crossed it out, because it sounded like a man feeling sorry for himself, and took another sheet.

Ressa had two loaves wrapped the morning after. She put one back. She wouldn't take money for the one she put in your bag; she says it was yours. I told her you'd have eaten it on a wall somewhere about the first milestone. Tell me if I was right.

Joren came to the workshop door with your note. He's read it standing up, flat-footed, the whole way through, and he wanted you told. He says he's working on it. He wasn't angry with you. He wanted you to know that most of all.

I went on Tuesday. Garrik's kept your washer in the arm and he says he isn't going to take it out. He wanted you told that too. The woman in the knitted hat says they won't know what they've got in Ardenmere. I'm inclined to agree with her.

He stopped there, with the pen lifted.

The guild's letter was on the shelf in the workshop, propped against the clock. He could see it in his mind as clearly as if it were on the table in front of him: the polite paragraphs, the stranger's signature, the word Routine in another hand.

He knew exactly what he wanted to do with it, which was to leave it out. He wanted to leave it on the shelf and write to Cael about bread and washers and Joren's heels, and say nothing about a review that might come to nothing, because if it came to nothing then the boy would never have had to carry it, and if it came to something there would be time enough then. Don't make a thing real before it is. He had lived by that sentence for years.

He had lived by it so long and so well that he had never once told Cael about Tuesdays, or the coupling, or the file he had watched opened at twenty-two, until the boy found each of them out for himself and came to him angry, standing in a workshop, asking.

Tell me things, Cael had said, across the bench. As they come. Not managed.

And Hesk had said, All right.

He sat with the pen over the paper while the clock ticked and somewhere to the north the canal gate sighed, letting the night water through.

Then he wrote it.

The guild has opened a review of my standing, because of the notice. They want a written account of who lives here, and I've sent it. It's routine, they say, and slow, and it will most likely come to nothing. I'll tell you how it goes, as it goes. I'm telling you now because you asked me to tell you things as they come, and I said I would, and I'm finding out that's harder to keep than I expected. Don't worry about it. I know you will. Worry about it a little, then, and then stop.

He read it back. It did not make the review any smaller, but it made him feel, for the first time in six days, as though he were not standing in the house on his own.

There were other things he did not write. There were things he had not written in thirty-two years, and he did not begin them tonight, and he did not let himself think about them any further than the edge of the page.

He did not seal the letter. He laid it flat on the table under the clock and set the pen beside it, so that he could add to it tomorrow, and the next day, and every day until the carrier's runner came up Fen Street. Then he turned out the lamp and went to bed, past the door that stood open a hand's width, and left it open.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

In Ardenmere, the next morning, Cael was at the Cinder House before the sun had cleared the roofs.

The Cinder House was a squat stone public house two streets below the yards, on a corner, with a sign over the door that had once been a painting of a hearth with a fire in it. Weather had taken most of the paint, so that what was left was a black square with some orange flecks round the edges, more ember than fire, which he supposed was the point. The shutters were up, and the whole building had the stillness of a place that only came alive at certain hours.

The yard was round the side, through a gate in a wall, and he found it by following the sound.

It was a square of packed dirt about thirty paces across, with high walls on three sides and the back of the public house on the fourth. The ground had been swept and watered so that it would not rise in dust, and in the middle of it, worn into the dirt, was a circle, not painted or chalked.

It was a shallow groove, a hand deep, that years of feet had walked into the ground as water walks a channel into stone. It was very slightly out of round, longer one way than the other, as though the fighters who made it had all preferred the same side. Lanterns hung on hooks along three of the walls, unlit, and a few crows were working the edges of the yard where last night's crowd had dropped things.

Lira was in the far corner with a post.

It was a thick wooden post sunk into the ground and wrapped in canvas gone grey with use, and she was striking it. Short strikes, very controlled, with the edge of the hand and the forearm and once or twice the heel of the palm, and between the strikes her feet moved in small steps that never seemed to go anywhere and never stopped. It looked less like fighting than like a long argument with the ground that she was winning on points.

She did not stop when he came in, only said, between one strike and the next, "You're on time."

"You said not to be late."

"People say a lot of things." Strike. "Mostly nobody listens." Strike, step, strike. "I'm mildly impressed. Sit. Watch. I'll talk while I do this. Ask things when you want to; you'll learn it faster that way than if I make a speech."

He sat on an upturned crate by the wall and took out the notebook.

Lira stopped, with her hand flat against the post, and looked at him.

"You're going to take notes," she said, "on me hitting a post."

"Is that a problem?"

"No. It's the most you thing I've seen you do, and I've known you a day." She laughed, a short, real laugh that surprised her as much as him, and returned to the post. "Right. The circuit. First thing. You've been reading that board like the circuit's a place. It isn't."

"Then what is it?"

"It's a habit." She struck the post, low, and stepped round it. "A few hundred people in this district all decided, one at a time, that they wanted to find out what they could actually do. Not what a guild says they can do. Not what an evaluation says. What they can do against somebody who means it. And there was nowhere official to find that out, because officially, people like us aren't supposed to want to. So they started finding out anyway. In yards like this. And they kept doing it, long enough that the habit grew rules."

"Who made the rules?"

"Nobody." Strike, strike. "That's the part people from outside never believe. Nobody sat down and wrote them. They just—happened. The way a path happens across a field because everybody's walking the same way."

"Like that." He pointed his pencil at the groove in the ground.

Lira followed the pencil and looked at the circle as though she had not seen it in a while. "Yes. Exactly like that."

She worked through the rules while she worked the post, and he wrote them down.

A fight in the circuit was called a bout, and a bout was made of exchanges, not rounds. An exchange began when the fighters came off their marks and ended when they broke apart, and it could last two seconds or two minutes. Bouts were arranged between the fighters, or between whoever spoke for them, and the terms were agreed in advance, and every bout had a Ledger-keeper.

"Ledger-keeper," Cael said.

"The person who writes it down." Lira stopped and wiped her palms on her trousers. "Every venue has one. At the Cinder House it's Vell. She keeps the book. She calls the bouts. She decides when it's over. Everybody on both sides of the rope has to trust her to write down what happened, and nothing else, because the whole circuit is only worth anything as long as the book is honest. If the book lies once, nobody believes it again, and then there's no circuit, there's just people hitting each other in yards." She shrugged. "Which there'd be anyway. But it wouldn't count."

"And if somebody cheats?"

"Then that venue stops getting fighters. Nobody comes back. That's it. That's the whole of the punishment." She went back to the post. "No Compact. No guild. No warden. Just everybody deciding at once not to come back."

"Is there a rule against killing?"

Lira hit the post once, hard, and let her hand stay against it.

"There isn't a rule. It isn't written down anywhere. There's nowhere to write it. But everybody acts as if there's one, and everybody's afraid of what happens to anyone who forgets, so it works about as well as a written rule would. Better, maybe." She looked at him over her shoulder. "Paths are open. Whatever yours does, you can use it. That's half of why people come here instead of fighting in a guild hall with someone in a white coat counting. But you don't kill anyone, and you don't keep going after Vell's called it, and you don't embarrass whoever vouched for you."

"What happens if you do keep going?"

"There was a man before my time. I only know it from people telling it. Bronze in the circuit, Ash Path, very good, very angry. Twice he kept going after the call. Vell warned him twice. The third time he put somebody down so badly they had to send across the river for a healer, which costs more than most people here earn in a year, and gets noticed by people we'd rather didn't notice." She went back to the post. "No yard in Ardenmere would have him after that. Not one. Last anyone heard, he was fighting under another name three towns over, for a tenth of what he used to draw here. It takes a while for a thing like that to travel. But it travels."

Cael wrote Ash Path, Bronze. Three calls. Gone. He looked at it, and added: Vell called it.

"The ratings. On the board. The letters after the names."

"Ah. The ratings." Lira went into a quicker combination, three strikes and a step, three strikes and a step, and talked in the gaps. "Circuit ratings borrow the registry's words, Copper, Iron, Bronze, Rank 1 to 10, because everybody already knows them. But they're not the registry's. The circuit doesn't care what your Arbiter said about you. It cares what Vell's seen you do."

"So your circuit rating could be different from your registry tier."

"It usually is. That's why half the people here are here. Guild rejects. People who failed an evaluation once and couldn't pay for the next one. People who've got a good Path in a bad family. People who never had a guild at all." Strike, step. "Your registry tier's a word somebody stamped on you at fourteen. Your circuit rating's a running total of what you've done since."

"And if you've done nothing?"

"Then you're unrated. Everybody starts unrated." She glanced at him. "Nobody stays unrated long. Either you climb, or you stop coming."

"How does Vell decide the rating? Is there a formula?"

Lira laughed again, and this time it was not a surprised laugh. "If there is, she's never shown it to anyone. As far as anyone can tell the formula is, I've watched a great many fights and I have opinions." She stopped and picked up a water skin from the foot of the post. "You win convincingly, against people who are rated themselves, often enough, and your rating goes up. You lose badly often enough and it doesn't. But it's not only wins. How you lose matters. Sometimes more."

"How does it matter?"

"Somebody who gets carried out of the circle because they wouldn't concede, and somebody who reads it right and concedes at the right moment and walks out. Which one gets offered more bouts?"

He thought about it. "The one who walks out."

"Most people from outside say the other one." She drank, and held out the skin to him, and he shook his head. "The circuit doesn't pay for stubborn. It pays for interesting to watch and hard to read. That's not the same as strongest, though strongest doesn't hurt."

"What's your rating?"

"Higher than my registry rank. Lower than I think it should be." She capped the skin. "Vell and I are in a long, polite disagreement about it."

"Who's winning?"

"Vell. She's got the book." Lira set the skin down. "I lost my first four bouts here. Four. Some of them badly. I was better trained than nearly everyone I fought, and I lost anyway, because doing a technique in an academy hall and doing it against somebody who's trying to put you in the dirt are not the same thing at all, and the only way anybody learns that is with their face."

"What changed?"

"I stopped fighting the way they taught me and started fighting the way that worked for what I've got." She shrugged. "It sounds obvious when you say it. It took four losses before I believed it." She tipped her head and considered him. "You might have it easier there, you know. You haven't got an academy's way to unlearn. Whatever you build, you'll be building it from the ground. That's slower at the start. It might be faster after."

"That's a strange sort of advantage."

"Most of the good ones are."

There was one more name before the morning was out, and Lira said it with feeling.

"Marrow." She had gone back to the post, and she hit it a little harder as she said the name, as though it had been his face. "You'll see him this afternoon. Big man, very clean hands, a slate on a string round his neck. He runs the book."

"The ledger?"

"No. The book. The bets." Strike. "Vell's book says what happened. Marrow's book says what people think's going to happen, and how much they'll pay to be right. He sets the odds. And he shaves them."

"Shaves them how?"

"A little. Never enough to call cheating. Just a hair the wrong side of fair, every time, on every bout, so that over a season it adds up to a nice house across the river for Marrow and a lot of people wondering why they never quite win." She stopped and pointed a finger at Cael. "Do not ever bet with Marrow."

"I haven't got any money to bet with."

"Good. Stay poor. It's safer." She went back to her combinations, and then, between one strike and the next, as though it were nothing, she added: "He had me at five to one against, my second month. Against Renn."

"Who won?"

Lira hit the post once more and let the strike sit there, her palm flat on the canvas.

"Marrow," she said.

By the time the sun was high enough to reach the bottom of the yard, she had stopped, and sat on the crate beside his. They had gone through the rest of it: how a bout began (Vell's word), how it ended (Vell's word again, or one fighter's own, or the plain fact of somebody unable to get up), what you owed to the table afterward (you reported, win or lose, and stood there until she was finished with you), and what a vouch was.

"Somebody who's fought here says they know you," Lira said, "and that you'll not waste the yard's evening."

"And if you do?"

"Then they've vouched wrong, and everyone remembers." She stretched her arms over her head until her shoulders cracked, and did not look at him. "It's not a thing you do for just anybody."

He wrote it down, and looked at it after he had written it for longer than the words needed, and then turned the page.

The yard began filling as the afternoon came on.

Chapter 11 — Homework

[Wary, grounded narration; let the unfamiliar district open a detail at a time]

They came in by ones and twos at first, and then in knots, through the gate in the wall and round the side of the public house, until the empty yard of the morning had turned, without any single moment when it happened, into a place where something was going to happen.

Somebody strung a rope round the circle on short iron stakes, an arm's length outside the groove, so that the crowd had a line to stand behind. Somebody else came out of the back of the public house with a bucket and a ladle and went round the rope selling water, and then a boy came out with a tray of hot pies and did better. The lanterns along the walls stayed dark.

It was afternoon, and the light came down into the yard over the west wall, and lay across half of the circle and left the other half in shadow. The shadowed side was where people chose to stand. Cael worked out why after a minute, when he saw a man shading his eyes on the sunny side: from the dark side you looked into the light, and saw everything, and from the light side you looked into the dark.

Lira took him to an upturned barrel at the corner of the rope, on the shadowed side, where the wall of the public house met the yard wall. From the top of it he could see the whole circle and most of the crowd.

"Best seat," she said. "Don't tell anyone."

"Why is it empty, then?"

"Because it's next to the drain." She pointed with her chin at a grating in the corner, and the smell came up to meet the pointing. "Everything good has a cost. You'll get used to it."

A woman came out of the back door of the public house carrying a folding table.

She set it up in the shade of the back wall, on the edge of the yard nearest the circle, without looking at anyone. She unfolded its legs one at a time and pressed each into the dirt with her boot to seat it. Then she went back inside and came out with a stool and a book. The book was a thick ledger in a dark cover, worn soft at the corners and darker still where hands had held it, and she set it on the table and squared it with the table's edge, as though the angle mattered.

She was somewhere in her fifties, not tall, with grey working through dark hair that she wore pulled back hard from her face. She moved without hurry and without wasting anything, and when she walked out to the circle and along the groove, slowly, looking down at it, Cael saw that she walked heel first and then flat, every step the same length, measuring.

He knew that walk. He had last seen it on a white sheet in a back room in Denvash, on a man nearly twice her size.

"That's Vell," Lira said, unnecessarily.

Vell walked the whole groove. Twice she stopped and pressed at the ground with the toe of her boot, and once she called something over her shoulder. The boy who had sold pies came running with a rake and smoothed out a patch where the dirt had rucked. Then she went back to her table and sat down and opened the ledger to a clean page, and only then did she look at the crowd, a single sweep from one end of the rope to the other, as if she were counting it.

Her eyes went past Cael on his barrel without stopping. He was nearly sure they had paused.

A large man with very clean hands was working his way along the rope with a slate hung round his neck on a string.

He was dressed better than anyone else in the yard, in a dark coat with good buttons, and he was perfectly friendly to everybody. People kept putting coins in his hand and he kept writing on the slate with a stub of chalk and saying something low and pleasant to each of them. He laughed a good deal. Every few minutes he wiped the slate with his sleeve and wrote it again.

"Marrow," said Lira, in a voice like a closed door.

After a while Cael took out the notebook and, without being sure why, began copying the slate each time Marrow wiped it and wrote it again: two names, a number beside each. As people paid, the numbers moved toward the name more of them were paying on, which made sense, but they moved a little further each time than the money did. Cael could not have said how he knew that, but the numbers had a rhythm, and the rhythm leaned, very slightly, the same way every time, like a wheel with one spoke a hair too long.

"What are you doing?" Lira said.

"Counting."

She looked at his page. She read it twice, and then she looked across the yard at Marrow, who was laughing at something a man had said and writing on his slate.

"Don't," she said.

"Don't what?"

"Don't let him see you doing that." She did not take her eyes off Marrow. "I mean it. People who count Marrow's numbers have a way of finding out that the yard's less friendly than they thought."

Cael closed the notebook. He had seen what he wanted to see, and it had been what she said it was, a hair the wrong side of fair. He was obscurely pleased about it, in the way he was pleased when a measurement came out where he expected, and he was also a little frightened, and the two feelings sat side by side without either one making room.

Vell stood up behind her table.

She did not shout. She simply said, in a voice that carried over the whole yard without seeming to be raised at all, "First bout," and the yard went quiet in a wave, from the rope nearest her out to the far wall, as if she had dropped a stone into it.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The first two fighters were both Copper.

Vell gave them out as they stepped over the rope, in the same flat, carrying voice. "Copper Rank 4, Stone Path." A woman of about thirty, broad through the hips and shoulders, with short hair and her sleeves rolled up past the elbow. "Against Copper Rank 2, Blade Path." A lean young man, quick in every movement, who came over the rope in a single hop and rolled his neck from side to side as he walked to his mark.

They stood on opposite sides of the circle, just inside the groove.

Cael was writing before Vell had finished speaking. Stone, Cu 4. Weight low and centred. Hands open, not fists. Feet— He looked at her feet. They were flat, and wide, and very still, and the loose grit round her boots shivered once and lay down, as the grit round Joren's boots had done at the low wall, a world away and a week ago.

Rooted, he wrote. Or something like it. Higher rank than Joren's. He looked at the young man. Blade, Cu 2. Weight forward. Right arm low and back, behind his hip.

"Begin," said Vell.

The young man brought up his blade.

Cael had read about Blade Path and had seen it once, on a flickering grey sheet, too fast to follow. He had never seen it close. It came out of nothing along the young man's right forearm, from just below the elbow and out past the knuckles, a narrow blade of pale light, steady as a ruled line, with none of a flame's flutter in it and none of a lamp's spill. It simply stood there in the air, hard and clean, with a thin bright line along its leading edge, and when the young man turned his wrist it turned with him and made a faint high sound, like a wet finger round the rim of a glass.

It looked about a hand long past the fist.

"Longer than that," Lira said quietly beside him.

He looked at her.

"Whatever your eye just told you," she said, without looking away from the circle. "Longer than that. Everyone's eye lies about it. It's light, it's not steel, it doesn't look like it should reach as far as it does." She tapped two fingers on her own forearm, in the air beyond her fist. "About eight inches past where his hand ends. Remember that."

He wrote Eight inches past the fist. My eye says less. And underlined says.

The Stone woman moved first.

That surprised him. He had expected the quick one to open, the one with the reach, and instead the woman whose whole plan must depend on getting close came off her mark and crossed the distance in two long steps, low, her hands coming up open in front of her. The young man answered at once. It was a short, tidy cut, aimed at her leading shoulder, not to finish anything but to mark her, so that the next time she tried to close she would remember what it had cost.

She took it.

Cael saw her decide to take it. It was a half-second before the blade landed, and it was very small: her shoulder turned a little toward the cut instead of away from it, and her chin came down, and she did not slow. The edge of light went across the top of her shoulder and opened her sleeve and the skin under it in a short, shallow line. She made no sound. She was already inside his reach by the time he had finished the cut, and her hands closed on his extended forearm, one at the wrist and one above the elbow, just behind where the blade began.

The young man pulled. Nothing happened. Her boots were flat on the packed dirt and the grit round them lay still, and he might as well have tried to pull his arm out of a wall.

He broke the hold the only way he had, by letting the blade go out like a lamp and twisting his arm small, and he slid free and skipped back three steps, and the first exchange was over. The crowd made a noise that was half a groan and half a laugh. The Stone woman went back to her mark with a dark line across her shoulder, rolled the shoulder once, and stood there.

She let him cut her, Cael wrote, fast. On purpose. To get inside. The cut cost less than the distance. He stopped, and thought, and wrote: If she'd dodged it properly she'd have been two steps further out, and he'd have cut her on the way in next time anyway, deeper, because he'd know her line. She paid now, small, instead of later, big.

The second exchange took four seconds.

She came in exactly the same way, and this time he did not cut at her shoulder, because she had shown him she would take that. He cut lower, at her lead leg, to stop the step. But she had not been going to step. She had been going to drop, and she dropped under the cut onto one knee and came up inside it with both hands already on his arm, and this time she did not hold.

She turned. She took his whole extended arm, blade and all, and turned it over and out against the joint, using his own reach as a lever. He went down in the dirt on his side with his arm locked straight above him and his face in the groove.

He slapped the ground twice with his free hand.

"Called," said Vell. "Stone Path."

The crowd's noise was very different this time. It was mixed. Some of it was a groan, from people along the rope who had paid Marrow on the quick young man with the reach, and some of it was a long, appreciative murmur from people who seemed to have understood something about what they had just watched. Cael could tell which was which by where the people stood. The groaners were mostly on the sunny side, and the murmurers mostly in the shade.

The Stone woman let go, stood up, and offered her hand, and the young man took it and was pulled up, and they touched fists. Then she walked to the table, with her sleeve dark across the shoulder, and stood there while Vell wrote. It was a short entry. Two lines.

After the bout ended Cael kept writing for a full minute, so as not to lose the shape of it.

Two exchanges. She lost the first one on purpose to learn where he'd cut. She won the second because he learned it too, and changed, and she'd guessed what he'd change to. He was faster. She was a step ahead the whole time anyway. The reach was his advantage and she made it the thing she held on to.

He looked at what he had written, and then he added a line underneath, in the smaller hand he used when he was not sure.

The second exchange is questions.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The second bout took the rest of the afternoon, or felt as though it did.

Vell gave them out as Bronze. "Bronze Rank 2, Iron Path. Against Bronze Rank 1, Stone Path." Cael looked at Lira when he heard Bronze, and she knew what he was asking before he asked it.

"Vell's Bronze," she said. "Not the registry's. Neither of them could get past the gate on the bridge with a card that said Bronze, I'd bet. But they're Bronze in that book."

"What's the difference in a fight?"

"Watch," said Lira, "and tell me."

It was a long bout, and nothing in it was fast in the way the first one had been fast. The Iron man was tall and heavy and very calm, and when he struck, he struck short and hard, with no reach to it at all, and everything he hit he seemed to hit in exactly the same place.

The Stone woman was older than the first one, grey at the temples, and she did not let him hit her anywhere if she could help it. She gave ground. She gave ground along the groove in a long slow curve and let him follow, and every time he had nearly caught her up she stopped, and set her feet. The grit lay down round her boots, and he struck her guard as if he were striking a wall.

It went five exchanges like that. Then six.

Cael filled two pages and started a third. He wrote down how each exchange began and how it ended and what each of them tried, and he began to see something he had not had words for before, which was that both of them were changing their minds. In the first exchanges the Iron man had come straight at her, every time, and every time he had been met by the wall of her stance.

By the third he had stopped coming straight. He came in at an angle, so that she had to turn to meet him, and turning meant lifting a foot, and when she lifted a foot the grit did not lie down. By the fourth she had seen what he was doing, and she had stopped turning; she let him come in at his angle and met him side-on, which was weaker, but which kept both her feet on the ground.

She's giving up strength to keep her feet, Cael wrote. He's giving up power to make her move. They're both paying for something.

In the sixth exchange something changed in both of them at once, and it took him a moment to see what it was.

They were tired. They had been tired for some exchanges already, he realized, but in the sixth exchange it started to make decisions for them. The Iron man's strikes were still in the same place every time, but he took a breath between them now, a short one, and she saw the breath and began to time her steps to it.

The Stone woman, for her part, had begun to set her feet a fraction later each time, so that there was a moment, at the start of every stance, when she was not quite rooted yet. He saw that too. Cael watched them both see it, one after the other, and he watched them both try to use what they had seen, and it was like watching two people play a board game who had each just noticed the other's mistake.

In the seventh exchange the Iron man struck at the moment before her feet set.

He did not strike hard. He did not need to. He hit her guard while she was still settling into it, and she went back a whole step and then another. Her heel came down on the edge of the groove and slipped, and for an instant she was off balance with her weight on one foot and the Iron man was already turning to bring the next strike round.

She held up her hand.

It was not a slap on the ground. It was an open palm, raised, as you raise your hand in a room to say that you want to speak. She held it there, breathing hard, with her heel on the edge of the groove.

The Iron man stopped his strike in the air.

"Called," said Vell. "Conceded. Iron Path."

And the crowd, which had been quiet for most of the bout, did something Cael had not expected. It applauded. It did not cheer, as it had for the Stone woman's lock in the first bout. It clapped, steadily, all along the rope, the shady side and the sunny side together, and the clapping went on while the two of them touched fists and walked to Vell's table, and the person it was for was not the winner.

"Why are they clapping for her?" Cael said.

"Because she read it right." Lira was clapping too, not very loudly. "Another breath and he'd have had her down, and maybe hurt, and she'd have been out for a month. She saw it a strike early, and she stopped it, and she'll be back in the circle next week." She stopped clapping. "She'll get more bouts offered off the back of losing that than he will off the back of winning it. He's dull. Strong and dull. She's interesting."

"How you lose matters," Cael said.

"How you lose matters," Lira agreed. "You were listening. I was starting to think you only listened to people's feet."

At the table, Vell was writing. It took longer than the entry for the first bout, three or four lines, and when she had finished she said something to the Stone woman that made her laugh. The Stone woman went off to the water bucket with her shoulders down and her hands loose, as though it had been a good afternoon after all.

He had six pages by the end of it, more than he had written about anything since the archive.

Lira was watching him read.

"You're not watching it like everybody else," she said.

"How am I watching it?"

"Like you're going to be tested on it." She leaned back on her hands on the barrel lid. "Everybody else on that rope was watching it to see who won, and to see if they'd been right, and to have something to talk about at dinner. You were watching it like homework."

He thought about that. It was not untrue. He thought that the difference was simply that he did not know yet what he was going to need, and so everything might be the thing he needed, and so he had to keep all of it. He did not say that.

"Is that bad?"

"No," Lira said, and then, after a pause, more quietly: "No. It's not bad."

She did not say anything else about it. But on the walk back down from the yards, through the long gold light of the end of the day, he noticed that she was walking a little closer to him than she had in the morning, and that she was looking at him from time to time out of the side of her eye, as he imagined she might look at an opponent she had begun to take seriously, rather than at a curiosity she had decided to be kind to.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

She went with him as far as the crossroads.

The board stood in the middle of the triangle with the evening light on it, orange and low, so that every notice threw its own small shadow across the one beneath it. The skewer woman had gone. The man with the weighted cords had gone. The triangle was full of people walking home, and none of them stopped at the board, and Lira did not stop either. She stopped at the edge of the triangle and turned round and folded her arms.

"You're going to put your name down," she said.

It was not a question, and he did not treat it as one. "Probably."

"Not probably." She shook her head. "You've decided. You decided in the second bout. Somewhere about the fourth exchange you stopped writing and you just watched, for about ten breaths, and when the pencil started again it moved differently. Faster. Shorter. Like a list of things you were going to need." She said it with plain satisfaction, the satisfaction of a person who liked being right about people and saw no reason to hide that. "I'm not showing off. You ought to know what your face does when you've made up your mind, because you plainly don't, and somebody should tell you."

"What does it do?"

"Nothing. That's how I could tell. Everything else about you is always doing something." She tipped her head. "So you can't bluff me. Which is going to be either very useful or very annoying, depending on what you end up wanting."

He did not know what to say to that. He was not even sure she was wrong.

"How do I put my name down?"

"Go to the Cinder House tomorrow, before the bouts, and find Vell at her table. Tell her you want a bout. Unrated. She'll match you against somebody." Lira's voice had gone practical. "She'll ask your age. She'll ask your Path. She'll ask who vouches for you."

"Do I need somebody to vouch for me?"

"You don't need it." Lira looked at the board, not at him. "Nobody can stop you walking up to that table on your own. But an unrated debut with nobody speaking for them gets matched carefully, which means cheaply, which means Vell puts you against somebody who won't teach you anything, because nobody knows whether you'll fold in the first exchange or last the whole bout, and she won't spend a real fighter's evening finding out." She was quiet a moment. Then, quickly, as if she wanted to say it before she had finished deciding to: "I'll vouch for you. If you want."

He had not expected it. It took him half a breath too long to answer, and she saw that half a breath, and for once she did not say anything about it.

"Why?" he said.

"Because I don't think you'll waste the yard's evening." She shrugged, the easy shrug that looked as if it cost nothing. "And because I don't vouch for many people, and I'd like to be right about one of them. Most people I could vouch for, I'd be wrong about. Most people don't stand in front of a board for eleven minutes."

"I'd want that," he said. "Thank you."

"Don't thank me yet." The corner of her mouth went up. "If you go down in the first exchange I'm going to tell everybody I've never seen you before in my life and you must have followed me there."

"Would they believe you?"

"I'm very convincing," said Lira. "Tomorrow. Cinder House, the middle of the morning, before Vell's had too much tea and started being kind to people. Bring the notebook. You'll want it after, whatever happens."

She walked away across the triangle toward wherever she went in the evenings, and did not look back. Cael stood at the edge of the crossroads and watched her go until the widest street had taken her.

Then he looked at the board, and at the word vouch on the bottom notice, written in brown ink by somebody who had pressed hard enough to dent the paper. Ledger-verified bouts only. No vouch, no walk-in.

He remembered Lira's voice in the yard that morning, with her face turned away from him, stretching her arms over her head: It's not a thing you do for just anybody.

He had been offered something, and he had taken it, and he had no idea what it cost.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Torvin was at the kitchen table that night, which Cael had not seen him do before. He was sitting at the end of it with a ledger of his own, a thin one with a cracked spine, and a stub of pencil, and he was adding columns with his lips moving. His wife was at the range. Yeni had the far end of the table, with a shirt across her knee. The woman who slept in her boots was eating soup with her boots on.

Cael sat down across from Torvin and waited until he had reached the bottom of a column.

"What does a vouch cost?" he said.

Torvin looked up. He looked at Cael for long enough that the pencil, which had been about to start the next column, came to rest on the page.

"Who's paying?" he said.

"The person who gives it."

"Then it costs them." Torvin went back to his column.

That seemed to be all. Cael waited, and Torvin's lips moved down the column, and reached the bottom, and he wrote a figure under it and drew a line. Then, without looking up, he said, "A vouch is a loan. You're the one borrowing. They're the one who's out of pocket if you don't pay it back."

"Out of pocket how? It isn't money."

"Didn't say it was money."

At the other end of the table, Yeni's needle had stopped.

"It's their name," she said. She did not look up from the shirt either. Cael was beginning to think that nobody in this house ever looked up when they were saying something important. "Round the yards, everybody's got a name, and the name's worth something. It's worth what people think it is. If somebody puts their name next to yours and you go down in a heap the first time you're touched, then the next time they put their name next to somebody, people remember the heap." The needle went in and out. "Do it twice and their name's worth nothing. Then nobody'll take their word for anything. Not for a fighter, not for a debt, not for what they saw happen."

"How long does it take to make a name worth something?"

"Depends who you are." Yeni bit the thread. "Who's vouching for you?"

"Lira."

Yeni's hands stopped. Across the table, Torvin's pencil stopped too.

"The Wind girl," Torvin said. "Four months."

"You know her?"

"Everybody knows her," said Yeni. "She lost her first four bouts in that yard and kept coming back. Nobody keeps coming back after four. Now people bet on her." She looked at Cael at last, a long, measuring look, the same look she had given him the first night when she had seemed to be taking his measurements for a coat. "Four months is a short time to build a name, for her. It's all the name she's got."

Nobody said anything for a moment. Torvin's wife scraped something in a pan. The woman in the boots finished her soup.

"Well," Torvin said, and turned the page of his ledger, and started on the next column.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

Upstairs, with the lamp still lit and the brothers not yet in from the river, Cael sat on his cot and turned back through the notebook, past the day's six pages, to the entry he had written on the rise three days ago in the last of the light.

Find somewhere to sleep. Find work. Watch everything. Show nobody anything. Be dull. Be competent. Be still here.

He had found somewhere to sleep. He had not looked for work, and the pouch he counted twice every morning would not last while he put it off. And tomorrow he meant to walk into a circle in front of sixty strangers, which was about as far from show nobody anything as he could get without standing on the board. Hesk had said it more plainly in the side room at Weaver's Row, leaning close: Don't let anyone see you move. Not until you know what you're doing.

He set both rules against what he actually meant to do. He did not mean to show anything. He meant to last, and watch, and keep his hands to himself, and come out knowing more than he had given away. The circuit was the one ladder in this city that did not ask to see a card, and the only way onto it was across that rope. He was bending a rule, and he knew which one, and how far. He told himself that bending a rule you could see was a different thing from breaking one you had forgotten, and he very nearly believed it.

He thought about the Stone woman in the first bout, choosing a small cut now over a larger one later, and he understood, sitting there, that this was closer to tomorrow than any of the morning's rules. He was not brave. He was fairly sure of that. He was going to walk into the circle because staying out of it would cost him more, over time, than walking in. He would be paying for something. He would just be paying now, small, instead of later.

But he would not be the only one paying.

He turned to a clean page and wrote at the top of it, in the private hand, smaller than the rest.

Lira's vouching for me tomorrow. Torvin says a vouch is a loan and I'm the one borrowing. Yeni says it's her name, and four months of it is all the name she's got.

She didn't tell me that. She made it sound like nothing.

He looked at the two lines. Then he wrote one more under them, and underlined it, once.

Find out what it costs her before I let her spend it.

Chapter 12 — Terms

[Wary, grounded narration; let the unfamiliar district open a detail at a time]

Lira was waiting for him at the board in the morning, sitting on the edge of a water trough with her canvas roll across her knees, eating an apple.

"You're early," she said.

"So are you."

"I'm always early. I just make it look like I happened to be passing." She threw the core over her shoulder into the trough without looking, where it bobbed, and stood up. "Come on. Vell sets her table out at ten, and the first one there gets her before she's tired of people."

They walked up toward the yards side by side through a grey, cool morning, under a thin high cloud that took the colour out of everything, and the district was busy in the ordinary way of a weekday, carts and barrows and the smell of bread. Cael let two streets go by. He had settled in the night what he was going to say, and how, but walking now every version he had built in the dark came out as an accusation or an apology, and he meant neither.

He said it anyway, plainly, at the corner where the lane started to climb.

"What does it cost you?"

Lira did not pretend not to understand him, and he liked her for that before she had answered.

"Who told you it cost anything?"

"Torvin. And Yeni." He kept walking, and so did she. "Torvin says a vouch is a loan. Yeni says it's your name. She says four months is all the name you've got."

"Yeni talks too much."

"Yeni hardly talks at all."

"Then she picked a strange thing to say it about." Lira walked half a street without saying anything, and when she did speak, the lightness had gone out of her voice, and what was left was level and careful, the voice she had used to tell him about the examiner. "All right. If you go into that circle and fold in the first exchange, people will remember that I said you wouldn't. Next time I vouch for somebody, Vell will look at me a little longer before she writes it down. Next time I say a fighter's good, people will say, she said that about the boy who folded. It won't ruin me. I've lost four bouts in that yard and I'm still standing in it. But it'll cost me something I worked for, and I'd rather it didn't."

"Then why do it?"

"Because I don't think you'll fold." She looked sideways at him. "I could be wrong. I've been wrong before. But I've watched you for two days, and I don't think so, and if you want to know what my name's actually for, Cael, it's for this. It's for saying what I think in front of people who'll hold me to it. Otherwise it's just a thing I keep in a drawer."

He thought about the drawer marked Springs, do not use, and did not say anything about it.

"I'm not going to win," he said instead.

"No."

"I mean I'm not going to try to. I'm going to try to last. And I'm going to watch him. And I'm going to come out of there knowing more about how he moves than anybody on that rope." He heard himself saying it and realized he had not known until this moment that it was a plan, rather than a hope. "That's what I can do. That's all I can do. I wanted you to know before you put your name down, in case it's not what you thought you were vouching for."

Lira stopped walking.

They were halfway up the lane, outside a yard where two men were taking turns throwing each other over a hip onto a pile of straw, and the steady soft thump of bodies landing came over the wall like someone beating a rug. Lira stood in the middle of the lane and looked at him for long enough that he began to wonder whether he had made a mistake.

"That's exactly what I thought I was vouching for," she said. "Nobody wins their debut. Nobody sensible tries. The ones who try to win are the ones who get carried out." She started walking again. "And listen. Don't do anything stupid in there to protect my name. You get hurt doing something stupid for my sake and that costs me more than you folding would. I'm not paying for that."

"What counts as stupid?"

"Refusing to go down when you're down. Standing up when you should stay on the ground. Trying something you saw somebody else do on a sheet once." She shook her head. "Keep your feet, watch him, and when Vell calls it, it's over. That's the whole job."

"That's the whole job," he said.

"And Cael."

"Yes."

"It's a good question," said Lira, not looking at him. "Asking what it costs. Most people never ask. They just take it." She lengthened her stride. "Come on. She'll have had her first cup by now."

Near the top of the lane they passed the gate of the yard where the woman had worked on her shoulder. She was not there, but the old man was, in his corner in the shade, set in the same stance as if he had not moved since the day before, and as they went by his pale eyes came round to Cael, then to Lira's canvas roll, then to the way the lane ran on toward the Cinder House.

"Tonight?" he said.

"Tonight."

"Then watch his feet, not yours." The old man's eyes went back to the wall. "Yours'll do what they do."

Lira waited until they were past the next gate. "You know him?"

"He told me watching's not nothing."

"Four months I've walked past that gate," said Lira, "and he's never said a word to me." She looked back over her shoulder, frowning, and then at Cael, as if he had grown an inch while she was not looking.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Vell was watching the empty circle when they came in at the gate, and she went on watching it all the way across the yard, as if it might do something interesting the moment she looked away. Her table stood in the shade of the back wall where it had stood the afternoon before. The ledger was squared to its edge, the pen lay across the open page, and a cup of tea steamed at her elbow. Apart from the crows, there was nobody else in the place.

She moved her eyes only when they had stopped in front of her. They went to Lira, then to Cael, and then back to Lira for a moment, and Cael knew that look from the workshop. It was the look of somebody checking a column and finding a figure entered where she had not expected one.

"Name," she said.

"Cael."

The pen moved, but not for long enough to be his name. It wrote something shorter. She did not ask for a second name, and he did not offer one.

"Age."

"Fourteen."

The pen stopped. It stopped for about one breath, and in that breath Vell lifted her head and looked at him properly, and he made himself stand there and be looked at. It was a thorough look, not an unkind one. It went over his face and his shoulders and his hands and the set of his feet. Partway through it he realised it was doing to him exactly what he had done yesterday to the Stone woman and the Blade fighter from the barrel yard, and doing it a great deal better.

She laid the pen down and folded her hands.

"You'll have had the terms explained to you."

"Yes."

"Explained and agreed are different animals. So you'll hear them from me, and then nobody can stand in my yard afterwards and say they didn't." She did not raise her voice; she did not seem to need to. "You come in unrated. You fight who I put across from you. It ends when I call it. Not when you've had enough, not when the rope's had enough, not when your friend there can't bear to watch." Her glance went to Lira as she said it, and returned. "Once you're over that rope, I'm the only one who stops it. Whatever happens in there, you carry it out of here yourself, whichever way it falls. Nobody's making you. If any of that sits wrong with you, tell me now and I'll strike the line, and there's not a soul in this yard who'll hold it against you."

"It doesn't sit wrong."

"Then say it back."

He looked at her.

"It isn't that I think you're deaf," said Vell. "I've had grown men nod along to all of that, and then stand in the middle of my circle shouting that nobody told them. Nobody goes in until I've heard it come out of their own mouth. I don't care how old they are."

So he said it back, slowly, and checked each part before he set it down, the way Hesk had taught him to call a load figure aloud. Unrated. Whoever she chose. Over when she said it was over, and for no other reason and at no other time. Nobody stopped it but her. Whatever happened, his to carry, either way. Nobody was making him. He did not use her words. He used his own, so that she could hear he had understood the terms and not just memorised them.

When he had finished, the corner of Vell's mouth gave a little. It was gone again before it could grow into a smile.

"Path," she said.

"Nothing to register."

Her eyebrows went up, slightly, and came down. That was all the comment it got. She did not ask him what he meant. She picked up the pen and wrote three or four words, not in the column but out in the margin of the page, and laid the pen down again across the book.

"Who speaks for you?"

"I do," said Lira.

It came out fast and rather loud, as though she had been holding it ready and was afraid the chance might go by. Then she stood with her arms folded and her chin up and dared the table to say anything about it.

Vell considered her for some time.

"Speaking for a boy of fourteen," she said. "Unrated. Nothing to register."

"Yes."

"You've been in my yard four months." Vell's voice stayed exactly where it was. "In four months I've not once seen you vouch for anyone."

"No."

"So why this one?"

Lira opened her mouth and then, to Cael's surprise, shut it again and thought. He watched her do it, with Vell's eyes on her, and he watched her put down the easy answers one by one, the shrug and the joke about being bored, until there was only the true one left.

"Because I asked him what he was," she said, "after eleven minutes at the board, and he didn't lie to me."

Vell held her eyes a breath longer. Then she dipped the pen and wrote a line beneath whatever it was she had put down for him. It was short, and he could not read it upside down.

"There's a Blade called Renn who keeps at me for work," Vell said, still writing. "Copper Rank 3. This season he's had eleven bouts and lost three of them. For an unrated debut tonight, he's what I have. Anybody easier isn't fighting, and nobody who's fighting is easier. He'll not go gentle on you for your age. That's not how this yard works, and you'd not thank me if it were. Somebody goes soft on you the first time, you learn something about this place that isn't so, and you pay for it later."

Cael thought of the card in the corner of the board, near the lost boot: Renn (Cu 3, Blade) wants work. Any evening. Cinder House. He thought of Lira in her second month, going down to Renn while Marrow collected.

"Renn, then," he said.

Vell nodded the way a man nods when a reading agrees with the gauge. "Fourth bout. After the lamps." She set the pen across the page. "Don't be late. And don't thank me. All I've done for you is put a line in a book."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Lira took him to the quietest place she knew, which turned out to be the roof of a cooper's shed two lanes over from the Cinder House, reached by a ladder that the cooper apparently did not know she used. It was flat and tarred and warm from the morning, with a low parapet, and from it you could see the tops of three yards and, beyond them, the first wall of the Ranked core going up the hill in the grey light. Cael thought of a different roof, with a chimney and a water tank, and a grey dog barking at a drainpipe, and then made himself stop.

"Blade," said Lira. She sat cross-legged on the tar with a stick of charcoal and drew on the roof between them. "You saw it yesterday."

"Pale light. Along the forearm, from below the elbow. Out past the fist."

"How far past?"

"Eight inches. My eye says less."

"Your eye's spent fourteen years learning how long an arm is, and it won't unlearn that in an evening." She drew an arm on the tar, and a fist, and a long thin shape past the fist, and then drew the shape again, longer. "Add the eight inches every time you look. The moment you stop adding them, you'll get hit."

"What does it do? When it hits."

"Depends how he holds it." She turned the charcoal in her fingers. "It's got an edge and it's got a flat. The edge cuts. You saw the edge yesterday, on the Stone woman's shoulder. The flat just hits, like being hit with a strap of something hot." She looked at him. "Renn will use the flat on you. On an unrated debut, everybody with a blade uses the flat, unless you give them a reason to stop. It's a courtesy. It still hurts."

"Does he give reasons to stop?"

"No. He's careful." She drew a small circle on the tar beside the arm. "That's what eleven bouts and eight wins means. Not fast, or not only fast. Careful. He doesn't take risks he doesn't need to take. Against you he won't need to take any." She looked up. "Which is good. A careful fighter is a fighter who repeats himself."

"You've fought him."

"In my second month." She drew a line through the small circle. "He put me down in the third exchange. I'd read everything he did in the first two. I'd read it perfectly. I knew exactly what he was going to do, right up to the moment I was on the ground looking at the lamps." She put the charcoal down. "He's got a thing he throws in the third exchange, when he's decided you're worth throwing it at. I'm not going to tell you what it looks like."

"Why not?"

"Because knowing what it looked like didn't help me, and it won't help you. You'll be watching for it, and you'll miss everything else, and you'll still go down." She shrugged. "If he throws it, you go down. Everybody does. That's not losing, that's arithmetic. If he throws it at you, it means you made him want to, and that's a better result than most debuts get."

Cael wrote that down. If he throws it, you go down. That means you made him want to.

"Watch the first exchange," Lira said. "Don't try to do anything in it. Give him ground and look. Everybody on that rope will be watching to see whether you last. You watch what he does while he still thinks you're no trouble."

"And if I can't tell the difference? Between watching and just losing?"

Lira considered that seriously, which he had not expected.

"You'll be frightened," she said. "That's fine. Everybody's frightened. I'm frightened every time, and I stopped counting the times a while ago. Being frightened's not the problem. The problem is when you get so frightened you stop looking. If you notice you've stopped looking, that's when it's not watching any more. That's when it's just being hit."

He did not say anything for a moment, because he was thinking about a page in a leather book, in Hesk's hand, which he had read three times on a wall by the merchant road with crumbs on his knees. The fifth entry. It said that fear could be a tool, so long as it kept you looking, and that the only kind worth worrying about was the kind that closed your eyes. Lira had never seen that page or heard of Hesk. She had arrived at the same place by a different road, through four lost bouts in a yard in Ardenmere, and she had said it to him on a cooper's roof in almost the same words.

This steadied him more than anything she had said all morning. Two people who had never met, and who had learned it in two different ways, had told him the same thing, and that made it a figure he could trace.

"Thank you," he said.

"For what?"

"For telling me that."

Lira looked at him as if he had said something odd, and then shrugged, and picked up the charcoal again. "Hips," she said. "Do you know about hips?"

"Hands lie," said Cael. "Hips have to go where the weight goes."

She stared at him. "Who taught you that?"

"My grandfather. On Tuesdays."

"Then your grandfather," said Lira, "has saved me about an hour," and she drew a pair of feet on the tar instead, and started on those.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

By the time the lamps were lit, the yard was full.

Lira had warned him on the walk down from the roof that it would be an ordinary sort of night: sixty people, perhaps a few more, and none of them there for the fourth bout. They had come for the second, a grudge rematch between two Iron-rated fighters. Cael found this a relief, because he had not wanted anyone to come for him.

The lanterns hung on their hooks along the three walls and threw a warm, uneven light, bright in the middle of the circle and soft at the edges, and outside the rope the faces of the crowd came and went in the swing of the lamps, so that he could see a mouth and then not see it, an eye and then not.

He did not watch the first three bouts; he watched Renn.

Renn was on the far side of the yard, by the wall, with two friends, and for most of the evening he did not do anything at all. He stood with his weight on one leg and his arms folded and watched the bouts with mild interest, and talked to his friends between them, and laughed twice, a man of twenty or close to it.

He was built heavily through the chest and shoulders, not tall, and he stood like a man who had carried heavy things for a living, with his knees a little soft and his back straight. When he walked to the water bucket and back, his stride was short and even, each foot set down as though he meant to stand on it a while.

Once, while the third bout was being called, he looked across the yard and caught Cael looking at him. He nodded, the nod you give somebody across a market, not unfriendly and not especially interested, and then he went back to talking to his friends.

Marrow was working the rope with his slate, and when he passed the barrel at the corner, Cael read the slate without moving his head. Renn, it said, and beside it a number so small it was barely worth betting on. Unrated, debut, and beside that a much larger number. And underneath them both, on a line of its own, Over-under: one exchange.

"What does that mean?" he said quietly. "The last line."

Lira had seen it too. Her face did not change. "It means Marrow's taking bets on whether you last more than one exchange," she said. "And his book says you don't."

"Is that a good bet?"

"For most debuts," said Lira, "it's free money."

At the table, Vell stood up. "Fourth bout," she said, and the yard did not go quite as quiet as it had for the first one, and somewhere along the rope a man laughed at a joke Cael never heard.

Cael stepped over the rope.

The groove was a hand deep and he felt it under his boot as he crossed it, a dip and then level ground. Inside the circle the dirt had been swept and watered, and it was firmer than it looked, packed down by years of feet into something nearly as hard as a floor. The lamplight was very bright in the middle, brighter than it had looked from the barrel, and he walked to the near side of the circle, stopped just inside the groove, and turned round.

Renn was on the far mark before him, working each shoulder round in turn, unhurried.

From the cooper's roof, Lira's voice came back to him in its own clipped rhythm. Add the eight inches. Out loud, in your head. First exchange, you look. Give him ground. Look.

"Renn," said Vell. "Copper Rank 3, Blade Path. Against unrated, debut. Vouched." A small pause, so small that probably nobody else in the yard noticed it. "Begin when you're ready."

Renn brought the blade up. It came out of nothing along his right forearm, as the young man's had the afternoon before, but it was not the same: it was steadier, and it did not make the faint high singing sound when he turned his wrist. It simply stood there in the lamplight, pale and hard and straight, with a thin bright line along one edge. To Cael's eye, before Renn had moved at all, it stopped about a hand past the knuckles. He made himself say that twice in his head, and disbelieve it twice.

Plus eight inches. He said it. Plus eight. He saw it, then, the way a drawing on a page changes when somebody tells you what it is: the real length of it, the place where the edge actually ended in the air, a long way further out than his eye wanted to believe.

Then Renn started toward him, strolling, and the first exchange taught him three things, in order.

The first was that an amble from a Copper Rank 3 covered ground faster than other people walked. Renn did not seem to hurry, and then he was there, inside the distance Cael had thought was safe, and the blade was coming.

The second was that Renn opened with probes. Two of them, loose, one high toward the head and one across toward the body, thrown off his front foot with no weight in them at all, like a man tapping a wall to find out where the hollow part is. They were meant to be seen, and Cael saw them. He gave ground along the curve of the groove, left, and the first went past his face with a faint hiss of air and the second went across the front of him with room to spare, hands high, knees bent, his arms doing nothing except being in the way.

At the rope, someone said something about a rabbit, and somebody else laughed.

The third thing was the important one, and he nearly missed it, and then he did not.

Renn's weight went back.

It went back through his rear foot, into the heel, and settled there, and his whole frame seemed to gather itself onto that heel the way a spring gathers when you press it. The probes had been front-foot work, light as talk, and this was something else: the frame loading. And in the instant after the heel settled—

The blade came round.

Cael saw it start and was a breath late, so that most of him got clear and not all of him. The flat caught him across the meat of the left shoulder as it went past, and it landed like an iron bar left too long in a stove, a broad hard slap that spun him a half-turn on his feet and drove the breath out of him in a grunt. Along the rope the crowd made its first real sound of the night, a pleased murmur that meant the evening was going the way everyone had paid for.

He did not fall. He finished the turn three steps back with his left arm hanging and his shoulder singing, and he was still on his feet, and still inside the groove.

Renn did not come after him but walked back to his mark and waited for Cael to find his, and he rolled his shoulders again while he waited, in no hurry about anything. Cael could find nothing in his face to be afraid of, and nothing to be flattered by. Cael was a few minutes' exercise for a rated man between bigger bouts, the kind of evening a careful fighter takes to keep his arm warm, and Renn bore him no ill will and spared him no thought.

At the table, Vell's pen moved.
