The shoulder hurt in a bright, exact way, as though it had been drawn on him with a hot wire. Cael put the hurt in a box and set the box down, and kept the heel out where he could see it.

Probes off the front foot, he thought. Truth off the back heel. Between heel and blade there's a gap, and that one I spent finding it.

Next time it's mine.

The second exchange began the same way: Renn ambled in, and the probes came, high and across, off the front foot, loose and conversational, and Cael gave ground on the curve, and did not look at the probes at all. He looked at the heel.

It went back. It settled.

And this time Cael went when the heel went, without waiting to see the blade it was loading. He went left and back, early, before the blade had started to come round, a whole quarter of a second sooner than he had moved the first time—

The strike did not come round.

Renn dropped instead. He went low, very fast, his blade arm flung out wide and high as a counterweight, the pale edge drawing a bright line up into the dark above the lamps, and his whole heavy body swinging round, leg first, through the place where Cael's ankles ought to have been. He was going for the legs. There was no harm meant in it. It was the answer a careful fighter keeps for a beginner who has worked out one trick and is too pleased with it, and it ends with the beginner flat on the ground and the rope laughing.

But Cael had already gone, early, before the sweep had committed to anything, and the leg came round through an empty place where his ankles had been half a beat before. He jumped the tail of the swing, clumsily, arms flung out like a boy clearing a ditch, and landed with both feet under him, and found Renn right in front of him.

The bigger man was still crouched from the swing, twisted half round, his hips facing Cael full on and his blade flung up and out on the far side. A short arm could have reached him. For the space of half a beat there was nothing at all between Cael and the middle of him.

Cael saw it. He saw all of it, the hips and the turned shoulder and the blade on the wrong side, and he wrote it down in his head as clearly as if he had had the notebook in his hand.

He did nothing with it.

Then the moment shut. Renn came up out of the sweep in one smooth motion, stepped back two paces, and stood looking at Cael across the bright middle of the circle. And then he rolled his shoulders: left, then right, slowly, settling them, as he had before the first exchange. Cael filed it at once beside the heel. Shoulders when he changes his mind.

There was a half-smile on Renn's face, not for Cael exactly but for the situation.

Something had shifted in the sound along the rope; it was no louder than before, but it had lost the comfortable note of people who already knew the ending, and here and there someone had stopped talking to watch.

At the table, Vell's pen moved again, and for longer.

When Renn came in for the third exchange, he did not amble.

He came balanced and quiet, with his weight in the middle of his feet, and the probes, when they came, were crisper, shorter, with something in them now. Something had been decided across the circle: Renn had stopped exercising, found a puzzle in front of him, and meant to finish it.

The probes came, high and then across, and Cael gave ground, and watched the heel.

The heel settled.

And then he was somewhere else.

He was off the line of the strike without knowing when he had left it. His weight was already through, his feet already placed, and the blade went past through the place where his chest had been, and he had not seen it go. He had not read it. Two exchanges and a shoulder he had paid for that quarter-second between heel and blade, and when the heel came down the quarter-second was simply not there to use. There was the heel, and then there was this.

The second strike grew straight out of the end of the first: the same cut, turned and sent back, slanting low across into the place where anyone who had got clear of the first would have to be standing.

He was not standing there.

He was standing outside its arc, with his weight already turning, and he had not chosen that either. His mind arrived at each new place after his body was already in it, and found it lit and waiting, and could not account for having come.

The third strike came up from below.

He did not see it start. He only felt the air of it, close, very close, a hand's width from his ribs on the left side, ripping upward past him into the empty space above the circle, and he heard the blade's faint hiss die away at the top of its arc. The yard had gone so silent that he could hear the lanterns creaking on their hooks.

He stood still, his heart hammering hard enough to feel in his teeth, with no notion at all of what he had just done.

The watching, he told himself, because whatever had happened needed a name, and any name would do for now. Two exchanges of watching. The body learns. He set the explanation over the thing and saw at once that it did not fit, as a lid cut for a smaller jar does not fit. Two exchanges' study of a single fighter could not have bought that. Nothing he could put his finger on came to that. And the middle of a bout was no place to stand doing arithmetic.

He left the lid where it sat, crooked, and got his hands up.

Because Renn was still there, a pace and a half away, finishing the figure, his weight carried all the way through and up onto his front foot, his blade high and his ribs open. It was the second time tonight Cael had stood within reach of a fully committed Copper Rank 3. He had read nothing this time and got out anyway, and now the man was open, and Cael did the only thing he knew how to do, which was nothing he had ever practised.

He threw a short straight punch at Renn's shoulder.

Renn did not even turn toward it. His left forearm brushed it off, idly, as a man brushes off a fly, without breaking his stride and without bothering to make a guard of it. Then he stepped off, back to his mark, and the third exchange was over.

Cael had not touched him all night.

He knew that, standing on his mark with his fist still stinging from the forearm. He had read two exchanges and paid for one of them with a shoulder. Then something had happened in the third that he could not account for, and in the middle of it he had been handed the cleanest opening of the evening and had answered it with a punch a child could have swatted. Seeing a strike coming was one craft and doing anything about it was another. He had spent two days, and an hour on a cooper's roof, and two exchanges in this circle building the first. He owned none of the second.

Across the circle, for the first time all night, Renn was paying attention to him: the narrow, careful attention of a tradesman holding up a part that has come off his own lathe in a shape he did not cut. He said nothing, because fighters did not talk mid-bout, but his shoulders went round again, left and right, and something in the way he stood packed itself tighter, lower, more closely round its own centre.

There's his serious weight, Cael thought. Eight wins in eleven, with the holding-back taken off.

The fourth exchange lasted four seconds.

This time there were no probes, no amble, no tapping at the wall. Renn came straight off his mark and threw a figure that was cousin to the one in the third exchange, strikes folded into each other, each one coming out of the end of the last. But it was stepped up past some point where reading it stopped being any use, because every strike shut the door the one before it had left open, and the whole of it came so fast that everything earlier in the evening seemed, looking back, to have been good manners.

The first fold Cael saw whole, heel and strike, and he moved for it, late.

He saw the second fold partly.

And then, though he had not decided to, he was reaching for the thing that had moved his feet in the third exchange, feeling about for it like a man patting his pockets for a key he had been holding a moment before.

There was nothing there. There were only his own plain reflexes, the ones that had been late all evening, and they were late again, and they had nothing to spare.

The flat of the blade caught his right side across the ribs. It was a clean, driving, expert blow, with all of Renn's weight behind it this time, and it lifted him off his feet and turned him in the air and put him down on his side in the packed dirt with every bit of breath gone out of him at once.

The ground pressed cold against his cheek, and overhead the lamps rocked on their hooks, or else the yard did. The crowd had become a long way off, much further than the rope, and it was shouting.

"Match," said Vell.

She did not raise her voice, and did not need to. The one word reached every corner of the yard, the shouting and the lamplight and the boy lying in the dirt, and after it nothing else that happened in the circle counted.

Chapter 13 — Tonight's Answer

[Wary, grounded narration; let the unfamiliar district open a detail at a time]

Air came back to him in pieces, as though someone on the far side of a door were handing it through a crack a mouthful at a time.

The first mouthful was tiny and hurt all the way down. The next was bigger. By about the fourth he could get an elbow under himself, and then a knee. He stayed there in the dirt with his head hanging and took stock, because taking stock was a thing to be doing that was not lying on the ground.

Right side, the ribs: a deep, bright band of heat from under his arm to the bottom of his chest, so that each breath had to go round it instead of through. But each breath did go, and nothing ground against anything when it did. So, probably, nothing broken. Probably.

Left shoulder: duller now, and warming by slow degrees toward the kind of ache that would be worse tomorrow than tonight.

And the left forearm, which he had not counted at all. He turned it over in the lamplight and found a long graze down the outside from wrist to elbow, crusted with the circle's dirt and stinging now that he knew about it. Where it came from, he could not say. It annoyed him in a remote, bookkeeping sort of way, like a figure in his own column in a hand that was not his. It might have been the last fall, or the sweep, or the middle of the third exchange, where his feet had been and he had not been with them.

He did not want to go near the third exchange. He laid the arm down.

Someone stood between him and the lamps. It was Renn, without the blade now, his right hand held out open at the height of Cael's face.

Cael took the hand. Renn brought him up off his knee in one easy pull, with the unthinking strength of a man who had spent years shifting loads a great deal heavier than any fourteen-year-old, and did not let go straight away. He kept hold until Cael's feet had agreed to stay where they had been put.

"Four exchanges," Renn said.

He said it flat, the way it would go in the book, but his eyes were busy on Cael's face the whole time.

"Do you know how many I mostly get, off a debut with no rating? One. Two, if they've got some nerve. Never four." His glance went to Cael's ribs, and to the way Cael was holding himself round them, and back. "And the third."

He stopped there and gave one short shake of the head. It was not a man refusing to believe something. It was a man putting a thing on a high shelf to come back to when he had the leisure to look at it properly.

"I threw the whole of that one at you," Renn said. "It doesn't miss. It missed."

Cael kept quiet. He had nothing to say that would have been accurate.

"What's your Path?"

There was no suspicion in it whatever. It was what one tradesman asks another across a bench when a piece of work has come out better than the tools should allow: what did you use?

"Nothing to register," Cael said.

Renn looked at him a while longer. Whatever he made of that, he kept to himself, except that the corner of his mouth went up a little, as if it was the best thing he had heard in the yard all night.

"Tell Vell you want me again," he said. "Leave it a month. By then you'll be worth my while." He let go of the hand at last. "And I want the second look."

It was not the kind thing a winner says to a loser on the way past. Renn meant it, and said it without any decoration at all. He gave Cael one pat on the right shoulder, the one that had not been hit, tipped his head toward Vell's table, half a courtesy to her and half a direction to him, and walked off to the rope. The crowd let him through and shut behind him, and its ordinary noise closed over the place where he had been.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Win or lose, you went to the table after, and you stood there until she was done with you. Lira had told him so on the barrel. He went, holding his right arm tight to his side.

Vell was writing, and he waited, and watched the pen. Four times now, from the barrel and from the rope, he had seen her close a bout in the book: the names, how it ended, which exchange, anything owed. Usually it took two lines. The Bronze pair had taken three, because of the concession.

This pen was well past three. It went, and paused, and went on, and not in the steady way a hand copies out something it already knows. It went as his own pencil went when he was trying to get a thing down before it faded on him, choosing each word as it came and crossing nothing out, because nothing had been written yet that was wrong.

Once she raised her eyes to him without lifting her head.

The look was flat and gave nothing back, and it was very thorough. It was the look of someone checking a sum she had not yet decided to believe. It rested on him the length of a breath, went back down to the page, and the pen added a little more.

She blotted the page and shut the ledger on it, and whatever she had written stayed in there.

"Result stands as called," Vell said. "Renn, by the flat, in the fourth." She rested her hand on the closed cover. "He wants a return in a month, and I'm minded to let him have it. When you've mended, come and find me, and we'll settle terms."

"Yes."

For a moment her look was almost something other than flat. Then it was flat again.

"You lasted longer than the book said you would," she said.

Over by the rope Marrow was wiping his slate clean with the side of his hand, and his face had nothing on it at all.

"Is that good?" Cael said.

"It's what happened." Vell squared the ledger to the table's edge and looked past him to whatever was next, and he understood that he had been sent away.

He was halfway back across the yard before it reached him: three people who knew what they were looking at had watched him move tonight. Renn across the circle, Vell from her stool, and Lira at the rope. He had not chosen to show any of them anything, and it had happened in front of them regardless.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

In the Cinder House yard, Vell did not open the ledger again until she had the place to herself.

That took most of an hour. The crowd went first, in a long slow drain out through the gate, still arguing about the second bout, which had gone the way the book said it would and had therefore been a disappointment to nobody but the loser. The pie boy went next, with his tray empty and his pockets heavy.

Marrow came and stood at the end of her table for a minute, as he did every night, and told her what the evening had taken, and she wrote the figure where she always wrote it, in the back. She did not ask him how he had come by it; years ago she had decided that Marrow's book was Marrow's business and the circuit's book was hers, and that the two must never be allowed to touch.

"The debut," Marrow said pleasantly. "That cost me."

"Did it."

"Everybody had him at one." He smiled. He had a very good smile and he knew exactly how much it was worth. "Over pays long, on a debut. I didn't lay it off."

"Then you'll lay it off next time," said Vell, writing, and after a moment Marrow went away.

The boy from the public house came out with a pole and began taking the lanterns down from their hooks, one at a time, starting at the far wall, so that the yard went dark in stages, from the outside in. Vell sat on her stool and let him. When there were only three lanterns left, the ones nearest her, she opened the ledger at the page and read what she had written.

Renn (Cu 3, Blade) over unrated debut (14; nothing to register; vouched, L.), fourth exchange, by the flat. Called.

That was the result. There was no name in it. The book did not carry the names of unrated debuts, only what they were; a name went into the book when the yard had a reason to need it, and most debuts never gave it one. It was two lines. It was all the book required, and it was all anybody coming to the book in a year, or ten years, would need in order to know what had happened in the yard tonight and who owed whom what.

Under it she had kept writing.

First exchange: debut gave ground on the curve, did not answer. Took the flat on the left shoulder off the true strike. Stayed up.

Second exchange: moved on R.'s rear heel, before the strike. Early. Read it. R. answered with the sweep; debut cleared it, was offered the opening after, saw it (I watched his eyes), did not take it.

Third exchange: R. threw the full figure.

She stopped there, as she had stopped when she was writing it, with the yard full and the boy standing in front of her holding his ribs.

She had kept this book, or one very like it, for longer than some of her fighters had been alive. Before that she had fought in yards like this one, and in better ones, for long enough to reach a rating nobody gave lightly and a body that told her about it every wet morning. She had seen, at a rough count she had once made on a winter night with nothing better to do, something over four thousand bouts. She had called nearly all of them. She did not remember most of them, and that was as it should be. The book remembered them. That was what the book was for.

She remembered Renn's figure.

She had watched him build it, over two seasons, a piece at a time. The first time he threw it, it had not been finished, and a woman with a Shield Path had walked through the middle of it and put him down. The second time it had been nearly finished. By the end of last season it had been finished, and she had watched him throw it nine times since, and she had written it down nine times.

Nine times the third strike had come up the lane, and nine times somebody had been standing in the lane, because that was where the first two strikes put you. That was the whole of its design. Nobody had to guess wrong for it to work. Guessing right was what delivered you to it.

She had written it down on a night in the summer against the name of the Wind girl, the one who had stood in front of her table tonight with her chin up and said I do. The girl had read the first two strikes as cleanly as Vell had ever seen anyone read them, and the third had put her in the dirt, and she had got up, and come back the next week, and the week after that.

Tonight it had not put anybody in the dirt.

Vell had been looking straight at it. She looked at every third exchange straight, because the third was where fighters stopped asking questions and told you what they meant, and it was where things happened that the book needed to know about. She had watched the boy's eyes, because a reader's eyes went to the place he was reading, and she had seen him go to Renn's heel in the second exchange like a man going to a door he knows. And in the third exchange she had watched his eyes go to the heel again. She had watched the heel settle.

And then the boy had not been where the strike was. And his eyes had still been on the heel. He had moved before they had left it.

She did not know what she had seen. She had sat at the table with the pen in her hand and the boy standing in front of her, and she had known that she did not know, and she had known that the book did not care whether she knew. The book cared what had happened.

There was a rule she kept for herself, which was not written down anywhere, because there was nowhere it belonged. She had made it on the night she called the Ash Path man for the third time, and he did not stop, and a woman had been carried out of this yard to wait for a healer from across the river.

Vell had written that entry afterward, and it had run to a page and a half, because she had written down everything she had seen, in order, including the two calls before and how she had made them and what she had seen in his face when he did not stop. And when people came to the table in the weeks after, wanting to know whether she had called it too late, or too early, or whether she had a grudge, she had opened the book and turned it round and let them read.

Nobody had argued with the page and a half. The circuit had survived it, and so had she.

Write what you saw, the rule went. Not what you understood. If you only write what you understand, the book is only as honest as you are clever, and nobody is that clever.

She dipped the pen.

Defender off the line before R.'s strike began. Not a read. I watched for the read and there was none. Eyes still on the heel. Off the second strike the same. Was not in the lane for the third. A hand's width.

Debut threw one punch, untrained. R. turned it with the forearm.

Fourth exchange: R. threw the figure without probes. Debut read the first fold, part of the second, and nothing after. Down by the flat, right side. Got up.

She read it back. It was eight lines more than the book needed, and every one of them was a thing she had seen with her own eyes from this stool, and not one of them said what any of it meant.

That was correct. She did not know what it meant. Neither, she thought, did the boy. She had looked at him while she wrote, with the yard still noisy round them, and she had seen a fourteen-year-old holding his ribs and waiting, as he had been told to wait, with nothing in his face at all.

Most of them had something in their faces at the table, after a first bout: shame, or fury, or a grin they could not stop, or the dazed look of somebody who had not known until tonight what it was to be hit by a person who meant it. He had had nothing. He had had the look of somebody who was keeping very still around something, so that it would not spill.

She thought about the margin, where she had written nothing to register that morning. She had heard that phrase before, now and then, from people who did not want to say their Path out loud in a yard, and it usually meant a bad draw they were ashamed of. It usually did not mean anything she needed to know.

She thought about him saying the terms back to her.

She had made a great many people say the terms back to her, over the years. Most of them said them in her words, in her order, as fast as they could, like children saying a lesson. He had said them in his own, slowly, as if he were checking each one before he set it down, and when he had finished she had known that he had heard every word and weighed it, and had decided to come in anyway. That was rarer than talent. She had seen a great deal of talent.

And she thought about the Wind girl.

Four months. Four bouts lost and then a long run that had made people start betting on her, and in all that time she had not vouched for anybody, though Vell knew for a fact she had been asked. Tonight she had stood at the table and said I do as if she were afraid somebody would take the words out of her mouth before she could get them said. Because I asked him what he was, after eleven minutes at the board, and he didn't lie to me.

Vell had not asked what he was. She had decided, in the morning, that she did not need to know.

She thought now that she had been right not to ask, and that she would not ask, and that she was going to watch very carefully all the same.

There was one more line to write, and it was not one the book required, and she wrote it anyway, at the bottom of the entry, smaller, in the space she used for things that belonged to her and not to the circuit.

Lasted four. Marrow's slate said one. Match him with care. Not soft. Against people who'll teach him something.

She blotted it, and closed the ledger, and sat for a moment with her hand flat on the cover in the light of the last three lanterns.

The boy from the public house was waiting with his pole.

"Go on," Vell said, and he took the last lanterns down, one, two, three, and the yard went dark, and she picked up the book and her stool and went in.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Lira held her tongue for a block and a half, which Cael would later learn was close to a record.

She had come off the rope an hour earlier, while Vell's yard was still roaring, and found him at the gate and fallen in at his side with no word at all. The two of them had gone out into the dark of the district together. Lamps were few in the lanes and far apart, and the dark between them was the real kind. Two corners on, the yard had dropped away behind them, and there was only the sound of their boots, a dog somewhere, and the river a long way off. Cael was walking carefully round his ribs. Lira was walking at exactly his pace, which was slower than her own, and she said nothing about that either.

Then it came out of her, aimed at the dark in front of them rather than at him.

"You almost had him in the second exchange. Once the sweep went by. Half a beat, he was crouched and turned and wide open to you. Put a hand on him there and it counts, even with arms as short as yours." She breathed out hard through her nose. "I nearly bit through my knuckle."

"I wasn't trying to win. I was trying to learn how he moves."

For three steps she said nothing. He could feel her changing her mind beside him, a shift in the air, like the side of a stove when somebody has just shut the damper.

"Oh. That's actually smarter." Her voice had altered entirely.

"Two probes," Cael said. "Always the same two, every time he starts." He had the whole bout stacked in him, page on page, and every line he gave her he was also checking for himself. "High first, then across. Front foot. Nothing behind them; they're for looking with. When he means it, the weight goes back onto the heel before anything else. He sits in it. A quarter of a second, less by the end. He rolls his shoulders when he changes his plan: once after the sweep, once before the last one. And the sweep is for somebody who's just found the heel and is pleased with himself. He was waiting for me to get clever."

"He was," Lira said.

"And when he stops testing and simply comes," said Cael, "that's the one to be frightened of. That was the fourth."

"That," said Lira, with feeling, "was the fourth."

She had watched it from the rope, and he could hear in her voice what the watching had cost her.

Then she was not beside him any more. He had gone two steps on before he noticed. When he turned back she was under one of the few lanterns in the middle of the lane, hands at her sides, stopped, and he understood that the talk had come round at last to the thing she had meant to say all along.

"The third exchange," Lira said.

He waited.

"On the roof I said I wouldn't tell you what that figure looks like, because knowing it doesn't help." She did not move. "I'll tell you now. The whole thing is built for the third cut. The first two aren't trying to hit you. They're steering you. Read the first one right and you go where it puts you. Read the second right and you go where that one puts you, and where it puts you is the exact lane the third one comes up." She gave it to him without any colour in her voice, like a reading off a gauge. "In my second month I read the first two as well as I've ever read anything, and the third laid me on my back staring up at the lamps. Everybody he's ever thrown it at has finished up staring at the lamps."

The lantern caught in her eyes. They had not left his face.

"Tonight it went by a boy on his first night in the circle, with a hand to spare." She put her head on one side. "Somewhere after the second cut you went where that figure doesn't send anybody. So I've a question. It's a small one, and I think it's fair."

He had known what it was since Vell's table.

"How?"

He had walked the whole way from the yard without readying an answer, and he knew he had done that deliberately. Readying one would have meant turning round to look the thing in the face and take its measure, and here in the dark he could admit, a little, that he did not want to. He had nothing to measure it with. In the fourth exchange he had reached for it and his hand had closed on nothing.

There was no showing it to her. He could not have done it again on demand, here between these walls, because she asked; he could not have told her what it was made of or promised it would ever come back. It was a single stone in a heap he could otherwise count, and it would not be counted, and every time his thoughts drifted near it they remembered urgent business somewhere else.

"Instinct," Cael said.

It was a true word that stopped a hand's width before the truth did.

Lira's eyes stayed on him. He was beginning to understand that she could tell, very exactly, when someone had handed her a real answer, or a false one, or a true one with its legs sawn short. He suspected she had a second sense as well, rarer than the first, for whether to collect on the difference now or leave the account open.

"All right," she said. "Instinct."

She walked on, and he went with her. Three streets went by, lanterns coming and going over them, before she spoke again, and when she did it was lightly, in the voice of someone making a note in a book of her own.

"That's tonight's answer," said Lira. "I'm writing down that it was tonight's."

[Steady, observant narration; let place, distance, and social position register]

They walked.

The district went about its late business round them: shutters going up, lamplight under doors, somebody in a window two streets over arguing cheerfully about the odds on something. A cart went by with its lamp swinging. A woman on a doorstep called a cat in by a name Cael did not catch, and the cat did not come.

His body had sorted its pains into their long arrangements by then, the shoulder stiff and the forearm stinging, and the ribs a hot band that made every breath a small negotiation.

He had lost, and it was in the book in two lines, and he had not touched Renn once. But he had walked out of the circle owning the working of one man. Bruises healed. What he had bought with them would not. A month from now, at Vell's table, he meant to have every piece of it ready.

Nearly all of it.

One piece of the evening he left unsorted. He did not so much as pick it up. He let it lie where it had fallen, whole and unexamined, in a corner of himself where he would know it was there without having to look at it. He had been doing that with a turnip cart since the road. Now there were two things in the corner, and he did not let himself count them, because counting them would have been the first step toward a word.

So he went home at Lira's side through the cooling dark: fourteen, beaten in four exchanges, his shoulder and his ribs charging him for every step. And he was certain, quietly and against all the evidence of the book, that he had won something tonight that nobody on the rope had been watching for.

At the corner by the well with the iron cover, Lira stopped.

"I go this way," she said, with a nod at the dark beyond the well that could have meant any of four lanes. Then she looked at him, at the way he was holding his side. "Torvin's has a yard with a pump. Put the cold on the ribs before you lie down, or you won't get up in the morning. Not too long. Count it."

"How long?"

"You'll know how long." She almost smiled. "You count everything."

"Lira."

She had already turned. She turned back.

"You didn't lose your name tonight," he said. "Did you?"

For a moment Lira only looked at him through the dark. Then she laughed, short and real, the laugh from the yard in the morning that had surprised her.

"No," she said. "Marrow did. He'd laid nothing off on the over." She walked backward a few steps down the lane, without looking behind her, without hitting anything. "Go and put your ribs under the pump, Cael. I'll see you at the yard."

And she was gone into the dark, and he stood at the corner by the well for a moment longer, holding his side, and then went home.

Chapter 14 — Claim, Evidence, Ruling

[Focused, analytical narration; make every lesson and useful loss legible]

He woke because one of the brothers dropped a boot, and for a moment, before he moved, nothing hurt at all.

Then he moved. The right side of his chest reported first, the hot band from under his arm to the bottom of his ribs, and the left shoulder joined in a breath later, stiff and thick, as if somebody had packed the joint with wet sand while he slept. Last of all the scrape down his left forearm stung where the blanket dragged across it, the scrape he still could not account for.

He lay still and let all three finish what they had to say, while the window over his cot went from black to grey and the brother whispered an apology to the boot and both of them went creaking off down the stairs toward the river.

Last night he had stood under Torvin's pump in the dark with his shirt off and counted, because Lira had told him to count, and he had stopped at sixty because sixty was what his ribs would stand. He could not tell whether it had helped. He could breathe, though every breath went carefully round the edge of something on its way in and out, and that would have to do.

He sat up in three stages, like a folding chair.

Yeni was awake on the next cot, lying on her side under her blanket with one eye open, watching him do it.

"Renn," she said.

"Renn."

"How many?"

"Four exchanges."

The eye closed again. "Torvin's wife had you at two," she said into her pillow. "Now she owes the one in the boots a bun."

He had not known that anybody in this house had had him at anything. He sat on the edge of the cot with his shirt in his hands and thought about a bet made over a kitchen table on a boy nobody there had seen fight, and he could not decide whether it made him feel better or worse. Both, probably. He was getting used to things being both.

Putting the shirt on took longer than it should have. He did the right arm first, keeping the elbow tight against his side, and then worked the left shoulder into its sleeve a little at a time, like threading a stiff wire through a hole that was slightly too small. When he had finished, Yeni's eye was open again.

"Left's the shoulder. Right's the ribs."

"Yes."

"Don't sleep on either." She rolled over to face the wall. "And don't let him tell you to rest. He'll tell you to rest. Rest is for people with savings."

She did not say whether she meant Torvin or somebody else.

In the kitchen the range was lit and the oats were on, and Torvin's wife stood over the pot with her wooden spoon. The woman who slept in her boots was at the end of the table eating a sweet bun with great slowness and pleasure, and she raised it to Cael when he came in, as somebody might raise a cup.

"Four," she said. "I said three or better. I'm a generous judge of people."

"You said three because you'd heard about the Wind girl," said Torvin's wife, without turning round. "Sit down before you fall down, boy. There's a bowl."

He sat. The bowl came, and with it a spoon and a hard look at the way he lowered himself onto the bench, and then Torvin's wife went back to her pot and said nothing more about it.

He ate slowly. Turning his head to the left was fine, and turning his body was not, and by the bottom of the bowl he had worked out exactly which movements cost what and put the list away in his head beside the other lists.

Torvin came in from the yard with a bucket and stopped in the doorway.

"Pump handle was wet at midnight."

"I used it."

"Lira tell you to?"

"Yes."

"She's right." Torvin set the bucket down by the range and looked at Cael for a moment the way he looked at coins, slowly, checking his own count. "I said fight in the street."

"It wasn't in your house."

"No." Torvin seemed to consider this from several sides and to find nothing wrong with any of them. "Four, they're saying."

"Four."

Torvin grunted. It was not quite approval, and it was not nothing. Then he picked up the oats pot with a cloth round the handle and set it on the table at Cael's elbow, so that there would be a second bowl if he wanted one, and went out again without another word.

Cael had a second bowl. It seemed rude not to.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The Cinder House yard was half in shadow when he got there. The sun was up somewhere behind the east wall, and the wall threw a long, clean shadow across the packed dirt, so that the yard was split down the middle into a grey half and a bright half with the circle's groove running through both.

Mist lay in the low corner by the drain, and the crows were working last night's leavings along the rope line, where the pie boy had dropped crusts and somebody had dropped a whole half pie and never come back for it.

Lira was at the post in the far corner, in the grey half. She did not stop when she saw him. She watched him walk across the yard to her between one strike and the next, and partway across he understood that she was not watching his face.

"Right side," she said, when he reached her. "And the left shoulder. You walk like a man carrying a tray of glasses."

"You were at the rope. You saw where he hit me."

"I'm not telling you what I saw. I'm telling you what I see." She struck the post, low, and let her hand rest against the canvas. "You're not sparring today."

"I didn't come to spar."

"Then what did you come for?"

"You said you'd see me at the yard."

She looked at him for a moment. Then she turned back to the post so that he could not see her face, which told him more than her face would have, and struck it twice more, a little harder than before.

"All right. Then you can stand there and learn something with one arm. Right arm. Hold it up. No, like this." She took his wrist and set his forearm upright in front of him, elbow down and palm toward his own face, as if she were propping up a fence post. "This part. The outside, from the wrist to the elbow. That's what you catch with."

She showed him the deflection, the one she had shown him at the board on the second day, the one every Wind student learned in their first month: catch, reset, send. She went through it so slowly that it stopped looking like fighting and began to look like a craftsman showing an apprentice how to hold a plane.

Her strike came in toward his face at the speed of somebody reaching for a cup, and his forearm met it on the outside and caught it. That was the first part.

"Now stop. Feel where you are."

He felt where he was. The strike had pushed his arm a little across his own body, and his weight had gone with it, onto the wrong foot.

"That's why there's a middle," said Lira. "Catching it moves you. Reset puts you back, weight in the centre, arm back on its line, and then you're ready to do something with what you caught." She took her hand away and brought it in again, just as slowly. "Catch. Reset. Send."

On send she turned his forearm for him, rolling it outward against her wrist, and her strike went away past his shoulder into the empty air as if it had changed its mind about where it wanted to go.

They did it twenty times before the sun reached the post, and then forty. The reset was where his ribs complained, because the reset meant a small turn of the body back to centre and the turn went right through the bruise.

The third time he flinched in it she saw, and after that she brought her strikes in from a slightly different angle so that the reset needed less turn, and she did not say anything about why.

"Why not teach me the other way?" he said, around the fiftieth. "Your way. Without the middle."

"Because you can't skip a step you don't own." Catch. Reset. Send. "When I skipped it, I'd done all three parts ten thousand times. I knew exactly what I was leaving out, and what it cost, and why I could afford it. You'd only be leaving out something you never had." She lowered her hand. "That's not a skip. That's a hole."

He thought about that through the next ten repetitions and found nothing in it to argue with, which was annoying.

He had brought bread. On the way he had stopped at the top of the second row of the market and asked the bread woman for two from underneath, watching her face as the nut boy had told him to. She had given him two from underneath with a small sour look that he took as respect.

He held one out to Lira now. She tore it in half, put one half on top of the post and ate the other in four bites, and then set her feet.

"Breakfast's between. Not before. Before, you're slow. After, you're late." She brought her hand up. "Catch."

So he ate his roll in the gaps, in pieces, between sets of ten. When the sun finally came over the east wall and the shadow began to shrink back toward it, Lira moved their work along with the shadow, a step at a time, keeping them both in the grey half until there was no grey half left.

He noticed it, and he noticed that she did it without looking, as people do things they have done so often that they no longer need to decide them.

He did not ask about it. There was probably a reason, he thought, and if she wanted him to have it she would give it to him, and until then it was hers.

She did not mention the third exchange, not once all morning. He kept waiting for it between the catches and the resets, and it did not come. Somewhere around the hundredth repetition he understood that she was not going to ask today, and that the not asking was something she was doing on purpose, as deliberately as she kept them in the shade.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The third notebook from Denvash had nine pages left in it.

He counted them that afternoon, sitting on the low wall in Torvin's yard beside the pump, under the stunted pear tree in the corner that had given up growing tall and grown wide instead, and then he counted them again, because nine was not many.

The front of the book was full of Ardenmere: the nut boy's map, the board decoded, the rules, six pages on two strangers' bouts and Marrow's numbers. The back held the things he had written from the other end, as he always did, in the smaller hand.

There was the archive entry and the gate entry, and on its own page, near the end, the dip between the hedges and the turnip and I don't think I did.

He closed it on that page without reading it again.

The paper stall was at the bottom of the market, near the fruit woman with no name. It was run by a man with ink on his cuffs who sold everything from single sheets to bound ledgers with marbled edges that cost more than a week at Torvin's.

Cael looked at the ledgers. Then he bought the cheapest thing on the table that still had a proper sewn spine: a thick, plain notebook with a grey board cover and paper so thin that the ink of one page would show faintly through the next.

It was a good deal more than he wanted to pay. He paid it, and wrote the figure in the back of the old book under the line he had drawn that morning, and took the new one back to the wall by the pump, where he sat with the pencil over the first page.

He had kept notebooks since he was eight, and every one of them had been the same kind of book. Things went into it as they came, in order, a bearing, a dog, a wall, a word on page seven, and that had always been enough, because the things he wrote down were mostly things that would still be there tomorrow.

This was different, and he could feel the difference in his hands. The bout with Renn was already less clear than it had been last night. Had the second probe, the one across the body, really come off the front foot, or had he only expected it to?

He had been sure on the walk home and was nearly sure now, and by next week he would be sure again in the wrong way, as you become sure of a thing you have told yourself often enough.

He wrote Log at the top of the first page and underlined it.

Then he wrote the first entry the way he had always written things, in sentences, and it came out like this:

Renn. Copper Rank 3, Blade. He opens with two probes, high and across, off the front foot. The true strike loads in his back heel about a quarter of a second first. I read the heel in the second exchange and he answered with the sweep. In the third I got out of the whole figure—

He stopped.

He read the line back. In the third I got out of the whole figure. It was true. He had been standing outside the figure at the end of it, and Vell had seen it, and Renn had seen it, and Lira had seen it from the rope. Yet the sentence sat on the page next to the heel and the probes as though it belonged with them, in the same hand and the same voice.

Anybody reading it a year from now would think he had done the third exchange the way he had done the second, by reading and moving. He had not. He did not know how he had done it, and the sentence did not know either. It simply did not say so.

That was what sentences did, he thought. They ran on. You put a true thing in at one end, and a guess came out of the other in the same coat, and nobody could tell them apart.

He tore the page out, carefully, along the spine, so that the binding would not loosen, and folded it and put it in his pocket. Then he took the straightedge from his tool roll, the little steel one he had made at twelve, and ruled the next page into three columns.

He thought about what to call them. Hesk's slates in the workshop had columns for load, figure and result, which were close but not right, because nobody here was hanging weights on a rig.

What he wanted was something that made each line prove itself before he let it stay. He thought about Vell at her table, and the way the yard went quiet when she spoke, and the one word she said at the end of a bout that made it finished.

He headed the columns Claim, Evidence and Ruling.

A claim was what he thought was true. Evidence was what he had seen with his own eyes that made him think so, and when, and how many times. A ruling was what he would do about it next time, and it was only allowed to exist if the evidence was there.

If somebody had told him a thing and he had not seen it himself, it could still go in. But it went in with a small h beside it, for heard, so that he would always know it was a figure somebody else had traced and he had not.

Never trust a number you can't trace back to where it came from.

He began again.

1. Renn. Copper R3, Blade Path (Vell's rating). Eleven bouts, eight wins (Vell, h).

Claim: the probes carry no weight. Evidence: off the front foot, high then across, every exchange but the last. Ruling: spend nothing on them.

Claim: the true strike loads in the back heel a quarter second before the blade. Evidence: first exchange, paid for with the shoulder; second exchange, moved on it and was right. Ruling: move on the heel, not on the blade.

Claim: he rolls his shoulders when he changes his plan. Evidence: before the first exchange, after the sweep, before the fourth. Ruling: shoulders mean a new plan. Stop expecting the old one.

Claim: the sweep is kept for people who have learned the heel. Evidence: second exchange, once. Ruling: one is not enough. Watch for it again.

Claim: the blade reaches eight inches past the fist. Evidence: Lira, h. My eye says less. Ruling: add eight until I have measured it myself.

It took him most of the afternoon. When he had finished he had a page and a half on a man he had fought for perhaps three minutes in all, and every line on it would hold weight, because he had tried each one and could tell exactly where it came from.

There was nothing on it about the third exchange.

He had not left it out by deciding to. It simply had nowhere to go. He had a claim, I got out of the figure, but no evidence, because he had not seen himself do it, and no ruling, because he did not know what he would do next time, and so the columns would not take it.

He looked at the empty place where it would have been and felt something that was partly relief and partly shame, and he could not have said which was larger.

He turned the notebook over and opened it from the back, as he always did, to the last page. This would be the other kind of page; things would go here that did not fit the columns.

Sitting on the wall with the pump dripping beside him, he made himself a rule about it: nothing went in the back until the front was finished for the day. The facts first, then the rest. If he could make himself keep to that order, he thought, the rest might stay a sensible size.

He wrote only one line, at the top of the last page.

There are things that won't go in the columns. I know where they are. I am not counting them yet.

Then he closed the Log and sat with it on his knee, listening to the pump drip, and did not open the old notebook to the page near the back, though he knew exactly which page it was.

[Steady, observant narration; let place, distance, and social position register]

The pouch said he had until the eleventh day.

He did the sum on the morning of the tenth at the kitchen counter, in small stacks of coins, twice. Torvin's week ran out tomorrow. After that the pouch would pay for three more weeks if he ate the way he had been eating, and four if he ate the way the brothers ate, which was mostly bread and whatever the river gave them, but it would not pay for five.

Find work, he had written on the rise. He had written it second, after find somewhere to sleep, and he had done the first and not the second, and now the second had come round to find him.

He went down to the river workshops in the late morning with his left arm held close, past the cobbler and the lantern woman and the cooper, to the doorway at the end of the row with no sign over it. The mender was not straightening a mangle today.

He had the clock with no hands open on his bench, its works laid out on a cloth in neat rows like a surgeon's instruments, and he was looking at them through a loupe and did not look up.

IF IT'S STILL HERE, said the doorframe.

"Something of yours broken?" said the mender, to the clock.

"Not today. I wanted to ask if you need anybody."

That made the man look up. He took the loupe out of his eye and gave Cael the same checking look he had given him over the mangle frame, and his gaze went to the arm Cael was holding close and came back.

"For what?"

"Sorting. Cleaning. Truing small things." Cael could not find a way to say the next part that would be true and not sound like boasting, so he said it anyway. "My grandfather makes instruments. I've worked at his bench since I was six."

The mender said nothing to that. He reached under the bench, felt about without looking, and came up with a little brass balance of the kind a spice seller uses, with a beam no longer than a hand. The beam was bent, though not much.

It dipped a hair to the left at rest, so that anything weighed on it would weigh light in one pan and heavy in the other, and you would have to hold it up to the light and squint along it to see why. He put it on the bench, laid his straightedge beside it, and went back to his clock.

Cael did not touch the balance at first. He looked at it.

Then he did what he had watched the mender do with the mangle, and what Hesk had done at the rig for as long as he could remember: he did not guess. He laid the straightedge along the beam and found the bend, which was not in the middle, as he had expected, but a little way out along the left arm, where somebody had probably caught it on the edge of a stall.

He clamped the beam lightly in the bench vice with a fold of leather between the jaws and pressed, not much, and then took it out and laid the straightedge along it again.

It was better, and not right. He pressed again, less, and looked, and found he had gone over very slightly, so he turned it and pressed back the other way with the pad of his thumb and no vice at all.

The fourth time he laid the straightedge along it, he could see no light underneath. He hung the beam on its pivot and let it settle, and the pointer swung, slowed, and came to rest dead on the mark.

"There," he said.

The mender put down his loupe and came round the bench to look. Without a word he took two identical brass weights out of a drawer and set one in each pan, and the beam dipped and rose and came back to the mark and stayed there. He took the weights off and looked at Cael's left arm again.

"Two afternoons. Not mornings; I don't talk in the mornings. By the piece, not by the hour, because I don't pay for people standing about thinking." He put the weights back in their drawer. "You'll sort what comes in, and sweep, and true the small things. You won't touch the clocks."

"I won't touch the clocks."

"And if you break something you'll pay for it out of what I owe you, and then you'll go." He went back round the bench. "Tomorrow. After noon."

That was all. Cael stood in the doorway a moment longer before he understood that he was being allowed to leave, and left.

On the fish steps below the carriers' hut a barge was unloading sacks of meal onto the landing, and three men were carrying them up to a cart one at a time on their shoulders.

The second man up was Renn. He was in a sleeveless shirt with a sack on his right shoulder, taking the slick steps two at a time as though they were level ground. At the top he swung the sack onto the cart without breaking stride and turned to go down for the next one. Then he saw Cael on the street above and stopped on the top step.

For a moment neither of them said anything. Renn looked at him as he had looked across the circle in the third exchange, briefly and carefully, a man checking a part he had not cut.

"Healing?"

"Slowly."

"Good." He went down a step, then stopped and looked back over his shoulder. "A month," he said, and went on down to the barge.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

He went to Vell's table on the fourth morning after the bout, when he could lift his left arm as high as his shoulder without his face doing anything about it.

The yard was empty except for Vell and the crows. She sat at the table in the shade with her ledger squared and her tea at her elbow, exactly as she had on the morning of the terms, and when he stopped in front of her she looked at him without speaking.

"Lift your left arm."

He lifted it to the height of his shoulder.

"Higher."

He lifted it higher and kept his face still. He was nearly sure he kept his face still.

Vell watched the arm, then the face, then the arm again. "Thursday," she said, and picked up her pen. "Not before. Renn's return stays where I put it, at the month. Between now and then you'll fight who I give you."

"Who?"

"Brenna." She wrote a short line. "Copper Rank 2, Shield Path. She lost to Dessa a fortnight ago in three exchanges and she hasn't stopped talking about it. She wants somebody she can finish quickly, so that people will talk about that instead." The pen stopped and Vell looked up. "If you're any use, you'll be somebody she can't finish quickly. That'll be good for both of you, and she won't thank me for it."

He nodded. He was watching the pen.

It had written a line beneath the line from four nights ago. He could see the shape of the old entry, the long one that had run well past two lines and on down the page, though he could not read any of it upside down.

But he could see where a name would go at the start of each entry, and he could see that at the start of his there was no name, only something shorter.

"You haven't written my name."

Vell did not look down at the page. She seemed to have known exactly where he was looking.

"No."

"Is that because I'm unrated?"

"It's because the book doesn't need it yet." She laid the pen across the ledger. "You're in the book as what you are. Unrated. Fourteen. Vouched. Lost to Renn in four exchanges, by the flat, called. That's everything anybody coming to this book will need to know about that night. A name goes in when the yard comes to see it."

"When will that be?"

"For most of them, never. Most of them come and fight and go home, and the book holds what they did, and nobody ever needs to know what they were called. It's no slight. It's what a book's for." She picked up her tea. "When the yard comes to see you, I'll write it. Not before. And not because you asked."

Standing there, he did not mind, though he had thought he would. He was in a book, in somebody else's careful hand, as exactly what he was and what he had done, and every word of it was something Vell had seen herself from this stool. It was a ledger he could check, and it had no word in square brackets in it.

"Thursday," he said.

"After the lamps. Third bout. Don't be late, and don't be early either. Being early makes people think you're frightened."

He went out through the gate in the wall. On his way back down he found the old result still pinned near the bottom of the board at the crossroads, gone pale in the rain: Dessa (Cu 5, Stone) over Brenna (Cu 2, Shield), third exchange, called. He read it twice, and remembered two men arguing behind him in the triangle on his first afternoon, and one of them saying that Brenna could not stand that it went to three.

He took out the Log, turned to a clean page and wrote 2. Brenna. Under it, in the first column, he put wants it over quickly, and in the second, two men at the board, h; Vell, h, and in the third column nothing at all.

The ruling would have to wait until Thursday. He was learning that most of them would.

Chapter 15 — Never Resets

[Focused, analytical narration; make every lesson and useful loss legible]

On the third morning Lira let him use both hands.

"Open hands," she said. "Touch only. If you hit me, I'll hit you back, and I've got two good shoulders and you haven't." She set her feet in the grey half of the yard, where the east wall's shadow still lay long across the dirt. "I'm going to come in slow. You're going to catch, and reset, and send, and if you get the send right you can try to touch me afterward. Anywhere. A finger on my sleeve counts."

"And if I don't get the send right?"

"Then I touch you. And I'm not slow afterward."

She was not, as he found out in the first minute. Her strikes came in at the speed she had promised, the speed of somebody reaching for a cup, and he caught them and reset and sent them away.

Then, in the half-breath after each send, while he was still working out where his own hand should go next, her other hand would arrive from somewhere he had not been looking. It touched his collarbone, and then his ear, and once the very end of his nose, lightly, with one finger, while she said "Nose," in a perfectly flat voice, and he was so surprised that he laughed and his ribs made him regret it.

"You're thinking after the send. Like the send's the end of something. It isn't. Nothing's the end of something until Vell says so."

They went again, and he stopped thinking after the send, and then stopped thinking about anything at all, as far as he could tell, except the place her shoulders went before her hands did. He caught, reset, sent, and in the half-breath after the send he put his left hand out, not far, only as far as the shoulder would allow, toward the place he thought she was going to be.

His fingertips touched her sleeve.

Lira stopped and looked down at her own sleeve as if a moth had landed on it.

"Well."

"You're getting slower."

"I am absolutely not getting slower." She set her feet again. There was a brightness in her face that he had begun to recognize, a morning brightness that did not come out later in the day, when the yard filled up and she had to be the girl who had lost her first four. "You're getting faster. There's a difference. Mostly to my pride."

"Or you're getting predictable."

Lira looked at him with deep and dignified offence.

"I am never predictable. I'm generous. I let you have that one, because you've got one shoulder and a face like a kicked dog, and I thought you could do with some encouragement."

"You didn't let me have it. Your weight went onto your left foot before the strike started. I watched it go."

"People who've just lost a sparring round say that sort of thing to cheer themselves up."

"I didn't lose it. I touched your sleeve."

"You touched my sleeve because I was being generous." She brought her hands up. "Again. And this time I'm going to be a great deal less generous, and you're going to stop watching my left foot, because I've just noticed I've been doing that for four months and I'm going to stop."

She did stop. He watched for it for the rest of the morning and it did not come back once, and that night he wrote it in the Log, in the column for evidence, with something very close to admiration. Told her the tell. She removed it in an hour. Ruling: never tell anybody their tell unless I'm sure I don't need it.

He looked at the ruling after he had written it, and did not like it much, and left it in, because it was what he had seen.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On Tuesday there was an afternoon card at the Cinder House, three bouts, and Lira took him to the barrel by the drain to watch a man called Baro.

"Just Baro," she said, before he could ask. "No other name, or none he uses. Nobody's asked. He turned up at the start of the summer and put himself down for an afternoon card, unrated, and he's been on the afternoon cards ever since."

"Unrated since the summer?"

"He's never asked Vell for a rating, and she's never offered one." Lira hitched herself up onto the barrel lid beside him. "People have opinions about why. Some of them say he's somebody who used to be somebody, across the river, and doesn't want the book to find out what. Some of them say he's just strange." She looked across the yard. "I think he's the most careful fighter in Ardenmere. I've watched him eleven times and I've never once seen him get hit anywhere he didn't choose."

Baro was standing by the far wall, talking to nobody: a man of perhaps thirty, lean and long in the arm, with close-cut dark hair and a face that did not seem to be doing anything at all. When he moved to take a cup of water from the bucket, Cael saw that he turned his whole body to do it instead of turning at the waist.

There was a stiffness low on his left side, in the back, which he carried as if it were part of his clothing.

Old injury, Cael thought. Bad one. He's built round it.

Vell gave Baro out as unrated, Blade Path, against a Copper Rank 4, Force Path, and the yard made a low, interested noise that was not like the noise it made for a debut.

The bout took two exchanges.

In the first, Baro brought his blade up, a pale, steady edge along his right forearm, and then simply stood with it hanging low. He let his guard drift a little open on the left side, the stiff side, so that anybody looking at him would see the gap and the stiffness behind it and put the two together.

The Force fighter saw it; Cael watched him see it. The man's whole frame turned toward the gap like a dog turning toward a sound, and he came in hard on the left, with a short driving strike that would have folded Baro over his own bad back.

Baro was not there.

He had not moved fast, which was the strange thing, and Cael made himself see it clearly. He had moved early, and only a little, a single pivot on his right foot that took the stiff side away and brought his blade arm round, and the Force fighter's strike went into the air where the gap had been.

In the same movement the flat of Baro's blade laid itself along the man's ribs, lightly, almost politely. It was not a blow. It was a note left on a table: I could have.

The second exchange was the same. Baro offered the left side again, more openly this time, and the Force fighter hesitated and then took it anyway, because it was so open, and because he could not believe that a man would show the same weakness twice unless it was real.

"Called," said Vell. "Blade Path."

The yard clapped, not loudly. Baro touched fists with the Force fighter and walked to the table and stood there while Vell wrote, with his weight on his right foot and his face doing nothing at all.

He fought again in the third bout, against another Copper Rank 4, Iron Path this time, who had watched the first bout from the rope and had plainly decided not to make the same mistake.

The Iron fighter did not go for the left side. He went for the right, the good side, where Baro had shown nothing. He went patiently and carefully, giving the gap on the left a wide and sensible berth, and in the third exchange Baro let his right foot slide, as if the packed dirt had given under it. For one heartbeat his right side was as open as a door.

The Iron fighter took the door.

And Baro, whose left side had been the bait all along and was still the bait, turned on the bad back as if there were nothing wrong with it at all, and put the flat of his blade across the man's chest, and that was that.

Cael sat on the barrel with the Log open on his knee and found he had not written anything since the first exchange.

"He beat two Copper Rank 4s in an afternoon, and they never touched him."

"He does it most weeks." Lira was watching Baro walk back to the wall. "People say the trick is the left side. It isn't. The trick is that every opening he gives you is one he's put there. If you can see it, he wants you to see it." She was quiet a moment. "You remember Renn's second exchange? After the sweep? When I said you almost had him?"

"Yes."

"Baro would have had you." She said it without any weight at all. "If that had been Baro, crouched and twisted with his hips open, and you'd stepped in, he'd have been somewhere else before your hand got there, and you'd have been on the ground wondering how. Renn was really open. Baro never is."

Cael thought about that. "Then how do you tell? Between a real one and bait?"

"You fight a great many people, and you get it wrong a great many times, and after a while you get it wrong less." She slid off the barrel. "That's the only way I know. If you find a quicker one, tell me."

He wrote it in the Log that evening, as entry three.

3. Baro. Unrated, Blade Path. Watched, two bouts. Old injury, low left back, carried stiff.

Claim: every opening he shows is bait. Evidence: four exchanges, two opponents, the left side offered three times and the right foot once; every one taken; every one empty. Ruling: until I can tell bait from a real opening, take only the openings I make myself. Take nothing I'm given.

He looked hard at that ruling, because it meant that against anybody good, for a long while yet, he would be taking nothing at all. He left it in. It was what he had seen.

"Shield," said Lira the next morning, sitting on the low wall at the side of the yard with the bread. "You've seen one?"

"The gate guard on Merchant Row, in Denvash. He never used it. It was on his badge."

"Then you haven't seen one." She tore her roll in half. "At Copper it isn't much to look at. The air goes thick in front of the forearm, about a hand off the skin. You can see it if you know where to look, a sort of shine, like looking through the side of a bucket of water. It's about so big." She held her hands apart, a little wider than her shoulders. "It goes where her arm goes. It doesn't move on its own and it isn't a thing she holds. It's more like the arm's got longer and flatter and harder, all at once."

"What does it do when you hit it?"

"Nothing. That's what it does. You hit it and you stop." Lira ate half of her half. "Hitting it is like hitting a door somebody's leaning on from the other side. Brenna knows that. So she doesn't block with it, exactly. She walks it at you. She puts it in your face and keeps walking, and hits you with the edge when you run out of room, and then walks some more."

"Does it cost her anything? Holding it up?"

"Breath, mostly. Shield's like Joren's stance, the way you told me about it." He had told her about Joren on the second morning, and the heel, and she had laughed until she had to sit down. "It's on, and holding it isn't free. But Brenna's strong, and she's stubborn, and she's never once in her life let it down in a bout until the bout was over."

"Never?"

"Not once." Lira finished the bread. "She doesn't reset. That's the thing about her. Most people come back to a guard between strikes. Even Renn does, a bit, between the probes and the real one. Brenna doesn't. She hits you and steps into the next one and hits you again, and she never comes back to where she started, because with that thing up she doesn't think she needs to."

"Then when does it come down?"

Lira looked at him sideways with the narrow smile she kept for the right question when she did not intend to answer it.

"That's your homework."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On Thursday night the yard was full, and Marrow was working the rope.

Cael did not watch the first two bouts. He sat on the barrel at the corner, on the shaded side, and watched Brenna.

She was standing by the water bucket with two other women, both bigger than her, talking with her hands in short chopping movements. He could not hear the words over the crowd and did not need to, because every few sentences she chopped the air with the edge of her left hand, low and flat, as a woman might bring a cleaver down on a block. Her friends nodded and one of them laughed, but Brenna did not.

She was about twenty, square-built, with cropped fair hair and a face that went red easily, and it was red now, though she had not done anything yet but talk.

She's still fighting Dessa, he thought. She's been fighting Dessa for a fortnight, and Dessa isn't here.

Marrow came past the barrel. Cael read the slate without moving his head. Brenna, and a short price. Unrated, and a long one. Underneath, on its own line, Over-under: two exchanges.

"He's moved your line," said Lira quietly, beside him.

"It was one, last week."

"It was one for Renn because you were nobody. It's two for Brenna because you lasted four against somebody better." She did not look at him. "That's the closest thing to a rating you've got right now, that number. It isn't Vell's. It's what a few hundred people with money think, and Marrow's shaved it. But it moved."

He looked at the number on the slate. It was only chalk, and Marrow would wipe it off with his sleeve in a minute and write something else, but it was the first figure in Ardenmere that had changed because of something he had done.

"Third bout," said Vell.

He stepped over the rope.

Brenna was already on her mark. She did not roll her shoulders or stretch or look at the crowd; she stood with her left arm up and bent in front of her body and her right fist cocked at her hip. She looked at Cael with an expression of great impatience, as though he were a queue she had been made to wait in.

"Brenna," said Vell. "Copper Rank 2, Shield Path. Against unrated. Vouched." The small pause. "Begin when you're ready."

Brenna was ready before Vell had finished the word.

The air in front of her left forearm thickened. He saw it happen. It was exactly as Lira had said, a shine in the lamplight, a little wider than her shoulders, standing a hand's breadth off her arm like the side of a bucket of water stood on end. Through it her face wobbled slightly, like a face seen through old window glass. Then she came at him.

She did not amble, as Renn had. She did not probe. She walked the shield straight at his face and kept walking, and the first exchange was over almost before he understood that it had begun.

He gave ground. He had decided to give ground, sitting on the barrel, and it was a good thing he had decided, because there was no time to decide anything now.

He went back along the curve of the groove, left, and she followed. She swung the edge of the shield at him, flat and low, the same chopping movement she had made with her hand by the water bucket. He got his right forearm up and caught it on the outside, as Lira had taught him.

It was like catching a falling door. The blow went through his forearm into his shoulder and through his shoulder into his ribs, and the ribs, which had not quite finished with Renn, told him about it at length. He reset, badly, and did not try to send. There was nothing to send. The shield was not a strike that could be turned away. It was a wall that was walking.

He went back three more steps. She came three more steps. And then he was at the edge of the circle with the groove under his heel, and she brought her right fist round the outside of the shield toward his ear, and he ducked under it and slipped sideways along the groove, and she turned to follow without ever once bringing the shield back in toward her body.

At the rope somebody said "Rabbit," and somebody laughed.

Brenna stepped back to her mark. Cael went to his. His forearm was ringing and he had learned nothing at all, except that Lira had been right about the door.

Fine, he thought. The first exchange is a handshake. You find out their distance.

In the second exchange, he watched her feet.

She came in the same way, straight, with the shield up and walking, and he went back the same way, along the curve.

But he was not looking at the shield now. He was looking under it, at her boots on the packed dirt, and he saw that she stepped into every strike off the same foot. Left foot forward, shield forward, chop. Left foot forward, shield forward, chop. She hit his forearm with the edge, and the jolt went through him again, and as it landed her right foot came up off the ground to bring her into the next one.

And the shield dipped.

It was not much. A hand's breadth, perhaps less. For the space of half a beat, while she was stepping through, the bottom edge of the shine sank toward her hip, as if the arm under it had relaxed for a moment to let her body catch up. Then the foot came down and the shield came back up and she chopped at him again.

He went back. He watched for it. He saw it again. Strike lands, she steps through, the shield dips. Strike lands, step, dip.

She doesn't reset, he thought. She doesn't come back to a guard. But she has to move her feet. And when she moves her feet, the arm lets down a little, because it's tired of being up, and she doesn't know.

He did not do anything with it. He went back along the groove, and let her walk him round half the circle, and got out from under her right fist twice, and at the end of the exchange he had a second bruise coming up on his forearm beside the first, and Brenna's face was redder than it had been at the start.

At the table, Vell's pen moved.

In the third exchange he gave her nothing at all.

He went back. He went sideways. He let the shield come and caught it and gave ground, and let it come again. He did not try to touch her or to get round it. He watched the dip, and counted it. Four times in that exchange it dipped, always on the same step, always for the same half-beat.

And he watched something else begin.

Brenna was breathing differently. She had been breathing hard since the first exchange, because walking a shield at somebody was work, but now there was a sound at the top of each breath, a short hard huff through her nose that came just before she stepped. It was louder every time.

Her face had gone from red to a darker red, and her mouth had set in a line, and halfway through the exchange she said something through her teeth. He did not catch it the first time. He caught it the second time.

"Stand."

He did not stand. He went back along the curve.

"Stand and fight."

At the rope, the noise had changed. There was laughter in it still, but there was something else now, an edge of real interest, the sound of people who had come for a quick finish and were beginning to wonder whether they would get one. Somewhere on the sunny side a man shouted "Hit him, Brenna," as if she had not been trying, and she heard it, and her face went darker still.

Vell called the end of the exchange. Brenna went back to her mark breathing like a bellows. She did not look at the rope. She looked at Cael, and her look had stopped being impatient.

The fourth exchange told him the thing he had come for.

Brenna came off her mark faster than before, and harder, and her first chop was so big that he saw it coming from her shoulder long before it reached him, and stepped away from it with room to spare. The huff came before the second one. He heard it, and moved, and the second chop missed him too. The third was the same.

They were not faster. That was what he saw, with a kind of cold surprise. Her strikes had grown bigger and louder, but they had not grown faster. They had grown slower, because she was putting everything into them, and everything took time to gather.

Frustration's a tell, he thought. It's the loudest one there is. It's louder than the heel, louder than the dip. She's telling the whole yard what she's going to do, a full breath before she does it.

He did not know whether that was in Lira's homework. He thought probably it was not. He thought it was something he had found on his own, in the dirt, with his forearm aching, and he held on to it as if somebody might take it off him.

He also thought, as he went back along the curve for what must have been the fortieth time that night, that his ribs had begun to hurt in a new way. It was not the bright, exact hurt of a fresh blow. It was a tiredness under the bruise, as if the bruise itself were getting heavy. Giving ground was not free either. He had been paying for every step.

Vell called the end of the fourth.

He stood on his mark and looked across at Brenna, and Brenna looked back, and he decided.

He had watched for four exchanges. He had found the dip and counted it. He had found the huff, and he knew what it meant.

If he went on giving ground he would go on learning nothing new. Sooner or later his ribs would give out before her breath did, and he would end up on his back having never once found out whether the dip was a real opening or only a thing he had seen.

Take only the openings I make myself, the Log said. He had written it two nights ago. But he had not made this one. He had found it. He did not know which column that belonged in.

"Begin," said Vell.

Brenna came. The shield came. He caught the first chop on his forearm, deliberately this time, and held his ground under it for the first time all night, and felt it go through his shoulder and his ribs and down into his heels. He heard the huff. Her right foot came up to step into the next one.

The shield dipped.

He went in.

He went in low and to his left, under the sinking edge of the shine and past it, toward her right side, where there was nothing but a cocked fist and an open shirt. He was inside the shield's reach. For half a beat he was exactly where he had meant to be, and he put his hand out to touch her, anywhere, a finger on her sleeve.
