And Brenna, who was twice his weight and had been walking a door at people for years, simply turned.

She did not bring the shield back up. She did not need to. She turned her whole body toward him on the foot she had just set down, and the edge of the shine came round with her like a gate swinging shut. It took him across the chest. It did not hit him so much as collect him. It lifted him off the one foot he had left on the ground, and walked him backward two steps, three, and then there was the groove under his heel and nothing under the other one.

He went down flat on his back across the edge of the circle, with the thick bright air of the shield standing over his chest a hand's breadth from his shirt, and Brenna's red face behind it, and her right fist cocked.

She did not throw it.

"Called," said Vell. "Shield Path."

Brenna stood over him a moment longer. Then the shine went out of the air, all at once, like a breath let go. She was breathing so hard her shoulders went up and down with it. She looked down at him with an expression he could not read at first, and then could.

It was not triumph. It was relief, and something else underneath the relief that looked a great deal like anger at herself.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

He reported to the table, as you did, win or lose.

Vell was writing. It took longer than two lines. It took about as long as the long entry had taken on the night of Renn, and once, without lifting her head, she raised her eyes to him and then lowered them again.

"Five," she said, when she had blotted it.

That was all she said. It was a number for the record, and he understood from the way she said it that she had been counting too.

Brenna was at the water bucket when he went past. She had a cup in her hand and had not drunk from it. She looked at him over the rim.

"You ran me round for four exchanges."

"Yes."

"On purpose."

"Yes."

She drank half the cup in one swallow and looked at him again over it. Her face was still red, though it had begun to go back toward its ordinary colour, and he could see her working out whether to be angry and deciding something else.

"You found the step. In the fifth. You came in on the step."

He did not say anything, because he did not know whether he was supposed to.

"Dessa found it in the third." She put the cup back on the bucket's edge with a click. "Took her two exchanges. Took you four." She looked at him for a moment longer, a hard, considering look, and then something in her square face eased, not much. "Next time stand and fight. It's dull, the running."

"Next time I'll have a better reason to stand."

Brenna snorted. It was nearly a laugh. She went off toward the gate with her friends, and he heard one of them say something, and Brenna said, quite loudly, "He's fourteen," as if that answered whatever the question had been.

Lira found him at the rope and walked him out through the gate and down the lane without saying anything for two streets, and he could feel her saving it.

"Well?"

"You went in on the dip."

"You saw it."

"I've fought her twice. It took me the second time to find it, and when I went in on it she did exactly what she did to you." She was quiet for a few steps. "The dip's real. It's not bait. She doesn't know she does it. But you can't go in on it unless you're quick enough to be through before she turns, or heavy enough that she can't turn you. You were neither."

"I know."

"I know you know." She looked at him sideways in the dark. "That wasn't the homework, though."

"What was the homework?"

"Whether you'd find it. Not whether you could use it. Nobody uses it the first time. I wanted to know if you'd see it." She looked ahead again. "You saw it in the second exchange. I watched your eyes go down."

He did not answer that, because he was thinking about Brenna's breath, the huff at the top of it, getting louder.

"She got angry."

"She always gets angry. That's why she lost to Dessa."

"It made her slower. Not faster. Slower. Everything got bigger and slower and louder, and I could hear it coming." He tried to put it into words that would hold. "It was a better tell than any of the others. It was the whole of her telling me."

Lira walked a little way without speaking.

"Yes," she said at last, in the voice she used for things she had not expected him to know yet. "That's true. That's one of the truest things there is in that yard. And almost nobody learns it from the losing side."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

That night, at the end of the cot, with the brothers asleep and the wheezing man whistling and Yeni's lamp turned low, he finished entry two.

2. Brenna. Copper R2, Shield Path. Lost, called, fifth exchange.

Claim: she never resets. Evidence: five exchanges; not once came back to a guard. Ruling: don't wait for her to reset. She won't.

Claim: the shield dips on the step through, half a beat, every time. Evidence: counted four in the third exchange alone; went in on it in the fifth and it was there. Ruling: the opening is real. I am not quick enough or heavy enough to use it yet. Not yet is a ruling.

Claim: frustration makes her bigger, slower and louder. Evidence: third and fourth exchanges; the breath before each strike; the strikes themselves got slower. Ruling: if somebody gets angry, they will tell me everything. Let them.

He read it through. Then he closed the front of the book, because the front was finished for the day, and opened it from the back.

He sat over the page with the pencil. It was harder to write in the back, where there were no columns to hold the words up.

Four exchanges I let her think I was running. I wasn't running. I was watching. But she didn't know that, and she got angry because of it, and that was how I learned the thing about anger.

I don't know whether that's a trick or a lie. It felt like both.

He stopped. He thought about the fifth exchange, and the moment he had decided, and the hot, tight feeling in his chest when he had made up his mind to stand under the shield and go in. He had been angry too. Not at Brenna. At the running. At being, every single time, the boy who went backward.

I think I was angry in the fifth, he wrote. I think that's why I went in. I'm not sure it was a decision. I'm not sure it wasn't her tell and mine at the same time.

Find out what mine sounds like.

He closed the book and put it under his pillow and lay on his back, feeling his forearm ache, and his ribs, and the new bruise across his chest where the edge of the shield had collected him. Five exchanges, one more than Renn.

He had lost again, and he wrote that down too, in his head, where the Log could not see it, and it weighed less than he had expected it to, and he did not yet know whether that was good.

Chapter 16 — The Air Before the Heat

[Focused, analytical narration; make every lesson and useful loss legible]

Lira caught him trying the skip on the second morning after Brenna.

He had been practising it at night, and he had not meant to tell anybody or to be caught. He was caught anyway, because she came round the corner of the public house earlier than usual and found him alone at the post in the grey half of the yard, going from catch to send with no middle, over and over, with his face screwed up.

She stood by the gate and watched him do it four times before she said, "Stop."

He stopped.

"Do it again. Slowly. I'll come in."

She came in at the cup-reaching speed. He caught her strike on the outside of his forearm and went straight on to the send without resetting, the whole thing in one movement, as he had seen her do it on the second day at the board, and her strike went away past his shoulder. Then her other hand came round from nowhere and rested, very gently, on the side of his neck.

"That's where you are. You caught it, and it moved you, and you didn't come back, and now your weight's on your left foot with nothing behind it. You sent my right hand away, and my left hand's come in through the door you left open." She took the hand away. "That's not a skip. That's the hole I told you about."

"It worked for you."

"It works for me because I know where my weight goes when I catch, without looking, and I've known it for years." She stepped back. "You've known it a week. Again. The long way."

He did it the long way, catch, reset, send, and she came in again and again. The third time he let his arm go round in the send without coming properly back to centre first, and her left hand was on his neck again before he knew he had done it.

"Again."

He did not do it a fourth time. He felt the moment in the catch when his weight went across, and he let the reset bring it home before he sent, and when her left hand came in he had a forearm in its way.

They went on until the shadow left the post. He made the hole twice more, early on, and then never again, because he had found the place where it happened. It was not in the send at all but at the very end of the catch, when the strike had pushed his arm across and he wanted to be finished with it.

Once he knew the place, it was a matter of not wanting to be finished.

She noticed, and he saw her notice, but she said nothing until they had stopped and she had sat down on the low wall at the side of the yard with the bread, and he had sat beside her, and she had eaten half her half.

"You're not a natural."

He waited.

"I'm saying it plainly, because if I said you were one you'd believe me, and it would be a lie, and I won't tell lies to anybody I train." She brushed a crumb off her knee. "A natural gets it right and couldn't tell you how. You get it wrong. You get it wrong the first time, every time, and then you see exactly why it was wrong, and then you don't do it again." She looked at him sideways. "Ever. I've been watching for it. I've made the same mistake a hundred times in my life. You make a mistake once and then it's gone, as though you've crossed it out."

"Is that worse than being a natural?"

"It's better," she said, after a moment. "Naturals coast. They go a long way on whatever they were born with, and then one day it runs out, and they're stuck there, because nobody ever made them learn how anything is put together." She looked at the post, where the sun had just reached the canvas. "You're the most efficient learner I've ever stood across from. Whatever you end up being, you'll have built it yourself, and you'll know where every piece of it came from. I'd take that over a natural every time."

He did not answer at once, because he was trying to find somewhere to put it.

"Nobody's ever said that. About the classification. That it might be a thing you build, and not a thing that happens to you."

"I wasn't talking about the classification." She stood up and held a hand out to pull him off the wall. "I was talking about you. They're not the same." She hauled him up, carefully, on his good side. "Up. We're not finished."

He wrote it in the back of the Log that night, after the front was finished, and it was the first line in the back that was not a worry.

Lira says I build. She says it's better than being born with it. I think she might be right, and I think I want her to be right more than I can afford to, so I'm writing it here and not in the columns.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The mender paid him on the third afternoon.

It was not much, a handful of small coins pushed across the bench without comment. It paid for two afternoons of sorting a tea chest full of hinges, hasps and screws into trays by size and kind, and for sweeping, and truing the spoke of a child's wheel and the arm of a pair of spectacles.

Cael counted it on the walk back along the river and found that it would not pay a week at Torvin's, though it would pay three days of one.

Slows the pouch, he wrote, in the back of the old notebook, under the figure. Doesn't stop it.

In the market, on the way home, a man at the fish stall looked up from his board as Cael went past.

He was the bearded cousin, the one who knew about fish. Cael had never bought anything from him, and had spoken to him only once, to ask what a long silver fish was called, after which the man had told him and gone back to his knife.

Now he looked up from the board with the knife in his hand, caught Cael's eye and nodded, a small downward tip of the chin of the kind men in Denvash gave each other across the depot yard, and then went back to his fish.

Cael walked on down the row with the coins in his pocket and his forearm aching, and for half a street he did not understand what had happened. Then he did.

The fish man had been at the rope, or somebody who bought from the fish man had been at the rope and had told him, and now a man Cael had never spoken to knew who he was and had decided that this was worth a nod.

He did not know what to do with that, and told himself it was only a nod. He put it in the Log that night anyway, in the front, because it was a fact, though he could not think what column it went in; in the end he wrote it in the margin with no column at all.

Fish man, bearded. Nodded. I've never spoken to him.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

The letter came on the nineteenth day.

He knew it was the nineteenth because he had been counting. The letter to Hesk had gone in the west bag on the fifth day, and the clerk had said about a week, and Hesk would have needed a day or two or three to write back, and then it would be another week coming.

He had worked out on the road that the earliest a letter could come was about the nineteenth, and the latest was about whenever Hesk decided, and he had tried very hard not to think about the second figure.

Yeni had it. She was sitting on her cot with her sewing kit open beside her when he came up the stairs, and she held it out without looking up from her needle.

It was folded and sealed with a dab of plain wax, and on the outside it said Cael, care of Torvin's, ROOMS (the O leans), Unranked District, Ardenmere, in Hesk's square hand. Below that, in another hand, somebody had written Torvin's — runner.

"Came at noon. West bag."

"Thank you."

"Mm." The needle went in and out. "People who get letters back stay longer still."

He sat on his cot by the window and turned the letter over twice before he opened it, because he could not quite believe it was not going to say something terrible. Then he broke the wax.

It was two sheets, written on both sides, and the first lines were older than the rest; he could tell from the ink, which was a shade paler, and from the hand, which had been steadier and slower when it began.

Cael,

Ressa had two loaves wrapped the morning after. She put one back. She wouldn't take money for the one she put in your bag; she says it was yours. I told her you'd have eaten it on a wall somewhere about the first milestone. Tell me if I was right.

He had eaten it on a wall. It had been the second wall, not the first milestone, but it had been a wall, and he sat on the cot and laughed once, quietly, and Yeni did not look up.

Joren came to the workshop door with your note. He's read it standing up, flat-footed, the whole way through, and he wanted you told. He says he's working on it. He wasn't angry with you. He wanted you to know that most of all.

I went on Tuesday. Garrik's kept your washer in the arm and he says he isn't going to take it out. He wanted you told that too. The woman in the knitted hat says they won't know what they've got in Ardenmere. I'm inclined to agree with her.

He read that paragraph twice. He could see the back room, the folding chairs and the sheet on its frame, and Garrik threading with his back to the room, though he could not see Garrik's face, and he thought that was probably how Garrik would have wanted it.

The next part was in the same pale ink, and it was about the guild.

The guild has opened a review of my standing, because of the notice. They want a written account of who lives here, and I've sent it. It's routine, they say, and slow, and it will most likely come to nothing. I'll tell you how it goes, as it goes. I'm telling you now because you asked me to tell you things as they come, and I said I would, and I'm finding out that's harder to keep than I expected. Don't worry about it. I know you will. Worry about it a little, then, and then stop.

He stopped reading.

He sat with the sheet on his knee and looked at the window, at the grey square of it with the rooftops in it and a line of somebody's washing, and did exactly what Hesk had told him he would do: he worried.

He worried about the guild letter with its polite paragraphs, and the workshop, and the drawer marked Springs, do not use with a bent bracket's space in it, and the canal gauges and the survey levels and the clock inside the walking stick. He worried that the review would not come to nothing. He worried that it would, slowly, over a year, while Hesk sat in the workshop waiting for it.

Then he made himself look at the other thing, which was harder.

Hesk had told him, and had not had to. He could have written about bread and washers and Joren's heels and left the guild out, and Cael would never have known until it was over, one way or the other.

Instead Hesk had sat at the kitchen table, Cael could see it, with the pen over the paper and the lamp lit, and had decided to put it in, because Cael had stood in a workshop and asked him to.

As they come, Cael had said. Not managed.

And in the letter he had written at the waystation, sitting at the end of a table with a stew he had not eaten yet, he had left out a turnip cart.

He read on. The ink went darker and the hand quicker, because this part had been written later, after his own letter had come.

Your letter came on the twelfth day, so the clerk was right about the week and I'm writing back the same evening. I read it at the table. I read the part about the fifth entry three times, which seems to be the family number.

I'm glad you rode the last miles. The carter sounds a decent man, and a Stone Path with turnips is a fine thing to have met on your first day. I'm glad of the waystation woman's coins and of the bread you didn't eat. I'm glad you're tired and your legs hurt and you're all right.

Write and tell me what Ardenmere is like. Not what the reference room said. What it's like. Who you've met. What you're doing with your days. Whether you've found anything you're good at that nobody there knew about. I'll be here.

— H.

He folded the letter along its creases and held it.

Whether you've found anything you're good at that nobody there knew about.

He thought about the circuit, about Vell's book with no name in it and Marrow's slate and Brenna's shield coming round like a gate, and about the third exchange against Renn, lying in its corner with the cart.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He wrote back that night, at the kitchen table, after the others had gone up.

He told Hesk about Torvin's and the O, and Yeni, and the nut boy and the sister who flicked his ear, and the board at the crossroads, and Lira, and how she had stood behind him for eleven minutes. He told him about the circuit without dressing it up or making it smaller.

He wrote that it was a ladder that did not ask to see a card, and that he had put himself on the bottom rung of it. He had lost twice now, he wrote, to a Blade Path man and to a Shield Path woman, and each time he had lasted longer than the time before.

I'm not trying to win yet, he wrote. I'm trying to learn how people move. You taught me where to look. I'm looking.

He told him about the shoulder and the ribs, because Hesk would want the truth about those and because they were healing, and about the mender and the spice balance and the two afternoons, and the fish man's nod.

He did not tell him about the third exchange.

He did not decide that quickly, and he made himself say the reasons one at a time in his head, the way you call a load figure.

It would be a week getting there, and Hesk would read it at the kitchen table with nothing he could do about it except sit with it for another week, waiting for the next letter. And there was nothing to tell, because he did not know what had happened; he had a claim and no evidence and no ruling.

If he wrote it, he would be writing a guess in the same hand as the facts, and Hesk would read it as a fact, because it came from Cael.

All of that was true. He knew, while he was saying it, that it was also exactly what Hesk had told himself for years.

Don't make a thing real before it is.

He wrote one more line instead, at the bottom, and he meant it.

Thank you for telling me about the guild. I know it was harder to put in than to leave out. I'll worry about it a little, and then stop.

Then he signed it, and folded it, and put it inside the leather book to keep it flat, and went up to bed with the feeling of a man who has paid a debt in one currency and taken on another in a different one.

Amrit Sole was the next night's third bout. Vell had told him so on the morning after Brenna, over the ledger. Copper Rank 4, Ember Path. He won't chase you round the circle. He won't need to.

He was older than Brenna, older than Renn, a heavy-shouldered man somewhere near forty with a shaved head and a short grey beard, and forearms that were shiny and hairless in patches, like a baker's after years of reaching into ovens.

He sat on an upturned crate by the wall through the first two bouts and drank water and spoke to nobody. When a boy tripped over his outstretched boots on the way to the pie tray, he caught the boy by the collar before he fell, set him on his feet, and gave him back the coin he had dropped.

"He cooks," said Lira, beside him on the barrel. "At the eating house by the lower bridge. Has done for years. He fights twice a month because he says it's restful."

"Restful."

"He says nobody shouts at him in the circle."

On Marrow's slate, the line had moved again. Over-under: three exchanges.

"He's an honest fighter. He doesn't feint much. He doesn't need to. But I'll tell you one thing, because you'll find it out in about four seconds anyway." She did not look at him. "He doesn't miss with the heat by much. And at Copper, Ember isn't fire, mostly. It's the feeling of standing too near an open oven. Until it's not."

"Third bout," said Vell.

Amrit stood up from his crate as if he had been called to a table, and stepped over the rope, and nodded to Cael across the circle with grave courtesy, and set his feet.

"Amrit Sole. Copper Rank 4, Ember Path. Against unrated. Vouched." The pause. "Begin when you're ready."

Amrit raised his hands. He held them loose and open in front of his chest, the palms turned a little toward Cael, as if he were warming them at a fire.

For a moment nothing happened.

Then the air in front of his hands began to move.

It was very slight, like the air above a road at midday or above the top of a stove when the iron has just begun to tick. The lamplight behind his hands wavered and the rope behind him seemed to ripple, though the rope was perfectly still. Cael saw it, and wondered what it was, and was still wondering when Amrit stepped in and opened his hands.

Heat came out of them.

It was not flame; Lira had been right. It was the breath of an oven with its door flung open, a wall of dry, hard heat that struck his face and his chest and his raised forearm all at once. It drove the air out of his mouth and made his eyes water so hard that for a moment he could not see.

He went back three steps without deciding to, and when his eyes cleared there was a smell of singed wool, and he looked down and saw that the cuff of his right sleeve had gone brown at the edge.

Amrit had not followed him. He was standing in the middle of the circle with his hands lowered, waiting, with the patience of a man who knew how long a loaf took.

The first exchange was over. It had taught him one thing, which he had nearly missed and then had not: the air had moved before the heat came. Not much before. Half a beat.

He went back to his mark and watched Amrit's hands.

In the second exchange he moved on the shimmer.

Amrit came in slowly, with his hands up and open, and Cael watched the air in front of them, and the moment it began to waver he went sideways, left, along the groove. The heat came out of Amrit's palms into the place where he had been standing. It brushed his right cheek and his ear in passing, hot and dry, and did no more than that.

Amrit turned to face him. The shimmer came again. Cael went again, right this time, and again the heat went past him.

Without the heat, Amrit's hands were only hands. They were big, and they were quick enough, but they were a cook's hands and not a fighter's, and when he swung a plain fist at Cael's shoulder it came round so wide that Cael could have walked under it. He did.

He came out on the far side of Amrit with his heart going hard and a grin trying to get onto his face that he did not let onto it.

At the table, Vell had stopped writing. She sat with the pen lifted above the page and simply watched, which he had not seen her do before.

In the third exchange he read the shimmer every time, and he began to feel something he had not felt in the circle before, which was that he knew what was going to happen.

The air moved. He went. The heat came where he had been. The air moved. He went. He was not trying to touch Amrit, any more than he had tried to touch Brenna. He was only trying to be somewhere else when the heat came, and he was managing it, exchange after exchange, and every time he managed it the knowing got a little surer and a little warmer.

That should have warned him. That was the line he put in the back of the Log, later. It did not warn him at the time.

He was watching Amrit's hands. He was watching nothing else. And across the circle Amrit had begun to watch him watching.

Cael saw it, at the very end of the third exchange, and did not understand what he was seeing. Amrit's eyes went to Cael's eyes, and followed them down to his own hands, and came back up. It was quick, and grave, and almost kind. It was the look of a cook who has noticed that the boy at the back door is not watching the pot but the hand that lifts the lid.

In the fourth exchange the air in front of Amrit's hands began to waver, and Cael went sideways, left, along the groove, and nothing came out of Amrit's hands at all.

The heat was not there. The shimmer was there, wobbling the lamplight, as clear as it had been every time before, but Amrit was holding it, keeping it in his palms like a breath held in the chest, and Cael had already gone. He was committed to the step, his weight going left, his eyes on the shimmer still.

And Amrit, who had not moved his feet at all, simply stepped after him and swung a plain closed fist into the meat of his right arm above the elbow.

It was not a heat strike, only a fist, a cook's fist with twenty years of lifting stockpots behind it, and it turned Cael half round and nearly put him down.

He stayed up. He stood on the edge of the groove with his right arm gone dead from the shoulder to the fingers, and looked at Amrit, and Amrit looked back at him, and there was nothing in Amrit's face but the grave courtesy he had had from the start.

He showed me the shimmer, Cael thought. He showed it to me on purpose. Like Baro's left side. He's put it there for me to see.

Vell called the end of the exchange. He went back to his mark with his right arm hanging and the feeling coming back into it in hot pins.

In the fifth exchange he tried to tell them apart.

He watched the shimmer and he watched Amrit's breath, because Brenna had taught him that the breath could talk. When the shimmer came the first time, Amrit's chest stopped moving. His shoulders went still, as a man's do when he braces to lift something. Cael went, and the heat came, and passed him.

The second time the shimmer came, Amrit was breathing. His chest went up and down under his shirt. Cael held. He held his ground for the length of a heartbeat, against everything his feet wanted, and the heat did not come, and Amrit's plain fist came instead, and he slipped it.

The third time, he could not tell.

The shimmer came and he looked at Amrit's chest and he could not see it moving or not moving. The lamp was behind Amrit now, and his shirt was dark, and Cael had a half-heartbeat to choose. He chose wrong. He held, and the heat came, full, from a pace away, and he got his left forearm up in front of his face, the scraped one, and the heat struck it like the side of a kettle.

He did not cry out. He went back four steps with his teeth shut and his forearm held away from his body as if it belonged to somebody else, and the sixth exchange came, and he knew before it began that it was going to be the last one.

He knew it with great clearness. He knew it the way he knew the bracket would fail when the needle swung.

Amrit came in, unhurried. He had seen the forearm. He was not going to chase it, and he was not going to spare it either; that was not how this yard worked.

He was simply going to walk Cael to the edge of the circle, where there was nowhere left to step, and open his hands from a pace away. Cael had been watching him do it for five exchanges. He could see the whole of it before it happened: the groove at his heel, the shimmer, no room left to the left or to the right, the full open heat at a distance from which there was no getting the arm up in time.

He would be burned. Not badly, perhaps. Badly enough. He would be burned in front of sixty people on Lira's vouch, and he would go down into the groove, and he would learn nothing from it at all that he did not already know.

The groove was at his heel.

The shimmer began.

He raised his hand.

He held it up, open, the palm toward Vell, the way the grey-templed Stone woman had held hers up in the second bout on his first afternoon in this yard. He held it there, breathing hard, with the heel of his boot on the groove.

Amrit stopped. The shimmer in front of his hands wavered once and went out, like a stove door closing.

"Called," said Vell. "Conceded. Ember Path."

The yard did not applaud him as it had applauded the Stone woman, and he had not expected it to. But there was some clapping here and there along the rope, not loud and mostly from the shaded side. One of the people clapping was a girl on a barrel by the drain who did not stop until he had walked all the way to the table.

Vell wrote a good deal, then blotted it and looked up at him, and her eyes went to his forearm, which had come up red and shiny from the wrist halfway to the elbow, over the old scrape, and then back to his face.

"Six," she said. Then, after a moment, in exactly the same voice: "That was the right breath. A breath later and you'd have been at a healer's in the morning."

"I know."

Amrit was waiting at the water bucket. He had a clean cloth in his hand, wet, and he held it out without a word. Cael took it and laid it over his forearm, and the cold went into the burn with a feeling so close to pain that for a moment he could not tell which it was.

"Keep it wet." His voice was low and unhurried and surprisingly gentle. "A long time. Longer than you'd think. Don't break the blister if one comes up; let it go down by itself." He looked at the arm. "It'll be red for a week and it'll itch for two. It won't mark you." He picked up his own cup and drank and set it down. "You were watching my breath, in the fifth."

"Yes."

"It was a good thing to watch." Amrit nodded, as if he had tasted something and found it nearly done. "Not good enough yet. But good." Then he went off through the gate into the dark, toward the lower bridge and the eating house, and did not look back.

Lira did not walk him home that night. She had a bout of her own to see across the district. She only came down off the barrel long enough to wet the cloth again at the pump by the gate and lay it back over his arm with more care than she would have admitted to.

"The right people clapped," she said. "And Vell said the right breath. I've never heard her say that to anybody." Then she was gone, and he walked back to Torvin's alone, with his arm held out from his side and something in his chest that was not a bruise gone warm and tight in a way he did not trust.

4. Amrit Sole. Copper R4, Ember Path. Conceded, sixth exchange.

Claim: the air in front of his hands moves half a beat before the heat. Evidence: every heat strike, six exchanges. Ruling: move on the shimmer. Not yet known whether this is every Ember Path or only him. Need more Ember to rule.

Claim: he can make the shimmer without letting the heat go. Evidence: fourth exchange; paid for with the right arm. Ruling: the shimmer is not the heat. It is the start of the heat, and the start can be held.

Claim: when the heat is real, his breath stops first. Evidence: fifth exchange, two out of three. Third one I couldn't see. Ruling: two out of three is not a ruling. Watch more.

Claim: when I was sure, I stopped watching anything but his hands. Evidence: third exchange. He saw me do it. Ruling: being sure is a tell.

He looked at the last one. Then he closed the front of the book and turned it over and opened the back.

I chose to lose tonight.

Renn, Brenna, they put me down. Tonight I looked at what was going to happen and said no, not that, and put my hand up. It was the first thing I've done in that circle that was completely mine. Not a read. Not the thing in the corner. Not running. I looked at it and I decided.

It's a strange thing to be proud of, a hand up.

Six exchanges. Four, five, six. Each one longer.

He put the pencil down. Yeni was still sewing by her lamp, and she looked across at him once, at the wet cloth on his arm, and went back to her seam.

"Ember?"

"Ember."

"Cold water. Not butter."

"Everybody keeps telling me that."

"Because everybody's had somebody tell them butter," said Yeni, and bit her thread, and turned the lamp down.

Chapter 17 — About Speed

[Focused, analytical narration; make every lesson and useful loss legible]

"Petra Voss," said Vell, at the table, on the morning after Amrit. "Copper Rank 3, Force Path. Sunday, second bout." She looked at his arm. "That'll be well enough by Sunday. Hers won't be your problem. Hers'll be the speed."

He went from the table to the low wall at the side of the yard, where Lira was sitting with her knees drawn up, waiting for the shadow to reach the post. She had the look of somebody who has been saving a piece of news since the night before and has finally decided she cannot hold it any longer.

"There's a wager on you," she said.

He looked at his forearm. It had come up in a long red patch over the old scrape, shiny and tight, with a blister the size of a thumbnail near the wrist that he was not breaking, because everybody had told him not to. He had slept with it outside the blanket.

"Marrow's always got a wager on me."

"Not Marrow." Her mouth was doing something at one corner that she was plainly trying to stop. "You know the two errand boys who work the east lanes? One's got a red cap. The other one's got a brother in the carters'?"

Everybody had seen them. They ran messages and small parcels from the river up to the yards and down again, in competition with each other, all day, at a dead sprint, shouting abuse at each other across whatever street they happened to be crossing. He had once watched the red-capped one leap a handcart rather than go round it, because the other one was going round it.

"They hate each other. Properly, since they were about six. And now they've got a bet on how many more bouts you'll need before your first win. Red Cap says two. The other one says never." She looked at him. "They've each put half a mark on it, which is more than either of them earns in a day. They told the pie boy, and the pie boy told the woman at the water bucket, and the woman at the water bucket told me."

"Which of them's going to win?"

"Red Cap, I think. He hates the other one more than he loves money, so he picked the opposite of whatever the other one said." She considered. "That's not a good reason to back somebody. But it's not the worst reason anybody's ever backed you."

Cael looked at the post for a moment. "I don't like it."

"I didn't think you would."

"I didn't come here to be talked about."

"You came here to fight in a yard in front of sixty people every week, and you keep lasting longer than anybody thought you would." She said it quite gently. "That's what being talked about is made of. You can't do one without the other. Not here."

He had known that without letting himself know it all the way. Not three weeks ago, standing on the rise above this valley, he had written Show nobody anything and underlined still here, and since then he had walked into a circle three times with a crowd round it.

Now a fish man nodded at him, and two boys he had never spoken to had put a day's wages on him, and somewhere at a water bucket a woman he did not know was telling people what he was.

"In Denvash I was the boy who wrote things down. That was all anybody knew about me. Garrik knew me, and Ressa, and that was a whole street, and it took fourteen years."

"This district watches its fighters the way farmers watch the sky. Nobody loves the fighters. It's that news out of the circuit is worth something, and anything worth something gets passed round. You can't stop it." She let her feet down off the wall. "The only thing you get any say in is what story they tell."

"What story are they telling?"

"Right now? The boy who keeps losing and won't stop coming back, and takes longer to put down every time." She shrugged. "It's a good story. People like it. It's the kind they cheer for when it finally comes good."

"What would be worse?"

Lira did not answer for a moment. She was looking at the post, where the sun had just touched the top of the canvas.

"The boy who's dangerous," she said, "and nobody knows why."

She said it lightly, but with great precision, every word set down in its place, and he understood that she had not made it up just now. She had been carrying it, and he thought he knew which night she had picked it up, and which exchange.

She stood up before he could say anything, and held out a hand. "Come on. One arm today. You can't catch with the burnt one."

He wrote it that night in the front of the Log, because it was a fact to be managed and not a fear to be sat with, and he wanted it to stay that way.

Being watched is information other people get to use. Losing is a story. When I stop losing, it will be a different story, and I need to know which one before it starts.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

In the afternoon of that same day, on the cooper's roof, Lira told him about Petra Voss much as Vell had. She did not draw anything on the tar this time. She sat with her arms round her knees and looked out at the first wall of the Ranked core going up the hill in the haze.

"She's seventeen. She's been in the circuit a year and a half. She's very good and she knows it, and she doesn't talk much, and she hits like a door slamming in a high wind."

"Force."

"Force at Copper isn't strength, not really, not the way people think." Lira held up her hand and made a short, flat push with it at the empty air. "It's more as if everything she hits gets an extra shove at the end, after her hand's already stopped, as though somebody behind you kicked you at the same moment she hit you. You've seen it. You said you saw a plank jump out of somebody's hands on your first day in the lanes."

He had: a woman throwing a short punch at a plank held up by her partner, and the plank leaving his hands as though it had been kicked from behind. He had written Force, or something like it.

"That was her?"

"That's her yard. She trains there every afternoon." Lira glanced at him. "Go and watch her if you like. It won't help."

"Why not?"

"Because she's quicker than you, and watching her won't make you quicker." She said it without any unkindness at all, just as she had said that's not a skip, that's a hole. "Whatever's there, you'll see it. You'll see her lace her boots and know which foot she favours; I'm not worried about your seeing. But you'll see things and not have time to do anything about them. That's what she does to people. She doesn't hide anything. She doesn't have to."

He went and watched her anyway, that afternoon, from the lane outside her gate. She was small, smaller than Lira, wiry and freckled, with her reddish hair in one tight braid down her back, and she was working alone at a sand-bag on a chain, hitting it with short, straight punches that did not look like much.

Every time she hit it, it jumped. It did not swing back and forth as a sack swings when you punch it; it leapt away from her fist on its chain as if somebody much larger had hit it, and hung at the end of its swing for a moment, and came back.

He watched her for an hour and wrote two pages, and on the way back down the lane his hands were not quite steady, and he could not tell whether it was the hour of watching or the thought of Sunday.

The next morning, on the way up to the Cinder House, they passed the gate of the old man's yard. The old man was in his corner in the shade, in the stance that was like nothing else in the lane, and the woman with the shoulder was there too, going through her sequence alone. She reached the fourth position and held it, and her shoulder stayed down, and she went on to the fifth.

The old man's pale eyes came round to Cael as they went by, went to the red forearm, and came back to his face.

"Six," the old man said, and his eyes went back to the wall.

Lira said nothing until they were past the next gate. Then she said, "Four months, and he's never said a number to me either," in a voice that was trying hard to sound offended and not quite managing.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On Sunday the yard was fuller than it had been for Brenna or for Amrit.

He noticed it when he climbed onto the barrel. The rope was two deep on the sunny side and three deep in the shade.

There were faces in the crowd he had begun to know: the fish man with his beard; the two errand boys, standing as far apart from each other as the yard would allow and both glaring; the woman who slept in her boots, with a pie; and, near the gate with her arms folded, not Torvin but Torvin's wife.

He found he did not want to know how many of them had come for the second bout.

On Marrow's slate the line had moved again. Over-under: four exchanges.

And Marrow, for the first time, looked at him.

It was only a glance. Marrow was going along the rope with his chalk and his pleasant voice and his clean hands, taking coins, and as he came level with the barrel his eyes went up from the slate to Cael's face and rested there for the length of a breath. It was a perfectly friendly look, the look a shopkeeper gives a scale that has begun, for no reason anybody can find, to weigh against him.

Then Marrow smiled and went on.

"Don't," said Lira quietly.

"I didn't do anything."

"I know. Keep not doing it."

"Second bout," said Vell.

He stepped over the rope.

Petra was already on her mark, looking not at the crowd or at Vell but at him, steadily, with a calm, narrow interest. She was standing very lightly, with her weight forward on the balls of her feet and her hands up in front of her face, loose. She looked like somebody waiting for a door to open so that she could go through it first.

"Petra Voss. Copper Rank 3, Force Path. Against unrated. Vouched." The pause. "Begin when you're ready."

The first exchange taught him how little he knew.

She came off her mark so fast that he was still deciding which way to go when she arrived. A short straight punch came at his face. He got his right forearm up in time, barely, and caught it on the outside, the way Lira had taught him a hundred times in the grey half of the yard.

The catch held. Then the shove came.

It came a heartbeat after her fist had stopped, out of nowhere, as if somebody behind his arm had put a shoulder into it, and it drove his forearm back into his own face and threw him off his feet. He went back three skidding steps and sat down hard on the packed dirt inside the groove.

He was up again before he had finished thinking about it, which was the one thing he did right in the first exchange. The rope laughed. Petra did not. She was already back on her mark, waiting, with her hands loose in front of her face.

There's no reset, he thought, on his own mark, with his forearm ringing. There's no time for one. You catch it and the shove comes before you've finished catching.

In the second exchange he saw the lean.

It was very small, and he would have missed it if he had not spent an hour in the lane watching her hit a sand-bag on a chain.

Before a punch she meant, a punch she was putting the shove into, her shoulders tipped forward. Not her head. Not her hands. The shoulders, both together, perhaps the width of a finger, as if she were leaning into a wind only she could feel. Her jabs did not have it. Her feints did not have it. Only the ones she meant.

He saw it for the first time halfway through the second exchange. He saw the shoulders tip, and he knew what was coming, and he started to move.

The punch hit him anyway.

It caught him on the left shoulder, the Renn shoulder, because he had moved, and moving had taken his face out of the way. But it had not taken the rest of him. The shove came after the fist and spun him half round, and he stayed up, and stood there with the shoulder singing and understood something that he did not like at all.

He had seen it. He had seen it clearly, a long way off, the way he had seen the dip in Brenna's shield and the shimmer in front of Amrit's hands. And the seeing had bought him almost nothing. It had bought him the difference between being hit in the face and being hit in the shoulder. She was simply faster than his seeing.

He saw the lean three more times before the end of the exchange. Each time he started to move the moment he saw it. Each time he was hit, or nearly hit, or hit a little less hard. Once he got all the way clear and heard the shove go past his ear like a slammed door in the next room. Once he did not get clear at all.

At the table, Vell's pen moved.

In the third exchange he tried moving earlier.

He reasoned it as he stood on his mark. If the lean came and he moved and she was still quicker, then he had to move before the lean finished. He had to move on the very start of it, the first tilt of the shoulders, before it had become a lean at all.

She came in. Jab, jab, nothing in them. Then the shoulders began to tip.

He went. He went on the very first tilt, so early that he was moving before he was sure, and her real punch went past his cheek into the empty air where his face had been. It was the first time all night she had missed with one she meant.

The rope noticed. He heard it notice.

So did Petra.

In the fourth exchange she did something new. She leaned, and he went on the lean, and her punch was not where his face had been. It was where his face was going. It met him coming the other way. It caught him on the side of the jaw, not hard, a glancing blow, and the shove came after it, and he went down on one knee and his teeth clicked together and he tasted blood where he had caught the inside of his lip.

He got up. He looked at her across the circle, and she looked back at him, with the same calm, narrow interest she had had at the start.

She did not know about the lean. He was almost sure of that. Her face had no idea that her shoulders were telling him anything.

But she knew that he was moving before her punches came. She had seen it in the third exchange. And she had done what Renn had done with the sweep. She had not tried to find out how he knew. She had simply stopped hitting the place he was and started hitting the place he would be.

She's learning faster than I am, he thought. She's learning me while I'm learning her, and she's quicker at that too.

The fifth exchange he tried everything he owned.

He tried Brenna. He gave ground along the groove and let her follow, and waited for her to get angry, so that she would get bigger and slower and louder. She did not get angry. The longer he ran, the calmer she became, and the calmer she became the quicker she was.

He tried Amrit. He watched her breath for the moment it stopped. It never stopped. She breathed in short easy puffs through her nose all the way through every punch, like a girl running for a cart she knew she would catch.

He tried the catch. He caught one punch she meant, square on the forearm, and held, and the shove came, and he leaned into it with everything he had, and it moved him anyway, a full pace backward, his heels plowing two short furrows in the dirt.

Nothing he owned was quick enough. Every piece of it worked. Every piece of it was a half-beat too slow.

The sixth exchange he lost by inches, over and over. He saw the lean and moved and was nearly clear. He saw the lean and moved and was clipped. He saw the lean and moved and she was waiting where he moved to, and he saw her waiting and changed his mind and moved again, and her second punch, which had no lean in it at all, only a jab, caught him under the ribs on the right side, the Renn side, and stopped his breath for a moment.

He was tiring, and he could feel it; his feet were slower than they had been in the first exchange and his hands were lower. She was not tiring at all.

The only thing he saw her pay was a small one: between exchanges she shook out her right hand at the wrist, once, as though the shove she put into other people came back a little way into her own arm.

At the rope the noise had gone strange. Some of it was the noise for a beating, the low pleased murmur of people watching what they had paid for. But under it there was something else. He heard somebody say "Seven," and somebody else say "He won't," and the first say "He will," and he understood that they were betting on whether he would last another exchange.

Vell called the end of the sixth.

He stood on his mark and breathed. He did not look at the rope. He looked at Petra's shoulders.

I can see it, he thought. I can see all of it. I just can't get there.

"Begin," said Vell.

The seventh exchange was very short.

She came. She jabbed, twice, nothing in either one. He let them go past and watched the shoulders. They began to tip. He went, on the first tilt, as early as he had ever gone. He went left, not right, because she had been waiting on his right for two exchanges. He did everything right. He would go over it afterward, line by line, and he would not find a single thing he had done wrong.

Her palm was there anyway.

It was not a fist. It was the heel of her open hand, flat, driven straight into his middle, below the ribs, and it arrived before he had finished going left. It arrived as if she had known he would go left before he did. And then the shove came after it, and it was the biggest shove of the night, and it lifted him.

He was in the air. Then he was not. He came down on his left hip across the groove, half in the circle and half out, and his face hit the packed dirt, and he lay there with his mouth full of the taste of earth and blood and no air in him anywhere.

"Called," said Vell. "Force Path."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

He reported to the table with his lip swelling and his hip a single deep ache and his breath still coming back to him in pieces.

Vell wrote, and blotted it, and looked at him, at the swelling lip and at the way he was standing on one leg.

"Seven," she said.

He nodded. He could not have said anything just then without his voice doing something he did not want it to do.

"Four," said Vell. "Five. Six. Seven." She said each number flatly, as if reading them out of the book, which perhaps she was. "Every time one more." She closed the ledger and laid her hand on the cover. "You'll come to the end of that sooner or later. Everybody does."

"What happens then?"

"Then you'll have to do something besides last. Go and get your lip seen to."

Petra was at the water bucket. She had a cup in each hand, and she held one of them out to him, which surprised him so much that he took it without thinking.

"What were you looking at?"

He drank, and the water stung his lip. "You."

"No." Petra shook her head, once, so that her braid swung. "Everybody looks at me. You were looking at something. From the second exchange. You kept moving before I'd started." She frowned at him, not angrily. It was the frown of somebody looking at a lock she had not seen before. "What was it?"

He thought about the Log. Never tell anybody their tell unless I'm sure I don't need it. He had written it the night he told Lira about her left foot and watched her take it away from him in an hour. He was not sure he did not need this one. He was fairly sure he would need it very badly, one day, in this circle, against this girl.

"I don't know," he said. "I was just watching."

Petra gave him the narrow, considering look a moment longer. He could see that she did not believe him, and he could see her decide that it did not matter yet.

"You're quick at it. The watching. Quicker than anybody I've fought." She drank her own water. "Not quick enough."

"No," he agreed.

"That's all right," said Petra Voss, quite seriously. "Nobody is, the first time." And she put her cup back on the bucket's edge, and walked off to her friends at the gate, and did not look back.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Lira had a wet cloth for his lip and nothing to say about the bout, and he was grateful for both. She walked him home through the dark by the long way round the market, where it was quieter, at his own pace, which was slow because of the hip, and at the well with the iron cover she stopped.

"You saw her shoulders."

He looked at her.

"From the second exchange. Before every real one. Your eyes went to her shoulders." She was not asking. "I've fought her twice. I never saw it."

"She doesn't know she does it."

"No. I don't think she does." Lira looked at him in the dark. "You didn't tell her."

"No."

"Good." And then, after a moment, as if it had surprised her to say so: "Good." She turned toward the four lanes. "Cold on the hip. Not long. Count it."

5. Petra Voss. Copper R3, Force Path. Called, seventh exchange. Down on the left hip.

Claim: before a punch she means, her shoulders lean forward, about a finger. Jabs and feints don't have it. Evidence: second through seventh exchanges, every committed strike I could see. Ruling: watch the shoulders.

Claim: she doesn't know she does it. Evidence: her face; she asked me what I was looking at. Ruling: don't tell her.

Claim: the shove comes after the hit. You can catch the fist and the shove still moves you. Evidence: first exchange, fifth exchange. Ruling: don't catch her. Don't be there.

Claim: when I moved early she moved her target to where I'd be. Evidence: fourth exchange, and the seventh. Ruling: she learns in the bout, as fast as I do or faster.

He stopped there and looked at the column of claims, and then wrote one more line across the bottom of the page, under all three columns, because it did not belong to any one of them.

I'm losing on speed now. Not on seeing.

He closed the front of the book and opened the back, and then he sat with the pencil until the lamp had burned down a finger's width.

Nought and four. Four, five, six, seven.

I can see everything now. I saw the heel, I saw the dip, I saw the shimmer, I saw the shoulders. And tonight I saw every single one of the things she did, a long way off, and I still couldn't get there.

Hesk wrote: your body is going to learn before your mind does. I think that's backwards for me. My mind's ahead. My mind's in the right place every time, and my body gets there after, and after is no use.

I don't know how you make a body faster. I don't think watching does it.

He looked at that last line and nearly crossed it out, because it frightened him, and he did not cross it out, because it was true.

Find out how, he wrote under it. Lira knows. Ask her.

He put the book under his pillow and tried to lie on his right side, because the left hip would not have him, and his ribs on the right would not have him either. In the end he lay on his back under the beam, and Torvin's voice said Lamps through the floorboards, as it did every night, and the last line of light under the door went out.

Seven exchanges: he had lasted longer than he had ever lasted and seen more than he had ever seen, and he had never felt further from being able to do anything about it.

Chapter 18 — Someone Else's Coat

[Focused, analytical narration; make every lesson and useful loss legible]

"How do you make a body faster?" he asked her, the morning after Petra.

Lira was at the post, in the grey half, and she did not stop. She struck it twice more, low, and stepped round it, and struck it again. He had learned by now that this meant she was thinking, and that the strikes were where she put her hands while she did it.

"You don't," she said at last.

"Petra's faster than me."

"Petra's been doing it for a year and a half, and she was probably quick to begin with, and she's seventeen and you're fourteen." Strike. "Some of it's just that. Some of it's years, and you can't buy years. But that isn't what you're asking."

"What am I asking?"

"You're asking why you saw everything and got there late." She stopped with her palm flat on the canvas and looked at him over her shoulder. "Aren't you."

He did not answer. He did not need to.

Lira came away from the post and stood in front of him in the grey half with her hands loose at her sides.

"When she leaned," she said, "what did you do?"

"I saw it."

"And then?"

"And then I knew what it meant, and then I moved."

"Three things." She held up three fingers. "You saw. You knew. You moved. Three steps. And Petra only had one. She leaned, and hit you." She folded two of the fingers down. "That's the speed. Not your legs. Your legs are fine. It's the knowing in the middle. It takes you a quarter of a breath to look at what you've seen and say to yourself, that's the lean, that means a punch, I should go left. She doesn't wait for you to say it."

"Then how do I stop saying it?"

"You do it so many times that the saying wears out." Lira shrugged, the easy shrug that never quite looked as easy as she meant it to. "You remember the gap? The move you were taught, and the move your body makes when there's no time to remember the lesson? Everybody who's fast lives in the gap. You don't live there yet. You live in the lesson. You see a thing and you look it up." She tapped his forehead with one finger, lightly. "In here. Every time. Like that notebook of yours."

He thought about the columns. Claim. Evidence. Ruling. He thought about how long it took him to rule on anything.

"I don't know how to stop looking things up," he said.

"I know you don't." She stepped back and brought her hands up. "So we're going to do one thing, over and over, until you stop. I'm going to show you something new today, and I'm going to hit you with it, and I'm going to keep hitting you with it until one morning you don't need to think about where it's coming from. It might take a month."

"A month?"

"It might take a year. I'm being generous." She set her feet. "It's one of mine. It's a bit unfair. That's why I like it."

It was a combination of three parts, and the first two were nothing.

She came in with a touch, high, toward his face, quick and light and empty, a tap on a door to see who was home. Then another, just like it, from the other hand. They brought his forearms up without his permission. Then she stepped.

And the step was the unfair part. She was two paces from him when she started it and she was inside his reach when it finished, and he did not see it cover the distance.

It was as if the ground between them had folded in the middle and let her across.

She had told him on the first day at the board that at Copper, Wind did not make you fast like a thrown stone. It made the world slightly more negotiable for a second at a time. He had not understood her then. He understood her now, with her already standing where she should not yet have been and his forearms up in the wrong place, guarding his face from two touches that were long gone.

Her right hand came round from his left side in a backhand, flat, at the height of his head, and stopped a finger's width from his ear.

"There," said Lira.

He had not moved at all.

"Again."

They did it again. He got his feet moving this time, and the backhand stopped a finger's width from the back of his head instead of from his ear. They did it a dozen times.

On the last few he began to build a counter. If the two touches came, he would not raise his arms for them. He would step back and outside instead, away from where the step would land, and bring his right forearm up for the backhand when it came, and catch it, and reset, and send. Lira let him build it. She watched him build it with her head on one side.

It worked once, out of a dozen. The rest of the time the step got there first.

"That's the one you'll use," she said, when the shadow had gone off the post. "The backhand. When I want to finish something in the morning and you're being annoying. I'll use it on you every day until you're not annoying about it."

She did. She used it twice the next morning, early on, while he was still loosening his hip, and both times the backhand stopped beside his ear before his counter was half built. He wrote it in the Log that night as if it were an opponent.

Lira, the step. Claim: two empty touches, then the ground folds and she's inside. Evidence: thirty times, two mornings. Ruling: step back and out on the second touch. Catch the backhand. It works one time in ten. That's one more than none.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The morning it happened was an ordinary one, and he would go over it afterward again and again, looking for whatever had made it different, and he would not find it.

He brought the bread. He had asked the bread woman for two from underneath, as he always did now. She had given him two from underneath without the sour look, as she always did now, and he took as a sign that the market had stopped thinking of him as new.

The yard was cool and still, and the crows were along the eaves of the public house, watching the dirt with the settled patience of birds who had worked out years ago that nothing that happened down there was food. The east wall's shadow lay across the yard in its long grey bar, as it lay every morning, and Lira was in it.

They warmed up with the deflection, catch, reset, send, which his left arm could do now nearly as well as the right, though the burn still pulled when he turned the wrist. Then she moved him about the grey half with a drill for the feet that she had introduced the week before, a box of four steps forward and back and across, calling the corners faster and faster until he lost the count and she laughed at him.

Then there was the bread, torn in half and eaten between sets.

They had been at it perhaps twenty minutes when she changed the pace.

He felt it change. It was not anything she said but a gathering in her shoulders and her feet, as if the morning had been a walk and now she meant to run. Her strikes came in quicker and stopped stopping short.

A touch on his collarbone was a real tap now, enough to sting, and a slap on his forearm when he caught it late was a real slap. He felt himself come up to meet it, all of him, the comfortable half-attention of the warm-up burning off like the mist in the low corner by the drain.

She's going to use the step, he thought. She's working up to it.

She came in with a touch, high, and another from the other hand. He did not raise his arms for them; he had built that much. He began to step back and out, as he had planned, to bring his right forearm up for the backhand when it came.

And his body did something else.

There was a feeling attached to it, and he would spend days afterward trying to set the feeling down in the back of the Log and failing every time. It was not a thought, and it was not a flinch either, the kind a hand makes from a hot pan. It arrived in the space between those two, quicker than the counter he had planned and somehow surer than any flinch.

It did not feel as though his body had overruled him. It felt as though his body had made a different decision on his behalf, in some room he had no key to, out of information he did not remember having been given.

He dropped.

His weight went down and sideways all at once, lower than he had ever put it, lower than Lira had ever asked of him, his left leg sweeping out behind him in a long arc across the dirt and his right knee folding under him and his whole body turning low beneath the line of the strike. He had never been taught it or seen anybody do it, not quite like this, and he had not chosen it.

It arrived exactly in time, so exactly that it could not have been timed on purpose, and Lira's backhand went over him.

He felt it pass, the wind of it on the back of his neck and in his hair, where his head had been a half-breath before, so close that the air itself seemed to drag at him as it went by.

He came up out of it on the far side of her, and he was off balance.

Not clumsy; that was not the word. He was off balance in a way his body had never been before. All his weight was in a place he did not know how to carry it, his feet set wider than he set them, his hips turned further than he turned them, and his arms ended somewhere he did not recognize, low and out to the sides.

He had once borrowed Garrik's coat in the rain, when he was ten, and the sleeves had ended halfway down his hands and the shoulders had sat on him wrong, and for the whole walk home he had felt like somebody else wearing his own body. It was like that: like standing in somebody else's coat, and finding that the sleeves ended somewhere he did not expect.

Lira stopped.

She did not stop the way she stopped at the end of a set. She stopped completely, all of her, as the yard had stopped in the third exchange against Renn, when he could hear the lanterns creak.

"How did you know that was coming?"

He looked down at himself. He looked at where his feet were, and his hands, as if they belonged to somebody who had just handed them back to him.

"I don't know."

"That wasn't your counter." She came round him slowly, a half-circle, as she had walked round him at the board on the first day. She was looking at the place where his feet had been, and the long scuffed arc his left foot had drawn across the dirt. "That wasn't your read. You were going back and out. I watched you start to go back and out. And then you didn't." She stopped in front of him again. "I've never seen you move like that."

"I don't know," he said again.

It came out quieter, and he heard how much quieter. Under the honest not-knowing, which he had been carrying for weeks now and had got used to, there was something new. It was not a puzzle any more. It was small and precise and cold, it sat just under his breastbone, and it was fear.

Lira looked at him for a long time.

He found himself watching her face while she did it, as he watched everybody's, and the watching felt different, aimed at her, like turning a gauge on something it had not been built to measure. He was looking for one thing, and he knew exactly what it was.

He had seen it on the face of the gate guard at Denvash, and the clerk at the record office, and Pellin, just for a second, behind the professional blankness. He was looking for the moment when somebody's face found out something about him and drew back from it.

It was not there.

He looked for it carefully, because its absence was information too, and he did not know yet where to file it.

What he saw instead was the face she wore on the barrel when somebody in the circle did a thing she had not seen before. It was neither alarmed nor arranging itself into calm for his sake. It was only working something out, quickly and completely, the way a person adds a new figure to a sum she thought she had finished.

Then she let out her breath, and she was Lira again.

"All right. Strange. Let's keep going."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

They kept going, but it was not the same.

She ran the deflection with him again, and the box drill, calling the corners at the same speed as before, and nothing she did was different. But he could feel her watching him in a new way, and feel himself being watched, and the two feelings rubbed against each other, so that neither of them could get back into the easy rhythm of the first twenty minutes.

They were careful with each other now. It was as if a room they both knew by heart had turned out to have a door in it, and they had shut it again, and neither of them could stop knowing where it was.

She used the step twice more before the shadow left the post, and both times he reached for it. He did not mean to, and he knew it was useless before he did it, and he did it anyway.

When the two touches came he felt for the thing that had dropped him, as he had felt for it in the fourth exchange against Renn. He reached into the room he had no key to.

There was nothing there.

There was only his own counter, the one he had built himself, back and out with the forearm up, and it was late both times. The first time Lira's backhand stopped beside his ear, and the second time it did not quite stop, and clipped him, and she said "Sorry," and did not sound sorry, and did not sound pleased either.

He filed that too. Whatever it was, it did not come because he wanted it, nor because the same strike came again, at the same speed, from the same girl, in the same grey half of the same yard. It had come once, for one exact moment, and then it had gone back into its room and shut the door.

"Enough," said Lira, when the sun reached them. She picked up the last of the bread from the top of the post, tore it in two and gave him the larger half without looking at him. "Same time tomorrow."

"Same time tomorrow."

At the gate she stopped and turned round, as she had stopped at the well corner on the night of Renn.

"Cael."

He waited.

She seemed to be deciding something, and he watched her decide it, and then decide something else instead.

"Your left foot. In the box drill. You're still turning it out on the back corner. Fix it."

And she went out through the gate.

[Steady, observant narration; let place, distance, and social position register]

He went to the mender in the afternoon, because it was a Wednesday and Wednesday was one of his afternoons, and because he could not think of anywhere else he wanted to be.

The mender had a tray of small keys for him, a hundred or more, all of them for locks that had long ago been thrown away. He wanted them sorted by the shape of their bits so that somebody coming in with a lock could be matched to a key without trying every one. Cael sat on the stool at the end of the bench and sorted keys.

His hands were not right. He dropped one, and then another, and he picked up a key and looked at it and could not see its bit for a moment, only a key, as though his eyes had forgotten what they were for.

The mender looked up from his clock once, at Cael's hands, and back at his clock, and said nothing.

Cael put the keys in rows, slowly, laying each one down beside the last and checking that its bit matched before he let go of it, and if it did not match he moved it and checked again. It did not matter that it was only keys.

He needed something in front of him that would do exactly what it was supposed to do when he did exactly the right thing to it. He needed something to obey.

By the end of the afternoon there were nine rows of keys on the bench, straight as a ruled page, and his hands had stopped.

The mender came and looked at the rows. He picked one key out of the sixth row, looked at its bit, and put it back exactly where it had been.

"Something broken?"

It was the same question as always, and it was not the same question.

"I don't know yet," said Cael.

The mender nodded slowly, as if that were an answer he had heard before and respected, and went back to his clock.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Lira did not go back to her post that afternoon.

She went back to the Cinder House yard instead, when it was empty. There was no card on a Wednesday, and the public house's back door was shut. The only people about were the crows and the pie boy, who raked the circle on the days there was no card and had finished raking it, and was asleep on a sack in the shade with his mouth open. She did not wake him.

She went to the middle of the grey half, where the shadow had been that morning, though there was no shadow there now, only flat afternoon light. She stood where Cael had stood.

Then she did it herself.

She did it slowly at first, standing with her weight back and out, as he had been standing when he started to build his counter, and she imagined her own backhand coming round from the left at the height of her head. Then she dropped. She let her weight go down and sideways, and swept her left leg out behind her in an arc across the dirt, and folded her right knee under her, and turned.

It was easy; that was the first thing she found. Her body knew how to put its weight that low, and how to turn under a line, because that was what Wind did best at Copper. It took you out of the place where things landed. She had been dropping under strikes since her first month at the academy.

It was not hard to do.

It was impossible to do in time.

She tried it again, faster, imagining her own step folding the ground and the backhand coming round, and went down, and was late. She tried it a third time and went early, on the second touch, before the step had even begun. She came up on the far side of an empty yard, grinning at nothing, perfectly safe from a strike that would have changed its line the moment it saw her go.

She tried it eleven times. She counted, because she had caught counting from him, and was annoyed about it.

There was no moment to go; that was what she found.

If you went before the step, the backhand followed you down. If you went after the step, it had already gone past where your head was. The only moment that worked was the exact one, the half-breath when the backhand was committed and could not change and had not yet arrived. She knew from every hour she had ever spent fighting that nobody could choose that moment. You could not see it coming and then decide to go. There was no time to decide anything in it.

You could only already be going.

She sat down on the dirt in the middle of the empty yard with her arms round her knees.

He had not decided it. She was sure of that now, because she had watched his face. She had watched him start his own counter, back and out, the one he had been building for three days, and she had watched it stop halfway, as if somebody had taken it out of his hands.

And then he had gone down into that drop, and come up out of it with his feet wide and his hips too far round and his arms low and strange. He had stood there looking at his own body as though it had come back to him from somebody else, slightly the wrong size.

It had not been his.

She knew how he moved by now; she had been watching him move every morning for three weeks. He moved like somebody who had read about moving and was checking the book against the world, neat and careful and always a quarter of a breath behind his own eyes. She had been using that quarter-breath against him every morning, and she knew exactly how wide it was.

That drop had not been a quarter-breath behind anything. It had been on time, and on time with her, with her own step and her own strike, as though it had known them as well as she did.

And it had had a shape.

She sat in the dirt and tried to see the shape again, and could not quite. It had been low and sweeping, and the left leg had gone out behind in that long arc, and the turn had come from the hip and not the shoulders. It was not a move she had taught him, nor anything anybody at the academy had taught her.

And yet, when she had done it herself just now, slowly, her body had understood it at once, as though it were a word in a language she spoke but had never heard said in quite that accent.

She did not like that, and she did not know what to do with it, so she set it down, carefully, beside the other things she had not known what to do with, and looked at the little row of them.

There were three now.

The first had been on the second day, at the board. She had been talking about the gap, and about moving before you decided to, and his hand had gone to his hip. It had gone to the strap of a bag he was not carrying, and stayed there, and his face had gone somewhere a long way off, down a road she could not see.

She had wanted to ask and had not. She had stood there and watched him come back from wherever it was, and she had decided it was his.

The second had been Renn's third exchange.

She had been at the rope, and had seen the heel settle as she had seen it settle in her own bout in her second month. She had known what was coming because she had been on the end of it: the first cut, the second, the third up the lane.

She had known exactly where the third was going to go, because she had once lain on her back looking at the lamps from the place where it went.

And he had not been there. His eyes had still been on the heel, and his feet had already gone. She had bitten her own knuckle so hard there was a mark on it for two days.

Instinct, he had said, in the lane, under the lantern, with his hand on his ribs.

She had written it down, in the place in her head where she kept such things, as tonight's answer. She had meant it when she said it. It was the kind of answer you gave when you did not have a better one, and she had decided to let him keep it until he did.

And now this. The third. In daylight, in the grey half of the yard, against her own strike, with nobody watching but the crows.

She had not pushed. She had stood in front of him with the question right there in her mouth, the next question, the one that came after I don't know. She had been about to say it. Then what was it? Do it again. Show me.

She had not said it, because of his face.

She had seen him search her face, quickly and thoroughly, as he searched everybody, and she had known exactly what he was searching for. She had seen it in other people's faces when she told them she had been sent away from the academy. It was the drawing back, the small polite step away that people's eyes took when they found out you were not what they had expected.

He had been waiting for her to do it. He had been bracing for it.

And she did not want to give him anything he could mistake for it. Not a question, not a frown, not an again, show me in the voice of somebody who needed an explanation before she would decide what to think of him.
