The rope was three deep on the shaded side and two deep in the sun, though there was no sun, only lanterns and the cold coming down out of a clear sky. The benches were full to the third row. There were faces he knew in all of them now, and that was a new thing, and he looked at it as carefully as he had looked at anything.

The fish man with the beard was in the second row with his arms folded. Torvin's wife was by the gate, and beside her the woman who slept in her boots, eating a sweet bun. The two errand boys were at opposite ends of the rope, as far from each other as the yard allowed, and both of them were watching him and not each other, which he thought was probably the first time in their lives they had both looked at the same thing. Further along the rope stood the girls from the wall in the lane of yards. Brenna was near the front with her two friends, her face already red, though she had done nothing yet but stand there.

Doss was by the gate in the wall, leaning on it, with his bad leg out straight and his pipe unlit in his hand. He must have come before his night at the warehouses. He saw Cael looking, and did not nod, and did not look away either.

Marrow came along the rope with his slate.

Cael read it without moving his head. Dessa, and a short price. Unrated, and a long one. But the long one was not as long as it would have been a month ago, and he could see why. Somebody had been paying on him, a little, all week, and Marrow had moved the number to meet them. Under the two names, on its own line, Over-under: five exchanges.

Marrow came level with the water bucket and looked at him for a moment, pleasantly, and for a moment longer than pleasant needed. Then he wrote something on the slate with his chalk and went on.

"Second bout," said Vell.

The yard did not go quiet. It went lower. He had heard it go lower for Dessa on both Sundays, and now it was going lower for her again, and he found it strange to stand inside the sound and know that some small part of it was for him.

Dessa came across the yard toward him before he had reached the rope.

Her eyes never once went to the rope or the benches. She came straight to where he stood by the bucket and stopped in front of him, square and solid, with her hair tied back so tightly that it pulled at the corners of her eyes. Close to, she was older than he had thought from the benches, nearer twenty than not, with a small white scar through one eyebrow and a face that did not seem to do very much.

"Vell will have told you," she said. "I want to hear the terms from you."

"She told me."

"Then say them."

So he said them, to her face, as he had said them to Vell on the first morning, in his own words and his own order, slowly, checking each one before he set it down. Unrated. He fought who Vell put across from him. It ended when Vell called it, and not before, and not for any other reason. Nobody stopped it but Vell. What happened in it was his to carry, whichever way it went. Nobody was making him.

Dessa listened to all of it without moving. When he had finished she looked at him for a breath longer, as he had seen her look at the Fenrow man's feet.

"Third row," she said. "Both Sundays. I saw you."

"Yes."

"With a book." It was not a question. "Good." She turned and went to her side of the circle.

He stepped over the rope.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

"Dessa," said Vell, from her table. "Copper Rank 5, Stone Path. Against unrated. Vouched." The pause, which was the same small pause it always was. "Begin when you're ready."

Dessa set her feet. The grit round her boots shivered and lay flat. Her hands came up a little, loose, in front of her hips, and her eyes went to his feet and stayed there.

The first exchange cost him the skin off two knuckles and bought him one number.

He had decided on the bench, on the first Sunday, that he would not be quick with her. The Fenrow man had been quick. He had thrown everything he owned at her in his first exchange and walked back to his mark afterward flapping his hands as if he had shut them in a door, and Dessa had not so much as shifted a heel. Whatever you brought her in a hurry, she kept. So Cael went in at three-quarter pace, and asked.

He asked the high line first, a touch toward her face with nothing behind it. Her left forearm was waiting before the touch got there. He let it land anyway, lightly, to learn what it was like, and it was not like a block at all; it was like putting his hand against a gatepost somebody had sunk in the dirt. He asked her left side, a step across, and the whole frame came round to face him in one piece while her boots stayed exactly where they were. He asked her body, low, a feint he never meant to finish, and her weight went over by the width of a thumb and came straight home.

The same feint again, and it moved her less. A third time, and it did not move her at all.

Three, he thought. Three, the same as the Fenrow man got. Lie to her once and she believes you. By the third time she knows your lies better than she knows your name.

Two more touches, one on each forearm, to be sure. They were like knocking at a house where everybody was at home and nobody was coming down. She did not answer with a strike. She did not follow him when he drew off. She stood on her mark with the grit flat round her and let him spend, and he spent, and when he circled back to his own mark all he had to show for it was a sting across the right knuckles and the count of three.

Along the benches a man laughed. It was the laugh a yard gave a mismatch in its first minute, the small one dancing round the big one and getting nowhere, and Cael did not turn his head for it. He watched Dessa's lips at her mark. Four and four.

I spent, he thought. She banked. That's what everybody's first exchange with her looks like. That's all right. It was meant to.

The second exchange was the one he had made, and it started with a mistake he meant.

Its whole idea had come to him on a plank bench, and been turned over on the wall by the pump, and finished at the mender's with his palms flat on the bench while a beam came to rest. Nothing in four pages said that her guard could be broken, by anybody, least of all by a boy lighter than she was, so he would not try to break it. He would make her put it up instead, over and over. Each time her frame turned to meet him it had to be built again where it now faced, shoulders and forearms and hips coming round and settling and locking, though her feet never shifted. She did it fast and she did it beautifully, and it was not free. He had watched her count stretch from four to seven across a long bout on a Sunday, and that stretch was the bill.

So the bill would be run up on his clock, not hers.

He came at her and stopped short, and held still a moment longer than anybody would. He gave her two touches where one was due, and then nothing at all where she had braced for two. He stepped across to her left and was back on her right while she was still coming round to the left, and he did it again the other way. There was no beat in any of it that she could lean her weight against. Every time he changed his mind, her frame had to change to meet the new one.

It did. She turned and built and locked each time without haste or waste, and she never once came after him, and her eyes never once left his feet. She would not spend.

But he could hear her breathing now.

Once, coming out of a stopped step, he drifted a thumb's width nearer than he had planned, and knew without seeing it how much of her was gathered and waiting for exactly that mistake. It was like leaning out over the lip of a well and feeling the cold breathe up at your face. He was not eager. He took himself back out by the road he had come in.

He broke off, with his own chest heaving harder than he liked. From the benches it must have looked like nothing at all: her frame standing where it had stood when Vell spoke, and a boy hopping round a wall for most of a minute and never once landing anything worth the name.

"Hit her, then!" somebody shouted, and laughed, and somebody else told him to hush.

Cael did not look at either of them. He watched Dessa go back to her mark, because he had nothing better to spend the next breath on, and he watched her the way he had watched the Fenrow man's feet and the Blade man's blade from the third row. She reached her mark and set herself, and the grit shivered, and her back foot, which ought to have been the last bolt shot home, came down a half beat after everything else.

He saw it.

It went through him like cold water. This was the second exchange, not the end of a long night. She was not tired the way she had been tired after six exchanges with the Blade man, low on her left side, her count drawn out long. But he had made her build that frame something like thirty times in a minute, to a rhythm she had not chosen, and the thirty-first had come down late.

On two Sundays he had seen it once a night, and only at the end. He had not thought he would see it tonight before the end, if he saw it at all. Whether it would ever show itself twice in one bout, he had no idea.

At her mark Dessa's lips moved. Six and six.

He stood on his own mark with his hands loose and his face as still as he could make it, and he did not move.

Every part of him wanted to go now. The window had been there three breaths ago, in front of his own eyes; if he went straight in, hard, while she was still counting, he might be inside the frame before the back foot had come down. His legs were already telling him so.

And that was exactly what the four pages said she lived on.

He had written it on the first Sunday, with the cold off the wall coming through his coat: She doesn't beat people. She stands there while they beat themselves. Every eager fighter in his notes had seen something and gone for it and found her at the end of it, weight already low and the sweep already on its way. Hurry was her income. He had not spent two Sundays on a plank to hand her his now, because his legs were impatient.

The late foot was not an order to go. It was a promise that the window would open again the next time she had to raise her frame to his count, and that he could make it open.

So he banked it.

He breathed out. He let his shoulders drop. He looked at her feet as if they had told him nothing, and when Vell said, "Begin," he went in exactly as he had the first time, at the same polite pace, as though he had learned nothing and planned nothing and had only questions left.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

To anybody watching, the third exchange began as a copy of the first.

The same three-quarter pace. The same polite touch at the high line, which her forearm met. The same step across to her left, which her frame turned to follow.

And then, before it had finished turning, the step back to her right, the one he had used in the second exchange. Her frame came round to meet it, as it had come round thirty times already, and began to build itself again where it had turned. Her back foot came down to lock it.

He was not waiting for it. He was already going.

He had timed it from the third row, the gap between the frame and the foot. He had clapped its rhythm on his knee on a plank bench until the old man beside him had asked him to stop. He went into it the way you go through a door you have walked through in the dark a hundred times, without looking for the handle.

For a half beat the frame was up and the foot was not under it. It was the only half beat in three bouts of watching when she was standing on the dirt instead of built into it.

He hit her.

It was the strike from the post, the only one he owned: short and straight, the back foot driving, the hip turning, the fist arriving last. It went in under her left forearm, which had come round a hair too high, into the soft seam below her collarbone where the frame had not yet arrived to cover it. It did not stop at the surface of her. It went on through, and he felt the whole of her give round it, the way a person leaning on a door gives when somebody strikes the door.

She went back half a step.

She went back off her mark, the mark nobody moved her from. It was the first ground she had given in the bout, and he had seen what came after the first ground she gave, four times, in two bouts, from the third row.

He was already going left.

He went off her line before her weight had finished dropping, while the yard was still drawing its breath at the half step. Every eager fighter in his notes had followed that half step in. He went the other way, outside, two long steps along the curve of the groove. Four times on the Sundays he had seen that sweep, and it came now the way it had come then, low and flat and much faster than anything else she owned, a long arc along the dirt that reclaimed the half step and whatever stood on it.

Nothing was standing on it. It went through the place where a fighter following her in would have been, and he was two strides wide of it, off her line, with nothing touching him, and already turning back to face her.

Dessa came up out of the sweep and onto her mark and set her feet. The grit shivered and lay down.

Then she looked at his face.

It was the first time she had looked anywhere but his feet all night. It was very quick. Her eyes came up from his boots to his eyes and stayed there for the length of a breath, and he saw something go across behind them. It was not anger and it was not surprise. It was the look of somebody adding a new figure to a sum she had thought she had finished. Her eyes dropped to his feet again. The frame went up. That was the end of the exchange.

The yard was making a new sound.

It was not loud. It was a low, turned-head murmur that ran along the rope and up into the benches and back. Eighty people were revising something all at once, and some of them had money on it. On the second bench a man wanted to know what he had just seen, and the man beside him told him, and got it wrong. Near the front, Brenna said something to one of her friends, sharp and short, and did not laugh.

He read her lips while she counted at her mark. Eight and eight. It was the longest count he had seen from her on any night.

She did not look at the yard.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

His notebook was empty for the fourth exchange.

He knew it, standing on his mark with his knuckles throbbing and his breath coming hard. Two Sundays on a bench had bought him one tell and one way to make it come, and both of them were used up. She would close that window now. Nobody as good as she was left the same window open twice. She had looked at his face, and she would not let a frame come late on his clock again tonight, not if he made her build it a hundred times.

What he had left was patience. Against Dessa, patience beat having no plan only as a cup beats bare hands when the river is coming up.

Still he went, no faster than before, braced to pay dearly and be given almost nothing back.

She advanced.

Every step forward he had ever seen her take, on both Sundays and in the first three exchanges tonight, had been ground taken back from somebody who had taken it. This one was not. She took it, and then another, and then a third. She came frame first, unhurried, with the grit shivering flat under each foot as it came down, and even while she came he could see the sense of it, the thrift. Patience had never been the point with her. Spending was the point. And the cheap thing now, the thing that cost her least, was to finish a tired boy before his notebook grew another page.

It was quiet and complete. It was a wall deciding to arrive.

He gave ground.

He gave it along the long side of the circle. That was the one thing he had kept back, the one line in four pages he had not needed yet. He had noticed it on his first morning in the yard with Lira, and written it down on the first Sunday from the third row. The groove was not quite round. It was longer one way than the other, as if all the fighters who had walked it into the dirt had preferred the same side. Going back along the long side, he would have two more steps before the groove arrived at his heel.

He took the first of them. And the second.

Dessa did not follow him round the long side. She cut across it.

She did not hurry. She simply walked the short way, straight across the middle of the circle toward the place where he would be when he ran out of long side, and the two steps he had banked were gone before he had finished taking them. The groove was at his heel. He could feel its edge through the sole of his boot.

The yard had gone silent. It was the silence of eighty people all doing the same sum at once and not liking where it came out. He could hear the lantern nearest the gate creaking on its hook.

He searched her advance for a rhythm. He had refused her rhythm all night, and he looked now for one he could refuse, some step he could make come early or late. He found none. There was no rhythm left in her to refuse. She was only coming, frame first, with her eyes on his feet and her lips not moving at all.

She rocked onto the front foot, and all her weight went with it.

What happened next, he did not decide.

His body was already going. It was not going back, though every line of the exchange said back; back was the groove, and the rope, and the dirt. It was not going sideways either, along the curve, where he had gone in the third exchange and where she would be waiting for him now. It went across.

His lead foot planted, and the whole of him turned on it, low, into the closing space beside her advancing shoulder. It was the space her frame was coming forward to fill, the space that was not there yet. Then it was there, exactly, for exactly as long as he needed it, and he was through it before it closed.

No thought went into it. Hardly any of him went into it.

It came as a word comes when somebody says the first half of a sentence and you know the rest before they finish, in a voice you cannot place. And it had come once before, on a grey morning in this same yard, with Lira's backhand going over the back of his head and nobody watching but the crows.

He came out of it inside her frame.

Her forearms were behind him. He was at her right side, at an angle no guard of hers had ever had to cover, since no one had ever got there to need it. Her weight was on her lead foot, still going forward into the place he had been. His was under him.

The strike was his. That part he could account for. He had made it a hundred times a morning for two weeks at a canvas post in the grey half, and his hip knew it and his back foot knew it, and it went where he sent it: short, rising, up into the hinge of her jaw under the ear, where nothing was guarding anything because nothing had been expected there.

Dessa went down.

She did not fall the way the Fenrow man had fallen, all at once. She went down in stages, a knee and then a hand, and sat back onto the dirt inside the groove. An arm went under her; she sent word to her legs to stand. Her legs did not answer. She tried once more, with great care, the way a carpenter tries a joint he has just glued, and they did not answer again.

She sat on the dirt and looked at nothing for a moment. Then she lifted her right hand off her knee and held it up, open, the palm toward Vell's table.

"Called," said Vell. Her voice was exactly as level as it always was. "Conceded. Unrated."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He had stood inside that noise four times while the yard made it for somebody else, and now it was coming the other way.

It reached him in pieces. A shout from the benches, a groan from the rope, coins clicking along from hand to hand, somebody laughing at the face of somebody who had lost. Near the gate a voice he knew went up high and broke, one of the errand boys, though he did not look to see which. And under all of it ran a quieter, stranger thing, which was his own name in the mouths of people he had never met, here and there along the rope, as though somebody had just told it to them and they were trying it for size.

He did not know what to do with any of that, so he did the one thing he did know, and crossed the circle to her.

Dessa was up already. She had a thumb pressed under one ear and was opening and shutting her mouth, testing the hinge of her jaw one slow bite at a time. When the woman from the water bucket came toward her with a cup, she waved it away without looking.

"Both Sundays," she said. "Third row. A book on your knee." She did not make it a question. "That window was measured. And you'd left my line before the sweep came, so you'd counted that as well."

"Yes."

"There'll be people tell you it was luck." She moved her jaw left and then right, once, and let it be, as if she had decided it would keep. "It was nothing like luck. Since I came to this yard nobody's read me that clean, and you did it sitting on a plank for a fortnight." She looked at him then, properly, as she had looked at his face in the third exchange. "What's your Path?"

"Nothing to register."

Both her eyebrows went up a little, the scarred one and the other, a small and honest surprise.

"I had you ready," she said slowly. "Unrated, four losses, lasts a long while, gives ground. I know what you do with a boy like that. I'd planned it out, and I came with it." She looked down at the groove, where her own sweep had scored a long curve through the dirt across her mark. "Only there's nothing written on you. No Path to learn the habits of. No school's lines to cut. Nobody but you has read those four pages, and every bit of tonight came out of them." Her eyes came back up. "The registry might call that a hole in you. I don't. I'd sooner face a Path I know, any night of the week, than a fortnight of you sitting on a bench."

"Rematch?"

He had not known he was going to say it until it was out.

"No." There was no heat in it at all. "Not yet." Her glance went down to his hands, and he saw that they had begun to shake; something close to warmth crossed her face and did not stay. "Go and fight some problem that isn't me for a while. I'd like to sit on the benches for once and watch you work it. Then we'll talk."

She turned to go, and turned back.

"And eat something," she said. "A win empties you worse than a loss. Nobody tells you that."

She went off to her side of the yard, and on the way, exactly as the four pages had her, she never once looked at the crowd. She did stop at the water bucket. She took the cup the woman had held out to her before, and drank, and handed it back, and gave the pie boy a nod.

Then he was alone in the middle of the circle, with dirt down one side of his neck and his right knuckles split, and his hands shaking.

It was the ordinary sort of shaking, he thought, spent muscle and nerves that had finished their work, the same as after Petra. It climbed his forearms into his shoulders and he let it climb. Under it he looked for anything else, and found nothing.

So he reached. He stood quite still with the yard going on round him and reached for whatever had turned him across that closing space, the way you reach after a word you had on your tongue a moment ago. He had reached like that twice in the grey half after the drop, and come back with empty hands, and he came back with them now. Whatever it was had gone back into its room and shut the door behind it, and had not even left an ache to prove it had been out.

What it had left was how he was standing. His feet were set wider than he set them, his hips turned further round than he turned them, and his weight was on the foot he did not usually trust with it. It was somebody else's coat again, with the sleeves ending where he did not expect.

He put himself right on purpose, a piece at a time, feet in and hips round and weight back where it lived, the way he would have reset a gauge that had been knocked.

Then he filed it, in his head, where nobody could see him do it. Second instance. He knew while he was writing it there what number it really was, and he left that for later.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

He went to Vell's table, because you went to the table win or lose, and read the second line upside down, as he had learned to read at nine across the bench from Hesk, with his hands still shaking and the lantern swinging a little on its hook.

Built the third exchange on the lateness of her frame. Timed it from the benches over two bouts, then made it come early in the second by working her frame to his count. Does his studying before he fights, and more of it than a few weeks in this yard explain.

Above it sat the line Vell had spoken aloud while she wrote, because the record was always spoken. "Result stands as called. Unrated, over Dessa, Copper Rank 5, Stone Path. Fourth exchange. Conceded from the dirt." The pen had paused, and gone on. "Witnessed and entered." At the head of that line, where a name would have stood, there was still no name, only Unrated (14; nothing to register; vouched, L.), the same as every other time.

The second line she had not read out to anybody.

She blotted it, and shut the ledger on her thumb, and lifted her eyes to his with nothing in her face at all.

"It's a compliment. Don't spend it."

Chapter 26 — The Honest Sort

[Measured, quietly confident narration; let competence arrive without swagger]

The yard was slow to let go of him.

People he had never spoken to came up to him at the rope, and said things, and went away again before he had worked out what they had said. A man he did not know shook his hand, hard, and told him he had had him at the over and had not expected to be paid on the other thing as well. A woman told him he was too thin. One of the girls from the wall in the lane of yards came past and said, "Brenna's furious," with enormous satisfaction, and was gone.

Brenna herself did not come near him. But when he looked across the yard she was standing by the gate with her friends, red-faced, and she was looking at him. She gave him one short nod, the kind you give across a street to somebody you have decided you will have to take seriously, and turned away.

He found the errand boys at the gate.

They were not running. He had never seen either of them standing still before, and it changed them. They looked younger than they did at a sprint, and smaller, and they were standing closer to each other than he had ever seen them stand. The one with the brother in the carters' was counting coins out of a little cloth purse into the other's palm, one at a time, with a face like a slammed door.

The boy in the red cap had his hand held out flat and his eyes on the coins, and he was not saying anything at all, which Cael suspected was costing him more than anything he had ever done.

The last coin went into the palm. The boy in the red cap closed his fist on it. Then he looked up and saw Cael, and his whole face came open like a shutter.

"Two," he said. "I said two. Two more, I said, the night of the cook. And the girl with the freckles was one, and this was two." He held up the fist. "Two."

"I said never," said the other boy, "and I'd say it again."

"You'd lose again."

"I'd say it again."

The boy in the red cap was not listening. He was digging in his pocket with his free hand. He came out with something wrapped in a twist of greased paper, warm, and pushed it at Cael so hard that Cael had to take it or let it fall.

"Pie," he said. "I bought it in the third exchange, when she went back off her mark. I knew." He looked at the paper in Cael's hands, and then at Cael, with great seriousness. "That's your share."

He turned and ran. The other boy stood for a moment, looking at the empty purse, and then he ran too, after him, and they went off down the lane in the dark shouting at each other in exactly the old way, and the sound of it went round the corner and kept going.

Cael stood by the gate holding a warm pie.

"Eat it," said Lira, at his elbow. He had not heard her come. "Dessa told you to eat something. I heard her."

He ate it. It was the pie woman's, two stalls along from the honest-weight man, and it was mostly gravy. He thought it was the best thing he had ever eaten.

Along the rope Marrow was wiping his slate clean with the side of his hand, slowly, the whole of it. He looked up as he finished and saw Cael by the gate, and smiled the good smile, the one he knew the price of, and did not say anything. He did not need to. He had been paying out all along the rope for the last quarter of an hour.

"Don't," said Lira.

"I'm eating a pie."

"Keep eating it."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

She walked him back to Torvin's and did not say anything for the whole of the way.

It was not the silence of the walk home after Renn, when she had been saving something up. He could feel the difference. She was not saving anything. She was simply walking beside him at his pace through the cold, with her hands in her pockets, while the questions stacked up beside her like crates on a quay. He could feel every one of them. She did not ask one. She had learned that after a bout he was a long way down, like a swimmer who has gone deep, and that anything she said before he came back up would go straight past him.

At the door under the leaning O, she stopped.

"Write it up," she said. "I'll be around."

She did not say where. He went in.

Yeni was on her cot with the lamp turned up and a shirt across her knee, and she looked up from the seam as he came in, which she did not usually do.

"Well?"

"Won."

The needle stopped. It stayed stopped for long enough that he noticed it. Then it went on, in and out.

"Took you long enough," Yeni said to the shirt. "Torvin's wife's won her bun back off the one in the boots. She had you at five. The boots had you at never." The needle went in. "She'll be impossible."

He sat on the end of his cot by the window with the Log. His hands had stopped shaking somewhere on the walk home, and he had not noticed them stop.

He did the front first. That was the rule.

6. Dessa. Copper R5, Stone Path. Won. Conceded, fourth exchange.

He wrote it in the three columns, as he wrote all of them, and kept it short. He had been inside it. He did not need it told to him again.

First exchange. Ruling: don't hit her guard. Hit the time it takes her to build it.

The second exchange took the most care, because it was about the cost of a frame that had to be built again every time it turned, and that idea would go beyond Dessa. Anybody who had to set themselves, Shield or Stone or Iron or anything else that stood still to be strong, would have to set themselves again when they turned, and every setting cost something, and a person who made them turn on his clock instead of theirs was spending their breath instead of his own. That was the kind of thing the Log was for. Ideas that went beyond the one fighter were the whole point of it.

Second exchange. Ruling: if somebody's strength has to be built, make them build it, on my clock. Then wait. The late foot came early.

Third exchange. Ruling: a window that can be made is worth more than one that's given.

The third took more lines than the other two together all the same, because he wrote every step of it as he had made it, and when he had finished he read it twice.

Then he allowed himself what he had paid for, and took his time over it. Two Sundays on a cold bench had turned into half a beat. Half a beat had turned into a strike, and the strike into the first time in his life he had walked out of a circle the winner. He had read her correctly. He had timed it correctly. He had been correct to go left. Every one of the three had been made out of watching and nothing else, and each of them had held under load, the way a bracket holds when every figure in it has been traced back to where it came from.

Anybody could have been walked through that page and shown a reason under every move, and there was not a reason on it that belonged to anyone but him.

The registry could call him what it liked. Nobody else had any claim on that page.

He sat with it longer than he needed to.

Then he came to the fourth exchange, and tried to put it in the columns, and could not.

Claim: in the fourth, when she advanced, I went across into the closing space and came out inside her frame.

That was true.

Evidence: I was there. Her jaw. She saw it. The yard saw it.

That was true too.

Ruling:

There was nothing to put there. He had not gone across. Something had gone across, and taken him with it, and put him down inside her frame with his strike ready. He could not do it again, and he did not know how it had been done, and a ruling that said go across into the closing space would be a lie, because he could not go across into the closing space. He did not even know where it had been until he was standing in it.

He drew one line through the three lines, neatly, so that the words could still be read underneath, and beside them in the margin he wrote back.

Then he closed the front of the book and turned it over.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The back of the Log opened at the page he had written on the night of the drop.

First instance. And under it the morning in the grey half, the backhand going over, the coat. And the small box round It wasn't mine, which he had drawn so that he would know when he came back to it that he had meant it.

He turned to a clean page and wrote, at the top:

Second instance.

He wrote it down as plainly as he had written the first. There was no decision in it and no warning. No plan had it in, or anything like it. It simply came, in a voice he could not place. Afterward he was standing wrong, with his feet wide and his hips round too far and his weight on the wrong foot, as he had been after the drop: the coat again, the sleeves ending in the wrong place. He had reached for it, standing in the circle with the yard shouting, and there was nothing to reach for. It had left nothing behind.

Same in kind as the first, he wrote. Same arriving. Same coat after. Same nothing when I look for it.

The two of them would bear one conclusion and no more, and after a while with the pencil he set it down.

Two instances is a pattern. I won't put weight on it till there's a third. So: watch, write it down, and don't guess.

He looked at it.

It was a good sentence. It was the kind of sentence Hesk would have written about a spring that had failed its test twice, and it was careful and honest and it did not claim anything it could not prove. It had exactly the right amount of doubt in it.

And it was not true.

He sat on the end of his cot with the Log on his knee and the lamp hissing, and looked at the sentence, and knew it the way he had known the bracket would fail when the needle swung.

It was not true because the column was not true. The column started at the drop because he had decided, on the night of the drop, sitting exactly here, that it would start there. He had decided it on purpose, knowing what he had left out, and he had written down that he knew. He had told himself it was better to start a column somewhere, knowing it was short, than not to start one at all. That had been right, that night. It had been the most he could do that night.

But it was not that night now. Tonight he had written Two instances is a pattern under it, and the sentence did not know that it was standing on a column with its first two figures missing. Anybody who read it a year from now would think there had been two. He would think there had been two, himself, in a year, because he would have read the sentence so often that it had worn a groove.

That was what sentences did. He had found that out at the pump on the first day of the Log, with a torn page. You put a true thing in at one end and a guess came out at the other, in the same coat.

He put the Log down on the blanket, open.

Then he reached into the pocket of his coat, which was hanging on the nail by the window. Down in the bottom of the inside pocket, behind the leather book, there was a fold of thin grey paper that had been there since the ninth day. He had felt it every time he put the coat on. He had never once taken it out.

He took it out now and unfolded it.

The creases had gone soft. The pencil had smudged a little where the folds crossed. It was the first page of the Log, the one he had torn out along the spine so that the binding would not loosen, and it said, in his own hand from the morning after Renn, with the ribs still hot:

Renn. Copper Rank 3, Blade. He opens with two probes, high and across, off the front foot. The true strike loads in his back heel about a quarter of a second first. I read the heel in the second exchange and he answered with the sweep. In the third I got out of the whole figure—

And then nothing, where he had stopped.

He read it three times. Then he took the pencil and finished the sentence, under it, on the torn page, in tonight's hand.

—and I didn't do it. I didn't read the third cut. My eyes were still on his heel. My feet had already gone. Vell saw it. Lira saw it. Renn said it doesn't miss, and it missed. I said instinct. That stopped about a hand short of the truth, and I knew it while I was saying it.

He looked at that for a long moment.

Then he reached under the cot for his bag and took out the third notebook from Denvash, the old one with nine pages left in it. He opened it from the back, to the page near the end that he had never let himself read again. There, in pencil, written in the dark on the night of Lira's question at the board, was the cart.

Day three. The road, the dip between the hedges, after midday. I was walking in the middle of the road. Then I was on the verge. Then a cart came round the bend behind me, fast, downhill. The hub touched my bag strap.

I told the carter I heard it coming. I don't think I did.

He laid the old notebook open on the blanket beside the Log, and the torn page between them, and looked at the three of them in a row.

Then he turned to the clean page under Second instance in the Log, and drew one line through Two instances is a pattern and the two short sentences after it, so that they could still be read underneath, and under the line he wrote what was true.

That's the column's count. It isn't the count. Here is the count, in order, all of it:

1. The cart. Third day, the merchant road, the dip between the hedges. On the verge before the cart came round the bend. (Old notebook, back pages. Nobody saw. I only have my word.)

2. Renn. Eighth day, the third exchange. Off the line before his third cut. Eyes still on the heel. (The torn page. Vell, Lira, Renn saw.)

3. The drop. Twenty-eighth day, the grey half, Lira's step. Under the backhand. My counter taken out of my hands. (Lira saw. A mark in the dirt.)

4. Dessa. Fiftieth day, the fourth exchange. Across into the closing space. (The yard saw. Her jaw.)

He stopped and read the four of them back.

He had known the sum. He had done it in his head on the night of the drop, sitting here, and decided not to write it. He had thought then that writing it was the step that would make it real. He found now, with the four of them on the page in his own hand, numbered, that it had been real the whole time, and that writing it did not make it any more real than it was. It only made it honest.

Four, he wrote under them. Not two. I've known since the drop. I started the column late on purpose, and I wrote down that I was doing it, and tonight I nearly built a sentence on it anyway.

What the four have in common, as far as I can see it:

No decision. None of them was a thing I chose.

Each one came at the exact moment, never early. Each time there was something coming at me that I couldn't have got out of by myself.

Two of them (the drop, Dessa) left me standing in the coat afterward. Renn, I don't remember how I was standing. The cart, I don't know. Write that down: I don't know.

None of them came when I wanted them to. None of them has ever come back when I reached for it.

That's all I've got. That's all the evidence holds. I'm not going to write down what it is, because I don't know what it is, and anything I wrote would be a guess in the same coat as the facts.

He folded the torn Renn page along its soft creases, carefully, and laid it inside the back cover of the Log, where it would stay flat. He did not put it back in his coat. It did not belong in a pocket any more. It belonged with the rest.

Then he sat with the Log closed on his knee.

He did not feel lighter, exactly. The four were exactly as heavy on the page as they had been in the corner. But they were on the page now, where he could see them and count them and turn them over, and not in the corner where he had to walk round them in the dark. He thought it was like the difference between knowing there was a stone in your boot and taking the boot off.

The stone was still a stone. But you could pick it up and look at it.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Twice since he came to Ardenmere he had handed her half an answer and let her take it for a whole one. He counted them going down the turning stairs, because he was much too awake for sleep and there was nothing else to do with his head. Under the lantern in the lane after Renn he had said instinct, and in the grey half after the drop he had said I don't know, and both had been true. Both had been cut off short at the knee, and both times he had left it to her to decide whether to come back for the rest, and she never had, and tonight, if he could help it, would not be the third.

She was on the step outside the street door, as he had half known she would be. She sat with her back against the frame and her knees drawn up, quite at home there, as if the step were a chair she had owned for years. The lantern over Torvin's door laid her shadow long and thin down the cobbles, and the leaning O above her laid down its own beside it.

By his reckoning she had allowed him one bout's writing-up, near enough to the minute, and he suspected she had counted it.

"First win," she said. "Well?"

"It feels like a data point." He sat on the step below hers. "Five bouts and one win. What I've got works on a patient defender if she has a tell, and if I can make the tell show. That's one sort of fighter. About every other sort, it says nothing so far."

"Mm." She let that lie where he had put it, perfectly friendly and not much impressed. "And underneath the data point?"

He looked at the dark street, and at the lantern light lying on the wet cobbles, and the short answer was right there, ready, the practised one and the cheap one. He did not want to pay that way any more.

"The third exchange I made," he said. "Two weeks of it, and it went exactly as I'd put it together. Ask me why about any step of it and there's an answer, and every answer's mine. I'm proud of it. I paid for it." He turned his right hand over and looked at the split knuckles. "The fourth wasn't like that. The going across, the bit that finished it. That was never in anything I planned, not even close. It didn't feel like a thing I'd built. It felt like a thing I'd—"

There the sentence ran out of road, and he let it stop.

"Borrowed," said Lira.

She set the word down carefully, the way you would put down a full cup on a table in the dark, near enough for him to reach and not pushed toward him at all.

He turned the word about in his head and looked at it from every side he could find before he answered.

"Maybe," he said. "I don't know yet."

She nodded, slowly, and left it there between them on the step, where either of them could pick it up again.

That was the thing in her he still could not name: she could go through the market like a thrown stone, and beat a pie man down to half his price for nothing but the joy of it, and tell him to his face that he was no natural. And then, when it counted, she could sit on a cold step and leave a silence at exactly the size it wanted, not an inch larger. They sat in the sounds of the street. Somewhere a cart went by with its lamp swinging, and two doors along somebody was arguing about a window, and the district went on with its evening and did not care in the least what the registry said.

The rest of it came to him in that quiet, ready to be said.

"In the back of the book tonight I wrote that it was the second time," he said. "Then I sat and looked at it, and it wasn't true, so I wrote down what was." This part wasn't for the street. He shifted round to look at her. "I've been counting from the wrong place, on purpose. Tonight I stopped."

In the lantern light he watched a question come into her eyes, and watched her look at it and then lay it down beside her on the step, carefully, as she had laid down borrowed.

"All right," she said.

"I won't guess at it. If you guess, you put the wrong thing in the book, and then you believe it because it's in the book." He made himself keep going. "Only, the day I'm sure what it is, you're first. Before anybody. Before Hesk."

Lira was quiet for a moment, with her chin on her knees, as if she were weighing the offer in both hands before she took it.

"I'd have been very offended if it had been anybody else."

Then she smiled, the real smile, not the one she spent on strangers or on Marrow, and it reached her eyes and stayed. She knocked her shoulder against his, lightly, the left one, the Renn one, which did not hurt any more. "And it was a good fight. Leave the rest aside a minute. You worked well tonight, Cael. You didn't waste a day of those two weeks."

"Thank you."

"It wasn't me in there with Dessa. I was at the rope biting my knuckle." She stood and put down a hand to pull him off the step, and when he took it she pulled him up carefully, on his good side, out of habit, though he had no bad side tonight. "Come on. Torvin's wife cooks the stew with real vegetables in it on a fighting night, and the brothers eat like wolves, so we'd better be in first."

"I've had a pie."

"You've had half a pie, and that boy's pies are mostly gravy." She opened the door. "Besides, you've the look of somebody who's just written down a thing he's carried for a month and a half. Writing it costs you worse than the fighting does. Nobody tells you that either."

He followed her in under the leaning O, and on the stairs, going up to put the Log away before supper, he was smiling, and had been for some while, and could not have said when it began.

Chapter 27 — Unrated, Over Dessa

[Measured, quietly confident narration; let competence arrive without swagger]

The kitchen at Torvin's was fuller than Cael had ever seen it, and louder, and it smelled of onions.

Torvin's wife had the big iron pot on the range, the one she used for oats in the morning, and it was full to the brim with something brown and thick that had carrots in it, and turnips, and barley, and pieces of what had probably, at some point, been a sheep. She was ladling it out into every bowl in the house with the air of a woman settling an account.

"Five." She put a bowl in front of the place at the end of the bench before Cael had reached it. "I said five. Sit down."

At the far end sat the woman who slept in her boots, arms folded, with no bun. She waited until he was sitting.

"I said never. Don't take it to heart. I'd seen you walk. You walk like a heron."

"Herons are very good at standing still," said Lira, sitting down beside him with her own bowl.

"Herons fall over," said the boots woman darkly.

The brothers were in, because the river was still too high for barges, and they had heard about the bout from a man on the fish steps who had heard it from his cousin. The cousin had been at the rope. They had one question between them, and an argument riding on it: in the fourth, which side of Dessa had he gone round?

"Her right," said Cael. "Across, not back. Inside her guard, on her right."

That was true. The elder brother held out his hand without a word, and the younger put a coin in it, and they went on arguing about something else entirely, happily, and did not ask how.

The wheezing man, who never came down to supper, came down to supper, and sat by the range with his bowl on his knee, and said nothing, and listened to all of it.

Yeni sat at the corner with a shirt across her knee, sewing between spoonfuls, and did not look up once. But when the boots woman said heron a second time, Yeni said, "Herons eat fish whole," without lifting her head. The boots woman did not seem to know what to do with that.

And at the far end of the table, where nobody usually sat, Doss was eating.

He had not been at a supper in all the weeks Cael had been at Torvin's. He sat with his bad leg out straight under the bench and his pipe beside his bowl, unlit, and ate slowly, and listened. Cael understood after a while that he must have come back from the yard to eat before going down to the warehouses. He would have been on his way to his night as soon as the bout was over, and had come here instead, and sat down.

Once, while the brothers were arguing about left and right, Cael looked down the table and found Doss looking at him.

Doss did not smile. He did not say anything. He gave one short nod, a small downward tip of his heavy flattened face, the kind men gave each other across a depot yard in Denvash. Then he went back to his bowl.

Cael sat with it. It weighed more than he would have thought. It was not a congratulation. It was more like a line in a ledger, written by somebody who had once had his own name in a book and then not, who knew exactly what went into the book and what it cost.

Torvin came through from the front room with a second pot, a smaller one, which turned out to be more of the same. He set it on the table by the first, which was empty, and stood a moment with the cloth still in his hand, and considered Cael the way he considered coins.

"Heard you put Dessa on the dirt."

"Yes."

"Good." Torvin wiped his hands on the cloth. He seemed to think about leaving it there, and then not to. "She's sat on top of that yard all season. Every Sunday, same as a clock. Folk have stopped going in against her at all, my wife says, and a yard where nobody goes in against the top is a yard that starts to go stale." He folded the cloth over his arm. "Does a place good to see the top of it move. Does the district good. Reminds folk nobody stays up there for ever." He looked at the empty pot. "Does my rent good, too, if they come to see you again and drink while they're at it. So."

He went back out to the front room.

The table was quiet for a moment.

"That," said Torvin's wife, into the silence, with great satisfaction, "is the most he's said at one go since my sister's wedding."

Lira leaned over to Cael and spoke under the noise that came back after. "Renn's going to be unbearable."

"Renn's up the river."

"Renn left word on the fish steps before he went." She was trying not to smile and failing. "With three different people, so it would get round. He said that if you won anything while he was away, everybody was to know it was his teaching. That he'd given you four exchanges to learn in, out of the goodness of his heart, and you'd been living off them ever since." She ate a spoonful. "The fish man told me this morning. He said Renn was very particular that it should be told properly."

Cael laughed.

He did not decide to. It came up out of him before he knew it was there, loud, a real laugh, unguarded, the sound of it going down the long table and making the brothers look round. He had not heard himself make that sound since a kitchen in Denvash. He had not known until he heard it how long it had been.

Lira looked at him sideways, and did not say anything, and went on eating.

He thought, briefly, while the noise of the table went on round him, of Alis on Weaver's Row with her raised hand. And of Joren, walking home along the canal with his heels down on purpose, working at it. He wondered whether either of them would have known the boy at this table, with dirt still on his neck and a split knuckle and a pie in him and a bowl of Torvin's wife's stew. He was not sure that he would have known him himself, a month and a half ago.

He thought they might. He thought Joren, at least, would have known the laugh.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

He wrote to Hesk that night, at the kitchen table, after the others had gone up.

The house was quiet round him. The range ticked as it cooled. Somewhere behind the low brown door there was no pipe smoke, because Doss had gone down to the warehouses with his leg and his pipe as soon as he had rinsed his bowl.

He worked out the days before he began. It was a habit now. His letter about the pin had gone in the west bag on the thirty-seventh day, and it would have come to Fen Street on about the forty-fourth. Hesk would have read it at the kitchen table that same evening and written back that same night, because that was what Hesk did. His answer would be on a carrier's cart somewhere on the merchant road at this moment, coming east, and it would come to Torvin's on about the fifty-first or fifty-second day. That was tomorrow, or the day after.

It would answer a boy who had seen one man with a pin and did not know what it meant. That boy was a fortnight gone. And this letter, about tonight, would come to Hesk on about the fifty-eighth day, a week after Hesk had already written to the boy with the pin. They were writing past each other, like two people walking toward each other on a long road in the dark, calling out.

He did not mind it as much as he had a fortnight ago. It was the way it was. You said the things that would still be true by the time they got there.

Hesk,

I won tonight.

It was the fifth bout. A woman called Dessa, Copper Rank 5 in the book here, Stone Path, the best defender in the yard. She wins by standing still and letting people beat themselves on her. I sat on a bench and watched her fight twice, a week apart, and wrote down everything she did, the way you taught me to watch a stance. At the end of the second bout I saw a thing she does when she's tired. Her back foot comes down a half beat after the rest of her has set. In the second exchange tonight I made her set herself so many times, on my count and not hers, that it came early. In the third I went into it.

She said afterward that it was the cleanest read anyone had made on her since she came to the yard. The woman who keeps the book wrote a line under the result that she didn't read out, and I read it upside down, and then she told me it was a compliment and not to spend it. I'm trying not to.

I'm all right. Split knuckle on the right hand, nothing else. Torvin's wife cooked something with real vegetables in it.

He stopped there, and held the pencil over the paper, because the next part was the part Hesk had asked for in his last letter. He had been carrying it for two weeks without finding a way to answer it.

Tell me what she's like.

He thought about Lira on the step tonight, setting borrowed down where he could reach it and not pushing it any closer. He thought about her keeping them in the grey half every morning without telling him why, for three weeks, until the morning she did. He thought about her hand on his shoulder in the mist, short and plain. He thought about her biting her knuckle at the rope, and saying Nose in a perfectly flat voice, and telling him he was not a natural because she would not tell lies to anybody she trained. And about her reading the notice twice, standing in the middle of the box drill, and saying This is built.

You asked what Lira is like, he wrote. I've been trying to work it out for two weeks.

She's fifteen. She's quicker than me at everything except watching. She tells me exactly what she thinks, all of it, and then lets me pick it up, and it's always heavier than what other people give me, and it's always the right weight. Every morning she tells me what she saw me do the day before, and I write it down, and she never once tells me what it means. She says that's mine. She's the only person I've met here who asked me what the word felt like from inside, instead of telling me what it meant from outside.

I think she's the first friend I've had who I didn't start out with. Joren I had before I could walk. I had to find this one.

That's as near as I can get. I'll keep trying.

He read it back. It was not enough, and it was true, and he thought Hesk would understand both.

There was one more thing he did not write.

The fourth exchange he left out of the letter. He had told the brothers that he went across instead of back, and that was true, and he told Hesk the same thing in fewer words, in the line about the win. But he did not tell him what had gone across, or that it was not him, or that there were four of them now on a page in the back of the Log in his own hand, numbered.

That made four things he had not told Hesk. He knew the number exactly. He had written in the back of the Log, on the night of the drop, that he would have to answer for all of them at once one day.

He had made a promise tonight, on the step, to somebody else, that she would be first.

He sat with that, and it did not feel like a betrayal of Hesk. It felt like the opposite of what Hesk had done with Tuesdays and the file. Hesk had kept things until he was sure, and then had not told them even then, and Cael had found them out for himself and come to him angry. Cael was keeping this until he was sure, too. But he had told one person that he was keeping it, and why, and that she would be first. And he had written down in the Log that he was keeping it from Hesk, so that it could not hide from him.

It was not the same. He thought it was not the same. He thought he would have to answer for it anyway.

— Cael, he wrote at the bottom, and folded it, and put it in the leather book to keep flat for the morning.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He went up to the yard in the dark the next morning, as he always did, by the lane where the ground began to rise. Lira caught him up at the corner by the chalk board, with the bread under her arm and her breath smoking, and they went up together without saying much.

The old man was in his corner, as he was on every morning Cael had ever passed that gate. There was no light in the yard yet but what came off the sky, grey and thin, and the woman with the shoulder had not come. He stood alone in the shade that was not yet shade, in the stance that looked like nothing else in the lane, with his feet set and his hands loose and his breath going up slow and white.

His pale eyes came round as they reached the gate. They went to Cael's right hand, to the split knuckles, and stayed there a moment, and came back to his face.

"Four," the old man said.

Cael stopped. Lira stopped beside him.

The old man's eyes went back to the wall. Cael thought that was all, as it had been all after Amrit, and had half turned to go on up the lane, when the old man spoke again, to the wall.

"You went the long side."

Cael looked at him.

"In the fourth. When she came at you." The old man shifted his weight, the small shift from one foot to the other. "That groove's longer one way than the other. Always has been. You knew it, and you went back along the long way to buy yourself two steps. That was well thought." He was quiet for a moment. "She cut across it. Took both your steps off you before you'd finished taking them."

"Yes."

"She'll know now that you know it's there. So will every fighter who was at that rope with their eyes open, and a few of them had their eyes open." The pale eyes came back to him, not old at all. "A thing like that works once. After that it's a habit, and somebody plans for it. Find another."

"I will."

"I know you will. That's why I'm telling you." The stillness came down over him again like a lid, and that was all.

They went on up the lane. Lira did not say anything until they were past the next two gates, and then she said, in a voice that was trying very hard to sound wounded and not managing it at all, "Five months. I've walked past that gate every morning for five months. I won a bout in the summer by a whole exchange, and he has never once told me about a groove."

"Maybe you didn't go the long side."

"I didn't know there was a long side." She shifted the bread to her other arm, as if it had offended her. "I'm going to go and measure it. With string. This afternoon."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Her report, in the grey half, was the longest she had ever given him.

She gave it walking the box drill at the slow speed, as always, with frost on the dirt and the crows along the eaves. She did not look at him once.

"First exchange. You showed her three feints and stopped. You didn't show her a fourth. Most people show her six. You touched her guard four times and shook your right hand after the third, so I knew it hurt." Back left. "Second exchange. You came in off the half beat nine times. I counted. You changed sides eleven. You let yourself get too close once, about halfway, and got out again before I'd finished breathing in. Your feet were quicker than I've ever seen them." Front right. "When she went back to her mark after the second, your eyes went to her back foot. I saw them go. Then you looked at her face, and then at nothing, and you stood still for so long that the man next to me said you'd frozen."

"I hadn't frozen."

"I know you hadn't. I'm telling you what he said." Back right. "Third exchange. You went into the gap before her foot came down. I couldn't tell you how long before; it was quicker than I can see. You hit her under the left forearm, and she went back, and you were going left before her weight dropped. Your feet went before her hips did. I watched them." Front left. She stopped walking.

"Fourth exchange," she said.

He waited.

"She came forward. Three steps. You gave her the long side of the circle, and she cut across it, and the groove was at your heel." Lira was quiet for a moment, looking at the dirt between her own feet. "And then you were going backward, and then you weren't going backward. And then you were inside her guard." She looked up at him at last. "That's all I've got. That's all I saw. I'm not going to tell you any more than I saw."

"I know."

"Write it down, then."

He wrote it down that evening, all of it, in the evidence column, in her words, with her mark beside it. When he came to the fourth exchange he wrote exactly what she had said, then you were going backward, and then you weren't, and nothing else, and he did not put anything in the third column beside it.

She tore the bread in half and gave him the larger piece.

"Vell says not this Sunday," she said, through hers. "She told me last night, when you'd gone to write it up. Rest your hands, she says. She'll have somebody the week after." She swallowed. "And Renn's still held, if he's back by the turn of the month."

"Did she say who?"

"She said she hadn't decided, and when she had she'd tell you, and not before, and not because you asked." Lira's mouth did something at the corner. "I think she says it to everybody. I think she's said it so many times she doesn't hear herself any more."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The pie boy was nailing the result to the board when they came down to the crossroads.

He had a hammer in one hand and three nails in his mouth, and a sheet of paper flat against the board with the heel of his other hand. It was the back of a bill for something, written in Vell's upright pencil, and he was nailing it up over the corner of last Sunday's card, where it would be the first thing anybody saw. There were already six or seven people standing round the board in the cold, waiting for him to finish so that they could read it. When he had got the third nail in, he stepped back and took the hammer out of the way, and they read it.

Result, Thursday: unrated (vouched) over Dessa (Cu 5, Stone), fourth exchange, conceded.

Cael stood at the back of the little crowd and read it over their heads.

There was no name in it. He had known there would not be. The board said what the book said, and the book said unrated, and that was what he was.

A man at the front read it aloud to the woman beside him, who could not see over his shoulder. "Unrated over Dessa," he said. "That's the boy. The one from Torvin's. The thin one."

"What's his name?"

"Don't know. Cael, somebody said. Something like that."

Lira, beside him, said nothing. She did not look at him. But he felt her not looking at him, and he knew she had heard it too.

Something like that.

He thought about Vell at her table on the Sunday morning, saying When the yard comes to see you, I'll write it. He had thought then that it was a strange rule. He thought now that he understood it a little better. Some of the yard had come to see him last night. Some of it had said his name. A man at the board this morning knew it, nearly. But the yard had come last night to see Dessa, mostly, and to find out whether the thin boy would last. That was not the same as coming to see the thin boy. When it was the same, he thought, Vell would know it before he did.

He did not mind waiting for it. That surprised him, and he looked at the surprise, standing at the back of the crowd with his hands in his pockets, and found it was true.

The book knew what he had done. Every line of it was something Vell had seen from her stool, in her own hand, and every word was true. It did not have a word in square brackets in it anywhere. It had unrated, and vouched, and over Dessa, and a line underneath that he was not supposed to have read.

That was enough to be going on with.

"That's you," said Lira, at last, very quietly.

"That's me."

She bumped his shoulder with hers and turned away toward the four lanes, and he went the other way, down toward the river.

[Steady, observant narration; let place, distance, and social position register]

He went by the lane of the river workshops, because it was the way to the carriers' hut, and because he wanted to.

The mender was in his doorway with the loupe in his eye and a clock on the bench. He did not talk in the mornings, and it was still the morning, though not by much. But as Cael came level with the door he took the loupe out and looked up, at Cael's face, and then at the split knuckles of his right hand. They were scabbed now and stiff, and he had been holding the hand a little away from his coat without noticing.

"Something broken?" said the mender.

Cael stopped in the street.

"No," he said. "Something worked."

The mender looked at him for a moment longer, the checking look, the one he gave a frame before he leaned on the lever. Then he grunted. It might have been approval. It might only have been a man clearing his throat on a cold morning. He put the loupe back in his eye.

"Wednesday," he said, to the clock.

The carriers' hut was busy. The west bag was hanging on its hook on the back wall, half full, with WEST painted on it in tall black letters, and the clerk with the inky fingers was behind the counter weighing a parcel on the little brass balance. Cael waited his turn. He thought about the old woman in the shawl saying because the clerk is young and thinks it's clever to know things, and looked at the clerk, who was perhaps nineteen and had ink on his cuff as well as his fingers, and who was not looking at anybody in particular.

He had decided this on the cooper's roof, and written down that he had decided it: same hut, same bag, nothing on the outside but what they already had. When it was his turn he handed the letter across. The clerk read the address aloud in his flat voice, 14 Fen Street, Outer District, Denvash, and weighed it, and named the price, and dropped it in the bag.

"Torvin's," the clerk said, looking up. "Isn't it."

"Yes," said Cael, and let the clerk see nothing in his face but a boy posting a letter home.

"Thought so." The clerk seemed pleased with himself. "There's nothing come back for you yet. West cart's only just in. If there's anything, the runner'll have it up to you by evening."

Cael looked past him, out through the open side of the hut onto the landing.

The west cart was standing at the bottom of the fish steps with its tailboard down, a long carrier's wagon with a canvas tilt over its back and two tired horses steaming in the cold. The carter was handing sacks of post down to a boy on the landing, and three passengers had climbed down off the tail and were standing about, stiff from two days on a board. One was a woman with a child. One was an old man with a crate of something that clinked.

The third was a man of about forty, in a plain dark coat creased from the road, with the collar turned up against the wind off the river. He had a small travelling bag in one hand. Under his other arm he held a flat leather case, the kind clerks carried papers in, and he was holding it in a particular way that Cael noticed without meaning to notice it. He held it loosely, against his side, the way you carry something that has very little in it, as if he had expected it to be heavier and had stopped being surprised that it was not.

The man looked up the fish steps at the district, the long slope of roofs going up toward the yards, and the haze over the market, and the leaning chimneys. He looked at it as Cael had looked at the city from the rise on his first evening, as something he would have to learn.

Then he turned to the boy on the landing and asked him something. The boy pointed up the steps, to the top, where the squat brown building stood with its board of notices that nobody read.

The man nodded, and picked up his bag, and went up the steps toward it.

Cael watched him go for perhaps two breaths. He watched him as he watched everybody, without deciding to. A stranger off the west cart, tired, with a thin case and his collar up, going to the post. Then the clerk said "Next," behind him, and somebody pushed past him to the counter with a parcel, and he stepped out of the way and turned toward the steps himself.

He did not write the man down.

He would think about that afterward. In a month and a half in Ardenmere he had written down nearly every stranger he had seen: the polite man at Torvin's door, the grey coat in the market, the old woman in her shawl, the Fenrow Iron, the Blade man from across the district. He wrote things down. It was what he did. It was the thing he had done before he had anything else.

But it was the morning after the first win of his life, and the sun had come out over the river, thin and cold and very bright. He had a letter in the west bag and a split knuckle and four pages that had turned into a fight, and four more lines in the back of a book that had turned into the truth. There was a girl somewhere up in the four lanes who would be first. He went up the fish steps two at a time, into the light, past the brown building with its door already shutting behind somebody, and did not look at it.

He was thinking about Sunday week, and who Vell would put across from him, and how he would watch them.

Chapter 28 — The Thin File

[Dry, precise narration; hold institutional pressure beneath the ordinary details]

Coss read the file for the fourth time with the lamp pulled close and the desk rocking under his elbow every time he turned a sheet.

The rocking came from the left front leg. Somebody had once folded a scrap of paper under it to make it sit level. The scrap had worked itself out since then, and lay on the floorboards a hand's width from where it was needed, grey with dust, as though it had given up. Coss had noticed it in his first minute in the room and had not picked it up. It was not his desk. The ring-stains on its top were the cups of other men, sent out here before him on other errands and gone again, and one of them had carved a small neat letter into the corner by the inkwell, an R or a B, and then thought better of it and stopped.

The room was over the front room of the post, up a stair so narrow that he had carried his bag up it sideways. It had one window, which looked down the fish steps to the river. Under the window there was a cot along the wall, and there was a chair, the desk, and a partition of planks between this room and the next one that did not quite reach the ceiling. Through it, earlier, he had heard somebody cough on the other side, and then a door, and then nothing.

He had slept in a great many rooms like it. He did not mind them. A borrowed room had nothing in it to distract you, which was more than could be said for most rooms a man owned.

He laid the six sheets out across the desk in the order he had taken them from the case, as he would have laid out tools on a bench, and looked at them all together.

Coss had been a field agent of the Guilds Compact for eleven years, and he was forty-one, and somewhere around his fourth year he had made his peace with not being a brilliant man.

He had shared a desk that year with a man who was. The man saw patterns everywhere: in the dates on a run of permits, in which way a witness looked when she lied, in the order a family hung its washing. About a third of the patterns were real. The other two thirds were the man's own cleverness, reflected back at him off things that meant nothing, and he could not tell the thirds apart, because to him they all shone the same. He had gone on finding them, faster and faster, until a report of his sent four agents into a valley after a smuggling ring that was only three farmers who did not like each other. After that he had been moved to a records office in a town on the coast, where he copied other men's reports into a ledger, and was not unhappy, and wrote a very fine hand.

Coss had watched all of that from the other side of their desk and taken a lesson from it that he had never once had cause to regret. Brilliance found things, but it found false things nearly as easily as true ones. Attention, put down patiently day after day and year after year, found the true things in the end, and very seldom found the false ones, because it was too slow and too dull to be fooled by its own shine.

So he had chosen attention. Most files were exactly as dull as they looked, and the few that were not usually said so early, if you were listening.

This one was not saying anything. That was what kept him at the desk with the lamp.

The first sheet was a copy of the registration. Caelen Hesk-ward. Registration 41-7843-V. The certifying office was on a street called Weaver's Row, in Denvash, and the officer was a Warden-Adjunct named Pellin, whose signature was small and quick and gave nothing away. The date of the Kindling was in the autumn, fifty-odd days ago. On the line for the classification there was one word in square brackets, stamped, and no tier, no rank and no Path.

The second sheet was the residential notice under Statute 14, Section 9. He knew the form, though he had never had cause to serve one, and he knew what it had been written to do. It took a residence away from a person in one line and then told whoever held the standing, very politely, what it would cost them to keep that person close.

The third sheet was a gate entry. Denvash, Outer gate, eastbound, on foot. It was dated the third day after the Kindling. It was passive, which meant that a guard had read the card in the ordinary way and the record had marked it and nobody had been asked to do anything about it. Eastbound from Denvash, on foot, was the merchant road, and the merchant road came here in two days, and anybody who knew the road would have guessed this city. That part was not strange.

The fourth sheet was the request for the sweep, routed to Ardenmere about three weeks after the gate entry. It carried an authorization code in the place where a name should have been, and one line of instruction.

Confirm location, status, and compliance.

The fifth was the sweep's return, in a clerk's round hand. Location: a lodging house known as Torvin's, Unranked District. Status: resident. Compliance: nothing observed. It was signed by the clerk of this post, per the report of the officer who had walked it.

The sixth sheet was Coss's own brief, which told him to follow up the sweep, confirm what it had confirmed, and summon the subject for compliance evaluation as procedure required.

That was all of it. He had carried six sheets of paper two days east on the merchant road in a case built for sixty, and he had known on the first morning out of Denvash that the case was light. He had stopped being surprised about it somewhere around the first milestone.

He was not surprised now. He was doing what he did with any file that bothered him, which was to set down, one at a time, not what it said but what it ought to have said and did not.

A non-standard result at Kindling set a procedure going. He had never handled a SHATTERED file himself; he did not know anybody who had. But he had handled three files for results the standard framework had trouble with, and they had all grown the same way, in the same order, as faithfully as a tree grows rings. The certifying district wrote a preliminary risk assessment within the first week, because the certifying district was frightened of being blamed for anything that came after. Then a residential compliance note followed, setting out what the household's standing now was and what it was likely to become. Then there was a cross-reference to the standing-holder's own file, because the residential notice threatened a guild review in so many words. When the Compact notified a guild under that statute, the guild opened its review by its own procedure, and the review had a number, and the number went into the file.

Denvash had a compliance office that produced risk assessments as regularly as a bakery produces bread. There was none here. There was no residential note beyond the notice itself. There was no cross-reference to any review. And at the head of the file, where every case he had ever been handed carried its case number in red ink, there was nothing at all. Nobody had opened a case. There was no handler named, nobody whose desk this sat on between visits.

It was not a case. It was some papers in a case.

He had once, on a training course in his second year, been shown a SHATTERED file from the archive, as a curiosity, by an instructor who liked curiosities. It had been very old and very thick. He did not remember anything that was in it. He remembered the thickness, and the way the instructor had had to use both hands.

He sat back. The desk rocked.

Then he took out the register.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Every field agent carried one. It was a small black book, newly printed each spring, that listed the authorization codes of every office an agent might lawfully take an instruction from, so that he would know a true order from a forged one. Coss's was this spring's. He had checked that before he left, as he checked it every spring, because a register a season out of date was worse than no register at all.

He laid the request for the sweep beside it and found the code.
