The mender was at his bench before it was properly light, with a lamp lit beside him and a clock open on the cloth. He did not look up when Cael stopped in the doorway, because it was the morning and he did not talk in the mornings.

"I can't come this afternoon," Cael said. "I'm sorry. Something's come that I have to answer by tomorrow."

The mender turned a screw a quarter turn and looked at it through the loupe. He turned it back an eighth. Cael waited, and was about to go, when the mender took the loupe out of his eye and looked, not at Cael, but at the doorframe beside him, where the four words were cut into the wood and filled with black paint.

Then he put the loupe back in.

"Wednesday," he said, to the clock.

Lira was waiting at the head of the fish steps with her right arm held a little stiffly at her side and a loaf under her left. She had tied her hair back the ordinary way again, with the knot coming loose on one side. The brown building stood beside her with its board of notices and its shut door, exactly as it had stood every morning for seven weeks. Cael could not look at it now without seeing a man in a dark coat climbing its steps off a cart.

"Shoulder?"

"The size of a loaf. I told you." She held up the real loaf. "Breakfast's between. Not before."

They went round the side of the building, on the river side, where a narrow paved walk ran between the post and the top of the river wall. Halfway along it three stone steps went down to a door below the level of the street. There was a board nailed beside it, as weathered as the one on the front, and somebody long ago had painted on it in careful letters: REGISTRY READING ROOM. OPEN TO ALL REGISTRANTS. MORNINGS.

Cael read it twice. He had walked past this building perhaps fifty times. He had never once come round this side of it.

"Told you," said Lira. "Nobody reads it."

He went down the three steps and opened the door.

The room was half under the ground, long and low, with a row of small windows set high up in the outer wall at the level of the walk, so that the light came in from above and the only things you could see through the windows were the feet of people going past. It smelled of paper and damp stone and lamp oil. Shelves ran down both long walls from the floor to the ceiling, and down the middle there was one long table, scarred, with three chairs at it and a lamp on a hook above.

At the far end, behind a smaller table of his own, sat an old man.

He was thin and grey and dry-looking, as though he had been kept on a shelf himself for years, and he had a pencil behind each ear and a book open in front of him that he was not reading. He looked up as they came in, at Cael and then at Lira, and then at the hour on a clock above the door, which said that the room had been open for perhaps four minutes. He did not seem surprised. He did not seem anything.

"Halden," he said. It appeared to be the whole of his greeting.

"I'd like the procedure for compliance evaluations," said Cael. "And whatever there is on non-standard classifications. And anything that tells you how the two connect."

Halden looked at him for a moment longer, the length of a breath, and in that breath Cael saw him take in the hour, and the boy's age, and the girl with the stiff arm, and decide not to ask a single question about any of it. Then he got up, slowly, and walked down the room to the left-hand shelves without saying anything. He took down one volume, and then reached higher for another, and then stooped for a third from a bottom shelf, and brought all three back and set them on the long table under the lamp, side by side.

"Handbook," he said, tapping the first, which was thick and newish and bound in brown. "District edition. Copied fresh four years ago." He tapped the second, which was thin and old and so brittle at the spine that it had been tied round with a tape. "Supplementary register. Non-standard designations. Nobody's copied it in my time, and I've been here nineteen years. Mind the binding." He tapped the third, which was fat and grey. "Index. Tells you where everything is in the other two, and is wrong about a third of it."

He went back to his own table and sat down and did not look at them again.

Cael lit the lamp over the long table. Lira sat down at the end with the index and opened it as if it might bite.

Above their heads, through the boards of the ceiling, somebody walked across a room. Cael heard it quite clearly: four steps, a pause, three more, the scrape of a chair. Then a sound began that he could not place at first, a soft regular knock of wood on wood, tock, a pause, tock, a pause, irregular but steady, like a slow clock that was not keeping time.

He looked up at the ceiling.

"That's him," said Lira, very quietly, without looking up from the index. "Isn't it."

"I don't know."

He did know. Somebody was sitting at a desk directly above them and writing, and the desk had a leg that did not sit flat, so that it knocked on the floor whenever the man leaned on it. He was reading the law that the man had used, in the man's own building, under the man's feet.

He opened the handbook.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

It was the hardest reading he had ever done.

It was not the words. He knew most of the words. It was that the words had been put together by somebody who did not want them to be found by anybody who did not already know where they were. Every section began by saying what it applied to and then said that this was subject to another section, and the other section was in another part. Sentences went on for half a page before their verbs arrived. A thing would be defined on one page as one thing and then, forty pages later, used as though it meant something slightly different, and the only way to know which was to have read both.

He read it the way he had read Renn's heel and Brenna's dip and Dessa's foot, and the way Hesk had taught him to read a load sheet with its headings torn off. He made a list on a clean page of the Log as he went, a line for every section he passed. He wrote down not what it said but what it was for.

Part One: who may be summoned. Part Two: how. Part Three: where. Part Four: what the evaluation is. This one says nothing; it points at two others. Either that's lazy or it's hiding something. Follow it.

He followed it.

The first thing he found that looked like a seam was in Part Two, an hour in, and for a few minutes his heart went fast.

A person under the age of sixteen years shall be summoned through the holder of the household standing under which that person resides.

He read it twice, and then a third time, because it was very nearly too good. The summons had not gone to any household standing. It had gone to him, by his own name, to a lodging house. If a person under sixteen had to be summoned through the holder of his standing, then the summons had been served on the wrong person and was no good, and would have to be done again, through Hesk, in Denvash, two days' road away and a week's post.

He looked for where it was qualified, because nothing in this book was ever allowed to stand on its own. He found the qualification in a note at the foot of the next page, in smaller print.

Where the household standing of such a person has been revoked under the statute governing non-standard classifications, the person answers in his own person from the age of fourteen years.

He sat back.

Statute 14, Section 9. The notice in the back of the old notebook, the one that took the house off him in one line and then told Hesk very politely what it would cost to keep him near. He had thought, at the kitchen table with the teapot, that it had only taken a house. It had done more than that. It had made him, before the law, a man of fourteen with nobody standing between him and a summons. Nobody would ever be sent a paper on his behalf again. They would be sent to him.

It was not a seam. It was a wall, and it had been built on the second morning after Kindling, and he had not even known it was there.

He sat with that for longer than he could spare. Then he wrote it down, plainly, in the list, Part Two: under sixteen goes through the standing-holder, except mine is gone, so it comes to me. Closed. Then he turned the page. There were thirty-odd hours left by his count, and the wall was not going anywhere.

The second false seam took him most of the next hour.

It was in Part Three, where the book said what could be done to a person who did not come. A filing for physical retrieval shall be countersigned by the registering officer of the district in which the person resides. At first he thought this might be something. A filing that needed a second signature needed a second man willing to sign it. But he found, in the index, after Lira had found the right page of the index for him, sighing, that the registering officer of an Unranked district was whoever kept the district's registrations. On this side of the river that was the clerk who sat at the counter in the front room of this very building, a floor above his head and a few paces to the left.

Part Three: retrieval needs a countersignature. The countersigner is the clerk upstairs. Closed.

The third one was not even a false seam. It was the index going in a circle. Section 40 of the handbook said see the Supplementary Register for designations not provided for here. The index sent him to the Register. The Register's own front page sent him back to section 40 of the handbook. He went round twice before he was sure he had not missed a turning. Then he wrote the index goes round in a circle at 40 and drew a small circle beside it. He felt, for the first time that morning, close to laughing, which he took as a sign that he was tired.

Upstairs the knock had stopped and started and stopped. Through the high windows, feet went past on the walk: boots, a pair of clogs, a dog's legs, a child's.

At noon, Lira shut the index with both hands.

"I'm no use with this," she said. She said it without any shame at all, as a fact about herself, like fast, not strong. "I read too quick. I read the page and I've got it and then I've got it wrong, because the next page says the first page didn't mean what it said. You read slow and you don't trust anything. That's what this book wants." She stood up and pushed her chair in. "I'm going to go and listen."

"To what?"

"To the district." She tipped her head at the ceiling. "He's been here three days. He's asked people things. Somebody's heard every one of them, because somebody always does. I want to know what he asked and where, and especially where he didn't." She picked up the loaf, tore it, put half on the long table beside his elbow and kept the other half. "You eat that. I'll find you at dusk."

She went out. Halden, at his table, watched her go without lifting his head, and then looked back at his book.

Cael ate the bread over the handbook, carefully, so that no crumbs went into the binding, and went back to section 40.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

He found it a little after the middle of the afternoon, and he very nearly did not.

He had gone back to Part Four, which said what a compliance evaluation was, because everything else had come to walls. He had read it once already, in the first hour, and found nothing in it but a definition. He read it again now, slowly, every word, and when he came to the end of the section he did not turn the page. He looked at the foot of it instead, at the band of very small print below the last line, where the book kept its notes. He had stopped reading the notes some time in the second hour because there were so many of them and they were so small.

A compliance evaluation shall assess the person summoned against the benchmarks of that person's recognized tier and Path, as these are set down in the standard evaluation framework.

And under it, in print so small that he had to bring the lamp down on its hook to read it:

Note 3. For classifications not recognized within the standard framework, see Supplementary Register, statute 19.

He untied the tape round the brittle volume with great care and opened it. The pages were brown at the edges and soft as cloth, and the print was older and blacker and cramped, and he found statute 19 a third of the way through.

Designations listed in the Second Appendix to this Register are not recognized within the standard evaluation framework. A person bearing such a designation may be evaluated only under senior evaluation authorization, and shall not be evaluated by standard district procedure.

He turned to the back of the volume. There were two appendices. The second began on a page that had come loose from the binding and been tucked back in, slightly crooked, by somebody's careful hand. At its head was a subheading he knew. He had copied it in a green book's handwriting at a table under a north window in Denvash, on the second morning after Kindling, and had not seen it since.

Deprecated and Non-Standard Designations, Pre-Compact Era Holdovers.

And under it, among the cramped black lines, his word, in its square brackets, with the same cold short sentence about practitioner safety risk that he could have recited in his sleep.

He did not move.

Then he made himself lay it out in order, as Hesk laid out a calculation before he let anybody hang a weight on it.

The summons ordered a standard compliance evaluation. A standard compliance evaluation assessed a person against the benchmarks of their recognized tier and Path, as the standard framework set them down. SHATTERED was not recognized within the standard framework; statute 19 said so, and the Second Appendix listed it by name. A person bearing a designation in the Second Appendix could be evaluated only under senior authorization, and not by standard district procedure.

So the evaluation the summons ordered could not be done. Not by this man, at this desk, in this district, under this procedure. The regulation said so in its own words. You only had to follow it from a note at the foot of a page to a brittle book nobody had copied in nineteen years, and on to an appendix that had come loose from its binding.

He did not let himself feel anything about it yet.

He had been wrong before about smaller things. He had been sure of Renn's figure right up until the third cut came up the lane. He had read a supplier's printed number and trusted it, and watched a bracket fail on the rig at less than twice its working load. A thing could look like a seam and be a wall with a crack painted on it.

So he did what Hesk did. Hesk read every load figure aloud before he signed the sheet, under his breath, because a figure said aloud had to get past your ears as well as your eyes, and ears were harder to fool.

He read the three passages aloud, in order, under his breath, in the hush of the half-buried room, with the lamp swinging a little on its hook above him. Part Four, note 3, statute 19, the appendix. Then the logic, step by step, out loud.

It held.

He read it aloud a second time, slower. It held. He read it a third time, starting from the other end, from the appendix back up to the summons, the way you check a column of figures by adding it from the bottom. It held. He read it a fourth time, the slowest of all, trying with every line to find the place where it would give, the way he had leaned on the bracket with his thumb on the bench at Fen Street, feeling for the bend.

Read a fourth time, it stood just as it had stood the first. Sitting there, he understood that this was the one test he would ever be able to trust, the only thing that told a true find from a hoped-for one. It was not how it felt when you found it. It was whether it was still standing after you had done your best to knock it down.

Something in his chest let go, very slightly. It was not relief, not yet. It was the small, plain satisfaction of a figure that had been traced back to where it came from. He let himself have it for exactly one breath. Then he took out the Log.

He copied all three passages word for word, with the section and note and statute and appendix, and the shelf each volume had come from, and the note about the loose page. He did it fast the first time, just to have it down, in case the lamp failed or the room shut or the building fell in. Then he turned the page and did it again, slowly, in the careful hand he kept for things that mattered, with every number checked against the book as he wrote it. He had a feeling, sitting there, that of all the pages in the Log this one would be read by more people than any other, and that some of them would be looking for a mistake.

Upstairs the knock had stopped. As he blotted the second copy he heard a chair go back above him, and footsteps cross the floor, and go down a stair somewhere inside the building, and a door open and shut. Through the high window at the end of the room he saw a pair of dark trouser legs and good plain boots go past along the walk toward the river, unhurried, and out of sight.

Halden came down the room at dusk to take the volumes back to their shelves.

He picked up the handbook and looked at the place where Cael's slip of paper still marked Part Four. He picked up the brittle register and tied its tape round it again, with old, careful fingers, and settled the loose page of the appendix back into the binding where it belonged. "Most of the people who walk out of here looking that pleased," he said, "are wrong about something." He did not say it unkindly. He said it as a carpenter might mention that a chisel was sharper than it looked. "If it turns out you're one of them, come back. I'll find you the next book."

The sky over the river had gone green and gold behind the core's walls, and the lanterns were coming on along the fish steps. Lira was sitting on the river wall at the top of the steps with her bad arm in her lap and her heels drumming against the stone. She jumped down when she saw him, and looked at his face, and he watched her read it.

They walked along the river toward Torvin's, the long way, because it was the way he went, and she told him what the district had told her.

The man in the dark coat had eaten at Amrit's on his first night and his third, alone, at the end of the long table by the window. Amrit had given him a bowl of the fish stew and exactly the ordinary amount of bread. He had asked at the carriers' hut which bag went west and when, and the clerk had told him a good deal more than that. He had stood at the foot of the lane of yards on Saturday afternoon for about as long as it took to read the board of yard prices, and then gone away again down toward the dyers'. On Sunday he had bought two skewers at the cart in the triangle while the yard was shouting for Brenna going down. He had asked the skewer woman what was on, and been told the circuit, and asked nothing more.

"Nobody in the yards was asked anything," Lira said. "Not one person. Not about you, not about fighters, not about the Cinder House. I asked the girls on the wall. They'd have told me. They tell me everything, mostly to annoy me." She looked at him sideways. "He doesn't know. Or he doesn't think it matters. Either way he walked right past it."

Cael thought about the margin of the Log, and three lines in it, and a polite man at Torvin's door a month ago asking for the circuit kid.

He did not say anything yet. He did not have it in a shape he could say. But he turned it over all the rest of the way home along the river in the dusk, and it did not get any lighter.

Chapter 32 — Three Flat Sentences

[Dry, precise narration; hold institutional pressure beneath the ordinary details]

He wrote the first draft at the kitchen table that night, after the others had gone up, and it was a page and a half long, and it was terrible, and he could not see why.

He had the three passages copied out in the careful hand at the top of the Log page. Under them he had the logic laid out in four steps, just as he had read it aloud in the reading room. All he had to do was put the two together on a clean sheet for a man in a dark coat to read. He had thought it would take a quarter of an hour.

It took him until the range had gone cold.

Every sentence he wrote wanted another sentence after it to hold it up. He would write that a standard evaluation assessed a person against a recognized tier and Path. Then he would find himself writing that he understood this might seem a narrow reading, but that he believed it was the plain sense of the section. He would set down statute 19, and then, without deciding to, add that he did not mean to suggest the evaluation was improper. He only meant that it could not proceed in the form the summons gave. He wrote that he hoped he would not be thought to be avoiding anything. He wrote that he was willing to be evaluated by whatever procedure the regulation did allow. He wrote, at the bottom, that he was sorry for any trouble it caused.

He read it all back, and it read like a boy standing at a desk with his hands behind his back, explaining.

Torvin's wife came down once, in her shawl, for something she had forgotten. She looked at him, and at the pages, and at the cold range, and she did not say anything. She cut a heel off the loaf and put it beside his elbow with a cup of milk, and went back up.

He crossed out the sentence about trouble. He crossed out the one about not avoiding anything. He read it again and it was better and it was still wrong. The wrongness was in something he could not put his pencil on, like a bracket that held at working load and bent at twice it and left you no mark to show where.

He slept for perhaps four hours. He dreamed that he was reading the handbook and every note at the foot of every page said see the note above, and woke with the window grey and his hand on the Log.

The frost was thick again in the grey half. Lira was sitting on the low wall at the side of the yard with her coat buttoned to the chin and her right arm inside it, not in the sleeve, and the bread on her knee.

"Don't ask about the shoulder," she said. "Give it to me."

He gave her the sheet.

She read it the way she read a bout from the barrel, which was the way she read anything she was not immediately sure of: once fast, to have the whole shape, and then again slowly, stopping, going back. She did not say anything. A crow came down onto the eaves of the public house and looked at them both and went away again.

"The law's right," she said at last.

"I know the law's right. I read it four times."

"I know you did." She tapped a line two-thirds of the way down with one finger of her good hand. "This. You've put down what statute 19 says. It's a fact, and you're stating it like a fact, and that's good. But then there's this whole next part." She ran her finger along it. "I understand that the summons was issued in good faith, and I do not wish to suggest that any officer has acted improperly, but I believe that on a close reading." She looked up. "Who's that for?"

"Him."

"No. It's for the argument you think he's going to make. You've written his argument for him, in advance, so that you can answer it." She shook her head. "You don't do that in a bout. You don't stand on your mark before the first exchange and say to Vell, I know he's going to come in high, and I want everyone to know I've thought about it. You just stand there. You let him come in high, and then he finds out."

"Somebody's going to argue with it. He's going to argue."

"Then let him find his own argument. He won't, because there isn't one. You read it four times; you know there isn't one. But you won't show him there isn't one by sounding frightened that there might be." She took the pencil out of his hand without asking and drew a line through the whole of the bracing part, neatly, so that the words could still be read under it, as he did in the Log. "Cut all that. You want three sentences. Flat. Like things that are already settled."

"Say them."

She thought about it with her head on one side and the pencil against her lip.

"A standard compliance evaluation can only assess a classification the standard framework recognizes." She wrote it at the bottom of the page in her quick slanting hand. "SHATTERED is not recognized within that framework." She wrote that. "The evaluation named in this summons cannot proceed under standard procedure." She wrote it, and put the pencil down. "Then the numbers. Then your name. Then stop."

He read the three sentences.

They were better at once, as much better as a bout became the moment you stopped explaining your plan to yourself in the middle of an exchange and simply did the next thing. There was nothing in them to take hold of. There was nothing in them that asked for anything, or hoped for anything, or was sorry. They lay on the page like three flat stones set in a stream, and you could walk across them.

"You want it to read like somebody who knows the law, not somebody who's scared of it," Lira said. "Being sure doesn't change what's true. All being sure changes is how often a man argues back from sheer habit."

"I am scared."

"I know you are." She said it plainly. "The page needn't know."

She gave him back the sheet. He sat on the wall beside her and wrote it out again clean, from the beginning, on a fresh page torn from the back of the old notebook. He wrote the three sentences, and then the handbook part and section and note, the register and the statute, and the appendix and the place where its page had come loose. Then he wrote Cael Hesk-ward, Registration 41-7843-V, and nothing after. It was eleven lines long. The first draft had been fifty.

Lira read it over his shoulder.

"That's good," she said. "That's very good. They made us read Compact paper at the academy, pages of it, so we'd know what a guild letter looked like when we got one." She made a face at the memory. "That doesn't read like a boy who found the law yesterday in a cellar with an old man pretending not to watch him. It reads like somebody who's been doing this for years and is a bit bored by it."

"Halden wasn't watching."

"Everybody in a reading room's watching." She broke the bread in half with her good hand and her teeth, and gave him his half. "You'll be all right this afternoon. I've read the page. The page is right."

She would not let him sit on the wall after that. She made him walk the box drill at the slow speed while she called the corners from the wall with her arm inside her coat. His hands were shaking, she said, and he would be no use at a desk with his hands shaking, and the box would give them something to do. She was right. By the time the sun came down the east wall into the yard and there was no grey half left, his feet were going to the corners by themselves, and his hands had stopped.

[Steady, observant narration; let place, distance, and social position register]

The post kept its hours by a clock on the wall of the front room, behind the counter, and when he came in out of the cold it said a quarter to the second hour after noon. He had come early, because he was always early, and because the paper said during the hours the post is open, and he did not want there to be any argument about which hours those were.

There was one bench, against the wall opposite the counter, under a board of notices exactly as unread as the one outside. He sat on it with the Log on his knee and the folded sheet inside the Log's front cover.

The clerk behind the counter was a sandy, soft man with ink on the side of his hand, and he was in the middle of a dispute.

Two men stood in front of him. One was a cooper; Cael knew him by sight from the lane of workshops, the one beside the man who made only buckets. The other had blue hands to the wrist from the dye sheds. Between them on the counter was a sheet of paper with two roofs drawn on it in chalk and a gutter between them.

"You told us Tuesday," said the man with the blue hands. "It's Tuesday."

"I said if you were still cross," said the clerk.

"I'm still cross."

"So am I," said the cooper.

The clerk looked at the two of them with the expression of a man who has been given a pig he did not order. Then he took a length of knotted string from under the counter and laid it along the chalk gutter, very seriously, while both men watched the string as if it might change sides.

"Still two knots," he said.

Cael watched the string. Everybody in this district, he thought, had a string. Lira had a string, and the clerk at the post had a string, and the old man in the yards probably had a string somewhere, and had never needed it. He wanted, absurdly, to laugh, and knew that if he did it would come out as something else, so he did not.

He opened the Log to the careful page and read the three passages one more time, silently, his lips hardly moving.

He had learned in the circle that the moment before an exchange was worse than the exchange. His body knew, somewhere under thinking, that waiting cost more than doing, and would not be talked out of the cost no matter how good the plan. He had done the work. He had read it four times out loud. He knew the citation was right as surely as he knew anything since Weaver's Row. None of that made the bench any softer.

At two, the clerk looked up at the clock and then at him, and jerked his head at a narrow stair at the side of the room.

"Up there," he said. "He's expecting you."

The cooper and the man with the blue hands both turned and looked at him, curiously, as he got up. He went up the stair sideways, because it was too narrow to go up any other way.

The room at the top was small and plain, with one window looking down the fish steps to the river, a cot along the wall under it with a blanket folded square, and a partition of planks on one side that did not quite reach the ceiling. There was a chair in front of a desk, and a man behind the desk. On the floorboards by the desk's left front leg, a hand's width from where it ought to have been, there was a small grey square of folded paper.

The desk rocked when the man leaned forward. Tock.

Cael had sat under that sound for most of a day. He knew exactly where to look for it, and the man saw him look.

"Caelen Hesk-ward," said the man.

He was about forty, as Torvin had said, with a thin face and close-cut hair going grey at the sides. He had a habit, which Cael saw almost at once, of pressing his thumb to the bridge of his nose when he looked at a paper. He had taken his coat off; it hung on the back of the door. He did not stand. He did not seem unfriendly. He looked at Cael the way the mender looked at a frame before he leaned on the lever: thoroughly, without any hurry, to see where it was not true.

"Cael," said Cael.

"The summons says Caelen."

"The summons is right. People say Cael."

The man considered that and seemed to file it. "Coss," he said, and touched the paper on his desk where his name was written at the foot, as if the name needed its evidence too. "Sit down. This is a standard compliance evaluation. I'll ask you some questions about your residence and your practice, and you'll—"

"Before you begin," said Cael, and took the folded sheet out of the front of the Log, and held it out across the desk. "There's this."

Coss looked at the sheet in Cael's hand, and then at Cael. Something moved in his face, the faint irritation of a man whose straightforward afternoon has just stopped being straightforward. He took it.

"What is it?"

"A procedural objection."

Coss read it.

Cael watched him read it, because the man's face was information. He watched the eyes go down the eleven lines once, quickly, to find out what sort of thing it was. He watched them stop at the three flat sentences, and go on, and come to the numbers. Then he watched Coss go back to the top and read it again, much more slowly, and saw the irritation go out of his face and something else come into it. It was surprise first, and under the surprise a thing Cael had not expected and took a moment to put a name to.

It looked like respect. It was not happy about being respect. It was there anyway.

Coss put the sheet down on the desk, and the desk rocked. For the first time since Cael had sat down, the man's eyes were really on him, and Cael thought they had stopped seeing a name on a summons and begun to see a new and unlooked-for entry in a file that had been strange from page one.

Then he picked the sheet up again at once, as though he needed a third look to be sure the second had not been a trick of the light. This time he read it with his lips moving. Cael heard him say the numbers under his breath, Part Four, section twelve, note three, and stop, and look at nothing, and go on. Supplementary Register, nineteen. Cael understood that he was checking them. He was not checking them against a book. He was checking them against the text of the regulation that he carried in his own head, well enough to test a stranger's citation without getting up from his chair.

"You found this yourself," Coss said. It was not quite a question.

"Yes."

"Where?"

"Downstairs." Cael looked at the floorboards between them, and Coss's eyes went down to them too. "In the reading room. Yesterday."

Coss sat very still for a moment. Then, very slightly, he looked at the floor of his own office as if he had just been told something about it. Cael would have missed it if he had not spent seven weeks watching people's faces for exactly this.

Coss put the sheet down again and kept his palm on it, pinning the problem to the desk until he knew what he meant to do about it. He looked at Cael.

"You've cited it the way it's written. All of it. Do you know how unusual that is?"

"One day, and good reason to take care over it."

"A day," Coss said after him.

"And most of a night."

Something went across Coss's face that was very nearly a laugh, and was put away again almost as fast as it came. He did not quite manage to put all of it away.

"Is it wrong?" said Cael, into the pause.

Coss did not answer at once.

He was quiet in the particular way of a man going back over his own certainty before he says something he will not be able to take back, running it again in his head from the beginning. Cael had done the same thing in the reading room the day before, the fourth time, from the bottom of the column up. He recognized it, and sat still, and waited.

"No," Coss said at last. He said it flatly, as a man says the reading on a dial that he would rather have read something else. "It's not wrong. A standard compliance evaluation can't be done on your classification. So the evaluation they sent me out here for is one I can't carry out." He let his breath out, and for a moment his composure slipped far enough to show what was under it. It looked to Cael like frustration, and not at him, but aimed at something past him, at the window or further. "Nobody will want this report. It'll be about as unpopular as a report gets."

"Why unpopular? You'd be keeping to the rules."

"The sweep that brought me out here was asked for by people who wanted no delay. They wanted the file resolved." Somewhere in the last few minutes, Cael thought, Coss had worked out that pretending with this boy would cost more than it could ever buy, and he spoke now with the plainness of a man who has done that sum. "What resolved means to them, I couldn't say. Closed one way or closed the other. I honestly couldn't tell you. But a boy of fourteen reading me the statute across my own desk and walking off with six weeks isn't going to look like resolved to anybody above me." He looked down at the sheet. "I write accurate reports. I won't enjoy writing this one. I'll write it anyway, because it's true."

"What happens now?"

"Now I stamp the summons closed, pending, and I apply to regional for a senior evaluator, because that's what the regulation asks for in your case." Coss picked up a stamp from the corner of the desk. He held it a moment, longer than stamping a paper required, and Cael understood that he was weighing something that had nothing to do with stamping. Then he brought it down on the summons with a good deal more force than the job needed. The desk rocked. Tock. "Senior authorization takes time. The file goes up to regional to be read, somebody qualified has to be found to evaluate it, and then they've to be sent all the way out to a district at the far end of everything. Six weeks, as a rule. Longer if the evaluators are busy, and they usually are."

Six weeks.

Cael did the sum at once, the way he timed a window in a bout. Six weeks was forty-two days. It was not an answer. It was room.

"Who asked for the sweep?" he said.

Coss looked at him.

"I don't know," he said. "That's true. It's also all I'm going to say about it." He set the stamp back exactly where it had been on the corner of the desk. "Don't ask me again. It wouldn't do either of us any good."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Coss shut the folder over the stamped summons and the objection and got to his feet, and Cael understood that the meeting was over.

"Thank you," he said, standing too.

He meant it, and he knew while he said it that none of this had been a kindness. Coss had done it because it was correct, which seemed to be the only way he did anything. To do your work correctly when the people who sent you would rather you did it some other way was a kind of honesty all its own, and a rare one, and Cael had not looked to be taught it by a man from the Compact.

"Don't thank me." Coss was looking at the window, at the fish steps going down to the river. "I can buy you time. Whatever it is they're really asking, the answer's not mine to buy you. That part's yours."

He turned from the window then with something in his face that Cael could not read, the look of a man weighing whether to say a thing that did not belong in an evaluation.

"May I ask you something?" he said. "Not for the file."

"You can ask."

"Six weeks. What will you do with them?"

Cael considered how much to give him, thinking of the reading room below this floor, of the three lines in the margin of the Log, and of Hesk's don't change what you do, and of the plain fact that for a quarter of an hour this man had been straighter with him than his post had any need to be; and so he chose something near the whole of it.

"Get stronger. Build a reason for people to notice if I disappear."

Coss's face changed. It was not approval and it was not alarm, but it lived on the same street as both.

Cael turned to go, and his eye fell, without his meaning it to, on the small grey square of folded paper lying on the boards by the desk's left front leg.

"It's not the floor," he said. "It's the leg. That's come out from under it."

Coss looked down at it as though it had been lying there through a great many visits by a great many men and not one of them had ever said so.

"So it has," he said.

Cael took the narrow stair sideways, and down in the front room the cooper and the man with the blue hands had gone, and the clerk was winding up his knotted string and did not raise his head as Cael went by.

It was only at the street door that he noticed what had never been asked: in all that quarter of an hour, Coss had not said a single word about the yards.

Chapter 33 — Expensive

[Dry, precise narration; hold institutional pressure beneath the ordinary details]

He came out of the post into the middle of the afternoon and stood on the step with the door shut behind him.

The street was exactly as it had been when he went in. A cart was going down toward the lower bridge with a load of barrels, and one of the barrels had come loose in its ropes and was knocking against its neighbour at every jolt. A woman was calling fish from the bottom of the steps in a voice like a gull's. Two doors along, somebody laughed about some matter that was none of his, a long, easy laugh that went on after the joke was over, and somewhere across the river a bell was ringing the hour for people with cards that opened gates.

None of it knew what had happened in the room upstairs. None of it would have behaved any differently if it had. He stood in the middle of all that ordinary noise and let it settle round him. It steadied him, as the sacks of flour coming off Ressa's wagon had steadied him once at a kitchen table, with a notice between him and Hesk.

Somebody would still bake bread tomorrow. A cooper and a man with blue hands would still be cross about a gutter.

Lira was sitting on the river wall at the top of the fish steps, exactly where she had sat at dusk the evening before, with her right arm inside her coat and her heels against the stone. She was not drumming them. She had the look of somebody who has been happening to pass a particular place for about an hour.

She got down off the wall when she saw him, and did not come toward him, and waited.

"Six weeks," he said.

Lira sat down on the wall again, quite hard, as though her legs had decided it for her.

"Six weeks," she said. "He said yes."

"He said it wasn't wrong. He checked the numbers in his head. He didn't need the book." He sat down beside her. The stone was cold through his trousers. "He stamped it closed, pending. Somebody more senior has to come. Six weeks, he says, as a rule. Longer if they're busy."

"And then?"

"And then somebody more senior comes."

She let out a long breath that went up white in front of her and hung there.

"He was decent," Cael said. He had not known he was going to say it until it was out. "He didn't want to write the summons. I don't think he wanted to write any of it. He said it was going to be an unpopular report, and he was going to write it anyway, because it was true."

"Decent men write summonses all the time," said Lira. "That's what they're for."

"I know."

"I'm not saying he isn't. I'm saying it doesn't change what's on the paper." She looked at him sideways. "What did he ask you about?"

"Nothing. He was going to ask me about my residence and my practice, and I gave him the objection before he could start." He looked down at the river going past the bottom of the steps, brown and quick. "He didn't ask about the yards, Lira. Not once. Not the circuit, not fighting, not Vell. He doesn't know."

She was quiet.

"He asked me what I was going to do with six weeks," Cael said. "At the end. He said it wasn't for the file."

"What did you tell him?"

He told her.

Lira looked at him, and he could not read the look at all; then, slowly, she began to smile. It was not the quick one she allowed herself when she had landed something. It was the slow one that started somewhere behind her eyes and took its time getting out.

"You told a man from the Compact," she said, "to his face, in his own office, that you were going to go and make yourself hard to lose."

"I told him the truth. He'd told me the truth."

"I know." She got down off the wall again and held out her good hand to pull him up. "That's the worst part. He'll have believed you."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

He did the front of the Log first, at the low wall by the pump in Torvin's yard, under the pear tree that had given up growing tall, because that was the rule.

Fifty-fifth day. Objection given before it began. Ruled right. Closed, pending. Six weeks.

Coss asked nothing about the yards. Says he doesn't know who asked for the sweep. I believe him. (Not evidence. A face.)

He turned the book over and opened it from the back.

He held the pencil off the page before he wrote, because the thing he wanted to write was not a fact yet and he did not want it to put on a fact's coat.

The man at Torvin's door, about the twenty-eighth day, asked for the circuit kid. He knew there was a circuit, and that I was in it. The grey coat with the pin didn't seem to know. Coss doesn't know. Coss has my whole file, all of it, the thin case, and it can't have the circuit in it, because he'd have asked.

So whoever the polite man was, he knew a thing the Compact's own file doesn't.

I don't know who he was. I don't know whether he's anything. I'm writing down that two different people have been asking two different questions, and I don't know which of them matters more.

He drew a short line under it, and then he did the arithmetic, because six weeks was a number and he did not trust any number he had not laid out on the page.

Forty-two days. The Cinder House ran a card every Thursday and every Sunday, and an afternoon card most Tuesdays. Vell did not put anybody in twice in one week who had come off the dirt looking the way he generally came off it. Renn was due back at the turn of the month, which was perhaps a week away, perhaps two. He could not fight more than six times in forty-two days and still be standing at the end of them. Perhaps not more than five.

Six bouts, then, at most. Six chances to be something more than unrated (vouched) on a lamp-wick bill nailed to a board.

He sat on the wall with the Log open on his knee and thought about what it would take for a district to notice that a boy had gone.

It would take people who knew his name and said it. It would take a book that had him in it, not as unrated but as a person the yard had come to see, so that if the person stopped coming, somebody would turn back the pages and ask why. It would take Torvin, who held a room and knew to the day when it was paid. It would take the mender, who had said Wednesday, and would look up from his clock on Wednesday afternoon at a doorway with nobody in it. It would take a fish man who nodded and a bread woman who gave him the loaf from underneath, and two errand boys, and a girl on a wall who told Lira everything to annoy her. It would take Lira, who would be first.

And Hesk, a week away by the west bag, who would know to the day when a letter that should have come had not.

He thought about the green book in Denvash. Three of them dead within weeks. He did not know what had happened to them. He knew only what had been written down, by somebody who had cared which kind of true got believed. But he thought, sitting under the pear tree, that whatever it had been, it had happened very fast, to people who had not yet had time to belong to anybody but the people they came from.

He wrote that down, in the back, with a line round it, so that he would know it was a guess.

I don't know that. It's what I think. I don't want to be somewhere nobody would look.

Then he closed the Log, and went up to the Cinder House, because it was a Tuesday, and there had been an afternoon card, and Vell would still be at her table.

She was. The yard had nearly emptied. The pie boy was raking the circle where the afternoon's last bout had scuffed it, and the crows were along the eaves. Vell sat in the shade of the back wall on her stool with the ledger open in front of her, finishing an entry. She blotted it before she said anything.

"You're not on this week," she said. "I told the Wind girl. Rest the hand."

"The hand's rested." He held it up. The split knuckles had healed to thin pink lines. "I want to fight. As often as you'll put me in, for the next six weeks."

Vell looked at him. It was the flat look, the thorough one, and it stayed on him for longer than it usually did.

"Why six?"

He had thought, walking up, about how much to tell her, and he had decided on nothing about the post. The book stayed clear of the Compact. Lira had told him that on his first morning in this yard, and Vell had said it to him herself in her own way, with nothing to register. He was not going to be the one who brought the Compact over the rope on a sheet of paper.

"Because I've got six weeks to get better in," he said. "I'd like to spend all of them getting better."

Vell considered that. She seemed to find it true up to a point, short of the whole way, with the rest of it belonging to somebody other than her.

"Renn's back at the turn of the month," she said. "I'm holding him for you, as I said I would. Before that, I'll put you in with somebody." She picked up her tea. "I'll tell you who when I've decided. Not before. And not because—"

"Because I asked," said Cael. "I know."

Something happened at the corner of Vell's mouth and was gone again before it had become anything.

"There's one more thing," he said.

She waited.

"My name." He made himself say it plainly, the way he had said the terms back to her on the first morning, in his own words, checking each one before he set it down. "You'll write it in the book when the yard comes to see me. You said so. Not before, and not because I asked. I'm not asking you to write it now." He took a breath. "But when you do, it's not Just Cael. It's Cael Hesk-ward. Hesk is my grandfather. I'd like the book to have it right."

Vell did not pick up her pen.

She sat with the tea in her hand and looked at him. He thought that she was looking past his face at something else, perhaps at a margin with nothing to register in it, or the long row of entries under no name at all, or a girl standing in front of this table with her chin up saying I do. He could not tell. Vell's face did not let you tell.

"Hesk-ward," she said at last, as if trying the weight of it.

"Yes."

"I'll keep it." She set the cup down. "Not in the book. The book has what the yard's seen, and the yard hasn't seen that yet." She touched two fingers, briefly, to the side of her own head. "In here. Where I keep the things that are mine. When it goes in the book, it'll go in right."

"Thank you."

"I've not done anything but listen," said Vell. She looked down at the ledger, and he understood he had been dismissed, and went. At the gate he looked back. She had not picked up her pen. She was sitting quite still at her table in the last of the light, with her hand flat on the cover of the closed book, looking at the circle.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

He wrote to Hesk that night at the kitchen table, after the others had gone up.

He worked out the days first, as he always did now. This would go in the west bag at noon tomorrow, the fifty-sixth day, at the carriers' hut, the same hut and the same bag as always, with nothing on the outside but the address they had already. It would come to Fen Street on about the sixty-third. Hesk would answer it that night, because that was what Hesk did, and the answer would come back up the fish steps on about the seventieth. By then the six weeks would be a third gone.

He could not write the fear. It would be a week stale before Hesk could do anything with it, and he would have to carry it alone at the table for that week. He could write what was true, though, and it would still be true when it got there.

Hesk,

Your letter came on the fifty-first day, on the same cart as a man from the Compact. I didn't know that until the next night. He came to Torvin's door and asked for me by my whole name, and Torvin told him the room's paid and that I pay on time, and nothing else. Torvin's wife wanted him told I eat my oats.

On Sunday he left a summons at Torvin's for a compliance evaluation, forty-eight hours, with physical retrieval if I didn't go.

I went. But first I read the law in the registry's reading room until I found where it doesn't fit me. A standard evaluation can only assess a classification the framework recognizes, and mine isn't one. I read it out loud four times, the way you read a load figure before you sign it. It held.

He checked it in his head and said it was right, and stamped it closed, pending. A senior evaluator has to come instead. Six weeks, he says.

He was decent about it. I don't know who asked for the sweep. Neither does he, I think.

You said don't change what I do. I'd decided the same thing on a roof a week before your letter came. I'm posting this from the same hut, in the same bag.

You'd have liked the appendix. Its page had come loose and somebody had tucked it back in crooked.

I'm all right. I'm telling you this as it comes, because you asked me to, and because I asked you to first.

— Cael

He read it over. It was true all the way through. It was not all of what was true. The four times something had moved him that he had not chosen were still in the back of the Log, numbered: the cart, Renn, the drop, Dessa. He had made a promise on a step to somebody else about who would hear them first, and he had not broken it. He counted what he had not told Hesk, as he always did now, and the number had not changed.

He folded the letter and put it in the leather book to keep flat for the morning.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Coss wrote his second report that evening at the borrowed desk, with the lamp close and the window gone dark over the fish steps, and it was the least pleasant document he had written in eleven years.

It was not long. He set down that he had attended for the compliance evaluation as summoned, and that before it could begin, the subject had presented a written procedural objection. He gave the citation, in full: the part, the section, the note, the register, the statute, the appendix. He set down that he had checked the citation against the regulation and found it correct. He set down that the standard evaluation could not lawfully proceed, and that he had marked the summons closed, pending, and filed for senior evaluation authorization as the regulation required.

Then he wrote the sentence he had known since the afternoon that he would have to write.

The objection was found, prepared and presented by the subject himself, aged fourteen, from the public reading room of this post, in the space of one day.

He read it back. It was accurate. It would sit on a desk above his own, in an office where somebody read authorization codes that his own register did not list. It would say to whoever sat at that desk that the file they had kept so thin had been read more closely in a day by a boy in a cellar than by anybody who had handled it in Denvash. He did not know how it would be taken. He had a fair idea.

He left it in. He blotted it, and sealed it, and set it by the door for the morning pouch west.

Then he got down on one knee on the floorboards, beside the desk's left front leg, and picked up the small grey square of folded paper. It had lain there, a hand's width from where it belonged, for the whole of his stay and for who knew how many men's stays before him. He folded it once more, to make it thicker, and lifted the corner of the desk an inch, and slid the paper under the leg, and set the desk down on it.

He leaned on the desk.

It did not rock.

He stayed there for a moment on one knee, with his hand flat on the desktop, very nearly smiling, alone in a borrowed room over a district he still could not read. Then he got up, and turned the lamp down, and lay on the cot with his coat over him.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

In the morning, after the post and before the yard, Cael went up to the crossroads.

The triangle was quiet at that hour, with frost along the shaded side of every street and the skewer woman's cart still covered with its oilcloth. The board stood on its post in the middle of it as it always did, with its notices on notices, its tacks and nails and the bent fork, the bottom layers gone into the grain.

The pie boy had nailed up a new card since yesterday. It was in Vell's upright pencil, on the back of a bill for candles, and it was for Thursday and the Sunday after. His own name was not on it. The word unrated was not on it either. Vell had said she would tell him who when she had decided, and not before.

He stood and read it twice anyway, from the top.

Under it, near the bottom of the board, gone pale in three days of weather, was Sunday's result. Lira (Cu 3, Wind) over Brenna (Cu 2, Shield), fifth exchange, called. Beside it somebody had drawn a tally of three small strokes in charcoal, and somebody else had circled them.

And under that, older still, he found his own: unrated (vouched) over Dessa (Cu 5, Stone), fourth exchange, conceded.

He looked at the card and the two results, one above the other.

Forty-two days. Six bouts, if Vell would give them and his body would take them. At the end of the forty-two days a person more senior than Coss would come out along the merchant road, two days from wherever such people were kept, with a file that was too thin and a question that nobody had told Coss. Cael did not know what the question was, or who was asking it. He knew only that a field agent who had been honest with him had said he could buy time and could not buy an answer. The time had been bought, and it was going down already, one cold morning at a time.

He could not make himself safe in forty-two days. He did not think anybody could have done that.

But he could make himself expensive.

He could make it so that if a boy at Torvin's stopped coming to the yard, a great many people would notice on the same day, and would say so, and would not all say it quietly. He could put his name into enough mouths that it would be awkward to take it out of them. He could stand in that circle often enough, and well enough, that a woman with a book would find one evening that she could not leave him off a card without a dozen people asking her why. He could make it cost something to lose him.

It was not much of a plan. It was a plan a boy could make standing in front of a board in the frost with his hands in his pockets. But it was his, and he had built it out of evidence, and every piece of it was something he could do tomorrow.

Behind him the street that went up toward the yards had begun to fill: carts with sand, a barrow of straw targets, somebody shouting at somebody about a rope. He heard quick feet on the cobbles that he knew without turning round, because he had learned their rhythm every morning in the grey half, with their weight a little forward on the front of the foot.

"You've been reading that board for eleven minutes." Lira came up beside him with the bread under her good arm.

"I wasn't counting," he said.

"I know. I was." She looked at the board, at the new card and the two results under it, and then at him. "Well?"

"Six weeks," said Cael.

"Six weeks." She tore the bread and gave him half. "Then come on. You're wasting them standing here."

They went up the street together toward the yards, into the morning. He did not look back at the board. He knew exactly what was on it, and he meant, before six weeks were out, to give it something new.

Chapter 34 — Efficient

[Patient, methodical narration; give training, failure, and discovery room to accumulate]

The frost had not gone off the yard when they came in through the gate, and the east wall's shadow lay across the dirt in its long grey bar with the post standing up in the middle of it like a man waiting for a cart.

Lira set the rest of the bread on top of the post and did not take her coat off; her right arm was still inside it, not in the sleeve, and she had stopped pretending that this was a choice.

"Go on, then," she said. "You've had it in your head since the board. Say it."

He said it. He had worked it out under the pear tree the evening before and again on the walk up, and it came out in order. There were forty-two days. The Cinder House ran a card on Thursdays and on Sundays and most Tuesdays in the afternoon, and Vell would not put him in twice in a week, and his body would not let him even if she did. At the very most that made six bouts, and he thought it was more honest to say five. Each one had to count, and each one had to be against somebody the yard would talk about afterward, so that his name went into more mouths than it had been in before. A boy whose name was in a great many mouths was a boy whose going would be noticed, and asked about, on the day a more senior man came along the merchant road with a thin file.

"So I want to fight," he said. "As often as she'll let me. I told her so."

"I know. She told me." Lira leaned her good shoulder against the post. "She said you stood in front of her table and asked for six weeks of bouts like a man asking for six weeks of bread."

"What did she say about it?"

"She said hm." Lira gave him the long look she gave him sometimes even now, after seven weeks. It was not suspicion. It was more like a person reading a contract she has already signed, to see what exactly she has agreed to. "You've got five bouts in the book. One of them's a win. That isn't a foundation, Cael. That's a first course of stones."

"Then help me lay the rest faster."

"Faster." She said the word back to him as if she were weighing it in her hand. "All right. But we do it my way, and you don't argue with my way until it's failed you at least twice." She held up one finger of her good hand. "Faster doesn't mean reckless. It means efficient."

"What's the difference?"

"Reckless is fighting six times because six is the biggest number on the page. Efficient is fighting as many times as you can and still walk into the next one whole." She pushed herself off the post. "You can lose. You've lost four times and you're standing here, and losing's cheap if you learn something. What you can't do is get hurt in a way that costs you the bout after. Every morning from now on is for the next one. Every night the Log turns round before you sleep, not two days later when you've forgotten what your feet did." She looked at the bread on the post and did not pick it up yet. "And you don't go in against anybody I think will break you, whatever Vell says, and whatever you say. I'll tell you. You'll listen."

"And if you're wrong?"

"Then I'll have been wrong carefully." She almost smiled. "That's the other half of efficient. I've watched people come up through that circle in a hurry. Most of them came up fast and went down faster, and then they weren't in the yard any more, and nobody could tell you where they'd gone." She stopped, and he saw her hear what she had just said, and what it sounded like to somebody who had sat under a pear tree last night working out who would notice if he went. "I don't mean like that."

"I know what you meant."

"Good." She took the bread off the post at last and tore it, one-handed, with her teeth, and gave him half. "Eat. Then the deflection, slow, while I watch your left foot. It's still turning out on the back corner."

"I fixed it."

"You fixed it on Tuesday. It's Wednesday."

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

The mender was at his bench when Cael came down the row of workshops after noon, exactly as though nothing had happened on Monday and nobody had ever stood in his doorway apologizing.

The lantern woman next door had all thirteen of her broken lanterns out on a plank in the thin sun, and was warming her soldering iron between her palms and talking to it, while the cooper beyond her knocked a hoop down. The mender's own doorway had no sign over it, only the four words cut into the frame at the height of a man's shoulder and filled in with black paint, as they had been on the first afternoon Cael ever stopped there.

IF IT'S STILL HERE.

He had read them perhaps fifty times. He had thought they were a joke at first, and then a warning to people who left things too long, and then simply the mender's way of answering the question every customer asked, when will it be ready. He read them again now on his way in, and they meant something else, and he did not stop to look at what.

"Wednesday," said the mender, without looking up.

"Wednesday."

On the end of the bench there was a crate of forty or fifty door hinges, black with old paint and rust, which had come out of a house by the dyers' that was being pulled down. The mender wanted to know which of them still swung true. He did not want them cleaned, or oiled, or mended; he wanted them sorted into two heaps, one that could go into somebody's door tomorrow and one that would only ever be iron again.

Cael sat on the stool at the end of the bench and opened and shut hinges.

It was slow work and he liked it, because you could not tell a true hinge by looking at it. Paint hid the pin, and rust hid the knuckle, and a hinge that looked like scrap would sometimes open as sweetly as a new one, while a hinge that looked clean would bind at the halfway and grind and stop. You had to hold it and work it and feel for the place where it caught, and after the first dozen his hands knew before his eyes did. Something in the first quarter-turn told him which heap it was going in, before he had finished turning it, and he made himself finish turning it anyway, because he did not trust that yet.

He thought about the six weeks while his hands worked, because there was nothing else in his head that afternoon to think about.

A hinge that was still true would go into a door, and somebody would hang it and swing it and forget about it for twenty years. A hinge that was not would go on the scrap heap and be carried off to the smith by the bridge, and in a week nobody in the district would remember it had ever been a hinge. He did not like where the thought was going. He turned the next hinge over in his hands and worked it, and it caught at the halfway, and he put it on the scrap heap and did not think about it any more.

At the end of the afternoon there were two heaps on the bench, and the true one was smaller than the other. The mender came down the bench with his loupe pushed up on his forehead and picked a hinge out of each, one after the other, without any hurry. He worked them both, and put them back on their heaps exactly where they had been.

He looked at Cael for a moment, not with the long look he gave a frame before he leaned on the lever but with something shorter than that, and plainer.

"Monday," he said.

"Monday," said Cael. "And Wednesday. For six weeks, at least."

The mender considered this, as if it had been a measurement.

"And after?"

"I don't know yet."

The mender nodded slowly, as he had nodded at I don't know yet once before over a tray of keys, and put his loupe back in his eye and went back to his clock. Cael went out under the four words in the black paint, and he did not read them, and he heard them anyway all the way up the row.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Vell was at her table on Thursday morning before the yard had properly woken, with her tea and the ledger and her stool set square to the back wall, and she went on writing when he came across the dirt.

"Tuesday," she said. "The afternoon card."

He stopped in front of the table. "Who?"

Vell turned the ledger a little toward the light and laid her finger on a line. He could not read it upside down at that distance, and she did not turn it far enough for him to try.

"There's a boy on tonight's card," she said. "Second bout. He's on again Sunday, the first, before the benches fill. Copper Rank 2, Ember Path. He works the kilns down by the brickworks, and he fights the way you'd expect from somebody who stands in front of a kiln all day." She took her finger off the page. "You'll have him on Tuesday if you still want him after you've watched him twice."

"Why him?"

"Because he's on the card twice before Tuesday, and you'll want to watch him." Vell picked up her tea. "And because you've already been taught Ember once. Amrit taught you. I'd like to see whether it stayed."

"Not because I asked."

"No. Not because you asked." She drank. "Go away. You're standing in my light."

He went to the rope that evening on the shaded side, by the barrel near the drain, with the Log open on his knee and the pencil going, and he watched the kiln boy fight.

He was about seventeen, broad through the shoulders and narrow at the hip, with forearms burned all over in small shiny patches, old and new together, and he came over the rope as if he were angry with it. When Vell said begin he went straight at the other fighter, a Force youth a little older than him, and Cael watched the air in front of his right hand go thick and wavering, as air goes over a road in summer.

Then the boy stopped breathing.

It was not a long stop, only the length of a swallow: his chest went still, and his mouth shut, and a half-beat later the heat came. Cael felt it from the rope, on his face, like an oven door opened across a kitchen, and the Force youth flinched sideways out of it and lost his footing on the groove.

Shimmer, Cael wrote. Then the breath stops. Then the heat. Same as Amrit.

He wrote it again after the second exchange, and after the third, and he made a mark beside it each time. Amrit had stopped his breath before the real heat two times in three, and Cael had had to learn to tell the third time apart, and had paid for it with a burned arm. This boy stopped his breath every time, not two times in three or four in five but every single time, as surely as a door creaks on the same hinge.

There was a second thing, which he saw in the fourth exchange and nearly did not believe. Before every strike the boy looked at the place he meant to hit. He did not glance there; he looked, the way you look at a nail before you bring the hammer down, and then he hit it.

The Force youth went down in the fourth. The kiln boy stood over him breathing hard, with the shimmer still going off his hand, and the crowd along the rope cheered him in the comfortable way people cheer a thing that has gone as it was meant to.

Cael looked at his page. It said breath, every time and looks where he's going to hit, and nothing else, because there was nothing else.

He sat with the Log on his knee while the next pair went over the rope, and he did not like it at all, and he could not have said why.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

"Gone," said Lira.

"What?"

"That's what you say." She stepped back out of the box drill and stood in the grey half with her good hand on her hip. "Every time a plan dies. The moment it dies. You say it out loud, so I can hear it, and then you do something else."

It was Friday. Her shoulder had gone from purple to a colour like old mustard, and she had taken her arm out of her coat that morning for the first time, and she was using it carefully, as if it belonged to somebody who might want it back. He had been building a counter to her step since the end of the month before, and this morning he had built it four times, and four times it had been wrong in the same way. He had seen the two touches and started back and out, and found her already inside, and gone on with the counter anyway, back and out, with her backhand stopped beside his ear while his forearm was still on its way up to a place she had left.

"I knew it was wrong," he said.

"I know you knew. I watched you know it." She tapped her own temple. "You saw me inside, you knew the counter was dead, and you finished it anyway, all the way, every step, as though you'd paid for it and you weren't going to waste it." She shook her head. "It's dead, Cael. You don't owe it anything. You don't get to keep a plan because it was a good plan five breaths ago."

"So I say gone."

"Out loud. Every time. Before you do the next thing."

"That's ridiculous."

"It's very ridiculous." She brought her hands up. "Do it anyway."

The first time, it came out of him as a mumble, half under his breath, a beat too late to be of any use, and she stopped and made him say it again. The second time he said it clearly, and felt his ears go hot. Along the top of the far wall the two girls who sat there in the mornings to watch the yard and eat whatever they had stolen from their mothers' kitchens put their heads together and laughed.

"Gone," said Cael, a third time, standing in the wrong place with his arm half up.

"Gone," said one of the girls on the wall, in a deep solemn voice, and the other one fell against her shoulder.

Lira did not laugh. She took a stub of chalk out of her pocket, made one short line on the side of the post where the canvas ended, and came back to her mark.

"That's three," she said.

By the end of the morning it was nine. He said it every time he finished building something and saw it fall down, which was nearly every time. Some of the times he said it before he had properly understood that the plan was dead, and then stood blinking while his body worked out that he was right. The word did not feel like a tool; it felt like a boy announcing his mistakes to a yard.

She did one more thing before the sun reached the post.

"Watch," she said, and stepped back, and became him.

She did it so exactly that for a moment he did not understand what he was looking at. She stood on her mark with her feet a little too square and brought her hands up and looked across at an opponent who was not there, with her chin tucked and her eyes very wide and very serious. Then she nodded, slightly, to herself, a small private nod, the nod of somebody who has just solved something; and only then, a full breath later, she moved.

The girls on the wall had stopped laughing and were watching her with their mouths open.

"Do I do that?"

"The nod?" Lira dropped out of him and was herself again, all at once, loose and quick. "Every time. You see it, you work it out, and you agree with yourself. Then you go." She picked up the last of the bread. "Anybody who's watched you twice could time you by it. I could. Renn will have."

He had not known the nod was there. He had felt the agreeing, the small click of a figure coming right, and he had never once thought that it showed on the outside, where anybody standing in a circle could see it.

"Gone," he said, to nobody, to the nod.

Lira looked at him, and then took out the chalk and made a tenth mark on the post.

"That one counts. That was a good one."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Sunday was the first of the new month, and Renn was not in the yard.

Cael had not expected him to be, exactly, but he had expected him somewhere. He had looked for him at the fish steps that morning among the men unloading, and at the market, and at the yard gate. The river had come up again in the week, and the barges that should have come down from the upriver farms on Friday had not come. Torvin's brothers had been at the table every night saying so, loudly, with their elbows on the boards.

He went to Vell's table before the benches filled.

"It's the turn of the month," he said.

"I know what day it is." She was ruling a fresh page. "He's not back. The river's holding everything above the weir. He could be three days, or ten. I don't keep a man's slot open for ten days on the chance of a river."

"So the hold's gone."

"The hold's gone." She drew the line to the edge of the page and lifted the ruler. "I said I'd hold him to the turn of the month. It's turned."

He stood there a moment longer. "When he's back, I'd like to ask again."

"Then ask him." Vell blew on the ink. "Not me. I made you a promise once already and the river broke it. If you want Renn, you go and find Renn, and if he says yes, you both come to me, and I'll see." She looked up. "He'll come up the fish steps like everybody else, when it stops raining up the valley."

So he went and stood at the rope on the shaded side, near the barrel, and watched the kiln boy fight for the second time.

It was the first bout, with the benches still half empty and the pie boy not yet going with his tray. The kiln boy was against a Blade this time, a tall girl of about sixteen with a long reach, and he went at her across the circle the same way he had gone at the Force youth on Thursday, angrily, as if the circle had insulted him. The shimmer came up off his hand, and his breath stopped, and the heat came.

Cael made a mark in the Log.

It happened again and again: the boy stopped his breath before every real heat and looked at every place he meant to hit. The tall girl worked out the second thing in the third exchange and moved her ribs away from where he was looking. The boy noticed nothing, and kept looking, and kept hitting where he had looked. In the fifth exchange she slipped one of his looks and put the flat of her blade across the back of his neck, and Vell called it.

Lira had come up the rope while he was writing, and she stood beside him with her arms folded on the top of it.

"That's two," she said.

"Every time. Both nights. He holds his breath, and he looks."

"Then he'll do it on Tuesday."

"I know." He looked at the page. "That's what's wrong with it."

She turned her head and looked at him properly.

"There's nothing wrong with it. He's seventeen. He's rated Copper 2 because that's what he is. Some people have a tell like a fire bell and nobody's ever told them." She looked back at the circle, where the tall girl was helping the kiln boy up and he was letting her, red in the face. "You're not used to easy. That's all. You've never had one."

Marrow came along the rope with his slate. He had not put the Tuesday card on it yet. He saw Cael reading the slate anyway, and smiled the good smile, and said nothing at all, which was not like him.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On Tuesday afternoon the yard was thin.

It was a working day, and cold. Along the rope there were perhaps forty people, most of them men from the yards and the river workshops on their way home early, with the girls from the wall, and the errand boys, and two of Brenna's friends, who had come because Lira had told somebody who had told somebody. Lira was at the barrel with both arms out of her coat now, and she did not wave.

The kiln boy came over the rope as if it had insulted him.

"Copper Rank 2, Ember Path," said Vell, and gave his name, which Cael heard and did not keep. "Against unrated. Vouched." She looked at her book. "Begin when you're ready."

The shimmer came up off the boy's right hand before he had left his mark. He looked at Cael's left shoulder, hard. Then he came.

Cael watched his chest.

It went still, and the mouth shut, and Cael went right, away from the shoulder the boy had been looking at, a full step outside the reach of the hand, and the heat went past his left side like a door of air pushed open and slammed. It was hot on his ear and on nothing else.

The second exchange was the same. The boy looked at his ribs, held his breath, and struck where he had looked, and Cael was a step outside it. He did not strike back, because he had planned not to; he wanted to see whether anything in the boy changed when he missed twice.

Nothing did.

The boy's face went darker. His breathing got louder at the top of every breath, but it still stopped dead before every heat, as if a hand had been put over his mouth. On his mark between the exchanges he glared across at Cael and rubbed the burned side of his right hand against his trouser leg.

In the third exchange Cael went in.

The boy looked at his head, and his chest went still, and Cael stepped left and forward on the stillness, before the heat. The heat went over his right shoulder and singed the air beside his collar, and he was inside it, close enough to smell the brick dust on the boy's shirt. His right hand came up from the hip, short and straight, the one strike he owned, the one Lira had made him throw at the post until his knuckles knew the canvas by heart. He stopped it with his knuckles touching the boy's jaw, just under the ear.
