The kiln boy stood there with his breath still held, and the shimmer going out of his hand, and his eyes very wide.

"Called," said Vell. "Unrated."

It had taken perhaps three minutes.

The rope made a pleased noise, the ordinary kind. The kiln boy let his breath go at last, all at once, and looked at Cael's fist by his jaw, and then at Cael. He did not look angry any more. He looked mostly surprised, like somebody who has been told a thing about his own face by a stranger.

"How'd you know where I'd be?"

Cael took his hand away.

"You look," he said. "Before you hit. You look at where you're going to hit."

The boy stared at him.

"Everybody does that."

"No. Not everybody."

He walked to the table and stood in front of it, as you stood, win or lose, until she was finished with you.

"Result stands as called," said Vell, writing. "Unrated, over—" and she gave the kiln boy's name again, and then, "Copper Rank 2, Ember Path. Third exchange. Called." The pen went on for a line, and stopped, and did not go on. "Witnessed and entered."

That was all; there were no extra lines tonight, or none that she wrote while he was standing there. He had been listening for them without meaning to, and he noticed that he had been listening and did not like it.

When he came off the dirt the errand boys were arguing about something, and the one in the red cap held his hand out flat, and the other one put something in it with a very bad grace. Marrow had paid out, by the look of him, and had paid out cheerfully, which meant he had taken more than he gave.

Lira met him at the barrel. "Well."

"It was easy."

"It was easy." Her face did not do anything. "And you don't trust it."

"No."

"Good." She handed him his coat. "Easy happens. Some days you get a boy who holds his breath and looks where he's going to hit, and it goes exactly the way you wrote it. It doesn't mean the hard ones have gone anywhere. They're still out there, waiting their turn. Don't start thinking you've got a method that works on people. You've got a method that worked on him."

"I know."

"I know you know. It's getting said all the same, so it's been said." She bumped his good shoulder, which was both of them, today. "That's one."

He wrote it up at the low wall by the pump in Torvin's yard before he went in, while the light went. It was the seventh entry in the Log and only his sixth bout, because the Log had counted Baro, whom he had only watched, and Vell's book counted nothing it had not seen fought. It was the shortest entry he had ever made.

Seventh. The kiln boy (I didn't keep his name), Cu 2, Ember. Claim: holds his breath before every heat; looks at where he means to hit. Evidence: two bouts watched, every time, both nights. Ruling: step outside the look on the stillness; in on the third. Won, third exchange, called.

He sat for a moment with the pencil. Then he added, under the ruling, where he would see it:

It worked because he had never been told. That's not the same as it working. Don't learn the wrong thing from this.

He looked at the line and did not cross it out, and went in to supper.

Chapter 35 — The Second Look

[Patient, methodical narration; give training, failure, and discovery room to accumulate]

The barges came down on Thursday morning, all of them at once, as though the river had been holding its breath above the weir for a week and had finally let it go.

Cael heard them before he saw them, from the carriers' hut at the bottom of the fish steps, where he had come with his letter for the west bag. A shout went up somewhere along the long quay, and then another, and then the particular racket of a great many men who have been idle for days and have suddenly been handed something heavy. By the time the clerk had read his address out loud to the whole hut, as he read every address, and hung the letter on the third hook, there were eleven barges along the quay and the planks were going down.

He walked along the river wall toward the noise, telling himself that he was walking that way because it was the long way to the yard, and that the long way was the way he went, and that Hesk had said not to change what he did.

Renn was on the fourth barge.

He was standing on the deck in a heavy oiled coat with the collar up, handing sacks down to a man on the quay, and he had a beard. It was not much of one, three weeks' worth and patchy along the jaw, but it made him look older and more tired and a good deal more like the men around him. He was laughing at something the man on the quay had said when he swung a sack down, and turned for the next one, and saw Cael standing on the wall.

He stopped with the sack in his arms. Then he grinned, slowly, all the way across his face, and set the sack down on the deck as carefully as if it were full of eggs.

"Third exchange," Renn called, across the water and the planks and three men carrying grain. "Called. A Copper 2 who holds his breath." He put his hand flat on his chest. "I heard it from a woman with a fish basket before we'd got a rope ashore. I want you to know I take full credit."

"You were a week up the river."

"I was there in spirit." Renn came down the plank with a sack on each shoulder, as easily as if they were coats, and dropped them on the stack and straightened up. He gave Cael the craftsman's look, the one that checked a joint, which went over him from his boots to his face and lingered for a moment on his right hand, where the Dessa knuckles had healed to thin pink lines. "You've grown. No, you haven't. You're standing differently." He frowned. "Who's been at your feet?"

"Lira."

"Course she has." He wiped his hands on his coat. "So. The month's gone."

"The turn of the month's gone. The river kept you. Vell says the hold's lapsed." Cael had worked out what he was going to say on the walk along the wall, and said it. "She says if I want you, I come and ask you, and if you say yes, we both go to her."

Renn looked at him. "You're asking me."

"I'm asking you."

"Not her. Not through Lira. You." Renn seemed to find this interesting in itself, as if it were a part on his bench he had not expected. Then he shrugged his big shoulders. "I said I wanted to come back with something you hadn't seen. I've got it. I worked it out up the river, poling, which is a good place to work things out, because there's nothing else to do between one bend and the next except think and get wet." He picked up another sack from the stack without seeming to notice that he had. "Sunday?"

"If Vell says Sunday."

"She'll say Sunday. She likes it when people come to her table already agreed. It saves her the trouble of thinking we're fools." Renn hitched the sack higher. "Ten o'clock. I'll be at her table with my hair combed." He started back toward the plank, and then turned round, walking backward. "And you'll want to know where I'm training. Everybody'll want to know. I'll tell you now, so you don't have to creep about asking. The middle yard on the lane, tomorrow afternoon. Come and look, if you like. I'll be glad to see you there."

"Why?"

"Because it won't help you," said Renn, and went up the plank.

Vell said Sunday, an hour later, at her table. She said it while she wrote the card, on the back of a bill for lamp oil. She wrote Renn (Cu 3, Blade) on the second line and unrated (vouched) under it, and blotted it, and held it out without a word to the pie boy, who took it away to the board at a run.

Renn had combed his hair, and he had also shaved half his beard and then stopped, and the effect was so strange that the pie boy looked at it twice on his way past.

"Second bout," said Vell. "Before the lamps. Don't be late."

"And not early either," said Renn, "or people'll think we're frightened."

Vell looked up at him then, for exactly one breath, with the look, not unkind, of a woman who has heard every joke a fighter could make at her table, and has kept most of them in a book.

"Go and finish your face."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The middle yard on the lane was a square of dirt between two high walls, smaller than the Cinder House yard, with a chalk circle on it instead of a groove. The chalk had been walked half away, and by the middle of Friday afternoon there were thirty people at its gate.

Cael had expected a few of Renn's friends from the fish steps, and perhaps a girl from the wall. He had not expected the errand boys sitting on the top of the gate like crows, or Brenna's friends in a knot at one side, or two old men from the third row of the Sunday benches leaning on sticks with their scarves up over their mouths. There was a man selling hot chestnuts out of a pan, and Marrow, very clean, at the back, with his slate under his arm and the chalk not out.

"It's because he told everybody," said Lira, at his shoulder. "On the fish steps, yesterday, all afternoon. Come and see what I've got for the boy." She had her arms folded on the top of the wall and her chin on her arms. "He's always been a show-off. It's half of why people like him."

"He told me it wouldn't help me."

"Then either he's lying, or he's right." She did not turn her head. "Which do you think?"

He did not answer, and took out the Log.

Renn was in the circle with one of his friends from the fish steps, a broad young man as big as he was, who had been given the job of being Cael. Cael worked that out in the first minute and felt his face go hot, and then made himself stop minding and watch. The friend stood on his mark with his hands up and his chin tucked and his eyes very wide, looking down at Renn's feet. Somebody along the gate laughed and said that's him to the life, and the friend nodded to himself, slightly, solemnly, before he moved, and the laugh got louder.

Lira did not laugh. She glanced at Cael sideways, once.

"Your nod," she said quietly. "He's put your nod in."

"I know."

"I didn't tell anybody about the nod."

"You didn't have to. He watched me for four exchanges." Cael wrote it down. He has the nod. "He watches too."

Renn did not use his blade. He fought the friend open-handed, with the flat of his palm where the flat of the blade would be, and he did the same thing over and over for most of an hour.

The first thing he did was come straight off his mark, with no amble and no probes. The friend had barely got his hands up before the first fold of the figure was on him, high, and the second came out of the end of it, low and across. It was the fourth-exchange figure from the first night, the one with no handshake in it at all, the one that had put Cael in the dirt, and Renn was throwing it from the first breath, from the mark, every time.

The second thing was the heel.

Renn came off the mark slower, the third time, and settled his weight into his back heel exactly as he had settled it in the lamplight two months before. It was the spring pressing down, the frame loading, and the friend went the instant the heel settled, left and back, exactly as Cael had gone in the second exchange of their first bout. Renn did not strike. He stood on his loaded heel with his hand still back and watched the friend land, and then he struck, once, flat, across the friend's shoulder as his feet came down.

The gate made a noise, and the errand boys hissed through their teeth.

Renn did it again, settling the heel and holding it, and the friend jumped, and Renn waited for him to land and struck. He did it a third time, and the friend, who was not stupid, did not jump, and Renn struck off the heel at once, for real, so that the friend got the flat across his ribs instead.

"Either way," said Renn to the gate, breathing hard and grinning. "That's the beauty of it. If he goes when the heel goes, I get him landing. If he waits, I get him waiting." He wiped his face with his forearm. "And there won't be a third exchange this time. I've had his third exchange once. I don't want it again."

Somebody laughed. Somebody else called out to ask whether that meant Renn was frightened of the third, and Renn laughed too and said yes, terrified, and the friend punched him in the shoulder.

Cael wrote until his hand ached.

He wrote from the mark, every time, and the false heel with a box round it, and wait or go, he takes either. Then he stopped, with the pencil over the page, because he was watching something Renn did between the drills that Renn did not seem to know he was doing.

Each time Renn finished a drill and went back to his mark to begin another, he rolled his shoulders, the left and then the right, slowly, settling them. He did it after the third drill, when he went from the figure to the false heel, and again when he went back, so that each time he changed what he was going to do next, the shoulders went round first.

Cael had written it down two months ago, in his first entry, on a page he had later torn out and kept in his coat. Shoulders when he changes his mind. Renn had found Cael's nod, and had not, apparently, found his own shoulders.

"You've gone quiet," said Lira.

"He's right. It won't help me. Not the way he means."

She turned her head on her arms and looked at him.

"Knowing the heel can lie doesn't tell me when it's lying," he said. "If I watch it, I lose either way. He's built it so that watching the heel is the mistake." He looked at the page. "So I don't watch the heel."

"You've watched that heel for two months."

"I know." He shut the Log. "Gone."

There was no post here for Lira's chalk. But she looked at him with her chin on her arms, and her face came alight, there in the middle of a cold afternoon, at a gate full of people who had come to laugh at him.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

They walked down the lane afterward in the dusk and he told her the rest, because it was not finished until he had said it to somebody who would argue.

"He throws everything from the mark. So everything starts in the same place and goes the same way, straight at me. The figure's built to go forward, and it's very good going forward. So I don't stand where it's going. When Vell says begin, I go sideways, before the first fold."

"Which way?"

"Left. His left." He had worked that out at the gate. "The blade's on his right arm. If I go to his left, it has to come all the way across his body to find me, and that's longer. And the figure has to turn to follow me, and anything that's built to go one way and has to turn—"

"Has to stop to turn." Lira finished it, and her voice had gone sharp and interested. "Even for half a breath. Even if he's very good."

"He is very good."

"He's very good," she agreed. "He'll turn it the first time. He'll turn it smoothly, and you'll get hit anyway."

"Probably."

"And the heel?"

"I don't look at it. I look at his shoulders." He told her about the roll, and what it had meant on the first night, and what it had meant at the gate. "He'll start with a plan. When it doesn't work, he'll change it. When he changes it, I'll see it, and I'll know something new is coming, even if I don't know what."

Lira walked on without saying anything.

"And when do you hit him?"

"Not till he's tired. He said there wouldn't be a third exchange. He's built a plan that ends early." Cael looked at his hands. "A plan that's built to end in two costs a great deal to keep going for five."

"And if he isn't tired? If it's the fifth and he's still fresh and you've got nothing?"

He had thought about that too, at the gate, and had not got an answer that he liked, so he said the only one he had.

"Then I'll say gone, and do something else."

Lira laughed.

"That's not a plan. That's a promise to have another plan." She stopped at the well with the iron cover, where she always stopped, and looked at him in the last of the light. "It's not bad, though. The sideways is good. You stole that from me."

"I watched it on Sunday."

"I know. Every bit of it." She looked down at the four lanes. "Steal the rest of it too, if it's any use to you. That's what it's for." She turned to go, and then turned back. "And Cael. If he catches you on the turn, it's going to be across the back. Don't be surprised by that. Be ready for it."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

On Saturday, in the grey half, she was Renn.

She did it so well that the girls on the wall stopped eating to watch. She had his stroll and his rolled shoulders and his big careless hands, and a way of sticking her chest out that was not quite Renn but was so exactly what it felt like to stand across from Renn that Cael laughed out loud. Then she came straight off her mark at him with no amble and no probes, open-handed, and he went sideways, left, and her palm caught him across the back of the neck as he went.

"Turned it," she said. "Again."

He went sideways again. She turned it again, and the palm landed across his shoulder blades.

"You're going too late. You're waiting to see me start." She went back to her mark and rolled her shoulders, Renn's way. "Don't wait. He's not giving you anything to wait for. Go on the word."

They did it thirty times. By the twentieth he was going on Vell's word, said by Lira in Vell's voice, which was nearly as good as her Renn. By the twenty-fifth her palm was landing on his arm instead of his back, because the turn was costing her; and by the thirtieth she was breathing hard and he was not, and she noticed it, and stopped.

"There," she said. "That."

She did the false heel for him twice, settling into her back foot with her hand drawn back and holding it. Both times he felt his whole body lean toward going, the old way he had learned in the lamplight, and both times he made himself look at her shoulders and not her feet. The second time, while he was looking at her shoulders, her palm came across his ribs.

"Gone," he said.

She made a mark on the post with her chalk, the twenty-sixth, in rows of five.

"The heel's in you. Deep. That's what two months of watching it does. He knows that. It's why he built the whole thing on it." She wiped her face on her sleeve. "You'll feel it go tomorrow. Let it go. Don't fight it. Just don't let your feet follow it."

The old man was standing in his gate at the top of the lane when Cael walked up past the yards at noon. He was sleeves rolled, in the stance that looked like nothing else in the lane, watching the woman with the shoulder work through her six positions, and he did not look round, because he did not need to.

"Tomorrow?"

"Renn."

The old man said nothing. The woman with the shoulder reached her fourth position and held it, and the old man watched her hold it, and nodded once.

"He's been up the river," he said. "Three weeks. Poling." He shifted his weight from one foot to the other, very slightly. "That's arms and back. It isn't legs."

Then he went back to watching the woman with the shoulder, and Cael understood that he had been given everything that was coming.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

There was a letter for him at Torvin's when he came in, propped against the salt crock on the kitchen table where Torvin's wife put things she considered important. It was Hesk's square hand on the outside, the answer to the Dessa letter, which meant that it had been written a week ago, at the table at Fen Street, on the night the Dessa letter arrived.

He read it on the low wall by the pump, before supper, in the last of the light.

Most of it was the bench, and Ressa's hinge, which had stopped squeaking at last, and the survey office's young men, who had dropped another level. Some of it was the guild. The review had been given a date to sit, the second week of next month, which was this week, or the one after, depending on which day Hesk had counted from. He wrote that he would go in his good coat and answer what they asked, and that Cael was not to spend a single night on it.

Then there was a line on its own near the bottom, set a little apart from the rest.

You told me how you built it, one piece at a time. Keep that. A win you built is the only kind that teaches you anything. The other kind only teaches you to want another.

He read that three times. Hesk could not know that there had been another kind on that night too, in the fourth exchange, going across, because Cael had not written it. But the line sat on the page exactly over the place where he had not written it, the way a level's bubble sits over the one low corner of a bench, and he could not stop seeing it there. Then he folded the letter and put it in the leather book, and sat on the wall in the dusk with the pear tree over him. He thought about a man in a good coat walking into a guild hall in Denvash this week, or next, to answer questions about a boy who had gone east. He could do nothing about it at all from here, and would not know for a week how it had gone.

"Supper," called Torvin's wife from the door. "And the boots woman says she's got a bun on Renn, and I've got a bun on you, so you'd better eat something."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On Sunday the yard was full by the middle of the afternoon.

The benches were out along the shaded wall with the third row full of old men in scarves, and the rope was three deep on the shaded side and two deep in the sun. Renn's friends from the fish steps had come in a crowd and taken the sunny side by the gate, where they made the noise of men who had spent three weeks on a barge and had been paid on Thursday. The man who had been Cael in the middle yard was among them, with a bruise on his shoulder that he showed to people.

Marrow's slate said Renn with a short price and unrated (vouched) with a long one, and under them, Over-under: three exchanges.

"He's taken Renn at his word," Lira said at the barrel. "No third exchange." She had her arms folded on the top of the rope and her hair tied the ordinary way, with the knot coming loose. "Everybody's heard him say it."

"So has Renn."

"So has Renn. And now he's got to do it in front of all of them." She looked across the circle at the sunny side, where Renn was standing among his friends with his coat off and his sleeves pushed up, laughing at something and rolling his shoulders. "That's the trouble with showing off. You've said it. Now it has to be true."

The first bout was two Force fighters, women of about twenty, and it went to the fourth exchange and was won by the smaller of them, and the old men in the third row approved of it. Cael did not watch it; he stood at the rope and breathed as he breathed at his mark, in and out, four and four, as he had seen Dessa do it, and it helped.

Then Vell stood up behind her table.

"Second bout."

The yard went lower. Along the sunny side, Renn's friends began to bang on the top of the rope with their open hands.

"Renn. Copper Rank 3, Blade Path. Against unrated. Vouched." The small pause. "Begin when you're ready."

He went over the rope.

Renn came over the other side of it, and as he walked to his mark the blade came up out of nothing along his right forearm, pale and steady and straight, with its thin bright line along one edge. Cael's eye told him it stopped a hand past the knuckles. He told himself plus eight and saw it then, the real length, a long way further out than his eye wanted to believe.

Renn stood on his mark and rolled his shoulders, left and right.

Cael watched them go round, and did not look at the heel at all.

"Begin."

Renn came off the mark with the figure, and Cael was already going.

He went on the word, as Lira had made him go thirty times in the grey half, before the first fold had started. He went left along the inside of the groove, toward Renn's left side, away from the blade arm. The first fold came high through the place where he had been standing and cut nothing. The second came out of the end of it, low and across, and it was aimed at where he had been too. Then Renn turned it.

He turned it smoothly, as Lira had said he would. The figure bent round after Cael like a river bending round a stone, and the third fold came across low and late. Cael saw it coming and could not get all of himself out of its way, and the flat caught him across the outside of the left forearm, over the old burn, with a crack like a strap brought down on a table.

It was not the shoulder this time but the arm, and the burn under it lit up white from wrist to elbow, and he heard the sunny side roar, and he kept his feet and kept going, left, round the curve, until Vell called the break.

He went back to his mark with his left arm hanging and the fingers of that hand not quite closing.

First exchange, he said to himself, in Lira's report voice. No probes. All from the mark. He turned it. He turned it well.

And under that, which was not for any report: The turn cost him something. His feet were wide at the end. He had to put the right one down hard to come round.

Across the circle Renn was breathing easily. He grinned at Cael, and lifted his blade arm an inch, the way a man lifts a cup to somebody across a room.

"Begin."

Renn came off the mark slower.

Cael felt the change in it before he saw it, and his eyes went where two months had trained them to go, down to the back foot. The heel went back. It settled. It was the spring pressing down, the frame gathering, exactly as it had been in the lamplight.

And his whole body leaned to go.

He felt it happen. It was not a decision; it was older than a decision, a groove worn so deep in him that his weight was already tipping before his mind had finished seeing the heel, left and back, the way he had gone in the second exchange of the first night. His left foot came up off the dirt to carry him.

He's built it so that watching the heel is the mistake.

"Gone," said Cael, out loud.

He put the foot down where it had been.

It was not graceful, only a stumble that did not quite happen, half a step begun and taken back, and it left him standing flat-footed and off balance in the middle of the circle with Renn's weight still sitting on the heel, waiting for him to land.

He had not jumped, so there was nothing to land. Renn struck anyway, off the heel, because a loaded heel has to go somewhere. It was a real strike now and not a waiting one, and Cael was flat-footed under it. He got his right arm up, and the flat came down across the meat of his right thigh instead, hard. His leg buckled and he went down on one knee in the dirt, and came up again before he had properly understood that he had gone down.

The sunny side roared again.

Renn did not follow it up. He stood a pace and a half away with his blade still out and looked at Cael, and his face had a puzzled crease between the eyes. He had heard the word. Cael saw him hear it and not know what to do with it, as you would not know what to do if a man you were fighting stopped to tell you the time.

"Called," said Vell. "End of the exchange."

Cael limped to his mark with the thigh a deep hot ache, as if somebody had driven a post into it, and the forearm worse, and stood on it and made himself breathe, four and four.

The heel was still in him like a stone in a shoe. But he had felt it go, and let it go, and his feet had not gone with it, and he was standing.

Renn stood on his own mark, looking at him.

Then he rolled his shoulders, left and right.

He's changing it, said Cael, to himself. Something new.

"Begin."

Renn settled the heel again. Cael did not move. He watched Renn's shoulders, and the shoulders did nothing, and the heel sat there loaded, and the yard went quiet. Nobody struck. Two seconds went by, then three. In the third row an old man coughed.

Then Renn dropped.

It was the sweep. It was the answer he kept for readers, the whole heavy body going low and swinging round, leg first, with the blade arm flung out high as a counterweight and the pale edge drawing a line up into the air. It was meant for a boy who had learned not to jump for the heel, and who would be standing still, flat-footed, his ankles exactly where the leg went looking for them.

Cael had seen the shoulders go round. He did not know what was coming, but he knew something was, and he had decided at the gate on Friday that whatever it was, he would not be standing where it expected him to stand. He did not jump. He went back. He took two quick steps straight back toward his own mark, out of the whole reach of the swing, and the leg went through the empty place where his ankles had been and found nothing.

Renn came up out of the sweep in one smooth motion and stood there, breathing.

He was breathing harder now; Cael saw it in his chest, nothing yet, only a little more, a breath that came from lower down. But the sweep was a heavy thing to throw at nothing, and it was the third heavy thing he had thrown in three exchanges, and it had not been the plan.

The sunny side had gone a little quiet. Somebody along the rope said three, and somebody else told him to be quiet.

"Called," said Vell. "End of the exchange. Nothing."

That was the third exchange. Cael went back to his mark and did not look at Marrow's slate, and did not need to, because he could hear Marrow's chalk squeak somewhere behind the crowd.

Renn stood on his mark with his blade out and his hand on his hip, and looked at Cael, and the grin had gone. It had not gone into anything angry, but into the narrow, careful attention of the first night, the third exchange, the tradesman holding up a part off his own lathe that was not the shape he had cut.

He did not roll his shoulders this time; he set his feet. Cael saw him look, not at Cael, but at the place on Cael's left where Cael had gone in the first exchange.

He's learned the sideways, Cael thought. He's going to throw it where I'll be.

"Begin."

Renn came off the mark with the figure. He did not throw it at Cael. He threw it at the left, at the empty place on the inside of the groove where a boy who went sideways would be in half a breath. It was very well done. If Cael had gone left on the word, he would have run straight into the first fold.

He did not go left. He went right, toward the blade.

It was the wrong way and he knew it was the wrong way. It was the side of the arm with the eight inches on it, and the only reason to go there was that nobody would. The first fold went past him on the left, into the place where he was not, and Renn's whole weight went with it. The figure had been thrown to go one way with everything behind it. To come back for Cael it had to stop, and turn the other way, against itself, across his own body.

Renn stopped it and turned it. He was very strong in the arms, and he dragged the whole figure back round by main force. The second fold came at Cael late and high, and caught him, as Lira had said it would, across the back. The flat went from one shoulder blade to the other with a sound like a door slammed in a stone passage.

He went forward onto his hands. The dirt came up into his face. He felt the whole yard shout above him at once, Renn's friends and Brenna's friends and the old men, and for a moment he could not find his breath anywhere.

He found it. He got his feet under him and stood.

"Called," said Vell, very level. "End of the exchange."

He did not know how he got back to his mark. He was there, and the yard was very loud, and his back was a sheet of heat from one side to the other. His thigh was a post and his forearm was a bar of white fire. Across the circle Lira was standing at the barrel with both hands on the rope and her knuckles pale, and she was not biting them. She was looking straight at him with no expression at all.

He looked at Renn.

Renn was breathing hard now. It was not a little harder. It was hard, through the mouth, with his shoulders going up and down. Cael watched him and saw what dragging a figure back against itself had cost him, the whole heavy weight of it hauled round by the arms. It was the arms and back that three weeks of poling had made, and the legs that it had not. Renn's right foot, the front foot, was set wide on the dirt, and it was carrying everything. He had put it down there to haul the turn round, and he had not brought his weight back off it yet, and his heel was a finger off the ground.

The front heel. Not the back one. The front.

He stood on his mark with his back on fire and looked at that heel, a finger off the dirt with all of Renn on the ball of the foot above it, and he understood that this was the thing. It was not a tell, or a lie, or a plan. It was only what four exchanges of hauling had done to a big man's legs, and it was there because Renn had built a plan to end in two, and was in his fifth.

"Begin," said Vell.

Renn rolled his shoulders.

Cael saw them go round, and knew that something new was coming, and did not wait to find out what.

He went straight in.

He did not go left, or right. He went forward, on the word, straight at the middle of Renn, into the one place no sensible person went against a Blade. A blade was only dangerous at its length. Inside its length, close in, it was a forearm with something pale stuck to it, and a forearm was only a forearm.

Renn's new thing was the figure again, from the mark, thrown high and across at the place where Cael would have been if he had stood. Cael was not standing. He was under it, inside it, so close that the first fold went over his head and behind him. The blade did not touch him. The forearm under it came down across the top of his left shoulder, heavy, a bone on a bone. He felt it shove him down and kept going.

He was inside. He was chest to chest with Renn, close enough to smell the river on his shirt, and Renn's whole weight was still up on the ball of his front foot, where the figure had thrown it.

Cael put his left foot behind Renn's front heel.

He did not kick it. He set his foot there, on the dirt, behind the heel that was a finger off the ground, as you might set a wedge behind a wheel. In the same breath his right hand came up from the hip, short and straight, with the back foot driving and the shoulder following and the fist arriving last. It was the one strike he owned. He did not throw it at Renn's face, or his ribs. He threw it at the middle of his chest, flat, and not hard, because it did not need to be hard.

Renn's weight was going forward, into the figure. The strike pushed it back. It went back onto a heel that could not come down because there was a foot behind it.

He went over.

He went the way a tall stack of sacks goes when you take the bottom one out, slowly at first and then all at once. His arms flew out. The blade went up into the air with its bright edge flashing, and he came down flat on his back across the groove with a sound that went out of him in one great hah. Cael went down with him, onto one knee beside him, because there was nowhere else for his legs to go, and his right fist went up over Renn's face, and stopped there.

Renn lay on his back in the dirt and looked up at the fist.

The blade went out along his forearm, like a breath let go.

"Called," said Vell. "Unrated."

For a moment the whole yard was quiet.

Then the old men in the third row began to stamp their feet on the boards, all together, slowly. The shaded side took it up with its hands, and then, after a long breath, the sunny side, because Renn's friends were river people and they had seen what they had seen. Up on the wall one of the girls was standing with both arms in the air, and the errand boys were shouting at each other.

Cael took his fist away from Renn's face and could not get up, so he stayed on one knee with his hand on the ground, breathing.

Renn lay on his back across the groove with his arms out and his chest going up and down, looking at the sky. Then he began to laugh. It started low, somewhere in his ribs, and came up through him until he was shaking with it, flat in the dirt in front of the whole yard, and he did not seem to mind any of it.

"The front," he said, when he could. "You took the front one."

"You were standing on it."

"I know I was standing on it." Renn wiped his eyes with the back of his wrist. "Five exchanges. I said there wouldn't be a third." He lay there a moment longer. "I let you have that, you know."

Cael got to his feet, which took two tries, and got hold of Renn's hand and pulled, and Renn came up off the dirt, which took both of them, and stood swaying a little, with his free hand on his thigh. They touched fists. Renn's hand was shaking, and so was Cael's.

"I came back for a second look," said Renn, quietly, under the noise. "I wanted to see the third exchange again. What you did that night." He shook his head. "I had a plan for everything you did. Every single thing. I had a plan for the heel and a plan for the sideways and a plan for you standing still." He looked down at his own front foot. "I didn't have a plan for you having a plan."

His friends shouted him down. One of them threw a hat.

Cael walked to the table.

He stood in front of it and waited, as you waited, while Vell wrote, and the pen went on for one line, and then a second, and did not stop.

"Yes."

Vell looked at him a moment longer, then down at the book again, and dipped her pen, and wrote something small, in the place where she kept the things that were hers.

"Go and put your arm in cold water. Not butter."

He could not walk properly on the way home, so Lira walked on his right side, the thigh side, without being asked, and did not say anything for a whole street.

Then she said, "Report?"

"I want it in your words. With the marks beside it." She looked at him sideways. "And then I want to tell you that you're an idiot for going right in the fourth, and then I want to tell you that it was the best thing you've done in this district. In that order."

He gave her the report slowly, because his back hurt when he talked, and she walked beside him through the lamps coming on and listened to every word of it and did not interrupt once, not even at gone.

At the corner where the lane of yards came down into the street, the old man was standing in the dark with his sleeves rolled down for once, against the cold, as though he had been on his way somewhere and had stopped. He had not been at the rope; Cael had looked for him there and not found him.

The old man looked at the way Cael was walking, and at his left arm, which Cael was holding against his chest because it was easier than letting it hang.

"Five," said the old man.

Then he turned and went on up the lane toward his gate, and did not look back.

Chapter 36 — A Week Behind

[Patient, methodical narration; give training, failure, and discovery room to accumulate]

Hesk read the letter for the first time standing up, in the workshop doorway, with the runner's footsteps still going away down Fen Street and the cold coming in round his legs.

He read it fast, the way you look at a gauge to see whether the needle is in the red before you look at what number it is pointing to. I won tonight. That was the needle. Everything after it was the number, and he could take his time over the number. He shut the door and went to the bench and read it again, with Ressa's oven hinge in the vice in front of him and a fine file in his hand, a stroke of the file for every line. If his hands were busy, his head did not run off in front of the words and decide what they meant before it had got to the end of them.

A woman called Dessa, Copper Rank 5 in the book here, Stone Path, the best defender in the yard.

He had never seen Dessa, or the yard. He knew the Cinder House only as two words in a boy's handwriting, and a book kept by a woman whose name he had written on the back of an envelope in case he forgot it. And yet he could see all of it perfectly well: a defender who won by standing still, and a boy on a bench watching her twice, a week apart, with his chin tucked and his eyes very wide, writing down the thing she did not know she did.

The way you taught me to watch a stance.

Hesk put the file down for a moment, and then picked it up again, because the hinge did not care what he felt, and that was the great comfort of hinges.

It was on that second reading, slower, with the file going, that he noticed what he had been too glad to notice the first time. In the third I went into it, the boy had written, and then, with nothing between, She said afterward that it was the cleanest read anyone had made on her. The letter did not say whether the winning had happened in the third or somewhere after it, or how; and a boy who wrote down the angle of a gate guard's thumb on a card would not leave out the exchange in which he had won his first fight. Not unless he meant to.

Hesk had spent thirty years reading load sheets that other men had filled in. He knew what a column looked like when a figure had been left out of it. It did not look empty. It looked very slightly too neat.

He looked for the anger, because he thought he might be owed some, and found instead something older and more tired that had his own face. He had kept a great many things in a great many neat columns for a great many years: Tuesdays, the provisions, the preliminary assessment, and a file he had once seen opened in a room above his own clearance. He had kept them from the boy until the boy found them out for himself and came to him angry, across the workshop bench, on the second day after Kindling. A few years, he had said in the side room at Weaver's Row, and he remembered the boy's face. If there was a figure missing from this letter, it was missing for the boy's reason. He would tell it when it was worth telling, or he would not, and either way it was not Hesk's to dig out of a letter with a file.

He answered that night at the kitchen table. He wrote about the bench, because the boy had asked for ordinary things, and about Ressa's hinge, which had stopped squeaking at last, and about the guild giving his review a date to sit. He told the boy not to spend a single night on it, though he knew perfectly well that the boy would spend several. Then he sat with the pen lifted over the last part of the page, and wrote one line about building, which did not ask about anything or point at any column, and left room beside it for whatever else might be true as well.

He sealed it and propped it on the shelf by the door for the morning, against the guild's letter, which had stood against the clock there since the second morning after the depot with Routine written across its corner in somebody else's hand.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Joren came three afternoons after that, and he did not walk past.

He had walked past every day for two months, and Hesk had watched him do it from the bench, through the window over the vice. Joren would come along Fen Street from the direction of his family's yard, flat-footed, with his heels set down hard at every step as though he were trying to press them into the cobbles. He would look straight ahead until the last moment, and then turn his head to look in, and then look away again very quickly, as if he had been caught at something. Hesk had never once let him see that he had seen.

This afternoon he stopped in the doorway.

"Afternoon," said Hesk, not looking up from the bench.

"Afternoon." Joren stood there. He had grown since the autumn, or else he was standing differently; he was a big boy, broad like his father, who had always filled doorways, and now he seemed to be trying to fill this one carefully, without leaning on the frame. "Has he written?"

"Every week."

"Is he—" Joren stopped, and seemed to look for a better word, and not to find one. "Is he all right?"

Hesk put down the file and considered how to answer, not because he did not know, but because he wanted the answer to be the true one and the right size for a boy in a doorway, and those were not always the same.

"He's lodging at a house with a sign whose O leans. He pays on time. He works two afternoons a week for a mender who doesn't talk in the mornings. He's got a friend who's teaching him to use his feet." He picked the file up again. "And he won a fight, the week before last."

Joren's whole face changed.

"A fight?" It was nearly a shout. "Cael? In a ring? Against somebody?"

"Against a woman who was very good at standing still, I gather. He watched her for two weeks and then found the thing she did when she was tired."

Joren stared at him, and then began to laugh, helplessly, holding on to the doorframe after all.

"That's him. That's exactly him. Two weeks. He'd have had a notebook." He wiped his eyes. "He'd have had a chart."

"I expect he did."

Joren stood in the doorway grinning, and then the grin went slowly, as if he had remembered something, and he looked down at his own feet on the step.

There was a word between them. Hesk knew Joren knew it, because the boy had written it in a note and left it in the gap in the wall where they had always left things for each other. Joren knew that Hesk knew he knew it, and neither of them said it. It sat in the doorway between them like a third person who had not been introduced, and Hesk let it sit there, because it was not his to say to anybody, and the one person whose it was had chosen who to say it to.

He did not say summons either; the summons was not in any letter yet, and there was nothing yet to say.

"I'm practising," said Joren, to his feet. "Patience. Like you said. Every morning, in the yard behind ours. I stand." He looked up. "With the stance. It's the only thing it does, standing. I thought if that's the only thing it does, I'd better be the best at it there is." He made a face. "It's very boring."

"It's meant to be."

"My father says I'm wasting my mornings."

"Your father," said Hesk, "has never stood still in his life, and has never been able to finish anything that needed it." He got up from the bench. "Come here a minute."

He had a level on the bench for the survey office, the fourth, with its glass set in its frame and the cement not yet cured. It had to be held exactly upright, without the smallest tremor, for the best part of an hour while the cement went off. He had been going to rig a clamp for it. He gave it to Joren instead, and showed him how to hold it, and where to set his feet.

"Don't move it," he said. "Not a hair. If the bubble moves, the cement sets crooked and some young man drops off a roof because his level lied to him."

Joren took it as though it were made of eggshell.

Hesk felt the stance come into the boy before he saw it, a kind of settling in the floorboards, very faint, as if the workshop had become a little heavier on one side. Joren's heels went down, and his knees softened, and his whole body seemed to go quiet from the feet upward, and the little bubble in the glass, which had been trembling, stopped.

Joren held it for fifty minutes without a word. Hesk worked at the bench and did not watch him, and watched him the whole time.

At the end of it Joren set the level down on the bench as gently as a sleeping child, and stood rubbing his arms, which had gone dead, and looked as proud as Hesk had ever seen him look of anything.

"Tell him," he said at the door. "When you write. Tell him my heels are down."

"I'll tell him."

"And tell him—" Joren stopped again. "No. Just that." He went off up Fen Street toward his family's yard, flat-footed, his heels set hard into the cobbles at every step, and he did not look back, because he did not need to look in at anything now.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The other letter came two days later, a week to the day after the boy had posted it, and Hesk read the first line and sat down on the step of the workshop in the street.

Your letter came on the fifty-first day, on the same cart as a man from the Compact.

He read it all the way through sitting on the step, with people going by in the street and a cart going past close enough to touch, and noticed none of them.

A man from the Compact at Torvin's door, asking for the boy by his whole name. A summons for a compliance evaluation, forty-eight hours, physical retrieval if he did not go. The boy had gone down into a reading room under the man's own floor and read the law until he found the place where it did not fit him, and read it aloud four times, the way you read a load figure before you sign it. He had walked into the man's office with an objection on a single sheet, and come out with the summons stamped closed, pending, and six weeks, and a senior evaluator to come.

He had done all of that eight days ago, two days' road away. He had done it on his own, or nearly; the letter did not say, but there was the girl, Lira, who told him the truth about his feet, and Hesk hoped very much she had been somewhere near. Hesk had known nothing about any of it; he had been filing a hinge for Ressa's oven door while it happened.

He read the line about the reading room again, and the one about the appendix, and the loose page tucked back in crooked. Then he sat on the step with the letter on his knee, more frightened than he had been at any moment since Weaver's Row, though there was nothing at all to be frightened about, because it was over.

That was the post, and it was nobody's fault. A letter took a week, and a week was the price of the boy being somewhere he could not be found by the next man who came looking for him in Denvash. Hesk had agreed to the price and helped to set it, and he had not understood until this moment, sitting on his own step, what it would feel like to pay it. It meant being frightened a week late, all at once, for something that had already been finished by somebody braver than he was.

He went back into the workshop and sat down at the bench and opened the drawer of springs, because he had a job for the survey office that needed one, and because his hands wanted something to do.

He did not look at what he was doing. He put his hand into the drawer as he had put it into that drawer ten thousand times, and the end of a broken coil spring that should not have been in there at all went straight into the heel of his palm.

He looked at it for a moment as though it were somebody else's hand, and then wrapped it in a clean rag from the bench and went out, and walked down to Merchant Row to the healers'.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

The healers' house on Merchant Row had a blue door and a bench along the wall inside for people waiting, and a smell of hot water and something green. On the bench there were a carter with a crushed finger and a woman with a coughing child, and Hesk sat down at the end of it with his hand in the rag and waited his turn.

A girl came through from the back with two basins of steaming water, one on each hip, and set them down by the senior healer's table without spilling either. She had a plain grey apron on, too big for her, with the strings wound twice round her waist and her hair pinned up out of the way. When she straightened up and saw him, her face went quite still.

It was Alis Trent.

He had not spoken to her since the morning of the boy's Kindling, when they had passed her two blocks from home on the way back from Weaver's Row. She had been on the other side of the street with a basket, and she had lifted one open hand to the boy without crossing, and the boy had lifted his. He had heard from Cael's letters and from Ressa that she had gone to the healers', and had not thought about what that meant. It meant this: a fourteen-year-old girl carrying basins in an apron too big for her, with her sleeves pushed up past the elbow.

She came over, wiping her hands on the apron.

"Master Hesk." She looked at the rag. "What have you done?"

"Put my hand in a drawer without looking."

"That's what everybody says." She knelt on the floor in front of the bench, and unwound the rag, and looked at the heel of his palm with her head on one side. "It's not deep. It's dirty. She'll want it washed and bound and she'll want to look at it after." She glanced back at the senior healer, who had the carter's finger in both her hands and did not look up. "She'll let me wash it. I'm allowed to wash things."

"Only wash?"

"Wash, and carry, and boil, and fold, and watch." Alis fetched a small basin and a cloth and knelt down again. "Not anything else until the spring. Not anything with the Path. She says I don't know what I'm listening to yet, so I'm not to go poking about in anybody with it till I do." She dipped the cloth. "This'll sting."

It stung. She was careful and quick and not at all frightened of the blood, and she washed the cut out three times, and then held it up to the window and looked into it, and washed it a fourth time because she was not satisfied. She was a good deal more thorough than the carter's finger seemed to be getting.

"Is it true," she said, to his hand, "that he's in Ardenmere?"

"It's true."

"Ressa told my mother." She folded a pad of clean linen. "Is he all right?"

Hesk had been asked that twice now in a week, and had answered it two ways, and found he had a third ready.

"He's lodging at a house where they make him eat his oats. He works two afternoons a week for a mender. He has a friend who's fifteen and very quick and tells him the truth about his feet." He watched her bind the pad on. "And he's learning things. He writes me every week. He's well."

All of it was true, and none of it was the word. Alis had seen the boy's face on the way home that morning and knew it had gone badly, but not how badly, or what it had been called, and she had not asked, and he did not tell her. He did not tell her about the reading room either, or the forty-eight hours, or the summons stamped closed, pending, or anything that had been in the letter now folded in the inside pocket of his coat. It was not his to tell, and she was kneeling on the floor of a healers' house in an apron too big for her, learning a trade, and she did not need to carry anything of his down Merchant Row tonight.

"Good," said Alis. She tied off the binding, and it was neat, neater than he could have done it with two good hands. "Tell him I carry basins." She almost smiled. "He'll laugh. He always said I'd be the one who ran a whole ward."

"He'll laugh," Hesk agreed.

She got up off the floor and took the basin away, and the senior healer came over afterward, as Alis had said she would, and looked at the binding and turned his hand in hers and said, "Who did this?" When Hesk said that the girl had, she grunted, and did not undo it, and went back to the carter.

He walked home up Merchant Row in the dusk with his bound hand in his coat pocket and the boy's letter against his chest, less frightened than he had been on the step, though nothing had changed. A girl had knelt on a floor and washed a cut four times when three was not enough. Watching her be careful had steadied him, as the boy had once written that the sacks off Ressa's wagon steadied him at a kitchen table with a notice on it.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The review sat on the Friday of the week after, in the small room on the upper floor of the guild hall by the canal, with the shutters half closed against the light.

There were three of them at the table: the reviewing officer from the guild's own office, a thin careful man with a portfolio, whom Hesk had met once when he came to look at the workshop and ask about the drawer of springs. The other two were members chosen by lot, as the guild's rules required. One was a lens-grinder from the Inner District whom Hesk knew only by sight. The other was a woman he had sat near at thirty years of guild suppers without ever once learning her name, which he realized only as he sat down. She was a gauge-maker with a shop on the canal, a small fierce woman with a magnifier on a ribbon round her neck. She looked at his bound hand and raised her eyebrows and said nothing.

The reviewing officer read out the notice in full, in the voice in which such things are read: Statute 14, Section 9; the residence; the standing; the paragraph that said what keeping the person close would cost. He read Hesk's own account after it, the one Hesk had written and sent and been asked for a copy of. The person named in the registry notice of the second day no longer resides at this address. He left on the morning of the third day for another city, where he is lawfully resident, and he goes with my full support.

"Is that still the case?"

"It is."

"He has not returned to Denvash?"

"He has not."

"Do you maintain contact with him?"

Hesk had known this question would come, and had thought on several nights about how to answer it, and had decided in the end that there was only one answer he could give and still be able to look at his own hands afterward.

"I write to him every week. He writes to me. I intend to go on doing both."

The lens-grinder made a small note. The reviewing officer looked at him for a moment over the portfolio.

"The statute does not prohibit correspondence," he said at last, as though he were reading it off a page in his head. "It concerns residence and association. Correspondence is—" He seemed to choose a word. "Not specified."

"Then I'll go on with it," said Hesk, "until somebody specifies it."

The gauge-maker with the magnifier made a noise in her throat that might have been a cough.

They asked him about the workshop, and about his work for the survey office and the canal company, and whether any of it was work in which the guild's good name could be said to rest on his. He told them it was levels and gauges, and that the young men at the survey office dropped them off ladders, and that the canal had not flooded anybody in thirty years on his figures. The lens-grinder nearly smiled. They asked whether he had made any application on the boy's behalf, to any office, for any exemption. He said he had not; there was none to make. They asked him whether he had anything to add.

He thought of a great deal he could add: a reading room under a man's floor, and a loose page tucked back in crooked, and four readings aloud. He thought of a girl he had never met who told the boy the truth about his feet, and a level held for fifty minutes by a boy whose father said he was wasting his mornings.

"No," he said.

They sent him out to wait on the landing, on a hard chair under a portrait of some guild master from before anybody now living had been born. He waited for most of an hour and did not look at the portrait, but at his bound hand, and thought about the cut being washed four times.

When they called him back in, the reviewing officer did not sit down.

"The guild has considered the notice and the member's account," he said. "It finds no present cause to act on the member's standing." He closed the portfolio. "The matter will remain on the book."

"Remain," said Hesk.

"On the book. Open." The reviewing officer looked at him with something that was very nearly apology and was not allowed to be. "If the Compact writes to us again, about this, we will be obliged to look again. If it does not, the book will stay as it is."

So it was not closed, and it was not lost either. It was a door left on the latch, which was, Hesk thought, walking down the stairs with his good coat buttoned, very much the shape of everything else this autumn.

The gauge-maker caught him up at the bottom of the stairs. She walked beside him without saying anything, out into the street along the canal, with her magnifier swinging on its ribbon, until they came to the corner where she would go one way and he the other.

"The drawer of springs," she said. "He asked me about it, that man, when he came to my shop. Whether it was usual." She looked at his hand. "I told him every workshop in Denvash has a drawer of springs, and that a man who doesn't is either a liar or a bad maker." She snorted. "He wrote it down."

Then she went off along the canal toward her shop, and Hesk stood on the corner, a little warmed, and still did not know her name.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

He answered the boy's letter that night at the kitchen table, with the lamp close and his bound hand stiff on the paper. It took him three sheets, not because he did not know what he wanted to say but because of choosing what to leave out.

He put in the review, plainly: that it had sat, that they had asked whether he wrote to the boy and he had told them he did, every week, and meant to go on, and what remain on the book meant. He put in the gauge-maker and the drawer of springs, because the boy would like it. He put in that he had checked the citation as well as he could from Denvash with no handbook, and that he was proud of the reading and of the four times aloud, and he left that short so that it would stay true.

Then he came to the fear, and sat a long time with the pen lifted. He could leave it out. It would do no good, and it could not reach back and change one thing that had happened at that desk upstairs at the post. But they had made a bargain, the two of them, one letter apart: I'd rather have the telling, he had written once, and the boy had written back, as it comes. So he wrote down the step in the street, and the week-late fear, in six sentences, and did not soften any of them.

He did not put in the hand, or the spring, which mattered to nobody but him and the survey office. At the bottom, because he had promised, he put in Joren's heels and Alis's basins.

He read it over once by the lamp. It was all true, and it was not all of what was true. He was not sure he had ever written a letter in his life of which both of those things could not be said.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

"Bronze," said Lira.

She said it as if she were reading the word off the side of a crate, to see whether it was the crate she had ordered.

It was Tuesday morning in Ardenmere, a week and a valley east of Fen Street. Vell had her table out for the afternoon card, and they were standing in front of it because she had sent the pie boy to the low wall to fetch them. Cael was standing more or less straight, which had taken him two days to manage. The back was a band of colour from one shoulder blade to the other, black at the middle and green at the edges, and it pulled whenever he lifted his arms. The thigh had a print on it the width of a blade's flat, a long dark bar he could have laid a ruler along. His left forearm, over the old burn, had swollen up like a loaf and was going down slowly in cold water from the pump.

Lira had not let him do anything on Monday but sit on the low wall in the grey half and watch her drill, and on Tuesday she had let him walk the box at the slowest speed she had. Efficient, she had said, when he argued. I said I'd tell you. I'm telling you.

"Bronze Rank 1," said Vell. "Blade Path. Her name's Sarel. She fights here a few times a season, when she's got nothing better on, and she's on Sunday because she asked for something on Sunday." She looked at Cael. "You'll have her if you want her. If you don't, I'll give her somebody else, and nobody will think the less of you. Most people in this yard wouldn't take her if I paid them."

"Why me?"

"Not to win." Vell set down her tea. "You've won three of seven in this book now, and two of them inside a week. Every one of them, you watched first, and found the thing, and the thing was there. I'd like to know what you do when it isn't. When there's nothing to find, or you can't find it fast enough to use." She looked at Lira. "She's quick. She's quicker than anything you've stood across from. And she's fair. She won't hurt you for the pleasure of it, and she won't make it easy for the pleasure of it either."

Lira was looking at Vell with her arms folded. "Survivable?"

It was not quite a question to Vell. It was the question Lira had promised to ask, on the first morning of the six weeks, by the post.

Vell considered her, and seemed to understand exactly what it was.

"Survivable. If he's sensible. And if you've taught him to fall."

Lira looked at Cael, and he looked back and saw her weigh it, as she weighed a bout between exchanges, and not like the answer she came to.

"He'll be sensible," she said. "I'll see to the falling."

Vell picked up her pen.

"She's on this afternoon, as it happens. Third bout." She was writing. "And Thursday. Watch her both times. I'd watch her with both eyes. I don't think it'll help you much. But I'd like to see what you write."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He watched Sarel fight that afternoon at the rope on the shaded side, near the barrel, with the Log open on his knee and the pencil ready, and he did not write much.

She was about thirty, long-legged and lean, with dark hair cut short as a boy's and a long scar down the outside of one forearm, the left, old and white. She worked, somebody at the rope said, on the scaffolds the builders put up round the new houses on the east road. She had the scaffold walker's way of standing, with her weight easy and her arms loose, like somebody who has long since stopped thinking about how high she is. She came over the rope without any hurry at all, and her opponent was a Copper Rank 5, a Force man with a reputation, and he was not happy to be there.

"Begin when you're ready," said Vell.

Sarel's blade came up along her right forearm, pale and straight, no longer than Renn's as far as Cael's eye could tell, and no brighter. Then she moved, and he understood why Vell had said what she had said.

She did not amble, or probe, or throw a figure from her mark; she simply arrived. She was on her mark, and then she was in front of the Force man, inside his reach, and the flat of her blade was already coming down on his shoulder. Cael was sure he had seen her start. He had not seen her cross.

It was not like Lira's step, which folded the ground. This was only a body that was very fast, faster than any body he had seen, so fast that the watching could not keep up with it. By the time his eyes had told him she's moving, she had moved, and struck, and was already going somewhere else.

He wrote closes very fast and looked up, and she had done two more things while he wrote it.

He stopped writing and watched her hips and her feet and her shoulders, all the places Hesk had taught him, and every place he looked she had already left. He tried to find the thing she did before she went. There had to be a thing; there was always a thing. The heel. The dip. The shimmer. The breath. The lean.

He could not find it, not because it was not there, but because by the time he had looked for it in one place, she had done whatever she did, and he was looking for the next one.

The Force man went down in the third exchange, on his back, with the flat of her blade resting on his collarbone.

"Called," said Vell. "Blade Path."

Cael looked down at the Log. It said closes very fast, and under it left foot?, crossed out, and shoulders?, crossed out, and something before she goes—, unfinished.

Lira had come up beside him at some point and was standing very close, with her shoulder against his good one.

"Well?"

"I couldn't write fast enough."

"No." She did not say anything else for a moment. "Nobody could. I couldn't, and I've spent half my life looking at fast people." She looked at the page. "That's the bout, Cael. That's what she's for. Not the page you couldn't fill." She took a breath. "You'll watch her on Thursday. You'll get one more line. Maybe two. And then on Sunday you'll go in with two lines against a woman who doesn't care about lines."

"And then?"

"And then you'll find out what you do when you've got nothing to look up." She bumped his shoulder very gently. "And I'll teach you to fall properly before then. Because you're going to."

On Thursday he watched Sarel again, against a Copper 4 Stone, and got one more line. She doesn't look at you. She looks at the space next to you, where you're going to be. He sat over the line on the low wall by the pump afterward, with the cold coming down, knowing it was true and not knowing what to do with it. Then he turned the page and wrote at the top of a clean one, Sarel. Bronze Rank 1, Blade. Under it there was nothing at all, and he left it like that, because nothing at all was the honest entry.

Chapter 37 — Nothing to Look Up

[Patient, methodical narration; give training, failure, and discovery room to accumulate]

"Again," said Lira. "And this time don't put your hand out."

He had put his hand out. He had put it out every time, eleven times that morning, because it was what a hand did when the ground came up at you, and every time she had stopped him and made him get up and do it again.

They were in the low corner of the yard by the drain, where the mist pooled in the mornings and the dirt was softest from the water that ran down off the public house roof. Lira had chosen it for that; she had said, with a perfectly straight face, that she wanted him to learn to fall on soft ground first so that he would have something to be disappointed about later.

"A hand out is a broken wrist. Or a broken arm, if she's heavy. You land on the meat. The side of your leg, your hip, your back across here." She slapped the back of her own shoulder. "Chin in. Roll. Let the ground have it. Don't argue with the ground. It's bigger than you."

"Is that a Wind saying?"

"It's a Lira saying. I've been knocked down more than anyone in this yard." She brought her hands up. "Again."

She came at him with the step, slowly, at half speed, and her shoulder came into his and took his feet. He went down sideways and tucked his chin and let his hip take the dirt and rolled, and his hand stayed folded in against his chest, and he came up onto one knee with mud down his whole left side and his back screaming where the bruise was.

"There. That one."

She made a mark on the post with her chalk, but not a gone mark. She had started a second column on the other side of the post for falls, and it had seven in it now, and the gone column had thirty-four.

The strange thing was that he had stopped noticing the word. It was Saturday, the eighteenth morning since the board, and he still said it every time a plan died, as she had made him promise. But it came out of him now without any heat in his ears, and sometimes before he had properly decided the plan was dead, so that his body was already doing the next thing while his mind caught up and agreed. It was beginning to feel less like a confession and more like a hinge.

They did the falls until the sun came over the east wall, and then Lira wanted the step at full speed, because she said she had been going slowly for him all week and her legs had forgotten what they were for.

She did it ten times: the two empty touches, high and quick, one from each hand, the ground folding, the backhand coming round at head height and stopping beside his ear. He got his counter half built on the fourth and on the seventh, which was better than one in ten. By the ninth she was breathing hard, because she had been up since before light and had already done an hour at the post before he came, and he could see the morning in her shoulders.

On the tenth she went too far.

It was very small. The backhand came round and stopped by his ear, as it always did, but her weight did not stop with it. It went on past the place where the strike had ended, a hand's width further, onto her right foot, the way a door goes on swinging after you have let go of the handle. She had to put the right foot down hard and wide to catch herself. For half a breath she was standing open, with her whole right side turned toward him and nothing between his hands and her ribs.

Then she was back, and loose, and grinning, and pushing her hair off her face with her wrist. "Again. No. Enough. Bread."

He had seen it once before, in the fourth exchange against Brenna three weeks ago, when she had gone in on Brenna's right and gone a hair further than she needed to. Brenna's cocked fist had come round and caught her on the side of the head as she came out. He had seen it at the rope, and he had decided at the rope that once was not a pattern, and he had left it out of her report.

That was twice.

He took the larger half of the bread and ate it and did not say anything.

He told himself that he would tell her after Sunday, because she should not be carrying a thing about her own feet into a week when she would be at the barrel watching him get hit by a Bronze. That was true. It was the kind of true that has its legs sawn short, and he knew it, and he ate his bread.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The yard was full on Sunday by the middle of the afternoon, and it was not full for him.

He understood that the moment he came through the gate in the wall. The benches were out, with the third row already crowded with old men in scarves, and the rope was three deep on the shaded side, but the noise of the crowd was not the noise there had been for Renn. It was not the noise of people who had come to see what would happen. It was the noise of people who had come to see something they already knew would happen, done well.

They had come for Sarel, who fought here a few times a season, Vell had said, when she had nothing better on, and when she did, people came.

Marrow's slate said Sarel with no price beside it at all. Under it was unrated (vouched), with a price so long it ran off the edge of the slate and had been chalked round the corner, and under that, Over-under: three exchanges.

"Three," said Lira at the barrel. "He thinks you'll last three. That's generous."

"Is it?"

"It's Marrow. It's whatever makes him money." She had her arms folded on the rope and her eyes on the far side of the circle, where Sarel was standing by the water bucket talking to the woman who sold the water, easy, with one hand in her pocket. "Remember the falling."

"I remember the falling."

"Chin in. Land on the meat. Don't argue with the ground." She was not looking at him. "And remember what it's for. It's not for winning. Vell said so and she's right. You find out what you do when there's nothing to look up. That's all."

"And if I don't find anything?"

Lira turned her head and looked at him at last. "Then you'll have found that. That's still something. Go on."

The first bout was two young Blades, and it was quick, and nobody remembered it.

Then Vell stood up.

"Second bout." She did not need to wait for the yard to go quiet; it had been quiet since she stood. "Sarel. Bronze Rank 1, Blade Path. Against unrated. Vouched." The small pause. "Begin when you're ready."

Sarel came over the rope.

She came over without hurry, as she had on Tuesday and Thursday. She was taller than he had thought from the rope, long in the leg and lean all through, and the scaffold walker's ease was in everything she did. She walked to her mark and stood on it, and she did not look at him; he saw her not look at him. She looked at the dirt just beside his left foot, and then at the dirt beside his right, as though she were measuring a floor for a carpet.

The blade came up along her right forearm, pale and straight.

"Begin," said Vell.

He watched her hips.

That was the first thing, and it was a mistake, and he knew it was a mistake even as he made it. He had decided on Thursday night that watching would not work and that he would watch anyway for one exchange, because he had to know, and because he did not have anything else. So he stood on his mark with his hands up and his eyes on her hips, and he waited for the thing she did before she went.

She went.

He saw her start; he was sure of that afterward. He saw her weight go forward, and he had time to think now, and to begin to move. Then she was in front of him, inside his reach, and the flat of her blade was coming down across his right shoulder. His mind arrived at that fact a long way behind his body. It landed like a plank dropped from a height, a broad flat slap that spun him and took his feet.

He fell.

He fell as Lira had taught him for four mornings, without putting his hand out; he tucked his chin and let his right hip have the ground, and rolled, and came up on one knee with dirt down his whole side. Sarel was already walking back to her mark.

Along the rope somebody laughed, not unkindly.

First exchange, he said to himself, in Lira's report voice. She started and I saw her start. I didn't see her cross. I fell properly.

That was all there was to report, so he got up.

In the second exchange he tried his one line.

She doesn't look at you. She looks at the space next to you, where you're going to be. He had written it on Thursday and looked at it for an hour, and it meant that if he went where he would naturally go, she would be there first. So when she came, he would go the other way.

"Begin."

She looked at the dirt beside his left foot. She went. He saw her go, and he went the other way, right, away from where she was looking, as fast as he had ever moved.

She was there.

She had not been looking at the left at all, or she had, and had seen him begin to go right, and had simply gone right as well, faster. He did not know which, and he would never know which. The flat came across his ribs on the right side, low, where Renn had put it on the first night, and it lifted him and put him down. He landed on his back across the groove with every bit of breath gone.

He lay there for a moment looking at the sky, which was white and very far away, and thought that he had fallen properly, chin in, on the meat, and had not argued with the ground.

He got up, more slowly than the first time.

He stood on his mark with his ribs on fire and his shoulder throbbing, and he understood something, all at once and quite clearly. It was not the comfortable clarity of a figure coming right. It was the other kind, the kind that comes when you have pushed hard on a bracket and felt it give.

Everything he did was watching; it was the whole of him. He watched, and found the thing, and planned from the thing, and it had beaten Dessa and the kiln boy and Renn, and kept him standing against everyone else. It was the oldest thing he owned, older than the Log, older than Ardenmere. Hesk had given it to him on a Tuesday in a community hall in Denvash. The third exchange is where they tell you the truth.

Sarel was not going to tell him the truth in the third exchange. She was telling it in the first, and the second, and every one after it, and it was simply too fast to read. By the time he had read anything, it was already over.

The watching was too slow for her. Not wrong. Too slow.

"Gone," said Cael, standing on his mark.

He did not say it loudly. But the yard had gone quiet between the exchanges, the way it did for a Bronze, and he heard it carry. Along the rope, on the shaded side, Lira's head came up. Across the circle, for the first time, Sarel looked at him and not at the dirt beside him. Her eyebrows went up a very little.

"Begin," said Vell.

He did not watch her.

He did not know what else to do, so he did what Lira did, the thing she had been trying to teach him for two months and that he had nodded at and gone on not doing, morning after morning. He moved. He did not move to anywhere, or decide where he would be and then go there. He moved small and quick and all the time, a half step left, a quarter step back, a shift of the weight, a turn of the hip.
