He did not plan any of it. If he had stopped to plan it, it would have been a plan, and she would have read it in the space next to him before he had finished.

He did not know where he would be in half a breath, and that was the whole point: if he did not know, there was nothing in the space next to him for her to read.

She came. He was somewhere else.

Not far, a hand's width perhaps, no more. The flat of her blade went past his left ear with a hiss, close enough for him to feel the air of it on his cheek. He had not seen it coming, or dodged it. He had simply not been where it was going, because he had not known where he was going himself.

She came again, from the other side. He was somewhere else again. The edge of the flat brushed his sleeve, and he felt it, and it did not land.

The third time she did not come. She stood a pace off, with her blade out, and looked at him.

The yard had gone very quiet. Along the rope, in the third row of the benches, an old man said huh, out loud, to nobody.

"Called," said Vell. "End of the exchange. Nothing."

He went back to his mark with his legs trembling. He had moved more in that one exchange than in the two before it together, and his body did not know how to do it. It was like trying to write with the wrong hand, and every step was a step he had to find, and he found them late, and badly. But they had been his, and she had not been able to read them, because there had been nothing in them to read.

Third exchange, he said to himself. I stopped watching. I didn't plan. She didn't land.

He looked across the circle. Sarel was standing on her mark with her blade out and her head a little on one side, and she was not looking at him at all now. She was looking at the empty dirt around him, the whole ring of it, a stride out on every side, the way a scaffold walker looks at the boards she has left to stand on before she decides where to put her feet.

Then she nodded, once, very slightly, to herself. It was not his nod. It was the nod of somebody who has solved something.

She's learned it, he thought. She's already learned it.

"Begin."

She came in, and she did not come in to strike.

She came in and stayed, close, very close, inside the reach of her own blade, and she did not try to land anything; she simply moved with him. When he took his half step left, she took hers. When he shifted back, she was there. She did not need to read where he was going. She only had to keep the space around him small, so small that there was nowhere for him to go that she was not already standing next to. She walked him like that round the inside of the groove, so near that he could hear her breathing, which was easy, and smell the lime dust from the scaffolds on her shirt, and see the old white scar down her left forearm. She walked him, a step at a time, toward the long side of the circle, where the drain was. He felt the groove come up under his heel.

He had nowhere left to go but down.

He went down. He did not fall; he chose it. He dropped low and rolled away sideways along the groove, chin in, on the meat. It was the first time he had ever used a fall for anything but surviving one. He came up a stride and a half away, on one knee, with the flat of her blade arriving late across his left forearm as he rose. It landed on the old burn, on Renn's swelling, which had only just gone down.

The white came up behind his eyes. He did not let go of anything.

"Called," said Vell. "End of the exchange."

He got to his mark without remembering walking there.

Fourth exchange. She learned it. She stopped trying to find me and made the place small. I went down on purpose. He stopped. My arm.

The arm was bad; he could feel the fingers of his left hand, but he could not make them close. He held it against his chest and breathed, and looked across at Sarel. She was looking at the arm, and then at his face, and her face did not do anything at all.

In the fifth he tried to hit her.

He did not plan that either. He had only the one strike he owned, short and straight from the hip, and he had decided that if she came close again, as she had in the fourth, he would throw it. He would not choose a time. He would throw it the moment she was there, at whatever was in front of him, without stopping to see whether it was a good idea.

She came close. He threw it.

It was slow, and he felt how slow it was as it went, the back foot driving and the shoulder following and the fist arriving last, every piece of it in the right order and every piece of it a breath behind her. She was not there when the fist arrived. But she had been there when it started, and his knuckles brushed the cloth of her sleeve on the way past. It was only cloth, the barest touch, the way a moth touches a lamp.

The rope heard it before he did. It made a sound, a short sharp intake all along the shaded side, as though forty people had all burned their fingers at once.

Then her flat came across his back, not hard, but exactly on top of the bruise Renn had left, which had been going green at the edges and now went black again all at once. He went down on his hands. The pain was not new; it was old pain woken up, the kind that knows the way. It sat on him like a second weight while he knelt there looking at the dirt between his hands and counting his breaths in, one, two, until there were enough of them to stand on.

"Called," said Vell. "End of the exchange."

He got up with one hand on his own knee. Lira was standing at the barrel, very white, saying something, the same few words over and over by the shape of her mouth. He could not hear them over the noise in his own ears, and he thought afterward that it had probably been chin in.

He stood on his mark for the sixth exchange and knew it was the last, and why. His legs had gone, in the fifth, somewhere between the strike and the ground, and they were not coming back today. He could still do the small quick moving, and he could feel how to do it now; it was there in him, new and clumsy. But he could do it only as fast as his legs would let him, and they would hardly let him at all.

"Begin."

Sarel came.

He moved small and quick and unplanned, as he had in the third, and for one breath, for two, he was somewhere else, and she was not there. On the third breath his legs were a half-step slow. It was a very small half step. It was all she needed.

The flat of her blade came across his ribs on the right side, exactly where she had put it in the second exchange. He was on his back across the groove before he had understood that he had been hit. The blade came down and rested on his collarbone, lightly, the way you would lay a ruler on a page.

"Called," said Vell. "Blade Path."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He lay on his back and looked at the white sky and breathed, because it was the only thing he could think of to do.

The blade went out along Sarel's arm, and then she did a thing that he did not expect, and that he heard the rope not expect. She crouched down beside him in the dirt, low on her heels, with her forearms across her knees, the way the scaffold people sat to eat their lunch. Her face was level with his.

She looked at him, in no hurry about it. Up close she was older than he had thought, with lines at the corners of her eyes from the sun on the scaffolds, and a nick out of one ear.

"How old are you?"

"Fourteen."

She nodded, as if that were a number she had suspected and wanted to have confirmed.

"Two," she said.

He did not understand.

"Two exchanges." She held up two fingers. "You tried the thing you know, twice, and it didn't work, and in the third you threw it away." She put the hand back on her knee. "You know what most people do, at your rating, against somebody quicker? They watch harder. They watch the whole bout. They're still watching when they're on their backs. They go home and tell everybody they nearly had it. Six exchanges of watching harder." She shook her head. "You quit in two. You said it out loud. I heard you."

"It wasn't enough. The other thing."

"No. It wasn't. It was the first time you'd ever done it. You can tell." She looked at his left arm, which he was holding on his chest. "It'll be better the tenth time. Or the hundredth. I don't know which. I'm not your teacher." She glanced toward the barrel, where Lira was. "She is, I'd guess."

"Yes."

"Good. She moves like that. You'll want to steal it off her." Sarel stood up, all in one easy movement. She did not hold out her hand to pull him up, but looked down at him for a moment longer from her full height, and the look was plain and direct and not at all soft.

"That was a good bout. Don't ask me for another one. You'll want to. Don't."

She went to the table. Cael lay on the dirt a moment longer, because he could, and then rolled onto his side, chin in, and got his knees under him, and got up.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Vell wrote for a long time.

He stood in front of the table and waited, as you waited, with his left arm against his chest and his ribs pulling at every breath, while the pen went down one line, and then another, and another, and stopped, and went on.

"Result stands as called," she said at last. "Sarel, Bronze Rank 1, Blade Path, over unrated. Sixth exchange. Called." The pen moved once more. "Witnessed and entered."

Then she looked up.

"Six," said Vell.

It was what she had said after Petra, counting, every time one more. It was not the same, and he heard that it was not the same, and she did not explain it, but went back to her book.

Lira was waiting at the barrel and did not say anything. She held out his coat, and when he could not get his left arm into the sleeve she put the coat round his shoulders instead. They walked out through the gate in the wall together, slowly, with her on his right side, the rib side, without being asked.

She did not ask for a report until they were two streets away.

"What happened in the second? Between the second and the third. On your mark. You said it."

"I said gone."

"I know what you said. I heard it at the barrel. Half the rope heard it." She was looking straight ahead. "What was gone?"

He did not answer at once, because it was hard to say and his ribs did not like it.

"The watching. All of it. The whole method. Everything I do." He looked at the cobbles. "It's too slow for her. It's not wrong. It's just too slow. By the time I've seen anything, it's over."

Lira was quiet. "And the third?"

"I did what you do."

She stopped walking.

They were at the corner by the chalk board at the bottom of the yard lane, under a lantern somebody had just lit, and she stood there in its light and looked at him. Her face did something he had not seen it do before. It was not the morning brightness, or the quick smile, or the slow one. It was nearer to the look of somebody who has been shouting into a well for two months and has just heard the bottom answer.

"Badly. I did it badly."

"I know you did it badly. I watched every step of it." Her voice was not steady. "You did it, though."

"For one exchange."

"For one exchange. Against a Bronze. On your first try." She started walking again, quickly, so that he had to hurry, which hurt. "You're an idiot. Tomorrow you're doing nothing at all. Nothing. And the day after, we start on it properly."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He wrote it up that night on his cot, by the light of Yeni's lamp, because he could not sit on the low wall by the pump or on anything hard. He wrote it at greater length than any entry in the Log, longer than Dessa, longer than either Renn.

Ninth. Sarel, Bronze Rank 1, Blade. Lost, sixth exchange, called.

Claim: I can't find her tell. Evidence: two bouts watched, both eyes. A page with three crossings-out on it. Ruling: there probably is one. I'm too slow to see it.

Claim: watching is too slow for her. Evidence: first exchange, I saw her start and didn't see her cross. Second exchange, I went against my own habit and she was there anyway. Ruling: the method is fine against people slower than my eyes. She isn't slower than my eyes.

Third exchange, I stopped watching and moved without deciding. She didn't land. Fourth, she learned it and made the space small. Fifth, I touched her sleeve. Sixth, my legs went.

He stopped there with the pencil.

I need a second way, he wrote. For people I can't out-watch. Something that doesn't go through my eyes first. Lira has it. She doesn't decide and then move. She moves and the deciding is in it, somehow, all at once. I did a little of it today, badly, for one exchange.

I don't know if I can learn it from watching her. That's how I learn everything. But this might be the one thing watching can't teach, because it's the thing that isn't watching.

I don't know. Write that down: I don't know.

He read it back, and it was true all the way through. He turned the book over to the back and sat with it open, and thought about the second way, and about Lira in the grey half moving without deciding. He thought about the backhand going on past the place it should have stopped, on her right side, when she was tired, and about a report given in the dusk with a thing left out of it, and a morning, yesterday, when he had seen it again and eaten his bread.

He did not write any of that down, and told himself he was too tired. He blew out his small piece of the light by turning his face to the wall, and lay awake with his ribs pulling and his arm on fire.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Lira made him do nothing on Monday, as she had said. He went to the mender in the afternoon and sorted washers one-handed, and the mender looked at his left arm and said nothing at all.

On Tuesday he could lift the arm to his shoulder, and on Wednesday morning, in the grey half, she made him stand by the post and watch while she showed him what he had looked like against Sarel.

She did the first exchange, standing on her mark with her feet too square and her hands up and her eyes very wide, fixed on an imaginary pair of hips, and she nodded to herself. The girls on the wall laughed so hard that one of them nearly went off it backward.

"You nodded. At a Bronze. You stood there and agreed with yourself, and she was already halfway across."

"I know."

"I know you know. I want you to see it." She did the second exchange: she was him going right, very fast, away from where she was looking, with his chin up and a look on his face of tremendous cleverness. Then she was him being hit, and she flung herself down sideways in the dirt so exactly as he had gone down that he felt the bruise on his ribs throb in sympathy. The girls on the wall applauded.

She got up, filthy and grinning.

"Now the third," she said, and stopped grinning. "The third I'll do properly. Because you did it properly, mostly, and you need to see what it looks like from out here."

She did the third.

She did his version of her moving, the small quick unplanned half steps, badly on purpose, a little stiff and a little late, exactly as he had done it. Then she did it again, her own way, loose and quick, and the difference between the two was as plain as the difference between a hinge that swung true and one that caught at the halfway. Then she did it a third time, his way and her way at once, and though he could not have explained how she did it, he saw at last where his stiffness was. It was in the hips. He was moving his feet and keeping his hips square, as if they still had to be ready for a plan.

"There."

"There." She stopped, breathing. "You see it?"

"I see it."

"Good." She put her hands on her knees for a moment. She had been going for most of an hour already, his way and her way and his way again, flinging herself in the dirt, and he saw in her shoulders that she was tired. "One more. Then bread."

She did the step for the end of it, as she always did: two empty touches, the ground folding, the backhand coming round.

And her weight went on past it, onto her right foot, a hand's width too far. She caught herself with the foot down hard and wide, and for half a breath her whole right side was open to him, and then she was back.

Three times.

He did not let himself eat any bread first.

"Lira," he said.

She was already turning toward the post for it, and looked round.

"When you're tired," he said, "you go too far on your right. After the strike. You don't stop where the backhand stops. You go on past it, onto your right foot, a hand's width, maybe more. You have to put the foot down to catch yourself." He made himself keep going. "For half a breath your whole right side is open. Anybody quick could have it."

She stood very still by the post.

"Show me," she said.

He showed her as she showed him, slowly, from outside: the touches and the step, badly, and then the backhand, and he let his weight go on past the end of it, onto his right foot, too far. He caught himself with the foot down wide and stood there open, exactly the shape she had been a moment ago.

Lira looked at him standing there.

"I lost a bout like that," she said.

She said it quietly, and not to him.

"At the academy. At the end of a season, against a girl who wasn't as good as me. She wasn't. Everybody knew she wasn't." She was looking at the dirt. "It went long. Seven exchanges. In the seventh I went in on her right and she caught me coming out, on the side of the head, and I went down. And I lay there and I didn't know why. I went over it for weeks. I went over every step, and I couldn't find it, and in the end I decided she'd been lucky." Her voice went odd. "She wasn't lucky. Was she? I was tired. And I went too far on my right."

"I don't know. I wasn't there."

"No. But I was." She looked up at him, and her face was doing two things at once, and he watched them both. One was a kind of startled gladness, very bright, like somebody who has found a coin they lost a year ago in a coat they had stopped wearing. "Cael. That's—" She laughed, a short shaky sound. "Nobody's ever—that's mine. That's a thing about me. All this time I've been walking round with it, and nobody saw it. My instructor didn't see it. I didn't see it." She put her hand flat on her own right hip, as if to feel where it lived. "That's useful. That's really, actually useful. That's the most useful thing anybody's ever told me about my own feet."

He had known she would be glad. He had not known she would be glad like that.

"When I'm tired," said Lira, half to herself, already turning it over. "It's when I'm tired. All right. All right. I can work with tired." Then she looked up again. He saw the other thing come into her face, the second one, slower, the one that had been waiting under the first.

"You said three," she said. "Just now. Under your breath. When I did it."

He had not known he had said it out loud.

"How many times have you seen it?"

He thought about lying for the length of one breath, standing in the grey half with the chalk marks on the post beside him. There were thirty-odd gones on one side and seven falls on the other, every one of them a thing he had done wrong and said out loud. He did not lie.

"Three. Saturday. Just now." He made himself finish it. "And once before that. At Brenna. The fourth exchange. You went in on her right and went too far, and she caught you on the side of the head."

Lira was very still.

"That was three weeks ago."

"Yes."

"You gave me a report." Her voice was quite level. "That night. In the lane. You gave me every exchange. You gave me the old men in the third row liking it." She was looking at him now, straight at him, with nothing in her face at all. "You didn't give me that."

"Once isn't a pattern," he said. "I didn't know if it was anything. I thought—"

"You ruled." She said it quietly. It was worse than if she had shouted. "I said no ruling. I said it twice. Give it me after, like a report, I don't want a ruling. And you stood at that rope and saw a thing about my fighting and decided it didn't count yet, and kept it." She took a breath. "Where did you put it? In your book. Did you write it down?"

He did not answer. He did not have to.

"In the back," said Lira. "You put my fight in the back of your book."

"I didn't write it anywhere. I kept it." He heard how that sounded. "I was going to tell you when I was sure."

"When you were sure." She said it after him, slowly, as if she were reading it off something. "That's what you do, isn't it. You keep it till you're sure. You keep everything till you're sure." She looked down at the post, and at the chalk, and back at him. "And Saturday. You saw it Saturday. That was twice. Twice is a pattern, in your book. I've heard you say it. And you ate your bread."

"I didn't want you carrying it into Sunday."

"That was my choice." Her voice went up, just a little, and she brought it down again at once. "It's my feet. My right side. My bout that I lost at the academy and never knew why. You don't get to decide when I'm ready to know about my own feet, Cael. Nobody does. Somebody decided things like that for me once, at a desk, and that's how I ended up on a wall in this district." She stopped.

He stood there in the grey half with nothing to say, because it was all true. He had kept it until he was sure, and he had been sure on Saturday, and he had eaten his bread.

Lira looked at him a moment longer, and then picked up the bread off the top of the post. She did not tear it. She held it in her hand as if she had forgotten what it was.

"Thank you for telling me," she said. "I mean that. It's the best thing you've ever given me, and I'm glad of it, and I'm going to use it." She put the bread down on the post again, whole. "I'm going now. I'll see you."

She did not say same time tomorrow.

She went out through the gate in the wall without looking back. He stood by the post in the grey half, with the bread beside him and the chalk marks under his hand, and listened to her quick feet go away down the lane until he could not hear them.

The girls on the wall had stopped laughing some time ago. One of them looked at him, and then looked away, as if she had seen something she was not supposed to.

He did not eat the bread. He stood there until the sun came over the east wall and there was no grey half left. He thought about a boy at a kitchen table in Denvash, two months and a lifetime ago, finding out that his grandfather had known for a few years, and about what his own face had done when he heard it.

He thought about four things on a page in the back of the Log that Hesk did not know.

Then he picked up the bread and went to the mender's, because it was Wednesday, and he did not know what else to do.

Chapter 38 — A Door

[Patient, methodical narration; give training, failure, and discovery room to accumulate]

Lira got as far as the board before she had to stop walking.

She had meant to go straight down the lane and through the triangle and on, anywhere, at the pace she used for markets, so that people got out of her way without knowing why. But at the board her feet simply stopped, as if somebody had put a hand on her chest, and she stood in front of it in the cold with her hands in her jacket pockets and pretended to read it. Near the bottom, nearly gone into the grain under the new card and last Sunday's Sarel… sixth exchange, was her own result against Brenna, with the three charcoal strokes beside it rubbed half away by a sleeve.

She was angry, and she let it be big, because she had learned long ago that if you tried to make anger smaller while you were still standing in it, it only went somewhere you could not see it and waited. So she stood in front of the board and was angry all the way through, at a boy with a notebook who had stood at the rope three weeks ago, seen a thing about her, and decided she could not have it yet.

Once isn't a pattern. She could see exactly what his face had done when he decided it: the chin tucked, the eyes very wide, the small private nod he did not know he did. It was the face she had watched him make a hundred times about other people's feet and had never once thought he would make about hers. And the worst of it, the thing she did not want to look at, was that she might have done the same, seeing a thing in his fighting once, and waiting to see it again, and calling it being careful.

But she would not have left it out of a report. Not after he had given her every other exchange so carefully, in the dusk, with the old men in the third row put in for evidence. It had looked like everything he saw, when it had been everything he saw except one thing, and he had decided which. A woman at a desk had once decided that a thing Lira had done in front of witnesses did not count, and Lira had stood there with her chin up and asked what was the exam actually testing, and that had been the end of the academy. She did not like that a boy who was the opposite of that desk in every way had put her in mind of it.

The skewer woman was setting up at the corner of the widest street, and she looked across at Lira standing still in front of the board, which Lira never did, and then looked away, which was kind of her. Lira turned her back on the board and walked on.

The other thing came up under the anger as she walked, slowly. She had not let it come up in the yard because she had not wanted him to see it. She let it now.

When you're tired, you go too far on your right.

She went over it as she went down through the triangle: the backhand, and the weight going on past the end of it, and her right foot coming down hard and wide to catch her. She had felt that foot come down a thousand times and never once thought about it, because it was simply what her right foot did at the end of a long morning, like her hair coming loose on one side. You did not think about your hair coming loose. It came loose.

And then the academy, and the seventh exchange against a girl who was not as good as her. Lira had gone over that bout for weeks, lying on her bed in the long dormitory with her eyes open, trying every step of it from every side, and she had never found it. She had decided in the end that the girl had been lucky, which was not a good answer, only the only one left.

It had been her right foot, and a hand's width, there the whole time in plain sight at the end of every long morning, and nobody had seen it: not her instructor, not the woman at the desk, not her.

A boy from Denvash had seen it, from a rope, on a cold afternoon, while his own heart was going so hard against his ribs that he had printed the rope into his palms.

She had stopped again, in the middle of the street, and she was smiling, and she was still angry, and both were true at once. A man with a barrow had to go round her, and said something she did not hear.

It was the strangest feeling she had ever had about another person, and she stood in the street and made herself look at it straight, because she did not believe in looking at things sideways. Somebody had looked at her and seen her exactly, all the way down to her feet. Nobody had ever done that before, not once, not anybody, not in her whole life. And then he had kept back the one thing he saw that she most needed to know.

Both of those were him; that was the trouble. You could not have the first one without the kind of person who did the second.

She thought, then, because she was honest with herself when nobody was looking, about a row of three things she kept in her own head.

The first was a hand at the board on the first day that had moved before it should have. The second was the third exchange against Renn on the first night. The third was a boy dropping under her backhand in the grey half, lower than she had ever asked him to go, and coming up standing in a way that was not his. She had never told him about the row, or that she had gone back into the yard alone that same afternoon, with nobody there but the crows and the sleeping pie boy, and tried the drop eleven times, and learned that it was easy to do and impossible to do in time.

She had kept that for seven weeks, and told herself she was waiting until he had something he wanted to tell her.

It did not make what he had done all right. It took some of the heat out, that was all, the way a bucket of water takes some of the heat out of a forge without putting it out.

She walked on, and did not go anywhere she had meant to go. She went where her feet had been going all along, two streets over from Torvin's, to a narrow lane she had walked down nine times in the last month on purpose and pretended each time that it was on the way to somewhere else.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

The chandler's shop was at the end of the lane, with its door open and a smell of tallow coming out of it, and candles hanging in bunches from the beam over the counter by their wicks, like onions.

The widow who kept it was sitting behind the counter dipping tapers. She was a small woman with a face as round and pale as one of her own candle ends, and she had told Lira, the first time Lira came in to ask about the room upstairs, that she did not let to fighters. Then she had looked at Lira's boots, which had been resoled twice, and her jacket cuffs, which were turned back and stitched, and said that she supposed fighters had to sleep somewhere, and that she would want two weeks paid first and no visitors after the lamps.

"I'll hold it till Wednesday," she had said, a week ago. "Then I'll let it to whoever asks."

It was Wednesday.

"I've come about the room," said Lira.

The widow looked up from her tapers.

"I said Wednesday, and you've come on Wednesday." She seemed faintly surprised by this, as if people seldom did. "Two weeks first."

Lira took the tin out of the inside of her jacket.

It was a small flat tin that had once held throat sweets, and the picture on its lid had worn away to a brown smudge. She had carried it ever since she came to Ardenmere, in the inside pocket where it pressed against her ribs when she sat down, and she opened it on the counter between the bunches of candles. Inside were the weeks of door, in small worn coins: the purse from Brenna, and the two summer purses before that, and every coin from every week she had eaten at Amrit's for half price because he had decided she was his. There was the money from the sparring hour across the district that she did not tell anybody about. There were three coins she had found in the groove at the Cinder House since the summer, dropped by people at the rope, and had kept because they felt like the yard's own.

She counted out two weeks, twice, the way Torvin did, not because she did not trust the coins but to check her own attention, and pushed it across the counter. There was not very much left in the tin afterward, and she shut the lid on what there was.

The widow counted it once, quickly, and swept it into a drawer, and took a key off a nail behind her.

"Stair's round the side. Mind the fourth step. It talks."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

The room was at the top of a stair so narrow and steep that Lira had to go up it with one hand on the wall, and the fourth step did talk, a long creak like an old man complaining.

There was a door at the top. It was a plain door made of four boards with a crosspiece, painted years ago in a green that had gone grey, with a latch, and a keyhole below the latch, and a scuff at the bottom where somebody had kicked it shut for years. She stood on the top step with the key in her hand and looked at it for a long time.

Then she put the key in and turned it, and the lock was stiff, and then it was not, and she pushed the door open and went in, and shut it behind her, and stood with her back against it.

The room was very small, smaller than the roof room in the tall house in the third lane, which she had shared with two sisters from the dye sheds who talked in their sleep about indigo. There was a bed frame with a straw mattress rolled up on it, and a hook on the back of the door, and a shelf. There was one window, looking down into the lane, with a crack across one pane that somebody had stuck over with a strip of paper. The ceiling sloped down on the window side so that she would have to remember not to stand up too fast in the morning. It smelled faintly of tallow from the shop below, and the floorboards were worn pale down the middle where somebody had walked from the door to the window, and from the window to the door, a great many times.

She stood there with her back against the door and listened to it be shut.

That was all she had wanted, and she had not been able to say it to anybody, not to Yeni, who knew everything anyway, and not to Cael. When he asked what she was saving for, all she had been able to say was a door, and then tell him not to make a face about it. It had sounded like nothing, and it was nothing, four boards and a crosspiece and a lock that stuck. But it was hers, and it shut, and when it was shut there was nobody on the other side of it who had any right to open it.

She had not had that since she left the academy, nor at the academy either, in the long dormitory with its rows of beds. And before the academy—

She did not think about before the academy. She had a rule about that, and she kept it, the way you keep a door shut in a house you have moved out of.

She sat down on the floor, in the middle of the pale worn strip, with her back against the bed frame and her knees drawn up. She sat there in the thin light from the cracked window and let herself think about the six weeks, for the first time sitting still long enough to do it.

They were half gone: twenty-two days spent, and twenty left. She had counted the days without meaning to, the way he would have.

In twenty-two days he had fought three times. He had beaten a boy who held his breath, and Renn, and nearly nobody had believed it about Renn until they saw it. He had lost to a Bronze in the sixth exchange, and in the third he had done the thing she had been trying to teach him for two months. He had done it badly, stiff in the hips, but he had done it, in front of the whole yard, against a woman the whole yard was afraid of. He had said gone thirty-four times at her post with his ears going red. Then he had said it once more at a Bronze with his ears not going red at all, and half the rope had heard him.

She had stood at the barrel with her hands on the rope and watched every one of those, and watched him get better. It was not the slow, careful getting better of the first weeks, when every morning bought a hand's width and cost a bruise, but something faster. He had found something, or it had found him, and he was coming up through the circle as she had said people came up who went down faster, and he was not going down, because he was being careful, and she had made him careful.

She thought about being his teacher, which she had never been to anybody before. She had been somebody's student and failed, and somebody else's student and been right in front of witnesses, and had walked the yards of this district on her own for months, losing. She had not known, when she put her name to a vouch for a boy from Denvash who said a word nobody had ever heard out loud, that it would feel like this. She had not known it would feel like watching something she had planted come up through the ground and turn out to be a different plant from the one on the packet.

And she thought, sitting on the floor, about being seen.

She had told him at the board on the first day that the examiner had failed her for being right in front of witnesses, which was true but not the whole of it. The whole of it was that she had stood in front of that desk wanting, more than she had ever wanted anything, for somebody who understood to look at what she had done and say yes, that, that's real. Nobody had; the examiner had not understood it, or had not wanted to. The witnesses had understood it and said nothing, because it was not their exam.

Then a boy from Denvash had stood at a rope, three weeks ago, and watched her skip the middle against Brenna in front of the whole yard. He had given it back to her in the dusk afterward, exchange by exchange, flat, with nothing added. You caught the chop and sent it with no middle. Three times. She went after it every time. He had not said it was good, and had not needed to. He had seen it exactly as it was, and said it exactly as it was, and that had been better than good.

And this morning he had seen the other thing, the bad thing, the thing that had cost her a bout and all the time since of not knowing. He had seen it just as exactly.

It was the same eyes; that was what she kept coming back to, on the floor. The eyes that saw the skipped middle were the eyes that saw the right foot. You could not have one without the other. You could only ask the person who had them not to keep half of what they saw in a pocket.

She would ask him tomorrow, and not like this morning, with her voice going up and the bread whole on the post and I'll see you. She would ask him properly. She would tell him the rule, plainly, as she told him everything, and let him pick it up, and it would be heavier than what other people gave him, and it would be the right weight.

And then she would show him the door.

She got up off the floor and went to the window and stood under the sloping ceiling without hitting her head, and looked down into the lane, where a dog was asleep on a step and a woman was hanging a sheet out of a window opposite. Two streets away, over the roofs, she could see a corner of Torvin's chimney with the smoke going straight up, and she found that she had chosen this room partly for that, without knowing it until now. She stood at her own window, in her own room, with her own door shut behind her, and let herself be proud, all the way through, without anybody there to see it.

Then she went down the stair, and the fourth step talked, and she said I know to it out loud. She went to her sparring hour across the district very late, and was shouted at, and did not mind at all.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He did not know whether she would be there.

He went up to the yard in the dark on Thursday morning anyway, as he always did, by the lane where the ground began to rise, with two loaves from underneath in his arms. He told himself that it was what he did, and that Hesk had said not to change what he did, which was true and was not why he went.

The gate in the wall was open and the frost was white along the foot of the east wall, and in the grey half, at the post, somebody was striking the canvas, low, twice, and stepping round it, and striking again.

He stopped in the gateway.

Lira did not stop. She struck the post twice more and stepped round it, and he understood from the strikes that she was thinking, and that the strikes were where she had put her hands while she did it. Then she stopped, with her palm flat on the canvas, and looked at him over her shoulder.

"You're late."

"I'm not."

"You're standing in the gate. That's late." She took her hand off the post. "Come here."

He came across the yard. She did not take the bread, but stood in front of him in the grey half with her hands loose at her sides and her weight a little forward, and she looked at him.

"Here's the rule. You see a thing about me, you tell me. When you see it. Not when you're sure. Not when you've decided I'm ready. Not after Sunday. When you see it." She did not raise her voice. "My feet. My fighting. Anything. If it's wrong, it's wrong, and I'll tell you it's wrong, and we'll both have learned something. But you don't keep it. Not my things. I'll put up with you keeping your own things as long as you like. I've told you that. I'm still not asking. But mine are mine."

"All right."

"Say it back."

He said it back in his own words, slowly, checking each one before he set it down. If he saw a thing about her, he told her when he saw it. Not when he was sure. Not when he had decided anything. He did not keep her things.

She listened to every word, and when he had finished she nodded once. "Good. That's done, then." She took one of the loaves off him at last and tore it and gave him half, and something came up in her face, slowly, as if it had been waiting behind a door. "It was still the best thing you've ever given me. I meant that too."

"I know."

"I'm going to fix it. Tired or not." She bit into the bread. "I've already started. I did the step at the post twenty times before you came, at the end of an hour, and I felt it go every time. Every time, Cael. I can feel it now. All that time—" She stopped, and shook her head, and went on more quietly. "A long time I couldn't find it. And now I can feel it every time."

He did not say anything, because he did not think there was anything to say that would be the right size, and he ate his bread.

Then she said, not looking at him, in the voice she used when a thing mattered more than she wanted it to look, "I took a room."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

It was two streets from Torvin's, at the end of a lane he had walked down perhaps twice, over a chandler's shop with candles hanging from the beam by their wicks, like onions. There was a widow behind the counter who looked at Cael and said, "No visitors after the lamps," before he had said anything at all.

"It isn't after the lamps. It's the middle of the afternoon."

"I'm saying it now," said the widow, "so it's said."

The stair went up round the side, so narrow that he had to go up it sideways, and the fourth step creaked under him like an old man complaining.

"It talks," said Lira, behind him. "Every time. I'm going to name it."

At the top there was a door.

She stopped him on the top step before he could reach for the latch, and went past him, squeezing between him and the wall, and took a key on a string out of her jacket, and let herself in, and shut the door in his face.

He stood on the top step looking at the door. It was green gone grey, four boards and a crosspiece, with a scuff at the bottom.

"Knock," said Lira's voice, from the other side.

He knocked.

There was a pause, a long one, longer than it needed to be, a pause somebody was enjoying.

Then the latch lifted, and the door opened, and Lira stood in it with one hand on the edge and the other on the frame. She looked at him as if he were somebody who had come to the wrong house.

"Yes?" she said.

He did not laugh, though he nearly did, and he saw her see him nearly do it, and her face went very straight indeed.

"I've come to see the room."

"Have you." She considered him, and then stood aside and held the door open. "You can come in. Mind your head. The ceiling comes down on the window side and it's not sorry about it."

He went in, and minded his head.

It was very small, as he had known it would be. There was a bed with a straw mattress on it and a blanket folded square at the foot, and a shelf. On the shelf there was a tin cup, and a comb, and the canvas roll, and a little flat tin with the picture worn off its lid. There was one window with a crack across the pane and a strip of paper over the crack, and a hook on the back of the door with nothing on it, because she was still wearing her jacket. He thought she had not taken it off since she got the key.

He stood in the middle of the room on the pale worn strip of floor and looked at all of it, one thing at a time.

"Well?"

"It's yours."

He had not known that was what he was going to say until it was out. She did not say anything, but shut the door behind him, very gently. It made a small sound as the latch dropped, the smallest sound, a click like a figure coming right.

"It shuts."

"I heard."

"It locks." She showed him the key on its string. "From inside. And from outside. Both. I can be in here and lock it, or out there and lock it, and either way it's locked." She seemed to think he might not have understood. "Nobody else has a key. The widow has one, for fires. Nobody else."

"Lira. It's a good door."

She looked at him, and then sat down on the end of the bed, quite suddenly, as if her legs had decided it for her, and looked at the door. She did not say anything, and he did not either. He stood under the sloping ceiling with his head bent, and the light came in through the cracked pane, and two streets away over the roofs, through the window, he could see the top of Torvin's chimney with its smoke going straight up.

"You can see Torvin's from here."

"Can you? I hadn't noticed."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

For Sunday's card Vell gave him Talis: Stone Path, Copper Rank 4.

"He's young," she said, at her table on Thursday. "Younger than Dessa. A good deal less patient. Stone like hers, and strong, and he's had a good season." She drank. "You'll want to watch him tonight. He's fourth on the card."

"It's four days since Sarel," said Lira, who had come up beside him. "He's still green across the back."

"I know how long it's been. I wrote it down." Vell looked at Lira. "Survivable?"

Lira looked at Cael's back, as though she could see through his coat to the colours on it.

"Survivable. If he doesn't go down on the ribs."

He watched Talis fight that night from the rope, near the barrel, with the Log open on his knee.

Talis was about eighteen, a big fair young man with a neck as wide as his head and a way of rocking on his heels between the exchanges, impatient, as if the circle were a queue he had been made to stand in. When Vell said begin he did not wait for anything, but went in, and Cael watched the grit come up off him as it had come up off Dessa, shivering all at once over his arms and shoulders and lying down flat. Then he was a gatepost with a temper, and he walked through a Copper 3 Blade in four exchanges, and the rope cheered.

Cael wrote it all down: the shoulders, which dipped a little before the right hand came; the hands, which Talis held low; the impatience, the rocking on the heels, the way the young man's face went red when a strike did not land. Then he wrote frustration — let him, because that had been a true thing about Brenna and might be a true thing again.

He did not write anything about the ground, or look at it. He had never once in his life looked at the ground.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On Sunday the frost had gone off by the middle of the afternoon, and the dirt in the circle was soft on the surface and hard underneath, and Talis came over the rope as if he were late for something.

"Talis. Copper Rank 4, Stone Path. Against unrated. Vouched." The small pause. "Begin when you're ready."

The grit came up off him and lay down flat, and he came.

Cael did what he had done in the third exchange against Sarel, and moved, small and quick and unplanned, with his hips loose this time, as Lira had shown him on Wednesday. But Talis was not Sarel, and the watching was not too slow for him, so Cael watched while he moved, and he began where the Log told him to begin, with the shoulders. The shoulders dipped. The right hand came. Cael was somewhere else.

But Talis was somewhere else too.

Cael had not seen him go there. One breath Talis was in front of him, and the next he was a stride to the left with his weight already planted, and the right hand that the shoulders had promised never came at all. It was the left forearm that came, heavy and grey with the grit, across the upper arm like a mallet on a stump. Cael went sideways and kept his feet, just, and Talis was already rocking back on his heels, impatient, waiting.

"End of the exchange," said Vell.

First exchange, said Cael to himself. The shoulders dipped before the right, and I read it, and he didn't throw the right. The shoulders told the truth about a strike he never threw. He crossed them off in his head. Not the shoulders.

In the second he watched the hands.

Talis held them low, loose, at the level of his belt, and Cael watched them and nothing else, all through the exchange, as he had watched Renn's heel once. They told him nothing until they were already moving. They did not set, or close, or draw back; they simply went, and by the time a hand had begun to go, Talis had already been planted somewhere for half a beat, and the hand was only the last thing to arrive. Cael got out of the first one. The second came from a place a stride off to his right that he had not seen Talis reach, and caught him on the hip with a short blunt thud like a door kicked shut. He felt it go right through him into his back, into Sarel's bruise.

Not the hands, he thought, on his mark, with his hip aching. The hands come last. Everything's already decided by the time the hands know about it. He looked across. He knows where he's going to plant before I do. Of course he does. It's his foot. But there should be something before it.

In the third he watched the face.

It was the last place left above the belt, and it had been true about Brenna. Talis was impatient, and impatient people told you things. So Cael went in on purpose, once, early, and put the one strike he owned onto Talis's forearm, short and straight from the hip, a touch and no more, to make him angry. It worked. Talis's face went red from the collar up, and his mouth went tight, and Cael thought good, let him, and watched the red face for whatever it would give away.

It gave away nothing. Talis did not look where he meant to go, the way the kiln boy had; his eyes stayed on Cael's chest. His temper did not make his shoulders talk, or his hands. It only made him plant harder, so that the next strike, when it came off the planted foot, came with more of the ground behind it. Cael got his forearms in the way of it and felt it jar them both to the shoulder.

Not the face, he thought, back on his mark. Not the temper. He had gone down the whole of Talis from the shoulders to the belt, the way you go down a column, and every line was empty. There was nothing left to look at, and Talis was still going to plant somewhere he could not see, and hit him from it.

In the fourth he watched everything at once, and it made no difference. Talis planted on Cael's left, where Cael had not seen him going, and the gatepost forearm came round low into his side under the ribs, on the left, the side Sarel had not touched. It did not land like a mallet, or a door. It landed like a beam swung end-on into a wall, all of it at one point, with the whole weight of the planted leg and the ground beneath the leg pushing it through. It was the strike he never saw building. He was looking at all of Talis, and all of Talis was still, and then he was on the ground.

He went down on his side with his cheek against the dirt and every bit of air gone out of him at once.

"Match," said Vell.

He could not get up yet. He lay with his face on the cold packed earth of the circle, and breathed, or tried to, and listened to the yard shouting above him. He thought about nothing at all for a moment.

Talis walked back to his mark.

Cael felt him go.

He felt it in his cheekbone, where his face lay against the ground, a faint, quick buzz, very small, like the hum in a table when somebody sets a heavy glass down at the other end of it. It came up out of the dirt into the bone of his face, and then, a half beat after it, Talis's foot came down, a stride away, and planted.

Talis took another step. The buzz came first, and then the foot.

Cael lay very still with his cheek on the ground.

Again, he thought, and Talis took a third step, and it came again: the hum in the dirt, and then, half a beat behind it, the foot. Every time. The ground knew where Talis was going to plant before Talis's foot got there. It said so, if you were listening with the right part of you, and Cael had not been. He had been listening with his eyes, at shoulders and hands, as he listened to everybody. It had never once occurred to him that a tell could live in the ground.

He got up eventually, slowly, with his left side feeling as though somebody had driven a wedge into it, and something catching under the ribs, sharp, whenever he breathed in all the way. He walked to the table, and Vell wrote. He did not hear what she said, and then he did.

"Result stands as called. Talis, Copper Rank 4, Stone Path, over unrated. Fourth exchange. Match." The pen moved. "Witnessed and entered."

Lira was waiting at the barrel. She had her hand on the iron stake at the corner of the rope, where it went down into the ground, and she did not take it off when he came up. She was looking at him with an odd expression. "Did you feel it?"

He stared at her.

"Through the stake." Lira tapped the iron with one finger. "I didn't, at first. I was holding the rope. In the third exchange I put my hand down on the stake to lean, and it was humming. Every time he was going to plant. A half beat before he put his foot down." She looked at him. "I thought you'd have seen it."

"I felt it. After. With my face."

Lira looked at the side of his face, where the dirt was.

"Well," she said, after a moment, "that's one way to find it."

"I wasn't looking at the ground."

"Nobody looks at the ground." She took her hand off the stake at last. "That's why it's such a good place to keep something."

Chapter 39 — The Plan That Survives

[Patient, methodical narration; give training, failure, and discovery room to accumulate]

He could not sit on the low wall that night, or on the cot either, without something under the ribs on the left side catching, sharp, every time he breathed in all the way. So he wrote the Talis entry lying on his right side on the cot with the Log propped against the wall and Yeni's lamp turned toward him.

Yeni had turned it toward him herself. She had looked at the way he came up the stairs, one at a time, with his hand flat on the wall, and said nothing at all. Then she had got up off her cot and moved the lamp a hand's width along the shelf, and lain down again, and gone back to her sewing in the half dark as if she could do it by feel, which she probably could.

Tenth. Talis, Copper Rank 4, Stone. Lost, fourth exchange, match.

Claim: he goes somewhere I don't see him go, plants, and strikes from where he's planted. Evidence: four exchanges. Every strike came from a place I didn't expect. Shoulders still. Hands low. Nothing in either.

Claim: the tell is in the ground. Evidence: I felt it with my face after he'd put me down. A hum in the dirt, a half beat before he plants. Lira felt it through the iron stake at the corner of the rope, in the third. (Lira, h. Mine, after.)

Ruling: I lost to a thing I wasn't looking at.

He lay there with the pencil in his hand after that. The brothers came up the stairs arguing about whether the river would freeze at the edges this year, and they went to bed still arguing, and went quiet, and the wheezing man by the door began his long whistle, like a kettle a long way from boiling.

I've been looking at hands and shoulders since the community hall, he wrote. Hesk taught me hips and feet. I kept the hips and feet and added shoulders and faces and breath. Every tell I've ever found has been on the body. A heel, a dip, a shimmer, a breath, a lean, a foot coming down late. All of them were somewhere I already knew to look.

Talis's wasn't on the body at all. It was under it.

So: I have a method. It works. It has holes in it, and the holes don't tell you where they are. That's what makes them holes. If I'd known to look at the ground, it wouldn't have been a hole, it would have been a place I looked. I didn't lose today because I watched badly. I lost because there was a whole place I'd never once thought to watch.

There will be others. I don't know where. That's the point.

Ruling, for every one from now on: before I look for the tell, look for where I haven't looked.

He read it back, and then did a thing that he did not put in the Log, because it was too foolish to write down.

Yeni had got up to go down to the yard. When she crossed the room in her stockinged feet, past the end of his cot, he put his hand flat on the floorboards beside the cot, palm down, and shut his eyes.

He felt each step come into the boards before it landed, very faint, a small give in the wood under his palm, and then the step itself. It was not like Talis; it was only a floor, and a woman walking on it, and boards that had been creaking in this house for longer than Torvin had been deciding about his sign. But it was there, if you put your hand down and listened with it.

"What are you doing?" said Yeni, from the door.

"Nothing."

"You're lying on the floor with your hand flat on the boards and your eyes shut." She did not sound surprised, because very little surprised Yeni. "That's not nothing. That's something I'd want to hear about, if I had the time."

"I'm listening to the floor."

There was a pause.

"Well," said Yeni, "it's got plenty to say," and went down the stairs, and he heard every one of them through his palm.

Hesk's letter had come on the Friday, two days before Talis, and he had read it three times that evening and then put it away in the leather book and not been able to read it again. He took it out now, on the cot, with his side aching, and made himself read it a fourth time.

The review had sat. They had asked Hesk whether he wrote to the boy, and Hesk had told them that he did, every week, and meant to go on doing it. They had found no present cause, and the matter would remain on the book, which meant that it was not closed and was not lost either. There was a gauge-maker who had told a man from the guild office that every workshop in Denvash had a drawer of springs, and that a man who did not was either a liar or a bad maker, and the man had written it down. Cael smiled at that, on the cot, and the smile made his side catch.

Then the part about the reading room: I'm proud of the reading, and the four times aloud. That was all Hesk said about it, and it was short, and Cael read it twice, and it was enough.

Then the part he had not been able to read again.

When your letter came, I sat on the workshop step in the street and read it there, and I was more afraid than I have been since the day at Weaver's Row.

He made himself read it to the end.

It was all over by then. You had already done it, and done it well, and I knew that by the second line. It made no difference. That's the post, and it's the price of where you are, and I'd pay it again. But you asked me once to tell you as it comes, and that's how it came.

He lay with the letter on the blanket in front of his face.

He tried to see it, Hesk sitting on the step of the workshop on Fen Street, in the street, where people could see him, with a letter in his hands and his big square face doing something Cael had never once seen it do, and he could not. He had seen Hesk prepared, and still, and careful, and sometimes angry, and once, across the workshop bench on the second day after Kindling, ashamed, but he had never seen him afraid. It had happened anyway, a week ago, on a step, where nobody but strangers could see.

And Hesk had written it down and sent it, because they had said they would tell each other as it came.

There were four things on a page at the back of the Log, and Cael had not sent any of them. He knew the number exactly, because he had counted it every time he sealed a letter since the night of the drop. He had told himself every time that it was not the same as Hesk's years of silence, because he had written down that he was keeping them, and because he had told one person that he was keeping them and why. That was true.

But on Wednesday, four days ago, he had stood in the grey half and listened to Lira say you keep everything till you're sure, and felt it land, because it was true. She had said it about one thing he had kept from her for three weeks, about her own feet. There were four things he had kept from Hesk for two months, about his.

He lay there with Hesk's fear on the blanket in front of him and thought about that.

Then he read the end of the letter, because he could not lie there for ever.

Joren says to tell you his heels are down. He held a level for me for fifty minutes without moving it. His father thinks he's wasting his mornings.

Alis carries basins. She says you'll laugh.

He laughed; he could not help it. He laughed on his side on the cot, and his ribs caught, and he went on laughing anyway, quietly, with his hand pressed against his side. Across the room Yeni's needle stopped, and then went on.

He wrote back that night lying down, with the Log for a desk. He told Hesk about Renn, and the false heel, and the front heel instead, and about Sarel, who had crouched down beside him in the dirt and told him two. He told him about Talis, and the ground, and Lira's hand on the iron stake, and that Lira had taken a room two streets from Torvin's, over a chandler's, with a door that locked from both sides, and that she had made him knock.

He told him about the right foot without saying it was Lira's; he said only that he had seen a thing in somebody he trained with and kept it three weeks too long, and that he had been told so, and that he had been right to be told. He thought Hesk would understand what he was saying underneath it, better than anybody.

He did not tell him the four.

He sealed it, and put it in the leather book to keep flat, and lay looking at the ceiling. The number had not changed; it was still four. But he had written down, in a letter that would be in Denvash in a week, that keeping a thing too long cost something. He knew that Hesk would read it on a step or at a bench and know exactly how much.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The last weeks came in hard.

The frost did not go off the yard at all now. It lay white along the foot of the east wall all day, and the dirt in the circle was hard as a floor. At Torvin's the brothers came in every night with their hands like boiled meat to say that the river was going to freeze at the edges, while Torvin's wife put a second blanket on every cot without being asked.

The left side of Cael's ribs got better slowly. For a week he could not breathe in all the way without the catch, and after that he could if he did it carefully, and after that he forgot to be careful and did not need to be. The back went from green to yellow to nothing, and the forearm, over the old burn, stopped swelling and went stiff instead, and Lira made him work it in the cold water from the pump every morning until his fingers ached with the cold instead.

She worked on her right side as she did everything, by doing it wrong on purpose until she could feel exactly where the wrong lived. She would go through an hour at the post until she was tired and her shoulders were down, and then do the step and the backhand and let her weight go on past the end of it, onto the right foot, and stop there, standing open, exactly the shape she had been, and say there to herself, quietly. Then she did it again, and stopped her weight a little sooner, and then sooner again.

"Tell me," she said, every time.

"Still a hand."

"Tell me."

"Less. Three fingers."

"Tell me."

He told her every time. He told her other things too, now, because the rule was that he told her when he saw them, and once he started there was a great deal to see. He told her that her left hand dropped a little when she laughed, which made her laugh and drop it. He told her that she pushed her hair off her face with her wrist before she did the step, every time, which was nothing, probably, only hair; but he had been told to say.

"It is only hair," said Lira. "But thank you." And she stopped doing it, and two mornings later she started doing it again, because, she said, it was nice to have one thing that was hers that nobody could use against her, and if anybody ever tried to read her hair she would deserve to lose.

He was working on the other thing, the moving.

It was the slowest thing he had ever tried to learn. The deflection had come in days, and the box in a week, and even the strike from the hip had come in a fortnight of a hundred throws a morning. This did not come in any of those ways, because it was not a thing you could do a hundred times; it was the thing that happened when you stopped doing things a hundred times. Every morning Lira came at him at a speed he could not watch, and he moved without deciding, and for the first few mornings his hips went square the moment he thought about them, and she would stop and say hips and he would say I know.

But it came, by the width of a hair a morning, and some mornings not at all. On a morning near the end of the fifth week he got through a whole set without her saying hips once, and did not notice until she stopped and stood there looking at him.

"What?"

"You didn't say it."

"Say what?"

"Gone." She had the chalk in her hand. "I came in with the step and you'd started the counter, the back and out, and you saw me already in, and you let it go and went somewhere else. And you didn't say it. You just went."

He had not noticed, but when he thought back she was right: he had seen her inside and been somewhere else, all in the same moment, with no word in between, like a hinge that had been oiled.

Lira went to the post, where the gone column had thirty-nine marks in it, in rows of five, with the last row one short. She made a fortieth mark, and then drew a line under the whole column, straight across, hard, so that the chalk squeaked on the canvas.

"That's the last one."

"I didn't say it."

"That's why it's the last one." She looked at the column. "That's why I make you say it at all. You say it till you don't need to say it. Then you've got the thing the word was for, and you can throw the word away." She put the chalk in her pocket. "Forty. I thought it would be more. You're quicker than you think."

"You said I was slow."

"I said you weren't a natural." She came back to her mark. "I never said slow. I'd never say slow. You're the most efficient learner I've ever stood across from. You just do it in the most annoying order." She brought her hands up. "Again. And if you say it, I'm rubbing out the line."

He did not say it, and through the rest of that morning he could not have said it if he had tried, because there was nowhere in the moving for the word to go.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He had watched Dellin twice before he knew he was going to fight him.

He worked that out on the night after Talis, going back through the Log, where the entries were, a Thursday and a Sunday in the third week, among the bouts he wrote down because he wrote down every bout. Dellin, Cu 3, Force, and half a page each time, not underlined, because they had been homework, as all the cards were homework, and he had filed them and turned the page.

Vell gave him Dellin on the Monday after Talis, for Thursday, after the lamps, the third bout, and said that Dellin had asked for him.

"Asked?"

"He watched Renn. And Sarel." Vell held her tea in both hands. "He says he'd like to see what you'll do with a man who doesn't care whether you see him coming." She looked up. "He's not clever, Dellin. He's never needed to be. He's very strong and he's done the same thing in the same way for three seasons, and it works, and he sees no reason to change it." She looked down again. "I'd like to see whether you can beat a thing that works."

He watched Dellin a third time on Tuesday afternoon, from the rope, near the barrel, with the Log open on his knee.

He watched the ground first.

He made himself do it, standing at the rope with his hand on the iron stake at the corner and watching Dellin's feet before he looked at anything else. There was nothing in the ground; Dellin was not Stone, and his feet were only feet. Cael put his hand on the stake anyway, every exchange, and wrote ground: nothing at the top of the page, and felt a little foolish, and did it anyway.

Then he watched the rest.

Dellin was a big man of about twenty-five, a carter, broad and slow on his feet, with very short hair and a face like a friendly loaf. He fought exactly as Vell had said. He opened every exchange with his left hand, high, toward the head, a punch that was not fast and was not meant to land, only to make you bring your hands up. As your hands came up his right went to your body, low, under them, a short heavy punch to the ribs, and it did not matter whether it hurt, because it was not the punch that put you down.

It was the shove after it.

Cael had felt Force once before, from Petra, when everything she hit had got an extra push at the end, after her hand had stopped, as if somebody standing behind you had kicked you. Dellin's was the same and three times as heavy. His right hand landed on the Copper 2 Shield's ribs, and stopped, and a half beat later the Shield went sideways across the circle as though he had been hit by a cart. He went down in the groove with his shield still up.

Left high, every time, Cael wrote. To bring the hands up. Right to the body under them. The shove after the right. That's the whole of it.

He watched the second and third exchanges, and it was the whole of it: left high, right low, shove. The Shield tried to keep his hands down for the left, and the left landed on his ear, not hard, and his hands came up for the next one anyway, because a fist at your ear is a fist at your ear.

He saw the other thing in the fourth.

The Shield had got clever and stopped putting his hands up for the left at all, and had taken it on his shield, and stepped back from the right. For one whole exchange Dellin's right had found nothing. Dellin had stood in the middle of the circle with his friendly loaf of a face getting red, and then he had changed.

He had not changed what he did, only how close he did it, coming in so near that there was no room to step back from the right. He took hold of the Shield's collar with his left hand, and held it, and hit him with the right, low, and the shove came, and the Shield went over and Dellin went down on top of him.

When it stops working he holds you, Cael wrote. Left hand on the collar instead of left hand high. Then the same right.

He sat at the rope with the Log on his knee and looked at what he had written. It was three entries now, on three days, and they all said the same thing, which was so rare that he did not trust it and went back through the two older pages to be sure; and they said the same thing. Left high. Right low. Shove. And when that stopped working, the collar.

He told me, he wrote. Three times. He doesn't care that I know. That's what Vell meant.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He built it that night on the low wall by the pump, in the cold, with the pear tree over him, while Lira sat beside him with her knees up and her coat round them and argued with every piece of it, because that was what a plan was for.

"Don't block anything. Anything he touches gets the shove. If I put my arm up for the left, he's touching my arm."

"It's only the left. The left doesn't shove. You said."

"I said the right shoves. I don't know that the left doesn't. I've never seen him land the left hard. I'm not finding out on Thursday." He wrote block nothing. "So the left comes high, and I don't bring my hands up for it. I go outside it, to his left, away from the right."

"His right'll follow you."

"His right can't follow me. It's aimed at where my body will be when my hands go up. If my hands don't go up, my body's not there." He wrote it. "That's the first exchange. I make him miss the right. That's all I do in the first."

"And the second?"

"The same. I need to see he'll do it twice. He will. He's done it three seasons."

Lira chewed her lip.

"And the third he takes your collar."

"In the third he takes my collar. When the right stops working, he comes in close and holds. He'll do it in the third, because it's the third time he's missed." He looked at the page. "That's the one. When he comes in for the collar, his left hand's out in front of him and his right's held back, waiting. He's square to me. Both feet. He has to be, to hold and hit. He's the biggest he'll ever be and he's standing still."

"So you hit him."

"So I don't let him get the collar. I go in when his hand comes out for it. Under it. Inside it." He looked at the strike, the one he owned, written at the top of a page long ago. "And I don't hit his body. I hit the hand that's coming for the collar, on the way past, to turn him, and then the one strike, from the hip, on the jaw, while he's turned."

"And if he doesn't take the collar in the third?"

"Then in the fourth."

"And if he doesn't take it at all?"

He looked at her. "Then I'll say gone, and do something else."

Lira looked at the page in the cold.

"That's the first plan you've ever made," she said slowly, "that doesn't need him to be stupid. Only to be what he is." She pulled her coat tighter round her knees. "I like it. I don't trust it. Plans don't survive."

"I know."

"They don't. Not in there. Something always happens."

"I know. I'm going to find out what."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Nothing happened.

That was what he wrote afterward, at the top of the entry in the Log, before anything else, in a hand that was not quite steady, on the low wall by the pump, with the lamps lit and his breath going up white. Nothing happened. He looked at it for a long time, because it had never been true before.

The yard had been full for a Thursday, three deep on the shaded side, and the lanterns were lit on their hooks along the three walls. Dellin came over the rope as if he were climbing down from his cart, heavy and easy and in no hurry, and stood on his mark and smiled across at Cael with the friendly loaf of a smile, like a man who was looking forward to something.

"Dellin. Copper Rank 3, Force Path. Against unrated. Vouched." The small pause. "Begin when you're ready."

Cael put his hand flat on the dirt at his mark for one breath before he stood, not knowing who saw him do it, and felt the ground, and there was nothing in it but cold.

Dellin came off his mark, and the left came high, toward his head.

He did not bring his hands up.

It was the hardest thing he had done since the second exchange against Renn, harder than going right into a blade. Every part of him wanted to bring his hands up for a fist coming at his face. He kept them where they were, and went outside, to Dellin's left, a long step, and the left went past his ear. Then the right came in low, under hands that were not there, at a body that was not there, and found air.

Dellin stood a moment, looking at the place where Cael's ribs should have been, and then laughed, a big pleased laugh, and went back to his mark.

First exchange, said Cael to himself. Left high, right low. I didn't block. He missed.

The second was the same: left high, Cael outside it, right low, into air. Dellin did not laugh this time, but stood in the middle of the circle with his friendly face going a little pink, and rubbed the knuckles of his right hand against his thigh as if they had been cheated of something.

Second exchange. The same. He's beginning to mind.

"Begin."

Dellin came off his mark and the left came high, and Cael went outside it, and the right came low, and found nothing. For the third time in three exchanges it found nothing. Then Dellin did exactly what he had done to the Shield on Tuesday afternoon, and to two other men on a Thursday and a Sunday in the third week.

He came in close. His left hand came out, open, for the collar.

Cael went under it.

He went in as the hand came out, just as he had planned it on the wall, under the arm and inside it, into the big square space in front of Dellin's chest. His left forearm met Dellin's reaching wrist on the way past and turned it. It was not a block. It was the outside of the forearm, wrist to elbow, meeting it and sending it on, a quarter turn further than Dellin had meant to reach, so that the big man's shoulder came round after his hand.

And the strike came up from the hip. Back foot driving, shoulder following, fist arriving last. It went into the hinge of Dellin's jaw, under the ear, where Dellin's own turned shoulder had left it open.

It was not a hard strike. He did not have a hard strike. He had a well-timed one.

Dellin's knees went. Not all the way. They went the way a table's legs go when you lean on it at the wrong corner, a sudden dip. He sat down in the dirt, quite gently, with a surprised look on his friendly face, and put one hand down behind him. He sat there looking up at Cael, and at the fist that had come back up and stopped, half an arm from his nose.

"Called," said Vell. "Unrated."

For a moment the yard did not seem sure what it had seen.

It had seen three exchanges in which nothing happened and a fourth that was over almost before it began, and the noise came up slowly along the rope, uncertain at first and then not, the shaded side first and then the sun. It was not the roar there had been for Renn. It was the other noise, the low pleased one, the noise of people seeing a thing done properly.

Dellin sat in the dirt and worked his jaw from side to side.

"Huh," he said.

Cael held out his hand, and Dellin took it, and Cael pulled, and it was like pulling at a cart that did not want to go anywhere. Then Dellin got his own feet under him and came up, and stood there swaying a little, and looked down at Cael from a long way up.

"You knew." He did not say it angrily. He said it to make sure of it. "The left. The right. My hand coming out. You knew what I'd do before I did it."

Cael opened his mouth to say that he had not known anything. He had watched three times and written it down three times, and on the third time he had seen that it never changed. He had worked out how likely it was that it would change on Thursday, and found it was so small that he could stand on it. It was not knowing. It was arithmetic.

He shut his mouth again.

It would not have meant anything to Dellin, or to anybody, standing in the circle under the lanterns with the yard still deciding how loud to be. A man had asked him whether he had known, and the true answer was a column of figures, and there was no room in a circle for a column of figures.

"I watched you," he said instead. "Three times."

Dellin thought about that, rubbing his jaw.

"Three times," he said. "Huh." He nodded slowly, as if putting it somewhere. "I'll have to start doing something different, then." He seemed faintly worried by the idea. Then he clapped Cael on the shoulder, gently, for a big man, and went off toward the water bucket, saying to himself, quite loudly, "Three times," as if it were a sum he had been set and could not quite make come out.

Cael walked to the table.

"Result stands as called," said Vell. "Unrated, over Dellin, Copper Rank 3, Force Path. Fourth exchange. Called." The pen moved. "Witnessed and entered."

Then the pen moved again, a second line and a third, which she did not read out. But when he turned to go she said, without lifting her head, "That was a plan."

"Yes."

"It held."

"Yes."

"They don't, as a rule." She blotted the page. "Write down why this one did. That's the part worth keeping."
