[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He wrote it down on the wall by the pump, under Nothing happened.

Eleventh. Dellin, Copper Rank 3, Force. Won, fourth exchange, called.

Claim: left high to bring the hands up, right low to the body, the shove after the right. When that stops working, the collar. Evidence: three bouts watched. The same every time, in the same order, for three seasons (Vell, h). Ruling: block nothing. Make him miss twice. Go in under the collar in the third.

It went exactly the way I wrote it. Every exchange.

He sat with that.

Why it held, he wrote, because Vell had told him to. Because he never changes, and I didn't ask him to. I didn't build it on a thing he might do. I built it on a thing he always does. Renn had a plan for me. Sarel had no plan and didn't need one. Talis had a thing I'd never looked for. Dellin has the same thing he had last season, and he's proud of it, and I let him keep it right up until it was the one thing in front of me.

A plan holds when it's built on what they are, not on what you hope they'll do.

And I put my hand on the ground at my mark first. There was nothing there. I want to keep doing that anyway.

He looked at that last line, and left it in.

Lira came out of the kitchen door with two cups of something hot that Torvin's wife had given her for them, and sat down on the wall beside him, and gave him one, and looked at the page over his shoulder without reading it aloud. She read Nothing happened at the top, and her mouth went up at one corner.

"Vell gave you Corbin."

He looked at her.

"While you were writing. She came out to the gate to tell me, because she said you looked busy." Lira blew on her cup. "Thursday week. The last week. The last bout of your six." She was quiet for a moment. "Do you know who Corbin is?"

"A Copper 3. I've watched him once. In the second week."

"He's had nearly forty fights in that yard. He's been on Vell's cards since before I came. Since before Dessa, before Renn." She turned the cup in her hands. "He's not the best. He's never been the best. Nobody's afraid of him. But everybody knows exactly how good he is, because he's always exactly that good. Every season. Every bout. He's the one people use."

"Use for what?"

"For measuring." She looked across the yard at the pear tree, which had given up growing tall. "Somebody new comes up through the cards, and nobody knows what they are yet. So people say, put him in with Corbin. And they see how long it takes. If you go down in two, you're a Copper 2. If you go five with him, you're a good Copper 3. If you beat him—" She stopped.

"If you beat him?"

"Then you're whatever's past Corbin. And everybody in the district already knows what that means, because they've all been measuring against him for years." She drank. "It's not fair. You beat Renn, and Renn's better than Corbin on his day. Nobody cares about Renn the way they care about Corbin. Renn's a show-off with a good figure. Corbin's a ruler."

He thought about that, looking at the page.

"So if I beat him—"

"If you beat him, it's not a new fact about you. It's a new fact hung on an old one, one everybody already believes. People can carry that kind. They'll carry it down the fish steps and into the market and across the bridge to their cousins." She looked at him. "That's what you said you wanted. On the first morning. Your name in more mouths."

"Yes."

"Then that's the bout." She finished her cup. "Corbin's the one they'll repeat."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He watched Corbin on the Sunday, from the rope, with his hand on the iron stake.

There was nothing in the ground, which he had expected and wrote down anyway, and nothing in the shoulders, or the hands, or the breath, which he had half expected from what Lira had said; and still he watched for an hour and found nothing at all.

Corbin was about thirty-five, and square, and not tall, with a bald patch he did not try to hide and a short brown beard going grey at the chin. He was Shield Path, which Cael had not known from the one bout in the second week, because Corbin had won that one in the first exchange and Cael had not had time to see. His shield was not like Brenna's, a pane wider than his shoulders held up to be walked at people, but small, hardly bigger than a dinner plate, a little patch of shine off his left forearm that he did not hold up. He let it come and go, there for a strike and gone again between, as if he did not like to spend it on nothing.

He did not chop with it, or get angry, or dip on the step-through, because, somebody at the rope said, he had trained the dip out of himself in his first season, before Brenna had been born, near enough.

His opponent was a good Copper 4 Ember, a woman, and Corbin gave her three exchanges and then took her apart in the fourth. He did it without any hurry and without anything Cael could find to write down, except that he did it, and Cael wrote nine lines, and every one of them was nothing.

Then, at the end of the third exchange, as the two of them went back to their marks, he saw it.

It was not in Corbin's body but in his eyes.

On his mark, between the exchanges, while the Ember woman breathed and set herself, Corbin looked at her feet. He did not look at her face, or her hands, or the shimmer coming up off her arm. He looked at her feet, carefully, for the whole of the pause, the way a man reads a page he means to answer. When Vell said begin, he moved before the Ember woman did, and he was in exactly the place her feet had said she would go.

Cael sat at the rope with the pencil stopped over the page.

He reads feet, he wrote. At the mark. Before the exchange. He watches how you set yourself, and he knows where you're going.

He looked at that, and then wrote under it, very small, He's me. He's a watcher. He's been watching for forty fights.

He sat on the low wall by the pump that night with it open on his knee and did not know what to do with it at all. Then, very late, with the cold coming down and the lamp going out in Yeni's window above, he thought about a big young man in a middle yard on the lane with a friend who had been given the job of being Cael. He thought of a heel settling back into the dirt and holding there, waiting, saying a thing that was not true.

He began to write very fast.

Renn taught me this, he wrote, at the bottom of the page, when he had finished. He'll take full credit. Let him.

Chapter 40 — Tier Equivalent

[Patient, methodical narration; give training, failure, and discovery room to accumulate]

Corbin came over the rope like a man stepping over a low wall in his own garden.

It was Thursday, the ninety-second day, the last week of the six, with the lanterns lit on their hooks along the three walls and the yard fuller than Cael had ever seen it on a Thursday. The benches had gone out along the shaded wall because there was nowhere else to put people, and on the end of the front one the errand boys were defending their places from a pair of dyers. Up on the wall the two girls sat with a bag of roast chestnuts between them, not laughing at anything.

Renn was on the sunny side by the gate, and had waved, and pointed at his own front foot, and laughed. Dessa was on the end of the third bench, beside an old man in a scarf, with her hair tied tight and her hands folded in her lap. He had looked at her once and she had looked back and given him nothing at all, and he had understood that she had come to watch him from the benches, as she had said she would, on her own schedule, and that she would tell him nothing about it.

Marrow's slate said Corbin, and a short price, and unrated (vouched), and a price that was not long at all. Under it there was no over/under, because Marrow had rubbed it out, and Cael could see the ghost of a 5 under the chalk where it had been.

"He doesn't know," said Lira at the barrel. "First time since you came. He couldn't make up his mind."

Corbin stood on his mark across the circle with his arms at his sides, square and not tall, with his bald patch catching the lantern light and his short beard going grey at the chin. He did not roll his shoulders or rock on his heels, or look at the crowd, or at Vell. He looked at Cael's feet.

Cael had known he would, and had written it down on Sunday night in a hand that would not keep still. He looked down at his own feet on his mark, as if checking them, and set them.

He set them to say left.

He did it as Renn had settled his heel in the middle yard on the lane, on purpose, for somebody to read. He put his weight a little onto his right foot and turned the left toe out a hair, along the groove: a boy who meant to go sideways to the left on the word. Every person in this yard had heard by now that the boy from Torvin's went sideways against Renn, and Corbin would have heard it, and watched it.

"Corbin. Copper Rank 3, Shield Path. Against unrated. Vouched." The small pause. "Begin when you're ready."

Corbin read his feet.

Cael watched him do it, and let him, and did not move them.

"Begin."

He went left, exactly where his feet had said, honestly, because the first exchange was a handshake and he wanted to see what Corbin did with a true read before he gave him a false one.

Corbin was there.

He was there before Cael was. He had moved on the word as if the word had been his own idea, and he was standing a stride to Cael's left, in the place Cael was going, with his weight settled and the little patch of shine coming up off his left forearm. It was hardly bigger than a dinner plate, and Cael's strike from the hip went into it out of habit, like a fist into a door that somebody has just shut, and stung all the way to his elbow.

Corbin's right hand came round, short, not fast, and hit him in the middle of the chest with the flat of the fist.

It was not a hard blow but a sensible one, and it knocked the breath out of him and put him back two steps and told him, as clearly as words, I was here first. Then the shine went out of the air off Corbin's forearm, as if he did not want to waste it on nothing, and Corbin walked back to his mark.

"End of the exchange," said Vell.

First exchange, Cael said to himself. I told him the truth with my feet. He read it. He was there first. He spends the shield only when he needs it.

He looked across at Corbin, who was looking at his feet.

Cael set them again to say left, exactly as before, with the weight a little onto the right foot and the left toe turned out along the groove, so that they said the same thing they had said a moment ago, when they were telling the truth.

"Begin."

He went right.

He went right on the word, against his own feet, against everything his feet had said, and Corbin went left. Corbin went exactly where the feet had told him, a stride to the left, smooth and early, to the place where a boy who meant what his feet said would be. The boy was not there.

For half a breath Cael was on Corbin's right side, the open side, the side without the shield, with nothing between his hands and the man's ribs.

He threw the strike.

The shine was there. He did not see it come; it was not there, and then it was there, the little plate of it, a hand off Corbin's forearm, which had come across the front of his body faster than anything about Corbin had looked. Cael's knuckles hit it and stopped. Corbin's elbow came round after it, short, into the top of Cael's left arm, and Cael went sideways and kept his feet.

But he had seen Corbin's face.

It was only for a moment, as the elbow came round. Something had gone across it and been put away again almost at once, not anger but surprise, a small clean surprise, the look of a man who has put his foot down on a stair in the dark and found it a stair lower than he thought.

Along the rope, on the shaded side, the old men in the third row made a low noise.

"End of the exchange," said Vell.

Cael went back to his mark rubbing his arm. Second exchange. I lied with my feet. He believed me. He was on the wrong side. He's quicker with the shield than he looks. Much quicker. He looked across. And it surprised him. Somebody lying with their feet.

Corbin stood on his mark.

He did not look at Cael's feet, but at the middle of Cael's chest, steadily, the way you look at the middle of a page when you have decided not to read it line by line. He had stopped reading the feet. One false read in forty fights, and he had stopped.

He's learned it, thought Cael. Already.

He had expected that, but not so fast.

"Begin."

Corbin did not move first.

That was the change, and it was all the change there was: he stood on his mark and did not move until Cael did. Cael moved as Lira had made him move every morning for three weeks, small and quick and unplanned, and Corbin did not try to read it, because he did not need to. He simply waited, square, with his weight in the middle of his feet. Wherever Cael went, Corbin turned to face it, a quarter turn and no more, without hurry, and the little plate of shine came and went off his forearm. It came when Cael was near and went when he was not, as if it were a lamp somebody kept turning up and down.

Cael went in twice. Twice the shine was there before his strike, and twice Corbin's fist came round after it, short and sensible, into his shoulder and then into his side. The second one found the left side under the ribs, where Talis had put his gatepost of a forearm eleven days ago. Something caught there, sharp, and he felt it all the way up into his teeth.

He did not let his face do anything. Corbin watched him not let it.

"End of the exchange," said Vell.

He got to his mark and made himself breathe, four and four, with the catch coming at the top of every breath in. He had thought it had healed, and it had not quite healed.

Third, he said to himself. He's stopped reading me. He waits. I can't get through the shield when he's waiting. And he's found the ribs.

He looked at Corbin, and Corbin was looking at his left side, not at his feet or his chest but at the place under the ribs where the catch was. Corbin had seen the Talis bout, of course. Everybody who used Corbin for a ruler had been at the rope for everything else, and Corbin had been at the rope too, for forty fights' worth of seasons, watching.

The fourth exchange was the bad one.

Corbin came for the ribs without hurrying it, forward a step at a time, square, with the shield coming and going, and every time Cael moved, Corbin's short fist went for the left side, under the arm. Cael got his arm down for the first. The second came in over it, and the catch went through him like a nail. He went down on one knee in the dirt and came up again before Vell could say anything, which he had learned from Lira: you came up before anybody could think you were not going to.

He went backward round the inside of the groove, toward the long side, toward the drain, with his left arm held in against his ribs and his breath coming short. Corbin followed him without any hurry at all, the most patient thing Cael had ever seen, more patient than Dessa, who had waited for you to beat yourself on her. Corbin was not waiting for that; he was simply walking a tired boy round a circle, a step at a time, toward the edge of it.

Cael felt the groove come up under his heel.

"End of the exchange," said Vell.

He was on his mark without remembering getting there, and the catch was there at the top of every breath, and his left arm did not want to come away from his side, and somewhere along the rope on the shaded side somebody had begun, quietly, to count. Four. Somebody else said five's what Marrow had, and somebody told them to be quiet.

At the barrel Lira had let go of the rope and folded her arms tight across her chest, as if she were cold all at once. He understood from her face, which had nothing on it, that she was not going to call anything, or say anything, or tell him what to do. It was his to carry.

He looked across the circle.

Corbin was on his mark, breathing a little harder than he had been at the start, not much, and looking at Cael. And then, as Cael watched, his eyes went down.

They went down to Cael's feet.

Cael stood very still on his mark.

He's reading them again.

Of course he was. He had stopped reading them in the third because the boy had lied with them once. But the boy was hurt now, and tired, with his arm in against his side and his breath coming short, and tired people did not lie with their feet. Tired people stood the way their bodies needed to stand, because they had nothing left over for standing any other way. Forty fights had taught Corbin that. You could not lie with your feet when you were on your last legs. It took too much.

So he was reading them again. He was reading them as he had always read them, for forty fights, because it had always worked.

Cael looked down at his own feet.

He set them to say left.

He did it slowly, so that it looked like what it was, which was a tired boy setting his feet. He put his weight onto his right foot and turned the left toe out along the groove. It was the same shape as the first two exchanges, exactly the same. Once it had been the truth, and once it had been a lie.

He saw Corbin read it.

He saw Corbin see the shape, and know it. It was the lie from the second exchange, the shape that said left and went right. And Corbin was a man who had been lied to once by that shape and had learned it, as he learned everything, in a single exchange. Cael watched him settle very slightly onto his own left foot, ready to cut across to his right. That was the place a boy would go who said left with his feet and meant right.

"Begin," said Vell.

Cael went left.

He went left, exactly where his feet had said. He went the way he had gone in the first exchange when he was telling the truth, because that was what he was doing. He was telling the truth to a man who had just learned not to believe it.

Corbin went right.

He went to the right, smooth and early, into the place where the liar would be. It was a very good move, the move of a man who had read a lie correctly and answered it before it had finished being told. To cut across to his right he had turned a quarter away from the boy, and his left arm, the shield arm, had gone round with him across the front of his own body. For half a breath, for less, he was a stride away from where Cael was, on the wrong side, with his weight going the wrong way, his shield on the far side of himself, and all of his square solid back turned a quarter toward the boy.

Cael was inside.

He did not remember deciding to be. He was simply there, on Corbin's left side now, close, closer than the shield, with the catch in his ribs going through him like a nail and none of it mattering. Corbin's shield arm was on the wrong side of Corbin. To come back across, the shield would have to come all the way round the front of the man who owned it. It was hardly bigger than a dinner plate, and very quick. But it was on the wrong side, and there was a whole square man in between.

The strike came up from the hip. Back foot driving, shoulder following, fist arriving last.

He stopped it a finger's width from the hinge of Corbin's jaw, under the ear.

He felt the shine come up beside his wrist, too late. It was there, the little plate, a hand off Corbin's forearm, which had come round the front of him faster than anything had a right to. It was a breath behind the fist. It had come round in time to guard a jaw that was not going to be hit, because the fist had already stopped.

Then Cael's left hand, which he had not been able to lift away from his ribs for an exchange and a half, came away from them on its own and went flat against the side of Corbin's chest. It did not strike. It was simply there, resting on the man's ribs, under the arm, exactly where Corbin had been putting his fist into Cael's all evening.

Corbin stood quite still.

Cael stood quite still.

They stood like that, in the middle of the circle under the lanterns, close enough that Cael could hear the man breathing, and the yard had gone so quiet that he could hear the lantern hooks creaking on the walls.

Then Corbin lifted his right hand, slowly. He opened it, palm out, and held it up toward the table.

"Called," said Vell. "Conceded. Unrated."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Corbin laughed.

It was a short laugh, and not a loud one, and it came out of him as though it had been waiting a long time for a reason. He stepped back from Cael, out of the strike's reach, and let the shine go off his forearm, and stood looking at him with his hands on his hips.

"You told me the truth," he said.

"Yes."

"The last time. With your feet." Corbin shook his head slowly. "The first time you told me the truth, and the second time you told me a lie, and I learned the lie. And the last time you told me the truth again, because you knew I'd learned the lie." He seemed to be going over it, step by step. "That's forty-one," he said. "Forty-one fights. Nobody's ever done that to me with the truth."

"I couldn't have done it twice."

"No," Corbin agreed. "I'll have learned that by morning." He held out his hand, and Cael took it, and Corbin's hand was hard and square and dry and steady. "Go and stand at the table. They'll want to know how long it took."

"Five."

"Five," said Corbin, and nodded, as though the number confirmed something he had always suspected about the world. Then he turned and walked off toward the water bucket, square and unhurried, a man stepping over a low wall in his own garden. On his way he passed Dessa's bench, and Dessa said something to him that Cael could not hear, and Corbin laughed again.

The yard came up behind Cael like weather.

It came up all at once and from everywhere, the shaded side and the sun and the benches. The old men in the third row were stamping on the boards, and the river workshops were shouting, and the errand boys were standing on the end of the front bench defending it from nobody. Up on the wall the girls had both stood up, and the bag of chestnuts had gone over and was rolling along the top of the wall, and neither of them was trying to catch it. Renn was shouting something on the sunny side by the gate, with his arms up. It sounded like mine. His friends were shouting him down.

Cael walked to the table with his left arm against his ribs, because it had gone back there as soon as it was allowed to, and stood in front of it.

Vell was writing, and she went on writing.

"Result stands as called," she said at last. "Unrated, over Corbin, Copper Rank 3, Shield Path. Fifth exchange. Conceded." The pen moved on. "Witnessed and entered."

Then she put the pen down, which he had never seen her do before a result was blotted, and looked up at him.

"Go home," said Vell. "Put that side in cold water. Not butter." She looked at him a moment longer. "And come to my table on Tuesday, after the afternoon card. Not before."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He did not get far toward home.

He got as far as the gate in the wall, with Lira on his left side now, the rib side, without being asked. Then he had to stand still in the gateway and breathe, carefully, with his hand pressed flat against the catch, while people went past him out into the street.

They went past him talking.

He had never heard so many people talking about a bout on their way out of the yard. They were not talking to him, and nobody stopped, though a few of them looked at him as they passed, to see whether he matched what they had just been told. But mostly they talked to each other, walking out into the dark street under the lanterns, and he heard pieces of it go past.

—Corbin, though—

—five, I said five, I said it at the third—

—conceded, he put his hand up himself—

—that's past Corbin, then, that is, that's—

Lira stood beside him in the gateway and listened to it go past, with her head a little on one side.

"There," she said quietly. "Hear that?"

"I hear it."

"That's not about you." She was not smiling; her face had the look it had at the barrel before a bout, quick and still at once. "Listen to it. Nobody's saying you're good. Nobody knows what you are. They're saying past Corbin. That's a thing they already know how to say. They've been saying it about other people for years." She looked at the street, at the backs going away under the lanterns, talking. "By tomorrow it'll be at the fish steps. By Sunday somebody's cousin across the bridge will have it. The boy at Torvin's went five with Corbin and Corbin put his hand up." She turned and looked at him. "That's the one they'll repeat. I told you."

"You did."

"I'm always right about the yard." She took his right arm, the good one, and put it through hers, which she had never done before. Without making anything of it she began to walk him out into the street, slowly, at his pace, which was the pace of an old man crossing a frozen yard. "It's the only thing I'm always right about. Come on. Torvin's wife will have put something on with real vegetables in it, and if we're not in before the brothers there won't be any."

They went along the dark street together, slowly, through the people going home talking. At the corner by the board somebody had already been with a stub of charcoal, and under the card for Sunday, in large untidy letters that were not Vell's, it said CORBIN PUT HIS HAND UP. Under that, smaller, in a different hand, five. The errand boys were standing in front of it arguing about which of them had written it.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

It was a Saturday, the six weeks' thirty-ninth night, very cold, and nothing happened in it at all until it did.

He was at Torvin's, on his cot under the window, with the Log open on his knee, late. The brothers had gone to sleep early because the river had frozen at the edges, just as they had said it would, and there would be no barges in the morning. They had argued about it until they fell asleep in the middle of the argument, one and then the other, and Yeni's lamp was turned low on the shelf, and the wheezing man was whistling by the door, long and thin. Downstairs Torvin had said Lamps up through the floorboards an hour ago, and the house had gone quiet round it.

He was going back through the six weeks.

He had begun it after supper because he could not sleep on his left side yet, or his back, and lying on his right side he could read. So he went back through the Log from the morning at the board, entry by entry, the way he read a column of figures before he signed it, from the top, slowly. Seventh, the kiln boy. Eighth, Renn, the front heel. Ninth, Sarel, two, with the longest entry in the book. Tenth, Talis, and the ground. Eleventh, Dellin, nothing happened. Twelfth, Corbin, five, conceded. Four wins and two losses. Six bouts in six weeks, as he had said under the pear tree, which he had not been sure his body would take, and it had taken them, just.

He was in the margin of the Dellin entry, at the line about putting his hand on the ground at his mark, when something changed.

He did not know what it was; that was the first thing about it. It was not a sound, and it was not a feeling, not quite, but nearer to the quiet that comes before a thought arrives whole, the moment when you have stopped working at a thing and it suddenly turns over in you, by itself, and shows you its other side. Except that there was no thought, only the quiet, and the turning over, and nothing on the other side yet.

But he knew that something had changed. He knew it the way he had known, in Pellin's office, that the sigil at the edge of his sight was looking at him.

He put the Log down on the blanket.

He sat very still on the cot, with his back against the cold wall under the window, as he had sat in the circle at Weaver's Row with his feet on the two worn places, and waited.

It came from behind the breastbone.

It came from the place where the sigil had gathered on the morning of his Kindling, small and risen, before it spoke one word and went out. That place had been dark ever since; he had gone looking for it in Torvin's yard on the twenty-eighth night, for an hour, and found only the place where a door should have been. He could feel that it was still dark. Nothing lit. No sigil came up out of it to the edge of his sight. But in the dark, the way words come up on the inside of your eyelids when your eyelids are open, something was written.

He read it.

He did not read it with his eyes, and he did not know what to call what he read it with. He read it as he had read the archive entry in the green book at a table in Denvash, under a north window: once, and then again, and then a third time, slowly, checking each word against the one before it, before he let himself believe any of it.

It stayed. It did not go out, as the word had gone out. It sat there in the dark behind his breastbone, quiet and plain, like a figure on a page once it has been written down.

Wind-adjacent.

He knew where it had come from.

He knew it at once, before he had finished the third reading, as surely as he had known that something had changed, and it did not come as an argument but as a fact, like the river being cold.

It had come from the grey half. It had come from two months of mornings in the shadow of the east wall, at a canvas post, with a girl who would not tell lies to anybody she trained. It had come from watching her step a hundred times from the inside with his arms in the wrong place, and once from the rope. It had come from the drop under her backhand that was lower than she had ever asked him to go. It had come from the fourth exchange against Dessa, going across, into the closing space, in a way that was not his. It had come from the third exchange against Sarel, when he had stopped watching and moved without deciding, the way she moved. That was the thing she had been trying to teach him for two months, and he had thought he was only learning it.

He had been gathering it. He had been gathering it all along, mornings and bouts and the long minutes at the rope, and he had never had any word for what it was he gathered. Now it had a name, or the beginning of one. Adjacent. Next to Wind, but not Wind. Lira's, and not Lira's. Partial. Undetermined. Unknown.

It was not an answer. It was a page with more on it than yesterday's.

He sat on the cot for a long time with the notice there in the dark behind his breastbone, and did not write anything.

Then he thought about Lira.

He thought about her in her room two streets over, behind her green door that locked from both sides, with Torvin's chimney in her window, and he thought about going there. He could see the whole of it, as he had seen it on the night of the summons, when he had shut the Log on the kitchen table and gone up through the dark to the window at the bottom of the roof stair. The habit of telling had begun that night, and he had been proud of it, and he could go now. He could knock on her green door, three times, soft, and she would open it with her coat on and say what happened. He could tell her.

I think I've got something of yours.

He tried the sentence in his head and it came out wrong, and he tried it another way, and it came out wrong again.

He had promised her on the step on the night of Dessa: when I know what it is, really know, you'll be the one I tell first. He did not know what it was. He knew what it was called, now, a little, and where it came from; he did not know what it did, or why, or how a thing could be collected by watching, or whether it would answer if he called it. He did not know whether it was a thing he had done or a thing that had been done to him.

And in the grey half, on the morning after he had named her right foot, she had stood in front of him with her hands loose at her sides and said mine are mine. You don't keep my things.

This was hers. Or some of it was. He did not know how much.

He took the Log up off the blanket and turned it over to the back, and wrote.

Not yet. I'm not hiding it. I just can't explain it yet, not even to myself. If I tell her now, she'll help me work it out, and afterward I'll never be sure which parts of the working out were mine.

He read it back.

He was not sure that it was honest.

He read it a second time and was less sure. It had the shape of a reason, and he could see the shape quite clearly, and he could not see whether there was anything inside it. It might be true. It might be the kind of true that has its legs sawn short. It might be a boy on a cot who had been told once, plainly, in the grey half, you keep everything till you're sure, keeping one more thing till he was sure, and writing down a good reason for it in his best hand.

He did not cross it out, but drew a line round it instead, a box, so that when he came back to it he would know he had not been sure.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Then, because he could not sit still with it any longer, he got up.

There was a narrow space between his cot and the wall, perhaps two strides long and one wide, where his bag stood and the cold came in under the window, and he stood in it in his stockinged feet on the boards. The brothers were asleep. Yeni was asleep, or was lying with her eyes shut and listening, which with Yeni was the same thing.

He thought about Lira's step.

Not the whole of it, with the touches and the backhand, but only the beginning of it, the part he had watched a hundred times from the inside and never once been able to see. The first drop of the hip, which started everything, a small dip and turn, so slight that from the inside it looked like nothing at all.

He did it.

He did it on purpose, slowly, at half the speed Lira would have done it. He dropped his hip the way he had seen her drop hers, and turned the way he had seen her turn, and put his foot down where he had seen her put hers.

It worked.

It did not work well. It worked so badly that anybody watching would have thought he was trying to step over something on the floor and had misjudged it. It was clumsy and slow, and nothing like the drop under her backhand, or the going across against Dessa, which had come out of him whole and perfect and not his. But for a moment, for one step, the boards between the cot and the wall were very slightly less firm about how far apart they were. It was the width of a hand, perhaps less: the space between where his foot had been and where it landed was a little shorter than it should have been, and he felt it go short under him, like a stair that is not quite the height you expected.

He had done it. Not had it done to him. Done it. On purpose. He had chosen to.

He stood there afterward in the narrow space, breathing.

He was breathing much harder than one slow step in his stockings had any right to make him, and his hip ached, the left one, deep in the joint, as if he had carried something heavy up a long stair on that side. It cost something, he did not know what or how much; he only knew that it had cost more than it should have, and that he had paid it, and that he did not know yet what it had bought.

He did it once more, to be sure.

It was worse the second time, slower and clumsier, and the boards were only a very little less firm, hardly at all, and the hip ached more after it. He did not do it a third time. He sat down on the end of the cot with his hand pressed to the hip and his breath coming short, and turned the fact over in his mind like a stone he had picked up off a road and could not yet tell the weight of.

Then he picked up the Log and wrote under the box.

I did it on purpose. Once. Badly, slowly, and it cost something in the hip and the breath that I can't measure yet. Twice, worse. But on purpose.

Every time before, it came when I didn't ask for it and wasn't there when I did. Tonight I asked, and it came. Not much. A little. Badly.

I think that's the thing that matters. Not that it's there. That it's started to answer when I ask.

He read that over, and it was true, and he left it.

He wrote to Hesk before he slept, because it was Saturday, and the letter would go in the west bag on Monday and be in Denvash by the Monday after. And he had found, sitting on the cot with his hip aching, that he wanted very much to write to somebody, when there was only one person it could be, and he could not write it to him.

Lira's drawn a line under the forty. I'll tell you about the forty another time; it's a long story and most of it is me saying one word.

Tell Joren I'm putting my hand on the ground at my mark before every bout now. He'll know why, or he won't, and either way he'll like it.

Tell Alis I laughed.

Then he sat with the leather book closed on his knee and counted, as he always did now, what he had not told Hesk.

The cart. Renn. The drop. Dessa. And tonight.

It was five.

He sat with the number in the cold, with the wheezing man whistling by the door. It was not that it had gone up. There was one person who was meant to be first. She was two streets away behind a green door, and he had not gone.

He blew out his small piece of the light by turning his face to the wall. He lay awake with the notice quiet behind his breastbone and his hip aching, and listened to the district's late sounds come up through the window.

On Tuesday the afternoon card went off without him, three bouts, and he stood at the rope and watched all three and wrote them down. Then the yard emptied, and the pie boy began to rake the circle, and the crows came down along the eaves, and he went to Vell's table.

She was finishing an entry. "Sit down," she said, and blotted it.

There was nowhere to sit but the dirt and the barrel, so he stood, and she did not seem to mind.

"Assessed-Copper," said Vell.

He waited.

"It's not a real rank. I want that said first, so you don't go thinking it is." She turned her tea a quarter turn by its handle. "It's a word I use. It means the circuit has watched you for long enough to say you fight at about Copper 5, or 6, on a good night, whatever the registry calls you. And the registry calls you nothing." She looked at the ledger. "Take it to Denvash and they'd not know what it meant. Take it across the river and they'd laugh. Nobody outside this district would give you a mark for it."

"But inside it," said Cael.

"Inside it, it's the difference between a boy people bet on for sport and a fighter people plan for." She picked up her pen and wrote a short line beside the long-standing one at the top of his page, which he could not read upside down, and she did not turn the book. "That's worth something here. It's worth more here than you know yet."

She blotted it.

"Is it worth anything to you?" said Cael.

He had not known he was going to ask it until it was out. Vell looked up at him, and something went across her weathered face, very nearly amusement, and was put away again.

"Liking a fighter has nothing to do with how I rate him. The book's honest or it's nothing, and an honest book's all that stops this circuit tearing itself to pieces over who's good." She looked at him a moment longer, and then said, more quietly, in a different voice, the one she kept for things that were hers: "For what it's worth. I do."

Lira was sitting on the low wall at the side of the yard with her knees up and her coat round them, in the last of the light. She had waited, and had not come to the table, but had sat on the wall, as she had sat on the river wall on the day of the six weeks, with the look of somebody who had been happening to pass a particular place for about an hour.

"Assessed-Copper."

She did not jump off the wall, but sat quite still for a moment, and then the slow smile began, the one that started behind her eyes and took its time getting out.

He walked beside her and did not say it.

He had it with him, behind his breastbone, quiet and plain, in the dark place that was not quite as dark as it had been. Wind-adjacent. It had been there at Vell's table and on the wall and in the gate, and it was there now in the lane. Every step he took beside her, it was there, and every step he did not say it.

The six weeks were spent. Somewhere on the merchant road, or at a desk two days west, somebody more senior than Coss was being found and sent, with a file that was too thin and a question nobody had told Coss. A girl with a green door was walking beside him in the dusk, pleased about a word that was not a rank, a girl who had drawn a line under forty and had told him, plainly, mine are mine.

"Same time tomorrow," said Lira.

"Same time tomorrow."

She went off up the lane toward the chandler's, and he stood at the well and watched her go until he could not see her, and then turned toward Torvin's, two streets the other way.

He did not know how long he could carry it, only that it would not be long. He thought, walking home with his hip aching, that it might be two weeks, if he was careful, and that he did not want to be careful, and that the thing behind his breastbone was partly hers. He thought that every morning he kept it from her in the grey half, it would get heavier. Nothing that has to be held is free.

Chapter 41 — The Back Pages

[Taut, clear narration; sharpen the danger without rushing the thinking]

He made the step again on Tuesday night, in the narrow space between his cot and the wall, after the brothers had stopped arguing and before the wheezing man began to whistle.

It was the fourth night running. He had told himself on the first night that he would do it only to be sure it was still there, and on the second that he would do it to see whether it came more easily, and by the third he had stopped telling himself anything and simply waited for the house to go quiet. Then he stood up in his stockings on the cold boards, with his back to the room so that Yeni would see only a boy standing by a window, and dropped his hip, and turned, and put his foot down where he had watched Lira put hers a thousand times.

The boards went short under him by the width of a hand.

It was no better than it had been on Saturday. It was slow, and stiff, and anybody watching would have thought he had stood up too fast and lost his balance and caught it again. When it was done his breath came short for a dozen breaths, as though he had run up the stairs from the street, and the ache came into the joint of his left hip, deep and dull, a little worse than the night before. He did it once more, because twice was the number he had set himself, and the second time the boards hardly changed at all.

He sat down on the end of the cot with his hand pressed against the hip and waited for his breathing to come back.

It did not get easier, but it did not go away either. On Saturday he had thought it might be a thing that happened once, like the word in Pellin's office, and then never again. Three nights later it was still there, every time he asked, small and clumsy and costing more than it gave. He did not know whether that was the beginning of something or the whole of it.

He took the Log off the shelf and turned it over to the back, past the boxed Not yet and the entry about the first night, to a clean page.

He had been putting off this page for three days. Every night he had opened the back section and looked at the white paper under the last entry, and closed it again, because what he wanted to write was not a fact. Everything else in the back of the book was a fact. The cart was a fact; the drop was a fact; the notice, with its plain words in the dark behind his breastbone, was the plainest fact of all. What he wanted to write tonight was a guess, and he had told Lira once, on a step under a lantern, that guessing was how you wrote the wrong thing down and then trusted it because it was written.

But he had been carrying the guess around for three days, and it had got no smaller, and he thought it would be better on paper, where he could at least see the edges of it.

He wrote slowly, in his best hand.

I think I'm borrowing something.

He looked at the line until the letters stopped looking like words. Then he went on under it, because one line on its own looked too sure of itself.

Not taking. It isn't all there, and it isn't mine the way Lira's Path is hers. She was declared at Kindling and it's been hers every day since, whole, to use when she likes. What I've got is more like the outline of how she moves, without the inside. It comes properly when something's coming at me and I haven't got time to choose. When I ask for it on purpose, slowly, by the cot, it comes too, but badly. It's like copying out a word in somebody else's handwriting. You can see whose hand it was meant to be. Nobody would mistake it for theirs.

I don't know how it got here. I don't know if "borrowing" is the right word. It's the least wrong word I've got.

He read it over. There was nothing in it that was more than he knew, and nothing that was less, and he left it.

The wheezing man had begun his long whistle by the door. Yeni's lamp was down to a bead, and when he looked up she had turned on her side with her face to the wall, which meant either that she was asleep or that she had decided to let him think so. He put the Log back on the shelf beside Hesk's leather book and lay down on his right side, the side that did not catch, and lay awake with the hip aching and the dark place behind his breastbone quiet and a little less dark than it had been.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

In the grey half on Wednesday morning Lira was teaching him to move without deciding, and he was watching her do it, and he could not stop thinking about the watching.

He had always watched her. That was what the mornings were. She did a thing at the post and he watched it, and then he tried it and she watched him, and between the two of them they found the place where his body and her body disagreed, and worked on it. It had never before seemed like anything but a lesson. This morning, every time she moved, he caught himself wondering what he was doing when he looked at her, and whether looking was all it was.

"Hips," said Lira.

"I know."

"You know, and they're still square." She stepped back out of the box and put her hands on her own hips to show him. "You're thinking. I can see you thinking. You're thinking about something that isn't this."

"I'm thinking about this."

"You're thinking about something near this." She looked at him with her head on one side, not cross, only interested. "Is it the rating? Because I'll tell you now, I'm still proud of it, and you're still past me, and if you want me to say it again I'll say it at the post in front of the girls on the wall."

"It isn't the rating."

"Then it's something you'll tell me when you tell me." She brought her hands up. "Again. Loose. And stop looking at my feet like they owe you money."

He did it again, and his hips were square, and she said hips, and he said I know.

She did the step at the end, as she always did. It came round with the two empty touches and the ground folding, and the backhand stopping by his ear, and her weight stopped with it, almost; it went on past by perhaps two fingers' width onto her right foot. That was better than three fingers. He told her so at once, as the rule said, and she grinned and said two to herself and pushed her hair off her face with her wrist.

He watched her do that too.

He had watched her push her hair back a hundred times, and her step a thousand, and her breathing and her shoulders and the way she leaned on the post with her good arm when she was thinking. He knew her movements as he knew the stairs up to his room at Torvin's, where to put his foot in the dark. And somewhere in all that watching, if the notice meant what he thought it meant, something of hers had come across into him without either of them noticing. He did not know whether it had come across in a day or in a month, or whether it was still coming across now, this morning, while she stood in the grey half pushing her hair out of her eyes.

She did not seem to have noticed anything, and she said something about almost everything; she had told him about his nod, and his hips, and the way his chin went up when he was pleased with himself. But then she had seen it, of course. I did what you do, he had said, under a lantern by the chalk board, and she had stopped in the street with her face doing something he had never seen it do. She had thought it was learning. So had he, at the time.

He wanted it to be true that she had not noticed, because that was easier, and he knew by now that wanting a thing because it was easier was a reason to be careful with it, not a reason to believe it.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

On Thursday the mender sent the lantern woman's boy up to Torvin's to ask whether he would come for an extra afternoon, because of the keys.

They had come out of the same house by the dyers' as the hinges, from the drawers of a desk that had gone for firewood. There were a few long door keys and a great many small ones for boxes and cupboards, and nothing left to try them in. The mender said that did not matter. A key that had been used for twenty years had a shape worn into it by the lock it fitted, and you could see the lock in the key, if you looked.

So Cael sat on the stool at the end of the bench with a loupe in his eye and looked at keys, and the mender was right. A key that had turned every day for years had soft bright edges on its wards where the lock's own pins had worn it. A key that had never been used was sharp all over, and a key that had been used for a while and then put away had both kinds of edge at once, the bright ones going dull again. By the end of the afternoon he could sort the pocket keys from the drawer keys, and could not have told anybody how.

He thought about Lira the whole time. The lock had not given the key anything. It had only been turned in, every day, a little at a time, until the key carried the shape of the lock whether anybody meant it to or not. It was a comfortable thought, and he did not trust it, because comfortable thoughts were the ones that let you stop asking questions. He set it on the side of the bench in his head with the other things he did not trust yet and went on sorting.

Walking back up the lane of yards at the end of the day, he passed the old man's gate. The old man was standing in it with his sleeves rolled down against the cold, watching the woman with the shoulder go through her six positions in the last of the light, and he did not look round.

"Assessed," said the old man.

Cael stopped. He had not told the old man; he had not told anybody but Lira and Torvin's wife, and Torvin's wife had told the boots woman, which was the same as telling the whole district.

"Yes."

The old man watched the woman reach her fourth position and hold it.

"Now they'll plan for you," he said. "Before, they bet on you. Now they plan." He shifted his weight very slightly from one foot to the other. "Different thing, being planned for."

Then he went back to watching, and Cael understood that he had been given all of it, and walked on up the lane.

That night, on the cot, he turned to the back of the Log and wrote the longest entry he had written there since the drop. His hand went faster as it went, and less careful.

I need more than one. One source is a story. Lira is one source. If there's anything to this at all, the next question is whether it's Lira, or whether it's anybody. Is it watching somebody a great deal that does it? Or is watching only the first part, and there's something else as well that has to be there, that I haven't found? I can't tell those apart from one example. Nobody could.

I need somebody else. A different person, a different Path. Watched as hard as I watched her, and then see whether anything comes, and whether it comes the same way, or a different way, or not at all.

He stopped with the pencil over the page, because the next thought had arrived while he was writing the last one, and it was not a comfortable thought at all.

If it was anybody, and not only Lira, then it was everybody he had ever watched hard enough. Renn's figure, Dessa's patience, the kiln boy's held breath, Sarel's closing, Talis planting where he could not see him go, Corbin reading feet at the mark: any of them. The woman with the shoulder, too, doing her six positions in the old man's yard every evening for three months while he walked past. Any of them might have left something behind in him, quietly, as the lock had left its shape in the key, and it might be sitting there now in the dark behind his breastbone with no notice on it yet, waiting.

On some nights, he thought, that would be the most exciting thing he had ever thought of, and on others the most frightening. Tonight, on the cot, with the wheezing man whistling and the hip aching, it was both at once, and he could not have said which was winning.

He wrote under the entry, smaller: Find out. Don't guess.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He chose Kestrel because he had watched him twice already and had never meant to fight him.

That was the first reason, and the most important. Kestrel was a Copper Rank 5, Force Path, who fought on the Sunday card once or twice a month. Vell would not put an assessed-Copper of fourteen into the circle with a Force man who had been at it for ten seasons. So Cael could watch him as hard as he liked without it being homework for a bout, and if anything came of the watching, it would not have come from needing it.

The second reason was that Kestrel was nothing like Lira. He was a big, slow-spoken man of about thirty who worked at the ropewalk along the river, long in the arm and heavy in the shoulder, with tar ground into the creases of his hands that no amount of washing would shift. He did not skip any middles. He fought as he walked, steadily and straight at you, and his Force did what Force did, which was to put a second, heavier push into you a half beat after his fist had stopped. It was the shove Petra had taught Cael, made slower and much bigger. If something of Kestrel's came across, Cael thought, he would know it was not Lira's.

The third reason was that Kestrel trained in the mornings, alone, in the middle yard on the lane where Renn had shown off his false heel, and anybody could stand at the gate and watch.

On the Sunday card Kestrel had the third bout, against a Copper 4 Blade from Fenrow, and Cael watched him from the rope on the shaded side with his hand on the iron stake. He did not watch him for the Log, with the pencil going. He watched him the grey-half way, the whole of him at once, and it was harder than he had expected to stop looking for things. His eyes kept going to the big man's heels, because the heels were where the shove came from, and every time they went there he caught himself building a plan for a bout that would never happen. Gone, he thought, without saying it, and brought them back.

Kestrel beat the Fenrow Blade in the fourth exchange with one shove that sent the Blade across the groove on his back, and walked to the water bucket humming.

Lira had come up beside him at the rope while he was watching, and had stood there without speaking, which was not like her.

"You weren't writing," she said.

"No."

"You always write." She looked at the circle, where the pie boy was raking out the furrow the Fenrow Blade had made. "You looked at him the way you look at me in the mornings. Not the way you look at the people you're going to fight."

He had not known it showed. He thought that perhaps he should have; she had found his nod, and his hips, and the way his chin went up.

"I won't be at the post tomorrow," he said. "Or Thursday, perhaps. I'm going to watch him train. At the middle yard. All morning."

Lira held his eyes and said nothing, long enough for the pie boy to come along the rope and go past them with his tray. He saw the question come into her face, and saw her look at it, and put it down beside her on the step that was not there, carefully, as she had put down borrowed under the lantern after Dessa.

"All right," she said.

It was the voice that meant she was not going to pick the question up. But she had put it down a little further away this time than she usually did, and at the well she said same time Tuesday, not tomorrow. He walked home to Torvin's with that sitting in his chest.

So on Monday he did not go to the grey half. He went up to the middle yard in the dark, with bread in his pocket, and stood at the gate with his back against the wall where Renn's friends had sat like crows, and waited.

Kestrel came at first light. He hung a sack of sand from the beam across the far end of the yard, on a rope he brought coiled over his shoulder. He stood in front of it with his hands at his sides while his breath went up white and came down again a dozen times, and then he hit it, not hard. His fist went in a hand's depth and stopped, and the sack hung there on its rope with the dent of his knuckles in it. Then, a half beat after the fist had stopped, the whole sack went up and back as though somebody had kicked it from below, and swung out to the end of the rope, and came back. Kestrel stepped out of its way without looking at it and hit it again.

Cael watched him do that for four hours.

He watched him as he had watched Lira for three months, which was not the way he watched an opponent. He did not look for a tell, and he did not take the Log out of his coat. He tried to look at the whole of the man at once, as you look at a stance when you want to know what it feels like to stand in it. He watched Kestrel's breath go down into his belly before every blow. He watched his weight settle very slightly into his heels as the fist stopped, as if he were bracing a door with his back, and the shove come out of that settling and not out of the fist at all. He watched until his own heels ached from standing and he had stopped being sure whether he was seeing the thing or remembering it.

At the end of the morning Kestrel unhooked the sack and coiled his rope and walked out through the gate past him, close enough to touch, smelling of tar and sweat and rope, and did not look at him once.

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

He tried it that night in Torvin's courtyard, after the lamps.

It was the same courtyard where, ten weeks ago, on the twenty-eighth night, he had sat on the cold flags for an hour looking for the Arbiter, and found only the place where a door should have been. The pear tree was bare now, and the pump had a skin of ice on its trough that somebody had broken with a stick and that had frozen again round the stick. He sat on the low wall with his coat buttoned to the chin, and when the house had gone quiet behind him, he closed his eyes and went looking.

He went to the dark place behind his breastbone, which was not quite as dark as it had been, and found the Wind there. It was not a word or a picture, but a sort of leaning in the dark, the shape the step had left when it went through him. He did not reach for it. He went past it, carefully, as you go past a sleeping dog, and felt about in the dark beyond it for anything that was not Lira's. He put the whole morning in front of himself, the heels settling and the sack going up a half beat late and the tar on the big hands, and reached for whatever it had left.

There was nothing.

But it was not the nothing he had found on the twenty-eighth night. That had been a closed door, flat and final. This was more like starting a nut on a bolt in the dark at Hesk's bench: the thread almost catching, and catching, and then slipping off, so that you knew there was a thread there and could not make it take. It was not an absence so much as something unfinished.

He sat on the wall for an hour, and it did not finish. At the end of the hour he made the Wind step once, on the frozen flags, to be sure he still could, and it came, clumsily, the stones going a hand's width short under his foot. So it was not the asking. He had asked twice tonight, and one thing had answered and the other had not.

He went up the stairs in the dark with his hand on the wall, and wrote nothing in the back that night but the date and Kestrel, first day, because everything else he could have written was either nothing or wanting, and he could not yet tell which.

Chapter 42 — Some of It's Yours

[Taut, clear narration; sharpen the danger without rushing the thinking]

On Thursday he went back to the middle yard, and this time Kestrel looked at him.

The frost had come down so hard in the night that the sack's rope was frozen stiff, and Kestrel had to stand under the beam beating it against his leg before it would take a knot. Cael was already at the gate. He had missed the grey half again, and Lira had said all right again on Wednesday evening at the well in the same voice as before, with the question set down a little further away from her this time. He did not like how far.

He watched as he had watched on Monday, without writing and without looking for anything, and tried to let it go into him as the mornings in the grey half had gone into him, a little at a time, without his permission. He did not know how to do that on purpose. Every time he caught himself trying to let something in, he was really only watching harder, and watching harder was what he did for a bout. It was the opposite of what he had done with Lira for three months, which had mostly been standing about in the cold while she showed him things, liking her. He had never before liked anybody in quite that plain everyday fashion, as you like the person whose mornings you share, and he could not see how it could matter. He thought it would be a very foolish thing to write down, and that he would probably write it down anyway.

At the end of the second hour, Kestrel stopped hitting the sack. He wiped his face on the shoulder of his shirt and looked down the yard at the gate, slowly, as though he had known Cael was there all along and had only now got round to it.

"You're the boy from Torvin's," he said. "Went five with Corbin."

"Yes."

"Second morning you've stood there." Kestrel came a few steps down the yard, not toward him exactly, but nearer, rolling his shoulders. Up close he was even bigger than he looked in the circle, and his voice was soft and slow, a voice that did not expect to have to be raised. "Vell put us down for something?"

"No."

"Then what are you watching me for?"

Cael had thought about this, walking up in the dark, and had not found an answer that was both true and short. So he gave the true one.

"I don't know yet."

Kestrel looked at him with no expression on his broad face at all. Then he nodded, as if that were a perfectly ordinary reason for standing at a gate in a frost for two mornings, and turned back to the sack.

"Stand inside the wall, then," he said over his shoulder. "Out of the wind. You'll lose your feet, standing in that."

So Cael stood inside the wall, out of the wind, and watched for two more hours. At the end of it the big man coiled his rope and walked out past him humming, and said "Morning" as he went by, as though they had known each other for years.

That night, on the low wall by the pump, the thread stayed exactly where it had been on Monday, almost catching and not catching.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On Friday morning he went back to the grey half, because two mornings away from it had been two too many, and because Lira was there.

She did not say anything about the two mornings. She tore the bread and gave him half, and then the box drill at full speed, and then the step, over and over. He was tired from two dawns at a gate and two nights on a cold wall, and she could see it, and she only came at him a little harder, as though she meant to find out how tired he was by experiment.

On the ninth time she came at him with the step, something happened.

It did not happen in his feet, where the Wind lived, but lower down and further back, in his heels. She came in with the two empty touches and the ground folding, and as she came his weight went down and back into his heels, both of them, at once, hard, as if he had braced his back against a door that somebody was pushing on from the other side. It was not his. He had never once stood like that in his life. It was not Lira's either; Lira never stood like anything, she was always going somewhere. It lasted for half a heartbeat, perhaps less. Then her backhand stopped beside his ear, and he was standing on his own two feet again in the ordinary way, and his heels were only heels.

He stood quite still.

"Late," said Lira. "You were late. You went somewhere and stopped."

"I know."

"Where did you go?"

"I don't know."

She looked at him, and he saw her see that he meant it, and put that down on the step beside the other things. "Again."

He did it a dozen times more before the sun came over the east wall, and his heels stayed his own every time, and by the end he could not have sworn to anybody, not even to himself, that he had felt anything at all.

He wrote it up that night on the cot: the two mornings of Kestrel, the two failed nights on the wall, the half heartbeat in the grey half, as plainly as he could. Then he sat looking at what he had written, because none of it would stand still.

Inconclusive, he wrote at last.

I can see three ways to read it. One: two mornings isn't three months. I watched Lira for three months before anything came, and I wasn't even trying. Two: Force doesn't come across the way Wind does, or not to me, for reasons I can't guess at. Three: the thing in my heels this morning was real, and was his, and I need a great deal more before I can say so. I can't tell which. I'm writing that down so that I remember I couldn't.

He turned back a page, to the boxed Not yet from the thirty-ninth night, with not sure it is honest written beside the box.

It had been two weeks tomorrow.

He had told himself, walking home from the well on the forty-second day, that he could carry it two weeks if he was careful. He had been careful, and the two weeks were nearly gone, and in all that time he had found out nothing that would make it easier to say. He had only found out that he did not know more things than he had thought.

He shut the Log and lay down on his right side and looked at the window until the bead of Yeni's lamp went out.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

"You've been somewhere else," said Lira, "for about a fortnight."

It was Saturday morning in the grey half, and she had stopped in the middle of the box drill to say it, with her hands still up. Then she let them down and stood with her weight a little forward and looked at him.

"Not distracted. You're here. You're doing the drills. But half of you's somewhere else, in some other talk, and I only get the scraps of mine." She tilted her head. "And you've missed two mornings standing at a gate watching a ropewalker hit a sack, and the girls on the wall told me before you did. Which you'll agree is not how it's meant to go."

"I know."

"I know you know." She did not sound angry. She sounded like somebody who has waited outside a door all afternoon and has decided to knock once, politely, and see. "I said I wouldn't ask. I'm not asking. I'm telling you that I've noticed, so you know I've noticed. That's all."

He had rehearsed this a dozen times, lying on the cot with his face to the window. In every version it had come out either too small or too strange, and he had stopped rehearsing it on Thursday because rehearsing it had begun to feel like a way of not doing it. Now she was standing in front of him in the grey half with her hands at her sides, and he did not want to say it here, by the post, with the girls on the wall eating their stolen bread and the frost on the dirt.

"Can I come to your room," he said. "This afternoon. Before the lamps." He heard how it sounded and went on. "I want to tell you something, and I want to tell it with the door shut. Your door. Because it's partly yours."

Lira was very still.

"Partly mine," she said.

"Yes."

She looked at him while the girls on the wall stopped chewing. He saw her pick up the question she had put down, two weeks ago, on the step beside her, and look at it, and not ask it.

"The third hour after noon," she said. "The widow has her nap then, and she won't say anything about visitors." She picked up the bread. "Bring the book."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He walked there with the Log inside his coat, against his chest, as Lira carried her throat-sweet tin.

The lane was empty in the cold. There was a dog asleep on a step, and a sheet frozen stiff on a line across the lane like a board, and candles hanging over the chandler's counter in bunches by their wicks. The widow was asleep in her chair behind them with her chin on her chest, and she did not wake when he went by. The fourth step talked. He went up the rest on the outsides of the treads, where they were quieter, and stood at the top in front of the door that was green gone grey.

He knocked three times, soft.

There was a pause, not a long one this time. Then the latch lifted and the door opened, and Lira stood in it with one hand on the edge. She did not say yes? She looked at his face, and whatever she saw there made her not say it, and she only stood aside.

"Mind your head."

He minded it. She shut the door behind him, and the latch dropped with its small click, and she turned the key in it from the inside and left it in the lock. Then she sat down on the end of the bed with her back to the wall and her knees up, and he sat on the floor on the pale worn strip in the middle of the boards, with his back against the shelf, because it was the only other place to sit.

It was very quiet. Two streets away, through the cracked pane with its strip of paper, Torvin's chimney was smoking straight up into a white sky.

He took the Log out of his coat and held it on his knees, closed.

"I'm going to say it badly," he said. "I've tried it every way, and every way's bad. So I'm going to say it in order, the way I'd give you a report, and you can stop me."

"I won't stop you."

"Two weeks ago," he said, "three nights before the six weeks were up, I was on my cot at Torvin's going back through the Log, and something came."

He told her about the quiet before a thought. He told her about the dark place behind his breastbone where the sigil had gathered at Kindling, and had been dark ever since, and how it had still been dark, and how something had been written in it anyway. He opened the Log to the back, to the page where he had copied it, and turned it round on his knee so that she could read it, and she leaned forward on the bed and read it with her lips moving very slightly, as she read the board.

She read it twice. Then she sat back against the wall and looked at him, and did not say anything, and waited.

"The drop," said Cael. "Under your backhand, in the grey half, the first time. Dessa's fourth exchange, going across. Some of Sarel. The step I did by the cot that night, on purpose, badly." He made himself keep looking at her. "I've watched you more than I've watched anybody in my life. Every morning for three months. I don't know how it works. I don't know if watching's even the thing, or only part of the thing. I don't know how much of it there is, or whether it's still coming.
