He stopped, because the next part was the part he had rehearsed most and trusted least, and then he said it plainly, because plain was the only way it came out true.

"Some of it's yours."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Lira heard it, and for a moment did not feel anything at all.

That surprised her. She had been sitting on the end of her own bed for a quarter of an hour before he knocked, with her knees up and her back against her own wall, getting ready to feel something, because a boy who said partly yours in the grey half with his ears going red was a boy who was going to say a thing that would need feeling about. She had guessed at it, the way you guess at the weight of a sack before you lift it. She had guessed that it was the drop, and Renn's third exchange, and the hand at the board on the first day; she had kept those three in a row in her head for months. She had guessed, some nights, that the row was all one thing. She had even guessed, once or twice, lying awake, that the one thing might have something to do with her.

But guessing at the weight was not the same as lifting it, and now it was in her arms, and for a breath or two she only held it and could not tell what it weighed.

Then the first thing came, and it was not the thing she wanted.

It was the desk. It came up out of nowhere, as it did sometimes, quick and sour: the long room and the woman behind the desk, and the feeling of something she had done with her own body, in front of witnesses, being turned over in somebody else's hands and made into something that was not hers any more. It lasted about as long as it took her to recognize it. She looked at it, and she thought, no, that's not this, and she put it down. She was proud of herself for that afterward; it had not been easy, and nobody saw.

Cael was sitting on her floor with his book open on his knees and his face very carefully not doing anything. She knew that face. It was the face he made at his mark when he had been hit somewhere that mattered and did not want the other fighter to know where. He was waiting to find out where she was going to hit him.

"All right," she said. Her voice came out steadier than she had expected. "I'm going to say this first, so it's said, because I think you're braced for me to pretend it isn't. That's strange, Cael. That is a very strange thing to be told on a Saturday afternoon in your own room. I don't want you thinking I think it's ordinary."

"I don't think it's ordinary."

"Good. Then we agree it's strange." She looked at the book on his knees, at the three plain lines copied out in his best hand. "And it says Wind."

"Yes."

"And you think it's mine."

"Some of it."

She sat with that. She waited for it to feel like something being taken, because that was what it would have felt like once, and it did not. She waited a while longer, to be sure, and it still did not.

What it felt like instead was stranger, and she had to go round it twice before she could find the edges of it. It was like coming home and finding a letter on the table in your own handwriting, which you did not remember writing, telling somebody something kind. It was something of hers, which she had not given, that had gone out of her anyway and done some good somewhere, and she was only finding out now, after the fact, when it was already done and could not be taken back or given again. It was a very odd way to learn you had been generous. She found that she did not mind it at all.

"It isn't theft," she said.

He looked up.

"I thought it might feel like that. Hearing it. I thought, if he ever says what it is, and it's me, it'll feel like the academy." She turned her hands over on her knees and looked at them. "It doesn't. You didn't take anything. You didn't even know you were doing it. You just paid me more attention for three months than anybody's ever paid me in my whole life, and something about you is built to take attention like that and make it into something you can use." She looked up again. "I don't know what that is. I don't think you do either. But it's not stealing. Stealing's when somebody's got less afterward. I haven't got less. I checked." She lifted her chin at the door. "I did the step at the post this morning before you came, twenty times. It's all still there."

Cael did not say anything. He looked at the floor between his boots, and she watched his face try three or four things and give each of them up.

"Thank you," he said at last.

"I haven't done anything but not be stupid about it, which is a very low wall to climb, and I'm a bit insulted you thought I'd struggle with it." But she was nearly smiling, and she let him see it, because he needed to see something.

Then she asked him the question that had come into her head while she was finding the edges of the other thing, and she asked it carefully, because it was not a question she knew how to ask.

"Does it feel like anything? Having it."

He looked up at her.

"I've had mine since I was fourteen," she said. "It was declared. The Arbiter said it, and it was mine, and I've never once had to wonder where it came from or whose it was. It's just the way my legs work. Having a thing turn up in you the other way round, I can't imagine." She hesitated. "If you don't want to—"

"No. I want to." He thought about it, frowning at the floor, and she watched him do it and did not hurry him. "It feels borrowed," he said. "Not in a bad way. Put on somebody else's coat, even one cut to your size, and it never sits on you the way your own does; you always know. It's like that. Except that this coat fits better every time I put it on, better than it should, for how long I've had it." He looked at his hands. "Either it's turning into mine, or I'm just getting handier at wearing coats that belong to other people, and I can't tell which."

Lira looked at him.

"I can't decide whether that's wonderful," she said, "or the strangest thing I've heard."

"Can't it be both?"

"Everything with you is both. I've given up being surprised." She said it with a fondness she did not bother to hide, because it was her room and her door was locked and there was nobody to hide it from. Then she reached down beside the bed and picked up her throat-sweet tin, for something to hold, and turned it over in her hands.

"Now I'll tell you something," she said. "Because you've told me yours, and it would be a poor kind of rule if it only went one way."

She told him about the row of three: the hand at the board on the first day, going to a strap that was not there; the third exchange against Renn; the drop under her backhand, lower than she had ever asked. She told him that she had kept the three in a row in her head with nothing written over them, and had never said so. Then she told him the worst of it, which was the eleven tries. She had gone back into the empty yard that same afternoon and tried his drop, her own backhand turned into his drop, eleven times, and had found that it was easy to do and impossible to do in time.

"You can only already be going," she said. "That's what I found out. You can't decide to do it. If you decide, you're late." She turned the tin over. "I kept that for months. I told myself I was waiting till you had something to tell me."

He was looking at her very hard.

"So you knew," he said.

"I didn't know. I had a row of three and a guess. That's not knowing. You taught me that." She put the tin down on the bed beside her. "But I wasn't surprised, today. Not by the thing. Only by it being me." She looked at the book on his knees. "Can I see the back?"

He held it out without a word, and she took it, and turned the pages slowly on her knees.

She read First instance and the drop. She read the four, numbered, in his careful hand, the cart and Renn and the drop and Dessa. She read What changed: me. She read the notice again, and then, under it, a box drawn round two lines.

Not yet. I'm not hiding it. I just can't explain it yet, not even to myself.

Beside the box, smaller, it said not sure it is honest.

She looked at that for a long time.

"It was about half," she said at last. "Honest. If you want to know." She did not say it unkindly. "The half that wasn't, you've just paid for, sitting on my floor." She closed the book and gave it back to him. "That's what the box is for, I suppose. So you'd know which half."

"Yes."

"Good. Keep the box." She got up off the bed and went to the window and stood under the sloping ceiling without hitting her head, looking out at Torvin's chimney. "You can show me the back whenever you like, now. You don't have to. But you can."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He went before the lamps, because the widow would be awake by then, and because there was nothing more that needed saying, and they both knew it.

Lira stood in the door and watched him go down the stair, and the fourth step talked under him, and he said I know to it out loud, which was what she said to it, and which he could not have known. Then she shut the door, and turned the key, and sat down on the floor in the middle of the worn strip where he had sat, because it was still warm.

She sat there until it was too dark to see the paper on the cracked pane.

She thought about the drop, and about Dessa's fourth, and about the third exchange against Sarel, when she had stood at the barrel with the rope printing itself into her palms and watched him move the way she moved. She had thought then that she was watching her teaching come up out of him. That was true. She thought now that it had not been the only thing coming up, and that she would never be able to sort the two apart, and that she did not want to. She thought that something she had been, every morning, without trying, had gone into a boy from Denvash and come out of him again in front of the whole yard against a Bronze, and that she had stood there and been proud of it before she knew what it was. She was still proud of it, now that she did.

It was the strangest present she had ever been given: she had given it herself, without knowing, and been thanked for it afterward on her own floor.

She thought about what she would do with it, and decided, sitting there in the dark, that she would do the plainest thing. She would go on teaching him. She would go on being exactly what she was every morning in the grey half, as she had been for three months, only now she would know, and he would know she knew. Whatever was coming across, if anything was, would come across between two people with their eyes open. That seemed to her a better way for anything to happen than the way most things happened.

And the next time he said I don't know about it, she would say neither do I, and mean it, and they would not know together, which was a different thing from not knowing alone.

She got up off the floor at last and lit her candle end in its tin cup, and saw by its light that she had been smiling without knowing it, as you find you have been humming.

Some of it's yours.

She thought she would keep that. Not in a book; she did not keep a book. In the place where she kept the things that were hers.

Chapter 43 — Three More Weeks

[Taut, clear narration; sharpen the danger without rushing the thinking]

He wrote to Hesk that night, at the kitchen table at Torvin's, after everybody else had gone up.

He had not meant to do it then. He had meant to sleep on it, and write on Sunday, and post on Monday as he always did, with the west bag at noon. But when he came in from the lane in the dark, Torvin's wife was banking the range and the table was empty and scrubbed, and there was a lamp on it, and he sat down at it with the Log and a sheet of paper and could not get up again.

He had told Lira. That had been the promise: when he knew what it was, really knew, she would be the first. He still did not know what it was. But he had found out, sitting on her floor, that not knowing was not a reason to keep a thing, only a reason to say I don't know beside it. And she had been the first, and now there was somebody second.

He sat with the pen over the paper while the range ticked as it cooled. Then he wrote.

Hesk,

There are five things I haven't told you. I've counted them every time I sealed a letter since the end of the first month, so I know the number exactly. I'm going to tell you all five now, in order, as plainly as I can, and then I'm going to tell you why I didn't before, and you can decide what you think of that.

The first was on the road, on the third day, before I ever got here. A cart came round a bend behind me and I stepped out of its way before I heard it. I told the carter I'd heard it. I don't think I did.

The second was my first bout, against Renn, in the third exchange. He threw a figure at me that should have caught me whatever I did, and I wasn't where it went. I didn't choose where I went. I tore the page out of the book where I'd written it, and kept it in my coat for a month, and didn't read it.

The third was in the yard, in the mornings, with Lira. She threw a backhand and I dropped under it, lower than I've ever dropped, in a way that wasn't mine. She asked me how I knew it was coming and I said I didn't know, and that was true.

The fourth was the Dessa fight. I told you I built the third exchange, and I did. I didn't tell you about the fourth, because I didn't build it. It happened the way the drop happened. Your line about a win you built sat on the page right over the place where I hadn't written it, and I read it three times.

The fifth came two weeks ago, three nights before the six weeks ran out, while I sat on my cot at Torvin's. Something came up where the Arbiter used to be, written in the dark. I'll copy it exactly, because you'd want it exact.

He copied the three lines from the back of the Log, letter by letter, and checked them twice.

I think it's Lira's. Some of it. I think it came from watching her every morning for three months, but I don't know that, and I've spent the last fortnight finding out how much I don't know. I can make the step on purpose now, badly. It costs something in the breath and the hip that I can't measure yet. I tried to get something from a second person, a Force fighter, by watching him two whole days. Nothing came that I could stand on.

I told Lira today. I'd promised her she'd be the first, before you, before anybody, and she was. She didn't flinch. She said it wasn't theft, and that she'd checked, and she hadn't got less.

Why I didn't tell you. At first it was because I didn't know what it was, and I didn't want to send you something that would frighten you a week late, with nothing I could do about it from here. You know what's in the archive better than I do. Then it was because I'd promised Lira first. Those are both true. But the first one is the same reason you gave me across the bench on the second day, and I was angry with you for it then, and I think I was right to be. So that reason's finished, for me.

You told me once to tell you as it comes. This is how it came. I'm sorry it came all at once.

I'm all right. I'm well. I'm not frightened, most of the time. I'll tell you the next thing when it happens, and not five things later.

— Cael

He read it over, twice, by the lamp. It was the longest letter he had ever written, and there was nothing in it that he did not know to be true. When he had finished the second reading, he folded it and put it in the leather book to keep flat for Monday, and then sat at the scrubbed table with the lamp turned low and counted, as he always did now, what he had not told Hesk.

There was nothing to count.

It did not feel as he had thought it would. He had thought it would feel like putting down something heavy, and it did a little, but mostly it felt like having opened a door in winter: colder, and a great deal more air. Somewhere in Denvash, in a week, a man would sit on the step of his workshop with this in his hands, and be frightened, and there was nothing Cael could do about that. He had decided it was better than the other thing anyway.

Torvin said Lamps through the floorboards from upstairs, though there was only one lamp left lit in the house, and it was Cael's. He turned it out.

On Sunday morning, in the grey half, Lira did the step for him on purpose.

She did not say she was going to. She was at the post when he came in through the gate with the bread, as she always was, and she took the loaves off him and tore them and gave him half. She's an old fighter who doesn't want to talk to anybody, and you're a boy everybody's started talking about, and if you come in with me she'll decide you're a show and shut the gate." She took her jacket off and folded it over her arm, so that she would look like what she was, a fighter come to ask a fighter something, and went in.

He waited in the lane by the wall for most of an hour. A young man came out through the gate rubbing his shoulder and walked off without looking at him. Then the dry voice started again, lower, talking to Lira, and he could hear only the shape of the conversation going back and forth across the yard: Lira's voice going up once, sharply, and coming down, a long silence, something short from the dry voice, and then Lira laughing as she laughed at Marrow when she had got the price she wanted.

She came out with her face pink with cold and something else.

"Thursday," she said. "The afternoon. Two hours. She wants a mark for it, which is too much, and I've paid half already and you'll pay the rest." She put her jacket on. "And she wants to look at you."

"What did you say to her?"

"I asked her what she'd studied for ten years and never once had anybody worth showing it to." Lira did her buttons up one by one. "And then I told her what you do, which I hope you don't mind, because it was the thing that did it. She'd heard the Denvash boy at Torvin's, and past Corbin, and thought it was talk. She asked whether it was true you watched Renn for two months and found his heel, and whether you'd quit watching in two exchanges against Sarel and done something else, and I said yes to both. And she was quiet, and then she said that she had never in her life met anybody who could do both, and that she supposed she'd better see one before she died."

"And you laughed."

"She meant it to be funny. I think. She's harder to read than Corbin." Lira started back down the lane toward the kilns, and glanced back at him. "You'll like her."

That night, on the cot, he wrote at the top of a clean page in the front of the Log: Feryn. Bronze Rank 2, Pressure. Three weeks. Under it he wrote: Pressure: heavy. Like weather. Like the air leaning on you (Vell, h). Don't (the eel woman, h). Corvane, Thursday. There was nothing else he knew, and he had stopped pretending long ago that a short page meant a lazy one.

On Wednesday morning, before the grey half, he went to Vell's table and told her yes, two days before she had asked him to. She wrote it down.

Chapter 44 — The Build

[Taut, clear narration; sharpen the danger without rushing the thinking]

Corvane was waiting for them in her gateway on Thursday afternoon with her hands folded on the head of a stick, and she looked Cael up and down twice, slowly, before she said anything at all.

She was small and spare and very straight, older than the old man at the top of the lane of yards, with grey hair cut close to her head like a boy's and a face all bones and weather. She wore a man's coat buttoned to the throat and a pair of boots that had been mended so many times that there was more mending than boot. Her eyes were pale and steady and did not blink much. When she looked at him, Cael had the feeling he sometimes had in Hesk's workshop, when Hesk held a part up to the window and turned it slowly, looking for the flaw he already knew was there.

"Taller than I was told," she said. "Thinner. Stands like a Denvash boy." She looked at his feet. "Somebody's been at his feet."

"I have," said Lira.

"I can see that. Not badly." Corvane turned and went into the yard, leaning on the stick, and they followed her. "You can stand by the wall, girl. If you talk, you go."

The yard was small and walled in brick on three sides, with the river going by beyond the fourth wall, which was only waist high, and the smell of the kilns coming over it. There was no groove and no circle, only a square of trodden dirt with a ring scratched in it with the point of the stick, and a sack of sand hanging from a bracket on the wall, patched all over. Corvane went to the middle of the dirt and stood there, and Cael went and stood across from her, because it seemed to be what she wanted.

"Your friend tells me you watch," she said.

"Yes."

"Tell me what you watch."

He told her. He told her about Hesk and the community hall, hips and feet, and the three exchanges. He told her what he had found since: Renn's heel and the dip in Brenna's shield, the breath before the heat, Petra's lean, Dessa's late back foot, and Corbin reading feet at the mark. He told her about Talis and the ground. He did not tell it well, because he had never had to say it all at once before, out loud, to somebody who was listening without any expression at all.

When he had finished, she was quiet.

"And Sarel?"

"I couldn't find anything. She was too fast. So I stopped looking."

"In two exchanges."

"Yes."

Corvane nodded slowly. Then she put the point of her stick into the dirt between them and began to draw.

She drew a figure, a plain stick figure such as a child draws, standing upright. In the middle of its chest she drew a spiral, coiled tight, round and round, smaller and smaller, until it was nearly a dot. Beside the figure she made a row of short strokes, one, two, three, four, like a tally.

"That's what you'll be standing in front of. Pressure. And everything you've just told me is no good to you."

She talked for a quarter of an hour without stopping, and it was the most anybody had said to him at one time since Hesk on the night before Kindling.

She did not talk the way Lira talked, quick and sideways and laughing. She talked the way Hesk talked about a load figure, flat and exact, leaving out everything a sensible person could work out for himself and assuming he was a sensible person. Every few sentences she touched the drawing with the point of the stick, the spiral or the strokes, and went on.

"A Blade strikes. A Force man strikes and then shoves. Ember heats. Every one of them has a moment, one moment, where the thing goes, and every one of them has to get ready for that moment somewhere in the body, and that getting ready is what you've been reading. The heel. The breath. The lean." She tapped the figure's feet. "Pressure has no one moment. It has to be gathered. It's built, the way you'd wind a spring, a turn at a time." She touched the spiral. "And while it's being built, the body has to hold it. Somewhere. All of it, the whole time, and it gets heavier with every turn. That holding is the only true thing a Pressure fighter will ever show you. Everything else he does is there to hide it."

"Where does he hold it?"

"That depends on the fighter." She tapped the spiral again, in the middle of the chest. "But it's always low and always in the trunk, never in the hands. The hands are where it goes, at the end. The hands are what everybody watches." She looked at him. "That's the mistake. Everybody who has ever stood in front of Pressure has watched for the moment it lets go. They watch the hands, or the shoulders, or whatever moves last. And by the time they see it go, they're already inside it." She drew a line from the figure's hands outward, a long one, across the dirt almost to his boots. "It doesn't come at you like a fist, from one place. It comes like the air leaning, all across the front of you at once. You can't step out of the way of it once it's come. There isn't room."

She tapped the row of strokes.

"So you don't watch it go. You watch it being built. A fighter who's building stands differently from a fighter who's only standing, and it's slow to see, and it's very small, and he'll be covering it with every other part of himself the whole time. But it gives you warning. Not much. If you see it early enough." She looked at the strokes. "That's heartbeats. Four, for me, when I was young. I'm Copper, and I was never a good Copper. A Bronze will build in fewer. A good Bronze, in one." She lifted the stick out of the dirt. "Now stand there, and I'll show you, and you can tell me what you see."

She stepped back to the far side of the scratched ring and stood.

It was a plain stance, feet a little apart, hands loose at her sides, the stick leaning against her leg. She did not seem to do anything. Then she began to walk, slowly, round the inside of the ring, and as she walked her hands moved: up a little, and out, and down again, like somebody explaining something with no words. Her shoulders went up and down with the walking. Her head turned to follow him.

"Tell me."

"Your hands are—"

The air leaned on him.

He had not seen anything go. There was no flash, no shimmer, nothing in her hands or her face. There was only, all at once, the air across the front of him going heavy from his knees to the top of his head, and pushing, as though somebody had laid a broad flat hand on his chest and arms and face at the same time, from a pace away, and leaned on it. It was not hard. He did not fall. He went back a full step with his heels sliding in the dirt, and the air let go of him as quickly as it had come, and he stood there with his breath gone short and his hands up in front of him, and Corvane was standing where she had been, with her hands loose at her sides.

By the wall, Lira had put her hand flat on the bricks.

"You watched my hands," said Corvane.

"Yes."

"Everybody does. Again."

She walked. Her hands moved. He made himself look away from them, at her shoulders, and the air leaned on him again, and he went back a step. She walked again, and he watched her feet, and the air leaned on him, and he went back a step.

"Again."

He did not know how many times she did it. Eight. Ten. He looked at everything he knew how to look at, the hips and the feet, the shoulders, the breath, her face. Every time he was looking at something, the air came and put him back a step, and every time he could not have said, afterward, when it had begun. By the eighth time his chest ached from being leaned on and his heels had dug two shallow troughs in her dirt, and he understood why the eel woman had laughed.

"What do you see?" said Corvane.

"Nothing."

"What did you look at?"

He told her: hands, shoulders, feet, breath, face.

"Everything that moves," said Corvane. "And what doesn't move?"

He stood there.

"I'll do it slowly. Watch what doesn't move."

She walked the ring once more, as slowly as an old woman walking to market, with her hands moving and her shoulders going up and down and her head turning. He did not watch any of it. He watched, as well as he could, all the parts of her that were not doing anything; it was harder than he had expected, like trying to listen to the silence between the notes of a tune. His eyes kept going to the hands, because the hands were moving, and he kept bringing them back.

And there, under the moving, low down in her body, below the ribs and above the belt, something was holding still.

It was very small. It was not a stiffness, exactly, nor a stillness you could have pointed at, but a kind of settling, as if the middle of her had gone heavier than the rest and stayed there while the rest of her walked about on top of it. Her shoulders went up and down, and it did not. Her hands drifted and turned, and it did not. It was as though she had swallowed a stone and were carrying it very carefully while pretending not to.

"There."

The air leaned on him, and he went back a step, but he had said it first.

Corvane stopped walking.

She stood in her ring and looked at him with her pale eyes, and for the first time since the gate her face did something: not a smile, but a small shift at one corner of the mouth, as if a smile had been considered and put away for a better occasion.

"Where?"

He put his hand on his own body, below the ribs and above the belt.

"Something stays still. When the rest of you's moving. It's like you're carrying it."

"How long before I let go?"

He thought back. "Two breaths. Perhaps two and a half."

"I built for four." She leaned on her stick. "So you saw it at two. Halfway." Her pale eyes stayed on him while a barge went by beyond the low wall. "Once is nothing, boy. Once is luck, or it's me walking slow for you. Again."

She did it again, and he saw it at two. She did it again, faster, and he saw it at one and a half. She did it again, faster still, and he saw nothing until the air was on him. She did it six more times, and he saw it three times and missed it three, and by the end he could feel his eyes aching in their sockets from looking at a thing that was not there, and he was more tired than Sarel had made him.

Then she stopped and sat down on an upturned bucket by the wall with both hands folded on the head of the stick, breathing harder than she wanted him to see.

"That's what you'll be doing. Against him. Only he won't walk slow for you, and he won't build for four. He'll build in one, or less, and he'll hide it under a great deal more than an old woman waving her hands about." She looked at the scratched figure in the dirt, which their feet had half rubbed out. "You'll read it late. Every time. If you're very good, and lucky, you'll read it a little less late each time, because that's what you are. I can see that's what you are." She looked up. "And it won't be enough. Not at Bronze. Not in three weeks. I want you to know that before you go in, not after."

"Then why read it at all?"

"Because a little less late is the difference between being knocked down and being knocked back." She nodded at the troughs his heels had dug. "And because there's nothing else, at Copper, against Pressure, but reading it. I looked for ten years. There isn't."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Lira had not said a word. When Corvane stood up and went into her house without saying goodbye, she came away from the wall and put Cael's coat round his shoulders, because he had forgotten he was not wearing it, and they let themselves out through the gate.

Corvane came back to the door before they had gone three houses down the lane. She stood in it with her stick, and called after them in her dry voice, not loudly.

"Boy."

He turned round.

"What's your word, boy? The one they gave you. Your friend wouldn't say. She said that was yours to tell."

He had said it out loud to very few people since Weaver's Row: to Lira on the first day, at the board, and to a man from the Compact across a desk at the post. It came out of him a little more easily each time, and it still never came out easily.

"SHATTERED."

Corvane stood in her doorway and considered it.

"Never heard of it," she said. "Good. I've heard of nearly everything." She looked at him a moment longer. "Come back and tell me what he does. Afterward. If you can walk." Then she shut the door.

They walked back through the kilns in the early dark, with the soot in the air and the river going by on their left. Lira did not say anything past the first two kilns. Then, at the corner of the brickworks, where the lane turned up toward the district, she said, "Ten years."

"What?"

"She lost to them for ten years, and then she studied them for ten more, and in all that time she never found anybody who could see the thing she'd found." Lira had her hands deep in her jacket pockets. "She told me that on Tuesday. Not like that. Sideways. She said she'd had forty students and none of them could ever see it, and she'd stopped showing it to anybody." She looked at the dark lane ahead. "Then you saw it at two, and she sat down on a bucket."

He had not thought of it like that.

"I can't do it," said Lira. "Build. I'm Wind; I haven't got anything to build with. But I can hold. I can stand there and get ready to step and not step, and hide it under something else, and you can try to see me getting ready." She glanced at him. "It's not the same. It's nowhere near the same. But it's the right shape, and it's what we've got, and we've got three weeks less three days."

"Every morning?"

"Every morning. And you'll draw that figure in the dirt with your eyes shut till you can see it standing up."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Supper at Torvin's was the stew with real vegetables in it, though nobody in the house had fought, because Torvin's wife had heard about Monday from the boots woman, who had heard it from the fish steps, and had decided that it counted in advance.

The whole table knew. The brothers had stopped arguing about the river to argue about the Bronze instead. The elder one held that Pressure was only Force made bigger, and the younger that it was a different thing altogether, like weather, because a man on the barges had told him so. Neither of them had ever seen it. They appealed to Cael, who said he had seen it that afternoon from an old woman with a stick and that it was not like Force at all. The younger brother was so pleased that he ate the elder brother's bread to celebrate.

Torvin sat at the head of the table and ate and said nothing until the bowls were nearly empty. Then he put his spoon down.

"Monday."

"Yes."

Torvin looked at him with the look he gave a coin he had already counted twice.

"Rent's paid to Sunday week. I looked." He picked his spoon up again. "And if you're carried home, they're to bring you in by the yard door. Not the front. People talk."

Torvin's wife hit him on the arm with her wooden spoon, not gently, and he went on eating as if he had not noticed.

At the far end of the table, where nobody sat, Doss had his bad leg out along the bench and his pipe beside his bowl. He did not look up until the brothers had gone up the stairs still arguing. Then he did.

"Corvane."

"She showed me how it's built."

"She showed you." Doss turned his pipe over in his scarred fingers. "Did she sit down?"

Cael looked at him.

"Afterward. On a bucket." He did not know how Doss knew to ask it. "She was out of breath. She didn't want me to see."

Doss was quiet until the range had settled and ticked twice. He put the pipe down beside his bowl with great care, as he always did, as though it were a tool on a bench.

"Then she saw something. She doesn't sit down for nothing." He looked at the range, where the fire was going down, and not at Cael. "I'll tell you one thing. It's the only thing I know about Bronze that's worth the breath. At Copper, people learn you over a season. At Bronze they learn you in an exchange." He tapped the knee under the table with the stem of the pipe, twice, as he did. "Whatever you do twice against him, you've done once too often. Remember that when you're standing there."

He got up, which took two movements, and rinsed his bowl at the basin, and went to the low brown door, and the smell of pipe smoke came out from under it a little later.

Cael sat at the table with his empty bowl and turned it over in his head, once too often, until Torvin's wife took the bowl away from him and told him he would wear it out.

That night, on the cot, he copied Corvane's figure into the front of the Log, with the spiral and the four strokes, as near as he could remember it. Then he wrote three pages under it, everything she had said, in the order she had said it. When he had finished, he read it through four times, and then once more aloud under his breath, as he had read the citation in the reading room. By the fifth time it had stopped feeling like something he had been told and started to feel like something he knew. He had begun to understand, since the reading room, that this was how it worked: a thing went into him from outside, as a word or a drawing, and stayed there, and was gone over, and one day it was his.

He sat with the pencil over that last sentence before he let himself write it down, because it sounded very like something else, and he did not know yet whether it was.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On Sunday Vell gave him a Copper 4 from Fenrow, a Stone man of about twenty-five who had come across for the afternoon card because he had heard there was a boy at the Cinder House who went five with Corbin, and he wanted to see for himself.

It was not the kind of bout anybody would talk about afterward, and Cael understood that before it began, and did not mind.

The Fenrow man was square and slow, with the grit coming up off him and lying down flat as it had come up off Dessa, and none of her patience. He rocked a little on his heels at his mark as Talis had, and looked at the crowd, and at Marrow's slate, and at the girls on the wall, and at everything except Cael.

Cael put his hand flat on the dirt at his mark for one breath before he stood.

The ground was cold, and hard under a soft skin of thaw. When the Fenrow man shifted his weight on his mark, something answered under Cael's palm, very faint, a small far-off hum like a glass set down at the other end of a long table. It was there and then it was not. Cael stood up and set his feet and did not let his face do anything.

"Copper Rank 4, Stone Path, of Fenrow," said Vell, and gave the man's name, which Cael heard and did not keep. "Against unrated. Vouched." The small pause. "Begin when you're ready."

In the first exchange he did nothing with it. He let the Fenrow man come, and plant, and strike, and was not where the strike went. He did not try to feel the hum through his boots; boots were not a cheek on the dirt, and he did not trust them. He watched instead, and found in the first exchange what he had half expected: the man's front knee bent a little before every step he meant to plant on, a small soft dip, as if the leg were testing the ground before it trusted it. It came a half beat before the plant, exactly where the hum had come under his hand.

Two of them, he thought, on his mark. The ground and the knee. Saying the same thing. He was very glad there were two. One tell was a guess. Two tells telling the same truth were a floor you could stand on.

In the second exchange he made sure. He moved, and watched the knee, and every time it dipped the man planted, and every time the man planted the gatepost forearm came round from the planted side, and every time Cael was a step outside it. The Fenrow man began to go red at the collar. He was not a fool; he could feel that he was missing in a way he did not usually miss. But he did not know why, and he did what most people did when they did not know why, which was the same thing again, harder.

In the third, Cael went in on the dip of the knee, before the plant, while the man's weight was still in the air above a foot that had not yet decided where to come down. He went under the gatepost forearm as it began to come round, inside it, and put the one strike he owned on the hinge of the jaw, short and straight from the hip, and stopped it there.

"Called," said Vell. "Unrated."

The yard made the low pleased noise, the ordinary one. The Fenrow man stood looking at Cael's fist by his jaw for a moment, and then laughed and shook his head and went to the water bucket. Marrow paid out without any trouble at all, as though it were a thing he did every week. It was over in less time than it took the pie boy to sell three pies.

Cael walked to the table and stood in front of it while Vell wrote, and the pen went down one line and stopped.

"Result stands as called," she said. "Unrated, over a Copper Rank 4, Stone Path, of Fenrow. Third exchange. Called. Witnessed and entered."

That was all, and there was nothing more in the book.

Lira was at the barrel with his coat. She did not say easy, and he did not say it either.

"That's what it's meant to look like," she said instead, quietly, as she held the coat for him to put his arms in. "Most of the time. When you've done the work. Nobody remembers it. It's not a story. It's just a bout you won." She did the top button of his coat up for him, which she had never done before, as if he were somebody's small brother. "You'll want more stories. Don't. A great many people in this district have been ruined by wanting a story every time."

At the top of the lane of yards, on the way home, the old man was standing in his gate in the dusk with his sleeves rolled down. He looked at Cael walking, at the way he was walking, which was the ordinary way, with nothing held against his chest and no limp.

He said nothing at all. He only nodded, once, very slightly, and went back to watching the woman with the shoulder.

Cael thought, walking on down toward Torvin's, that it was the best thing the old man had ever said to him.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

Lira took him up on the cooper's roof that evening, because she said there were some things she did not want to say anywhere a wall could hear them.

They went up the ladder at the back of the cooper's shed in the last of the light and sat on the flat part of the roof with their backs against the chimney stack, which was warm from the cooper's fire below. From up there you could see the whole district going down to the river in its lanes and its smoke, and the lower bridge with its lamps coming on, and beyond the bridge, across the water, the Ranked core going up in its pale stone toward the hill, with all its windows catching the last of the sun.

Lira looked at it without saying anything, her chin on her knees.

"I've been doing a thing," she said at last. "In the mornings. Since you told me. I don't know if I should."

He waited.

"I've been doing things slower." She did not look at him. "Not all the time. Just now and then. The step, mostly. I catch myself doing it a little slower than I need to, so you'll see it better. And then I catch myself catching myself, and I don't know whether to stop." She pulled her knees up and put her arms round them. "Because if it's watching, then I'm helping. And if it isn't watching, I'm only teaching you badly, and you've got a Bronze in fifteen days."

He thought about that seriously, because she had said it seriously.

"Hesk wrote me something once," he said. "When the man with the pin was walking about. Don't change what you do. Because changing it is the loudest thing you can do, and you never know who's listening." He looked at the bridge. "I don't know if that's right here. But I don't know what I'm doing to you every morning, and you don't either, and if we start changing things to make it happen more, then we're doing something on purpose that neither of us understands." He stopped, because he had not known he thought that until he said it. "I'd rather you just did what you do. The way you did it before you knew. Fast, when it ought to be fast."

Lira was quiet.

"That's what I'd decided too," she said. "On the floor, on Saturday, after you'd gone. I decided I'd go on being exactly what I was. And then the very next morning I did it for you slow, on purpose, and told myself that was only so we'd both be looking. And every morning since, I've caught myself doing it slow without meaning to, and not noticed till the third time." She laughed, short and not very happy. "It's harder than it sounds, being what you were before somebody tells you what you are."

"I know."

She turned her head and looked at him then, and he saw her see that he did know, better than anybody she had ever met, and saw her put that down carefully somewhere she would keep it.

"All right," she said. "Fast, when it ought to be fast. And if you see me going slow, you tell me. That's the rule." She leaned her head back against the warm bricks of the chimney. "Mine are mine. Even the slow ones."

They sat on the roof until the Ranked core had gone grey, and then dark, and the lamps came out one at a time along the lower bridge. Then they climbed down the ladder in the dark, and at the well with the iron cover she said same time tomorrow, and he said it back, and they went their two ways.

Chapter 45 — Word Ahead

[Taut, clear narration; sharpen the danger without rushing the thinking]

Lira could not build, but she could hold, and for three weeks she held.

She stood at her mark in the grey half every morning with the frost on the dirt and the post at her back, and got ready to step, and did not step. She kept the readiness in her for a breath, or two, or three, while she did everything she could think of on top of it to hide it: she walked, and rolled her shoulders, and talked to him about the bread, and pushed her hair off her face with her wrist, and once, to make the girls on the wall laugh, sang the first two lines of a song about a miller's daughter. Then, when she had held it as long as she meant to, she went, with the two empty touches and the ground folding, and her palm came across his ribs or his shoulder or the back of his neck, and she said, "When?"

"Your second breath."

"I started on the first."

"I didn't see it on the first."

"Then that's when you saw it." She went back to her mark. "Again."

It was not Pressure, and they both knew it. A Wind fighter getting ready to step did not hold anything heavy in the middle of her body as Corvane had; she held a lightness instead, a sort of tilt, as if the whole of her had decided to fall forward and was only waiting to be allowed. It was a different thing to look for, in a different place. But it was a thing that did not move under things that did, and it had to be found the same way, by watching what was not happening, and that was the part he had to learn.

He learned it slowly.

On the first morning he saw her readiness twice in thirty. By the fourth morning he was seeing it nine times in thirty, and by the end of the first week he was seeing it more often than not, and she had begun to change how she hid it. She stopped walking and stood still instead, and talked, and a person standing still and talking turned out to be much harder to read than a person walking, because there was so little to tell the holding from. Then he learned that too, a little, and she changed again.

"You're getting better," she said on the eighth morning, breathing hard. "And I'm getting better at hiding it. So it looks the same. That's what it'll be like in there. Remember that. He'll be getting better at hiding it while you're getting better at seeing it, and it'll feel like you're standing still."

In the afternoons, when she went to her sparring hour across the district, he drew Corvane's figure.

He drew it in the dirt of Torvin's yard with a stick, by the pump, and in the margins of the Log, and on the back of a bill from the mender. Then he drew it with his eyes shut, on the inside of his eyelids, the stick figure and the spiral coiled tight and the row of four strokes, until he could see it standing up and walking about on top of the stone it was carrying. Yeni watched him draw it once by the pump, from the kitchen door, and said nothing, and the next day there was a stub of red chalk on the low wall where he sat, which he had not put there.

He did not tell anybody else about the step.

He practised it at the post when Lira was late, and by the cot at night, on purpose, as he had done since the thirty-ninth night. It was still clumsy. It was a little less clumsy than it had been, or he thought it was; the boards went short under him by the width of a hand, and once, on a night near the end of the first week, by perhaps a hand and a half. It still cost his breath and his hip, a little less each time, or a little more, depending on how tired he was before he began. It still never came clean when he called it.

Once, in the second week, it came without his calling it at all, in the box drill at full speed. Lira came at him from the corner he had not called, and the ground went short under him and he was out of her way before he had decided anything. She stopped dead, with her palm still out, and looked at him.

"That."

"I know."

"Do it again."

He could not. That night he wrote it in the back of the Log as the fifth instance, the first since the notice, and the first in the grey half since the drop. But in the yard he tried for the rest of the morning and it did not come once, not when she came at him from the corner he had not called and not when she came at him from the one he had. By the end he was so tired from trying that his hips had gone square again. She stopped at last and sat on the low wall with her elbows on her knees, and he sat down beside her and they ate the bread.

"It's not going to be reliable. Not yet. You've had it a month. It'll want a season before it comes when it's called. My step didn't come when I called it for a year after I was declared, and it was mine from the day it was declared."

"I haven't got a season. I've got eleven days."

"Then on the twelfth day you'll have what you've got, and not a crumb more. Worrying through the eleven won't add a crumb, and not worrying won't take one away." She tore her bread and gave him half. "So don't spend them worrying. Spend them on the build. The build's yours. The step's—" She stopped, and looked at the bread in her hand. "The step's whatever it is. Don't stand in a circle in front of a Bronze waiting for it to come. If it comes, it comes. Read the build."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On the second Thursday Vell gave him a Copper 3 Shield from the dyers' sheds, a boy of about seventeen with blue hands, whom Cael had watched twice in the autumn and written down as careful. He was careful still. He held his shield up as Brenna had held hers, a pane wider than his shoulders, a hand's breadth off the forearm, like the side of a bucket of water stood on end. He walked it at people as if it were a door he meant to shut on them.

He also dipped it on the step-through, as Brenna had before she trained it out, a finger's width at the bottom edge, every time.

Cael saw the dip in the first exchange and let it go by, and in the second he stepped in under the dipped edge as it came and put the one strike he owned on the boy's jaw, and stopped it there, a finger short.

"Called," said Vell. "Unrated."

That was all of it. It had taken less than two exchanges, and the yard made the ordinary pleased noise, and the boy from the dyers' let his shield go out like a lamp and stood looking at the fist by his jaw.

Then he did something Cael had not expected. He did not go to the water bucket. He stayed where he was, in the middle of the circle, and looked at Cael with his blue hands hanging at his sides.

"Is it true?" he said. "You've got a Bronze coming?"

Cael looked at him.

"Monday week," said the boy. "That's what they're saying on the dye vats. A Bronze Rank 2, from away, and you. Is it true?"

"Yes."

The boy whistled through his teeth, softly.

"Rather you than me," he said, without any spite in it at all, and went to the water bucket.

Cael stood in front of Vell's table while she wrote. He was thinking about the boy's question and not about the bout, and it was the first time he had ever stood at the table without thinking about the bout he had just fought. He did not know whether that was a good thing.

"Result stands as called," said Vell. "Unrated, over a Copper Rank 3, Shield Path. Second exchange. Called. Witnessed and entered. They're talking about Monday on the vats, then."

"He said so."

"They've been talking about it on the fish steps since the day after I told you." She blotted the line. "I didn't tell anybody else. You didn't. The girl didn't. It's a funny thing about a yard. You can keep a thing in a book for thirty years and nobody knows it's there. You can keep a Bronze off the board for three days and the whole district knows he's coming and who he's coming for."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On the second Saturday there was no card, and Vell made the card.

She did it at her table in the middle of the empty yard with the frost still white along the east wall, writing on the backs of old bills in her upright pencil, one bout to a bill. The pie boy stood by to run them to the board. Cael had come to the post for the grey half and found her already there. She had said "Here," in the voice she used for it, and he had come across the dirt and stood in front of the table.

She finished a card and gave it to the pie boy, and he ran.

"Monday," said Vell. "Noon. I've set the gate. You'll not pay it." She laid the pen across the page. "Say the terms back to me."

He looked at her.

"You said them to me on the first morning," said Vell. "Before Renn. You've not had to since, because you've not been in front of anything that made me want to hear them again. Say them."

So he said them, standing in front of her table in the cold, as he had said them on the first morning, slowly, checking each one before he set it down. He came in unrated. He fought whoever she put across from him. The bout ended when she called it. Once he was over the rope, nobody stopped it but her, and what happened inside it was his to carry out. Nobody was making him do it.

Saying it, he heard that it meant more than it had meant the first time, and not because the words had changed.

Vell listened to all of it without moving.

"Good. He may not like the look of you when he sees you. That's his to say, and yours to answer. Not mine." She picked up a fresh bill and began to write on it, and he understood that he had been sent away.

Lira was at the post. She had watched the whole of it from the grey half and had not come over, and when he came back she did not ask what Vell had wanted. She gave him the bread, and then she stood in front of him with her hands at her sides and her weight a little forward.

"I've decided," she said.

He waited.

"Survivable." She said it carefully, as if she were reading it off the side of a crate. "If you fall properly. If you don't stand up into anything he's built at his full weight. If he goes heavy and you're still on your feet and there's nothing left to find out, you go backward, and you keep going backward, and you lose long. I don't care how it looks." She looked at him hard. "That's the ruling. I said I'd make it and I've made it. You'll listen."

"I'll listen."

"You'll listen, and then in there you'll do whatever you do." She almost smiled, and did not let it get very far. "I know. I've watched you. But I've said it, and you've heard it, and that's what I promised on the first morning of the six weeks." She turned to the post and struck it, low, twice. "Box drill. And this time, when I hold, I'm going to talk to you about the weather the whole time, and you're going to find it anyway."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The district knew.

It came to him a piece at a time, as a leak in a roof does, by a wet place and then another. Feryn's name was not on the board, because Vell never put a bout with a gate on the board; the gate was all the notice it got. But by the second Saturday somebody had chalked a small square in the corner of the board, under Sunday's card, with a B in it and an arrow pointing at nothing. Then somebody else had chalked a ? beside the arrow, and somebody else again had rubbed the ? out and written Monday.

The errand boys had a bet on it. Cael heard it from them before he heard anything else, on the fish steps, where the one in the red cap was explaining it to two girls with baskets. It was a mark each, which was more than either of them had ever had at once in their lives. Red Cap had the boy lasting three exchanges and the other one had him lasting one, and they had each spent several days trying to get the other to raise the stakes.

"He'll say gone," said Red Cap to the girls, with great confidence, "and then he'll do the thing."

"What thing?"

"The thing he does," said Red Cap, who did not know.

Renn was taking full credit. Cael heard that on the long quay from a woman with a fish basket, and then from Renn himself, who came down off a barge with a sack on each shoulder to tell him about it.

"I've told everybody," said Renn. "I've told them all. I taught that boy everything he knows, and I let him win, and now he's going to go and lose to a Bronze and make me look bad." He set the sacks down and grinned. "That's the story. It's a good story. Don't spoil it."

"I'll try."

"Don't try. Lose properly." Renn looked him over with the craftsman's look, the one that checked a joint, and the grin went for a moment. "Pressure," he said, more quietly. "I fought one once, at Fenrow, years ago. A Copper. I couldn't see anything. It was like fighting the weather." He picked up his sacks again. "Watch his middle, not his hands. That's all I've got, and I got it by lying on my back."

"Somebody else told me that."

"Then two people have told you, and you'd better listen." Renn started up the plank. "And I'll be at the rope. On the sunny side. Shouting."

Marrow had a slate already, though there was nothing on the board. Cael saw it from the gate of the Cinder House on the second Sunday, when Marrow was standing by the barrels with his very clean hands folded and the slate on its string round his neck. On the bottom of it, under the Sunday prices, he had written in small careful chalk Monday: F. (Bronze 2) — unrated., with no price beside either. He saw Cael reading it and smiled the good smile and, for the first time since Cael had come to Ardenmere, said something to him directly.

"I can't price it," said Marrow. "I've tried for a week. Every number I write is either too long or too short, and I can't tell which." He turned the slate over to show him the other side, which was covered with rubbed-out figures. "You've ruined my week."

"I'm sorry."

"No, you're not," said Marrow, quite pleasantly, and turned the slate back.

And on the scaffolds round the new houses on the east road, when he went that way to the mender's with a basket of mended hinges, Sarel called down to him from three storeys up.

She was sitting on a plank with her legs hanging over the edge and her lunch on her knee, among the scaffold people, with her short dark hair full of lime dust, and she leaned down to look at him as easily as if she were sitting on a bench.

"Pressure, I hear," she called.

He stopped in the road and looked up.

"Yes."

She looked down at him, chewing. The scaffold people round her had stopped eating to listen.

"Fall properly," she called. Then she went back to her lunch.

Dessa found him at the board on the Monday evening, the last Monday but one, in the dusk, when he had stopped to look at the chalk square with the B in it.

He did not hear her come. She was simply there beside him with her hands in her pockets and her hair tied tight, looking at the board as he was looking at it, as though they had arranged to meet there and read it together. She had a way of arriving that was like her way of fighting: you did not see her come, and then she had been there for some time.

"Monday," she said.

"Yes."

She read the board a little longer. A cart went by behind them toward the triangle with its lamp swinging.

"I'll be at the gate," said Dessa. "Not the benches. There won't be benches, not on a Monday." She did not look at him. "I watched you from the benches for Corbin. I'd like to watch this one standing up."

"Why?"

She thought about that seriously, as she thought about everything.

"Because he won't be trying to find out what you are," she said. "Everybody you've fought here was. Renn was. I was. Corbin, all the way to the fifth." She turned her head and looked at him at last, with the small white scar through her eyebrow pale in the dusk. "A Bronze doesn't bother. He already knows what he is, and he'll find out what you are by standing on it. I want to see what you do when somebody isn't curious."

He did not have an answer to that, and she did not seem to want one.

"Afterward," she said, "if you can still stand. You and I have a talk owing." She took her hands out of her pockets. "Not this month. But it's owing."

Then she went off up the street toward the yards, and he stood at the board in the cold, looking at the B and the arrow, and at the word Monday.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Hesk's letter came on the last Tuesday, propped against the salt crock on the kitchen table.

He knew what it was before he touched it. It was the answer to the five, written at the bench or the kitchen table in Fen Street a week ago, on the night the five arrived; it had come as fast as a letter could. He took it out into the yard and sat on the low wall by the pump with it, in the cold, and turned it over twice in his hands.

Then he opened it.

Cael,

I read your letter on the workshop step, which seems to be where I read your letters now. I read it twice. Then I went inside and put the kettle on and did not drink any of it, and then I sat down and read it again.

I'm not going to tell you I wasn't frightened. I was. I am. I'm frightened in the way I was frightened on the step about the summons, a week late and all at once, and I've decided that this is simply what it is to have you somewhere else. You told me as it came. I'll tell you the same: I was frightened, and then I was proud of you, and I'm both still, and I expect I'll go on being both.

You asked what I think of your not telling me. I think you had reasons, and I think one of them was mine, and I think you've paid me back for the bench on the second day more handsomely than I deserved. I'm not angry. I've no right to be, and I'm not.

I don't know what it is either. The archive tells you what became of four people, as far as anybody wrote it down. It doesn't tell you what any of them ever did. Don't go looking in it for an answer it hasn't got.

Keep the record. You'd keep it anyway, but keep it the way you'd keep a load sheet somebody's life might hang on, because it might. Show the back of it to nobody but her.

And remember what I said to you in the side room at Weaver's Row. Don't let anyone see you move. Not until you know what you're doing. When I said it, I knew none of this. I find I'd say it again.

Tell the girl thank you, from me, for not flinching. I've met a great many grown men who would have.

— H.

He read it three times on the wall, in the cold, with the pump dripping beside him into its iced trough. Then he folded it carefully along its own folds and put it in the leather book with the others.

He sat there a while longer. He thought about Hesk on the step with the kettle boiling inside and not drinking any of it. He thought about I've no right to be, and what it had cost a man like Hesk to write that down. He thought about the side room at Weaver's Row, which seemed a very long way off now: a tree outside the window growing at an angle, and Hesk's prepared stillness, and that sentence said for the first time.

Don't let anyone see you move.

On Monday, at noon, he was going to stand in front of forty people or fifty or a hundred and a Bronze Rank 2, and he did not know what he was going to do there, or what might come up out of him without asking. He did not know whether he would know what he was doing. He thought he would not, mostly. He thought that the only honest answer to Hesk's sentence was the one Lira had given him on the low wall: read the build, and don't stand in the circle waiting for anything else.

He went in to supper. Torvin's wife looked at his face and gave him a bun she said she had been keeping for the boots woman, who had not deserved it.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

On the last Wednesday the mender gave him back a key.

It was one of the small ones from the tray, from the desk that had gone for firewood, a little brass box key that Cael had put on the pile of keys that had lived in somebody's pocket every day for years. The mender laid it on the bench in front of him without a word, and beside it a small tin cash box with a dented lid, of the kind people kept under a floorboard.

"Came out of the same house," said the mender. "Out of the wall, when they took the chimney down. Locked." He did not look up from his clock. "I tried the ones you'd said were used. Third one."

Cael picked up the key and turned it over. The bright worn places on its wards caught the light from the window, where the lock it had lived in had shaped it, a little every day, for longer than he had been alive.

"What was in the box?"

"Letters." The mender considered his clock. "A woman's. To a man who went downriver and didn't come back. Thirty years." He moved a wheel a hair with the end of a pin. "The family have them now. They didn't know they were there."

Cael put the key down very carefully beside the box.

"You've a good eye for what's been used," said the mender. Then, much later, while Cael was sorting washers one-handed into their tins: "Monday."

"Monday. The Bronze."

"I know what Monday is." The mender did not look up. "I meant Monday here. After." He moved another wheel. "And after?"

It was the third time he had asked it. Cael had said I don't know yet twice, and both times it had been true.

"I'll be here. Monday and Wednesday. As long as you'll have me."

The mender nodded slowly over his clock, as though a long figure had come right at last, and said nothing else at all for the rest of the afternoon.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On the last night before the bout he could not sleep, and did not try very hard.

He lay on his right side on the cot with Yeni's lamp down to a bead and the wheezing man whistling by the door, and he did the thing he had done on the night before Kindling and the night before Renn and every night before a bout since: he went through it. Not the fight, which he did not know, but everything round it, the things he could count.

He counted three weeks of mornings in the grey half, twenty-one of them, and one morning in the box drill when the step had come without asking and never again. He counted Corvane's figure, drawn perhaps two hundred times. He counted two bouts won, a Fenrow Stone and a dyers' Shield, neither of which anybody would remember, both of which had been easy because he had done the work. He counted the money for Corvane, and the money for the gate, which Vell had said he would not have to pay because he was fighting in it, and Lira had said that was the only sensible thing anybody had said about the whole affair.

He counted what he knew about Feryn, which was what Vell had said, and what Renn had said, and what Corvane had said and shown him in a brick yard by the river. It came to a page and a half. He had gone into his first bout with Renn knowing nothing at all. He had gone into Dessa knowing everything there was to know. This was the first time he had gone in knowing a page and a half about a man he had never seen, and the page and a half was mostly about what he would not be able to do.

He found that he was not frightened. He looked for it, honestly, as he would have looked for a tell, and it was not where he expected it. There was something else there instead, in the same place, and it was a great deal more like wanting.

He wanted to see it. He wanted to stand in front of the thing the eel woman had laughed about and Renn had lain on his back under, and find out what it was, and what he was, standing in front of it. It was not a sensible thing to want, and he knew it. He wanted it anyway, the way he had wanted to know what the word meant in Pellin's office, before he knew enough to be afraid of it.

He thought that probably said something about him, and did not write it down.

He woke before the light, as he had woken on the morning of Kindling, and lay still and took stock, as he did on days that mattered: ceiling, the beam across it with its old nail holes, the wheezing man asleep, Yeni's cot empty already, the grey of an Ardenmere morning in the window, which he had stopped seeing months ago and saw again now on purpose. He got up and dressed and went down, and Torvin's wife put a bowl of oats in front of him without a word, and stood over him with her spoon until he had eaten all of it.

Lira was waiting outside, on the step under the leaning O, with her canvas bag over her shoulder.

He knew the bag. It was the one she carried things in that she thought he might need and would not have thought to bring: a cloth, a flask of water, the end of a loaf, a strip of linen rolled tight. She had carried it to every bout since Dessa. She stood up when he came out, and read his face as she read the board.

"You didn't sleep."

"Some."

"That's not an answer." She fell in beside him. "I'll let you off today."

They walked up through the district in the cold, toward the Cinder House, not hurrying. A sleet had begun somewhere over the river and was coming in slantwise, small and grey, not settling. At the corner by the board somebody had rubbed out the Monday in the chalk square and written TODAY instead, very large.

"Whatever happens in there," said Lira, not looking at him, "you've already done what you could with the time there was. I want you to believe that before you go over the rope. Not just hear it. Believe it."

"I believe it. Mostly."

"Mostly will do." She bumped his shoulder with hers, the left one. "Today, mostly will do."

Chapter 46 — Bronze

[Taut, clear narration; sharpen the danger without rushing the thinking]

Vell counted the yard once from her table, as she always counted it, and made it forty-one.

It was a poor number for a Bronze. On a Sunday afternoon in good weather a Bronze in her circle would have had the benches out and the rope four deep, and boys on the wall, and Marrow sweating. But this was a Monday at noon in the last of the winter, with a grey sleet coming in slantwise off the river and melting as it touched the dirt, and a gate on it five times the price of a bench. Everybody who had come had walked out of a day's work to be there, or paid somebody to do it for them, or simply not gone in. So forty-one was a good number, and she wrote it at the top of the page in the small hand she kept for things that were hers: Forty-one, sleet, Monday noon. Then she looked at who they were.

They were people who knew what they were looking at. The old men from the third row had come without their benches and stood in a knot by the drain with their scarves over their mouths. Dessa was by the gate in the wall with her hair tied tight and her hands in her pockets, alone. Corbin stood beside the water bucket, square, saying nothing to anybody. Sarel had not come, and Vell had not expected her to; the girl Lira was at the barrel, where she always was, with her arms folded on the top of the rope and her face giving away nothing. Renn was on the sunny side, though there was no sun, with a few of his friends from the barges round him, all of them quieter than she had ever known them. And the boy was at the rope on the shaded side, with his coat off and his hand flat on the iron stake at the corner, as though he were listening to the ground.

She knew why he did that. She had watched him find it.

The pie boy came across from the gate with the coin bag, and she weighed it in her hand without counting it and put it under the table. Then Feryn came in through the gate in the wall.

He came in as she had seen him come into three other yards in three other cities over five years, talking over his shoulder to somebody behind him, easy and loose and pleased with the day. He was taller than most and built for use, not for show, in a coat that had been good once and was now only warm. He had been nineteen and a Copper the first time she saw him, on a wet night in a yard three days south of here, and he had lost to a one-armed man and laughed about it all the way to the water bucket. He was twenty-four now, or near it, and a Bronze Rank 2, and he moved like a man who has been hit by a great many good fighters and has stopped finding it interesting. She had watched him win more bouts than she could have named without the books, and she had liked him every time, which she did not often say about anybody.

Halfway across the yard he saw who it was at the rope with his coat already off.

He stopped as a man stops who has walked into a door he thought was open. Then he looked at the boy, a long plain look, and turned round, and found her table, and came across to it.

"No."

He said it quietly, but the yard was very quiet, and the sleet was not loud, and forty-one people heard him.

"He's a child."

"He's fourteen," said Vell.

She had known it was coming. She had known it on the morning she told the boy that Feryn was coming, and every morning since, and she had decided long before this one what she would say. It was harder to say it to his face than she had thought, and she said it anyway.

"You posted for any opponent with a rating a keeper would sign. I've signed his. Assessed-Copper, in my hand, five weeks gone. He's won two since, and four of the six before it; that's thirteen bouts in my book. I still call him unrated at the rope, because the registry gives me nothing to write there, but the line's in my hand and my name's under it. He's entered under witness, and the purse is met, and the gate's paid." She turned the ledger round on the table so that he could see the page. "Those are the terms. They're the terms you wrote."

Feryn bent over the book and read the page, all of it, with his finger moving down the lines. She had seen a great many fighters stand at her table and complain about what was in her book. She had seen very few read it first. She marked it to his credit and did not let it show.

"I posted for interesting opponents." He was still reading. "I didn't post for somebody who's still growing into his boots."

"Then you should have written it better."

He looked up at her.

"I don't decide who stands in my circle. I decide who I put across from whom, and what happens inside the rope, and when it stops. That's all I decide. The consent question is his. It isn't yours to answer, and it isn't mine." She turned the book back round. "If you want to know whether he means it, ask him."

She had not always thought that.

Thirty years ago, when she was new to the book, she had turned a girl away from her rope because the girl was too young and too light and had a look in her eye that Vell did not like, and Vell had been certain she knew best. The girl had gone downriver and fought in a yard where the keeper did not care how old anybody was, or what look they had in their eye, and nobody there had called anything for her. Vell had heard about it a month later, from a carter.

She had thought about it through the whole of that winter. In the end she had decided that a keeper who chose for a fighter whether he was fit to stand had stopped being a keeper and become something else, something nearer to an owner. A fighter's word over the rope was the one thing in the circle that was entirely his, and the circle stood on it, as it stood on her word inside the rope. You did not protect people by taking their word away from them. You protected them by being very, very good at the call.

So she would not overrule him. But she had already decided, sitting at her table with the sleet on her shoulders, exactly where the call would be.

She knew Feryn's weights. He had two of them, and she had watched him use both. There was the weight he carried on tour, when he was being polite to a town and did not want to put anybody in the healers' for a gate: loose and strolling and very nearly kind. And there was the other one, which she had seen four times in five years, when somebody had made him take them seriously, and which had ended all four bouts inside an exchange. If the boy made him go to the second weight, she would be on her feet. The first exchange after that which could only hurt the boy, and not teach him anything, she would end. She would not wait for him to stop getting up. He would not stop getting up of his own accord; she had watched him in thirteen bouts now, and only once had he put his hand up, against a cook, when there was nothing left in the bout for him to learn.

Feryn had gone to the rope.

He did not go round it to the boy's side. He stood on his own side with his hands resting on the top of it, and looked across the circle at the boy, and the boy looked back. Vell watched Feryn not ask how old he was, which was what nearly anybody would have asked, and which he already knew.

"Whoever stands in front of Pressure, do you know what it does to them?"

"Not all of it." The boy's voice was perfectly steady and rather quiet. "I've spent three weeks finding out what I could. A woman who lost to it for ten years showed me how it's built. I can tell you where you'll hold it, and about how long, if you're slow." He did not smile. "You won't be slow. That's the part I can't find out from anybody. The benches can't tell me, and neither can she."

"Who talked you into it?"

"Nobody. Vell told me you were coming, and what you were, and I asked her for it." The boy looked at him across the circle. "I'd like to know what three weeks bought me. I can't find that out by watching."

Feryn did not say anything. He was weighing him, and Vell knew what he was weighing, because she had weighed the same things: whether the answer had been learned by heart, and whether anybody behind the boy was pushing. He looked for it. She saw him look past the boy at the rope behind him, and along it, and find nobody there but the girl at the barrel with her arms folded, who looked back at him as flatly as a shut door.

"All right," said Feryn at last, as a man shuts a gate behind him. Then he turned round and looked at Vell. "Note that I objected."

"Noted," said Vell, and wrote it. "So is his answer."

She wrote that too.

Then she stood up behind her table, and the yard went lower, and she said the rules for the witnesses as she always said them: that it went until somebody conceded, or could not go on, or until she called it; that her call stood; and that nobody was killed, by circuit custom, which was older than any law. She had said them a thousand times. Today she listened to herself say them.

"Feryn. Bronze Rank 2, Pressure Path. Against unrated. Vouched." The small pause. "Begin when you're ready."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Cael went over the rope and stood on his mark, and the sleet came down on his bare arms and melted there.

He set his feet. He did not nod. He looked across the circle at Feryn and watched what did not move.

Feryn left his mark walking.

That was the first thing that was wrong. Nothing came off the mark at him, no rush, no probing hand. Feryn only strolled the inside of the groove at an easy pace, open hands carried at the height of his belt, working the stiffness out of his shoulders as a carter does before the first load. Once he stepped half a pace to his left, to no purpose Cael could find. He turned his head to follow Cael with a mild, friendly look on his face. All of it was moving, and Cael let all of it go past him and looked under it, below the ribs and above the belt, for the thing that stayed still.
