He could not find it. That was the second thing. Corvane, walking slowly in her brick yard, had carried her stone so carefully that once he knew where to look he could see it. Feryn was not carrying anything. Every part of him was as loose as every other part; there was no place in the middle of him that had gone heavier than the rest. Cael looked and looked and found a man strolling about in the sleet, and while he was still looking, the roof fell in: the air itself, come down on top of him.

It was not like Corvane's. Corvane's had been a hand laid on his chest. This was the whole sky.

There was no place where it struck him. It was everywhere at once, all the air between them gone solid together and coming down on him and forward, and his guard did not break so much as fold. The air slammed his own forearms flat against his chest, and the breath left him in a hiss between his teeth. Then he was on the ground, all along his back, without having seen it coming. He lay in the wet dirt of the circle with the sleet falling into his open eyes and the noise of the yard arriving from somewhere a long way off, like voices through a wall, and did the accounting, because the accounting was the only thing he could do: breath gone; ribs ringing deep where his own arms had hit them, the left side catching under the old place; nothing grating; nothing broken.

Somewhere above him Vell was counting, level and unhurried, as she counted when somebody was down and not moving.

He got his breath back in pieces. At six he rolled onto his knees. At eight he was standing.

Feryn had not come after him. He waited at the centre of the circle with his weight easy and his hands at his sides, watching Cael get up with mild professional interest, like a man waiting for a cart to pass so that he can cross the road.

He's being polite, thought Cael. That was him being polite.

"End of the exchange," said Vell.

He went back to his mark and stood on it and made himself breathe, four and four, with the catch at the top of every breath.

First exchange. I couldn't find it. He doesn't carry it the way she did. Everything's loose. He looked across at Feryn, who was rolling his shoulders. He rolled his shoulders just before. And then a while after that it came. Three heartbeats. Four. The roll's not it. The roll's what he puts on top of it. So what's under the roll?

"Begin."

This time he did not try to see the whole of him. He narrowed, as Corvane had made him narrow in the brick yard, to the one place: below the ribs, above the belt, the middle of the man. He let the shoulders roll without him. He let the hands drift and the head turn and the feet stroll, and he kept his eyes on the plain cloth of Feryn's shirt where it went into his belt, and waited for it to do nothing.

Feryn rolled his shoulders. Again that purposeless half pace to the left.

And under it, in the middle of him, something went still.

It was not much. It was less than Corvane's had been, and much less than Lira's holding in the grey half, which he had learned to see more often than not. It was the faintest settling, as if the cloth of the shirt had for one moment stopped moving with the breath underneath it. But it was there, and it stayed there while the rest of him went on strolling, and Cael saw it and knew what it was.

He saw it late. He knew he had seen it late even while he was seeing it; there was not time to get out of the way, and nowhere to get to, because the thing that was coming would come across the whole front of him at once. But there was time for one choice, and he made it.

He did not meet it. He turned his guard edge-on, his left forearm leading, slanted across his body like a roof slanted to throw off rain, and he turned his shoulders behind it.

The air came down. It was as huge as before and as patient and as wrong. It hit the slanted forearm and did not stop there but went along it, down it and off it, part of it going past him instead of into him. The part that did not go past drove him back across the circle with his boots skidding in the wet dirt and ploughing two long furrows through Vell's rake lines, one pace and then two. It did not put him down. He came to a stop at the edge of the groove with his weight still on his feet and his breath still in him, and his left forearm was a single bar of ache from the wrist to the elbow, right over the old burn, as though the whole weight of what he had shed had run down the bone and settled there to stay.

Then the yard did a thing he had never heard a crowd do: not a cheer, but a breath, forty-one people drawing it in together.

Feryn had stopped walking.

His eyes went from Cael to the two furrows in the dirt and back. Something in the easy surface of his face tipped, very slightly, like a cup set down on a table that is not quite level.

"You read that," he said.

He did not ask it. It was a fact, put out for the whole yard to hear, and for Vell's pen, and for his own benefit.

"Three weeks, and you read it." He rolled his neck, slowly. "Nobody reads the build. Folk watch my feet for twelve months and the build goes by them every time."

He talks when he changes his mind, thought Cael. Like Renn's shoulders. He held his arm against his side and filed it.

"End of the exchange," said Vell.

He stood on his mark and did the arithmetic, because his arm was telling him to.

He had read the build in the second. He had read it halfway, perhaps, or a little less, as he had read Corvane's at two breaths in four, and it had kept him on his feet and cost him an arm. He could not spend the arm twice. Reading it halfway was not enough; he needed to read it at the beginning, before Feryn had built anything at all, at the moment Feryn decided to build, if there was such a moment, and if it showed. Corvane had never told him whether it did. Corvane had never seen anybody read it that early.

Across the circle Feryn had set his feet.

He was not strolling now. That was the change, and Cael saw it and felt the cold go down his back. Feryn stood quite still on his mark, with his hands loose and his shoulders level and his weight in the middle of his feet, and when Vell said begin, he did not walk at all. He only stood there, and looked at Cael with interest, and talked.

"Where are you from?"

Cael did not answer.

"Not here," said Feryn. "You stand like a city. Somewhere with walls." He shifted his weight a hair from one foot to the other. "I've fought in a city with walls. Hated it. Everybody watches you from the top."

He was hiding it under stillness, and under talk. Cael understood it at once, because he had seen it done for three weeks in the grey half by somebody who was much better at it than she would ever let anybody know. A person standing still and talking is harder to read than a person walking, he had found out on the eighth morning. There's so little to tell the holding from. Feryn had learned in one exchange to do what it had taken Lira a week to find. Cael watched the middle of him, under the talking, under the stillness, and the stillness was everywhere and there was nothing to tell it from.

Then, very early, much too early, before Feryn had finished his sentence about walls, before he had shifted his weight again or done anything at all, the cloth of his shirt stopped moving with his breath.

It was the beginning. It was the decision. Cael saw it, and his body was already going.

Afterward, on the cot, he would try to put what happened into its proper order on the page, and fail. He did not decide to step and then step. The step was already happening, with his whole weight in it, before anything in him that made decisions had been consulted. It was a long, low, slanting glide that his legs did with a sureness he had never put into them, quick the way air goes through a doorway when somebody opens a window at the other end of the house. It was familiar and not his. It did not carry him back from the air. It carried him round it, out past the whole edge of the place where it was going to come.

Behind him, the spot he had just left took the whole weight of the air. Its edge went past him: a hard drag at his sleeve and down the side of his body, solid, close enough to count as a touch. Then he was standing on the far side of it, at an angle no slip and no dodge should have been able to reach, balanced, with his guard up and Feryn's open flank in front of him an arm's length away.

The yard was silent. It was not the held breath of the second exchange, but a real silence, forty-one people and the sleet and nobody moving. Where the air had furrowed it, the dirt was still settling; he could hear it. He heard Vell's pen stop.

He did not take the flank.

By the time his thinking had caught up with where his feet had put him, the opening had already begun to close; Feryn was already turning. And the honest truth, standing there in the sleet, was that he did not know what he had just done, nor whether he could ever do it twice. It had come when the air came. It had not come once in three weeks when he called it, at the post, by the cot, in the box drill. It was not a tool he had picked up. It was something that had used his legs.

Feryn turned to face him.

For a breath he only looked. Then the yard came back all at once, a wall of noise from every side, Renn shouting on the sunny side and the old men by the drain stamping in the wet, and Feryn seemed deaf to all of it. His eyes stayed on Cael the way Cael's own eyes had stayed on Renn's front heel in the fifth exchange, once he had found it: the look you give something that has just crossed out everything you wrote about it.

"End of the exchange," said Vell. Her voice was very level.

Then Feryn settled.

There was no other word for it. All the slackness left him, the strolling ease and the friendly interest with it. Everything he had been carrying round the yard for three exchanges was set aside like a coat taken off and laid over a chair, and what stood there instead was a Bronze Rank 2 at his working weight, which Cael had never seen and understood at once.

"Last one, then," said Feryn. There was no talk in his voice any more. There was nothing in it but what he meant.

On the way to his mark, his forearm burning and his ribs catching and the sleet coming down, Cael saw that there was a choice in front of him, and made it.

The safe thing was to go backward. He could circle, and keep his distance, and make Feryn spend the last exchange chasing him round the groove, and lose long and look well doing it. Lira would not have minded. Vell would not have minded. Nobody in the yard would have said a word. He looked at the safe thing and put it down without any fuss. Looking well had never been the point of asking for this bout. He had asked for it so that he would know. There was only one thing still to know: how much his reading could hold against Feryn's whole weight, with nobody keeping anything back on either side of the rope.

He set his feet and looked at the middle of Feryn's shirt.

"Begin."

Feryn came in fast.

He came in fast and straight, and the speed changed everything, as everybody had told him speed changed everything, Lira and Vell and Corvane and the eel woman laughing with her arms in a tub. The build was there all the same, and Cael saw it. He saw it, folded small and tight under a man coming at him at a run, the faint settling in the middle of the shirt, as early as he had caught it in the third. But it bought him almost nothing now. Feryn was building as he came and closing as he built, and the half breath Cael had had in the third was a quarter, and the quarter was a sliver, and the sliver was almost nothing at all. His reading had not got worse. Reading was simply not enough any more.

He read a release coming, and he called for the step.

He called for it as he had called for it by the cot, deliberately, with his whole attention, the hip dropping and the turn. It did not come. Whatever had moved his legs in the third exchange kept to its own dark place and did not answer, because he had asked it to. So he slipped instead, with his own feet, his own trained slip, short and quick and honest, to the left, outside where the air would come.

The air did not come.

Feryn had not let it go. He had built it and held it and not released it, and Cael had slipped round a thing that was not there. And Feryn's hand, which had been at his side, was already where Cael was slipping to. Feryn had learned in the third exchange that the boy went round. He had stopped trying to hit where the boy was, and put his hand where the boy would go. Once too often, said Doss, somewhere at the back of Cael's head, a beat too late to be any use.

The hand closed on Cael's right shoulder in the middle of his slip.

There was no blow, and no wrench. Feryn simply agreed with him. Cael's own slipping weight went into the hand, and the hand took it and joined it and turned it, a few degrees, gently, so that all of Cael's speed going left became all of Cael's speed going down. The yard turned over. There was just time to understand that the throw was his own, and that all Feryn had done was choose its direction.

Halfway through the fall, too late to decide anything, he noticed the grip.

The hand on his shoulder did not let go. The turn was finished; his weight was already gone past any recovering; there was nothing left for the hand to do that the ground would not do better. It stayed anyway. Feryn's fingers kept their grip for as long as a slow count of one, pressing, when the lightest brush would have been enough, and went most of the way to the ground with him before they opened. It was nothing, a small thing in the middle of a large one. He put it away at the back of his head all the same, because it did not fit, and he kept everything that did not fit. Then the ground hit him along the whole of his right side at once, shoulder and hip and ribs together, and knocked the thought and his breath and the rest of the bout out of him in one blow.

He lay in the wet dirt with the sleet coming down on his face and did the accounting from a long way off. Everything hurt in the general way. His right shoulder and hip, where the ground had come up. His ribs on both sides now, the left catching again under the old place, the right new. His forearm, wrapped all the way round the bone. Nothing hurt in the sharp particular way that meant broken. He gave his body the order to stand, and it sent back an answer: presently. He got an elbow under him. The yard tilted and came level and tilted again.

"The match is called," said Vell.

She was very close. She had left her table. Every corner of the yard heard her, and she had not raised her voice.

"Feryn, Bronze Rank 2, by incapacity. So entered."

Part of him put a protest together: Count me. I'm getting up. Count me. The rest of him, the part that kept the book, looked at the protest and set it aside. Six more breaths went by before he had his feet under him, and when he had them he was swaying. The margin was gone and would not come back today. The fourth exchange had proved it: whenever Feryn chose to be fast, reading by itself put Cael on the ground inside four seconds. There was nothing left for a fifth exchange to teach him. It would only hurt him, and he would have gone into it, and Vell had known that he would.

Her call was not early. It was exact. She had ended it at the very moment it stopped being able to give him anything but damage, and he understood, standing there swaying in the sleet, that this was the whole art of what she did.

"Good call." It was true, and the book ought to have it from his own mouth.

"I know." Vell turned for her stool and her book.

All the noise of the yard he left at a distance, where it belonged.

He walked to the table, because you walked to the table, win or lose, and stood in front of it with his left arm held against his chest and his right side aching from the shoulder to the knee. Vell was writing. The sleet had got into the corner of her page and she had blotted it and gone on.

Feryn came to him there.

He came straight across the circle, ahead of Renn and the old men and the people with money in their hands, ahead of everybody, and Cael marked that he did it at once, before anything else. He held out his hand. Cael took it with his right, which hurt less, and Feryn closed his own round it and pulled once, smoothly, so that Cael was standing straight instead of swaying, and then let go. He was careful about it without making any show of being careful.

"What tier are you?" said Feryn.

It was the question. Sooner or later everybody asked it, one way or another, and long ago Cael had settled how to meet it: first, and plainly, before it could be found out sideways.

"SHATTERED."

Behind him he heard Vell's pen stop.

He watched Feryn's face. Gates and registry counters and boarding-house tables had given him a full list of the ways a face could take the word: a step back; a carefully emptied look; a nod a beat too quick; a glance toward the door. He watched to see which one it would be.

Feryn's face did none of those things. His eyebrows lifted, and what came into it was not fear, or even fear well hidden. It was appetite. It was the plain, unguarded hunger of a man who has been doing a thing for a long time, and doing it well, and has just been handed a problem from outside everything he knows.

"Huh," said Feryn.

He kept looking: at the sleet on him, the sway in his knees, at fourteen years of boy still upright in the circle.

"I stood in front of Bronze panels for a year," he said. "Months of it. Every Path there is in the room with me, and every way of using one. I've never once seen a thing I couldn't put a name to afterward." Slowly he shook his head, and what was in the shake was respect: not the sort a man puts on for the rope, but the sort he keeps. "The third exchange. I know what I saw. I've no idea what I was fighting."

"That makes two of us," said Cael.

Feryn laughed. It came out of him short and surprised and real, as though it had been knocked loose.

"Eat with me," he said. "Tonight. I'm paying."

Vell had lifted her eyes from the book. Both her eyebrows were up, and on Vell that was as good as a speech. Feryn saw it.

"What?"

"I've watched you win in three cities," said Vell, going back to her page, "and I've never once seen you buy anybody so much as a pie."

"Nobody's been worth a pie," said Feryn. He looked back at Cael. "Well?"

By then Lira had come round the rope. Cael saw her past Feryn's arm, standing by the barrel with her arms folded and her mouth pressed flat over something that was not disappointment, and that was working hard to keep from being pride. She caught him looking, and nodded once, short. It meant go, and it meant I want every word of it afterward, and it meant something else under both of those that he did not have a name for and did not need one.

His ribs hurt. His arm got stiffer with every minute he stood there. He had lost in four exchanges, in the sleet, with forty-one people watching.

"All right," he said. "I'm hungry."

Amrit's was full by the time they got there, because the sleet had driven everybody indoors who had anywhere to be driven to, and half the people at the two long tables had been at the rope at noon.

They went quiet when Feryn came down the three steps and ducked in under the lintel, and then they went loud again, very carefully, in the way people talk when they want you to know they are not talking about you. Two men from the river workshops shifted along a bench without being asked. Feryn thanked them as if they had given him a horse, and sat down with his back to the little windows and the river going by grey outside them, and Cael sat down across from him, which took two tries and a hand on the table.

The girl who carried the bowls came out. She put down in front of Cael a bowl of the fish stew with twice the bread beside it that she put beside anybody else's, and in front of Feryn a bowl of the same stew with exactly the ordinary amount.

Feryn looked at the two plates of bread, and then at the hatch, where a large man with a shaved head was looking at a pot.

"I see," he said.

"He decided I was his," said Cael. "After I lost to him. In the autumn."

"You lost to the cook."

"He's an Ember Copper 4. He's very good."

"I'm sure he is." Feryn tore his ordinary bread in half with great dignity. "I've lost to worse. I once lost to a man with one arm, on a wet night, three days south of here, when I was nineteen." He dipped the bread. "He used the stump. Nobody had ever told me you could use the stump. I lay on my back in the rain and thought about it for some time."

Cael laughed, and his ribs caught, both sides at once, and he had to put his spoon down and hold the edge of the table.

Feryn watched him do it with professional interest.

"That's the right side as well now," he said. "From the ground. And the arm." He looked at Cael's left forearm, which was lying on the table like a thing that belonged to somebody else, swollen and hot over the old burn. "Eat. You've spent more today than you think you have. Everybody does, the first time they stand in front of it."

He ordered more when the bowl was gone, without asking, and then more again. Cael ate all of it. He had not known he was hungry until he started, and then he could not stop, and Feryn sat across from him with his elbows on the table and told stories.

He told them as Cael wrote the Log, exactly and without mercy, and they were all at his own expense. There was the one-armed man. There was a yard in a farming town where the circle was shared, on the days there was no card, with a goat; the goat had wandered back into it during his bout. He had refused to step on it, and his opponent had not shared his feelings about the goat, and he had lost. There was his first Bronze evaluation, at twenty-one, in a long cold room in front of a panel of three. He had been so frightened that he had built far more than he meant to and let it go all at once, at the wall, as the panel had asked. It had blown every paper off the panel's table and out of the window into a canal.

"They passed me," said Feryn. "I've never known why. I think they were afraid not to."

"What did they write?"

"Nobody knows. It's in the canal." He drank. "I asked, years after. The senior assessor said she remembered the day perfectly and that I had a great deal of promise and no idea where to put it. Which was true. It's still true some days."

Cael laughed until his ribs made him stop, and then sat holding the table with his eyes watering, and Feryn waited for him with the patience of a man who has been laughed at in a great many eating houses and has learned to take it as a compliment.

At the hatch, Amrit looked up from his pot, once, at the two of them, and then looked down again.

But they had not come to Amrit's for the goat, and neither of them pretended they had. When the second bowl was gone Feryn put his cup down on the table and squared it there with one finger, as if it had to sit exactly so. It was the first careful thing he had done all evening.

"Your third exchange," he said. "I'd like to go through it with you. If you'll let me."

"All right."

"Six years now, I've made my living letting go on people." He said it plainly, as a fact about his trade. "Every way there is of getting out from under it, I've seen. The trained slip. The panic dive. The man who goes down flat because he's decided the ground is safer. I've fought Wind, real Wind, ranked, declared, people who'd been doing it since they were your age." He looked at the cup. "That wasn't any slip I know, and it wasn't fright. And you're no declared Wind, or you'd have said Wind when I asked you, and you didn't." He looked up. "You went before I let go. You didn't go away from it. You went round it, as if you knew where all the edges of it were going to be before I'd built them." He waited. "How?"

So it had come. Lira had asked him nearly the same thing in the grey half, months before, and he answered Feryn as he had answered her. It was the only answer he owned, and Feryn had paid for a true one, not a clever one.

"I don't know yet."

Feryn looked at him. Cael let him look. He had nothing to hold up and nothing to hide. Between their two cups lay the plain truth, and it was not finished.

"Yet," said Feryn.

"I keep a book." With his good hand Cael gave his own cup a single turn. "Everything I can't explain goes in it. Everything in it gets explained in the end, or ruled out. This one's sat in it a good while now." He looked at the river going by the window. "It happens when something's coming at me and I haven't time to choose. I can't call it. Calling's never worked. I asked for it today, in the fourth, when you came in fast." He felt his mouth go up at one corner, without much humour. "You saw how that went."

Feryn did not say anything.

Cael watched him turn the answer over. He watched him notice that it was not an answer, and weigh it, and decide, quite visibly, not to push at it. That was rare enough that he marked it. Most people pushed at a thing they could not explain, or backed away from it; he had a catalogue for both. Feryn only nodded slowly. It was how a man might leave a good bout half fought, on purpose, sure that the second meeting would pay better.

"When you figure it out, I want to know."

It had the same sound as his all right in the circle, a gate shut behind him. It was not a politeness. It was a thing he was putting in his own book, with Cael's name against it.

"You'll be somewhere I can find you?"

"I'm always somewhere," said Feryn.

Cael understood that this was how people who travelled the circuits said yes.

He paid, as he had said he would, and counted the coins out onto the table more carefully than he had done anything else all evening. At the top of the three steps, out in the street, the sleet had stopped and the cold had come down behind it, hard and clear, with the lamps lit along the lower bridge and the river loud underneath. Feryn stood for a moment in the doorway of the eating house and looked at Cael once more, the whole bruised, standing catalogue of him, and shook his head again, slowly, in the same plain way as at the table.

"Fourteen," he told the street, or himself.

Then he went off along the river toward wherever touring fighters slept, laughing quietly to himself in the dark.

The notice came while he still had the pencil in his hand.

It came as the first one had, thirty-seven nights before, on this same cot. There was no sound and no light, and nowhere it could be said to come from. There was the quiet first, the hush in which a whole thought gets ready to arrive, and then a turning over, and then, in the dark place behind his breastbone where nothing had lit since the word, something written.

He had not been waiting for anything. He had been paying in a bout.

It had been a slow walk back from Amrit's, as slow as his legs would let it be. He had not gone up to Lira's. It was long past the lamps, and the widow had said what she had said, twice, and Lira's door locked from both sides. At the corner by the well with the iron cover he had stopped and looked up the lane toward the chandler's, and then gone the other way. In the morning he would tell her every word of it, in order. She had asked for that with one nod at the barrel, and she would have it first.

Torvin's had been asleep. He had gone up the stairs a step at a time with his good hand flat on the wall and sat down on the end of his cot, and Yeni's lamp, turned down to a bead, had been turned up a little toward him by a hand that came out from under the next blanket and went back again.

Then he had opened the Log on his knee. The arm he wrote with was the arm that hurt, and every line cost him, and he had never had so much to pay in. Every exchange went in by his usual rule. First the event; next the read, and the moment it came; last the price of the read, and the thing it had bought. It was the fifteenth entry in the Log since the autumn, and the fourteenth bout in Vell's book, because the Log had counted Baro, whom he had only watched.

Fifteenth. Feryn, Bronze Rank 2, Pressure. Lost, fourth exchange, by incapacity. Vell's call.

First: didn't read it at all. Everything loose; nothing to find. The roof came down. Flat on my back, up at eight.

Second: read the build late, about halfway. Turned the guard edge-on and shed some of it down my left arm. Skidded two paces and stayed up. The arm paid.

Third: read the build at the start, before he'd built anything, while he was standing still and talking. Earliest I've ever read anything. And the step came. On its own. Same as always. Round it, not away.

Fourth: read it fine. The margin was gone anyway. He'd learned I go round, so he didn't let go at all. He put his hand where I'd go. I called the step and it didn't come. Thrown with my own speed.

The ruling had been short.

Reading is necessary. Reading isn't enough. He didn't beat what Corvane showed me. He was only faster than me at it. The drawing's right. It needs somebody quicker standing in front of it.

After that he had turned the book over and written, under the last entry in the back, Sixth instance. Feryn, third exchange. The step. Not called. Came when the air came. And he had flexed his forearm, carefully, and sat there with the pencil, asking himself whether the account was settled, and that was when the answer came, in the dark, without his asking it anything at all.

Now he did not move for a long time.

He read it once, and again, and a third time, slowly, checking each word against the one before it as if it might have shifted while he looked away. It had not shifted. It sat in the dark beside the other one, the Wind one, plain and quiet. Where there had been one line of figures there were two.

Pressure-adjacent.

He copied it into the back of the Log letter for letter, as he had once copied the first, and then wrote the first out again above it, so that the two lay on one page where he could see both at once. Then he did what he did with anything new. He laid it against the record to see where it went.

The Wind had cost three months. Three months of mornings in the grey half with Lira, watching her step until something in him had taken its shape without being told to: hundreds of hours. And even then the notice had waited until the shape had come up out of him under pressure, and not only once, but in the drop and against Dessa and against Sarel. It was the one example he had, and it was a long one.

Feryn he had never seen before noon today. He had heard of him from Vell, and from Renn, and from the eel woman on the fish steps. He had spent three weeks learning Pressure at the brickworks end from an old woman with a stick, who drew it for him in the dirt, and who had built in front of him for two hours together and leaned the air on him a dozen times; and no notice had come out of any of it. Of Feryn himself he had seen one bout, his own, four exchanges, the last of them over in four seconds.

If watching was what did it, the sum would not come out. He tried it every way he could think of and it would not come out. Three months of mornings for the one; four exchanges for the other.

So it was not the watching, or it was not the watching by itself.

He went back through the four exchanges more slowly, as he hunted through any bout for the place where it had turned. Before the notice, before he had known there was anything worth marking, some clerk at the back of his head had already set a marker down, and he came to it now: the fall, and the hand on his shoulder.

The grip had not let go. The throw had been over, his weight gone past any getting it back, everything the hand had been there to do already done, and still it had held him, one full beat, a pressed second of grip where a touch would have served, riding him halfway to the ground before it opened. He had set that aside in the circle because it fitted nowhere. Now it might fit.

His hand was not quite steady when he wrote.

Second fragment. Pressure-adjacent. From Feryn, I think. Not from watching, or I can't make the watching add up: one bout of him against three months of her. His air touched me three times in the bout, and Corvane's a dozen times in her brick yard, and nothing came from either. What's different is the hand. In the fourth, with the throw already finished, he kept hold of my shoulder. Held. One second, perhaps less, through my shirt. Suppose this thing can travel through a touch: then a single second of a hand might have done the work that three months of looking did.

He stopped and read it over, and made himself put down the next part before he could stop believing it.

Might. One data point. I wrote that exact thing about the first notice, that one might be chance, and I'm putting it down again here, in the book, where I'll have to see it every time I want to stop doubting. I don't know that the touch did this. All I can say is that the watching never comes out right, however I add it, and the hand is the single thing left over that won't go in with the rest. That isn't the same as knowing.

He leaned back against the cold wall under the window, careful of his ribs, and thought about Kestrel.

He turned back through the pages to the two days at the middle-yard gate and the two nights on the wall by the pump, and the half heartbeat in his heels in the grey half that he had never been able to trust, and the word he had written under all of it: Inconclusive. He had given three reasons it might have come to nothing. Two days of watching were not three months; or Force did not cross, or did not cross to him; or the thing in his heels had been real and only wanted longer.

He read them again and saw that there were four now.

Kestrel, reread, he wrote, under the rest. A fourth reason: for two mornings I was knocking at the wrong door, because with him the watching alone was never going to do it. Two days at a gate, and he never once came nearer than an arm's length, except going past me with his rope.

I don't know that either. I don't know what matters. Time, touch, the person, the Path, or some other thing there's no word for yet. For the record, then: is it every touch, or only some? Must it last? Did he have to mean anything by it?

He looked at the last question, and under it, slowly, he wrote:

He didn't mean anything. He was throwing me. If anything passed, it passed through a hand whose only business was putting me on the ground.

Then he sat and looked at the whole page. It was more than he had ever put in the back of the book in a single night. There was one thing still to pay in, and it had no column, since none of the columns were for how a day had felt.

A professional had beaten him in four exchanges, and had been a professional in every one of them. He had been read and outrun, and his own speed had been turned into the throw that laid him on his side in the wet, with forty-one people watching. It was all still on him, every separate hurt: the ribs on both sides now, the forearm wrapped round its bone, the whole right side of him from shoulder to hip where the ground had come up to meet him, and the six breaths it had taken him to stand.

At the foot of the page there was room for one more line, and he used it.

Loss, by incapacity, on Vell's call, to Feryn (Bronze Rank 2, Pressure). The call was right. I read him in three of four. Corvane's drawing holds. The step came once, when it chose, the way it always does. Got: the read, a dinner, an open account with a man who's always somewhere, and maybe a second door I never knew about. Paid: one arm, both sides, a fall. Three weeks went in, and what came out was more than I'd paid for.

He looked at it. Then he wrote one more line, because it was true, and because he did not think he would believe it in the morning unless it was written down.

I've never lost anything and felt less like I'd lost it.

He shut the book and set it on the shelf beside Hesk's leather one. He lay down very carefully on his back, which was the only way left that ought not to hurt, and it hurt anyway. He lay looking up at the beam with its old nail holes in the light of Yeni's lamp. Behind his breastbone, side by side in the dark, sat the two things, the one that leaned and the one that pressed, and he listened to the wheezing man begin to whistle.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

In the morning he went to the grey half before the light, because he had said he would tell her first, and he meant to.

He walked very slowly. The frost had come down hard behind the sleet, and the lane was white, and his right hip had stiffened in the night so that every step up the hill was a separate conversation. When he came in through the gate in the wall Lira was already at the post, in the dark, striking it low, twice, and stepping round it, and she stopped when she heard him and turned round.

She looked at the way he was walking. She looked at his left arm, which he was carrying against his chest because it would not hang, and at his face.

"Sit down," she said. "Before you fall down and I have to put a mark on the post for it."

He sat down on the low wall. She sat beside him, close, on his right, the side the ground had not had, because it was the side that was left, and did not give him any bread yet.

"Every word," she said. "In order."

He gave it to her in order, the four exchanges and Vell's call and What tier are you?, and Amrit's two plates of bread, and the goat, and the canal. She laughed at the canal and put her hand over her mouth. Then he told her the third exchange again, slower, and she did not laugh. Then he told her the fourth, and the hand on his shoulder that had stayed a beat too long, and what had come after midnight on the cot.

She stopped him there, before he could take the book out.

"In the fourth," she said. "When he went heavy. You didn't go backward."

"No."

"I said you'd do whatever you do." She looked at his arm, lying across his chest. "I'm not sorry I said it. And I'm not sorry you didn't. I've been sitting up half the night trying to work out which of those I am, and I'm both." She shook her head. "Go on. The cot."

He took the Log out of his coat and opened it on his knee and showed her, and she read it in the grey light with her lips moving very slightly, both notices one under the other in his careful hand.

She read it twice.

"His," she said.

"I think so."

"Not watching."

"I don't think so. Not only." He told her the arithmetic, and the grip, and the one data point, and Kestrel at the wrong door. She listened to all of it without saying anything, with her shoulder against his and her breath going up white beside his in the dark.

When he had finished she sat looking at the two notices on the page while the sky over the east wall went on paling.

"I don't know what that means," she said at last.

"Neither do I."

"Good." She took his good hand and turned it over and put a piece of bread in it, the larger half, though he had not seen her tear it. "Then we don't know together. That's better than you not knowing on your own on a cot with your face to the wall." She looked at the notice again. "Two doors."

"Perhaps."

"Perhaps two doors." She almost smiled. "One of them's mine, and I didn't know about it for three months. The other one's a man you met at noon and had supper with." She shook her head slowly. "I don't think either of us is going to like the next one, whatever it turns out to be."

He ate his bread. It hurt to breathe in while he chewed, so he ate it slowly.

The light came up grey over the east wall, and the frost went pink along the top of it, and the girls came and sat on the far wall with their stolen breakfasts and looked at his arm and then, kindly, looked away. Somewhere down in the district a cart was going over the cobbles toward the lower bridge, and the fish steps would be starting, and the board would be saying TODAY to a day that had gone.

He thought about Hesk's letter, and don't let anyone see you move, and forty-one people in the sleet holding their breath when the step had come. He would write to Hesk, the next thing as it came, and not five things later.

"Survivable," said Lira beside him, not as a question, looking at his arm.

"Survivable."

"Then tomorrow you're doing nothing. Nothing at all. And the day after—"

"We start on it properly."

"We start on it properly," she said, and stood up, and held her hand down to him to pull him off the wall, on his good side. He took it, and she pulled, and he came up.

On Wednesday the mender looked at his arm across the bench, and at the way he was standing, and said, "No."

"You can sort with one hand," the mender agreed, without looking up from his clock. "And you'll drop half of it, and I'll have to sort it again. Monday." He considered. "If it's still there."

So Cael went out under the four words in the black paint and stood in the row of workshops with nothing to do, which had not happened to him since Denvash. He told her. She did not draw the four strokes beside it this time. She drew one.

She looked at it, leaning on her stick.

"I lost to them for ten years," she said. "And I studied them for ten more, and I had forty students, and I never once knew that it showed there. At the start. I thought the start was inside where nobody could see it." She tapped the single stroke with the end of the stick. "And it shows."

"I did." She did not sound pleased to have been right. She looked at his arm. "It'll be enough one day. Against somebody. Not him, not this year. But somebody." She got up off the bucket, slowly, with the stick, and stood looking down at her drawing in the dirt. "You'll come back. When you've seen it again."

It was not a question, and he did not answer it as one.

She went into her house and did not say goodbye, as before. But this time she left the drawing in the dirt, with its one stroke, and did not rub it out with her boot.

He walked home through the brickworks in the early dark with the soot in the air and the kilns glowing red in their doorways, slowly, with his arm against his chest.

He thought about the six weeks, which had run out on the forty-second day and were five weeks behind him now. He thought about a senior man from the Compact with a thin file, who had not come yet and who must, by every count he knew how to make, be on the road by now, or at a desk two days west packing a case. He thought about Coss saying that he could buy time but not an answer, and about how much of the time had already been spent.

He thought about two lines of figures in the dark behind his breastbone where there had been one. There were two doors, perhaps, where he had thought there was only one, and he did not know where either of them went, or which of them he had come through, or whether there were others in the dark he had not found yet. He did not know what Kestrel had been, or what Feryn's hand had been, or whether Lira's three months and Feryn's one second were the same thing at all.

He knew that his ribs hurt on both sides, and that his arm would be stiff for a week, and that he had been read and outrun by a man who wanted to know the answer as much as he did.

At the top of the lane of yards the old man was standing in his gate in the dusk, with his sleeves rolled down against the cold, watching the woman with the shoulder hold her fourth position. "Yes."

"Four," he said.

Chapter 48 — An Ordinary Tuesday

[Restrained, watchful narration; keep the evaluation pressure close and human]

Properly, it turned out, meant a column.

Lira was at the post when he came in through the gate on Thursday with the bread, and she had already chalked it. Beside the gone column, which was ruled off at forty, and the falls column, which had stopped at nine, there was a third column now, narrow and new, with nothing at the head of it but a small W and nothing under the W at all.

"That's yours," she said. "Every time you ask for it, a stroke. Every time it comes, a ring round the stroke. And every time it costs you something, you tell me what, and I'll put a word beside it." She took the loaves off him and tore them and gave him half. "You said on Sunday you'd write it down every time. You haven't."

"I've written it."

"You've written that it costs. That's not the same as writing what." She pointed the chalk at him. "A little is a word. Worse is a word. Can't feel my foot is three words, and if you ever say it to me I'll want to know. But it goes on the post, where I can see it, and not only in the back of your book where I can't."

He looked at the empty column, and then at her.

"Is this the rule?"

"This is the rule." She put the chalk in her pocket. "Eat. Then ask."

So he ate, and then he stood up in the grey half with his left arm held against his chest, because it would not yet hang without hurting, and asked.

The step came slowly, as it always came when it was asked for, as if he were reading it aloud from a page in poor light. His hip dropped and his body turned and his foot went down, and the frozen dirt between where it began and where it landed went short by the width of a hand. Then his breath went, and the old dull ache came into the joint of his left hip, and he stood there with his good hand pressed against it, breathing as if he had run up from the river.

Lira made a stroke on the post and put a ring round it.

"What?"

"Breath. The hip. About the same as Sunday."

"Same," she said, and wrote it beside the ring in small letters. "Again."

He did it again. It was worse, as the second always was, and the ground hardly changed under his foot.

"Worse," said Lira, and wrote that, and made a ring that was only half a ring, because she said that was fair. Then she looked at the two strokes, chewing, with her head on one side.

"And the other one," she said.

He had known she would ask. He had known it since Tuesday, on the low wall, when she had read the second notice twice with her lips moving and said two doors in the voice she kept for things she would come back to. He had thought about the answer on the long walk to the brickworks and back yesterday, and he gave her the one he had found.

"I haven't tried it."

"Why not?"

"Because it doesn't go anywhere in particular." He looked across the yard at her, and at the girls coming along the far wall with their stolen breakfasts. "Feryn's went on everything in front of him. All at once. The Wind's only my feet. If I ask for the other one, it'll go wherever I'm facing." He did not look away. "And you're in front of me."

Lira stood quite still with the bread in her hand.

He thought for a moment that she would laugh, as she had laughed at the eel woman, and he would not have minded. She did not. She looked at him as she looked at a guard she had not seen before, the whole of it at once, and then she nodded, slowly, as if he had told her the right answer to a question she had not quite known she was asking.

"Then not me," she said. "Not the girls on the wall. Not the post, either; it's Vell's." She turned and looked at the empty end of the yard, where the grey half ran out against the drain. "Somewhere with nobody in front of it. When your arm can lift a cup."

"When my arm can lift a cup," he agreed.

"Good." She went to her mark. "Box drill. Slowly. And keep that arm out of it, or I'll tie it to you."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He posted the letter to Hesk at noon.

He had finished it the night before at the kitchen table, after everybody had gone up, with his left arm lying on the table beside the paper like something he had brought home from the market and not yet put away. It had not been a long letter to write. He had promised in the last one to tell the next thing as it came. This was the next thing, and it had come only two days ago, and he knew exactly what it had to say.

Hesk,

I said I'd tell you the next thing when it happened, and not five things later. This is the next thing.

I lost to the Bronze on Monday, in the fourth, on Vell's call, and she was right to call it. The arm's stiff and the ribs catch; nothing's broken; it'll be a week. He bought me supper afterward and told me about a goat.

That night, after midnight, on my cot, there was another one. I'll copy it exactly, as I did the first.

He had copied the three lines letter by letter from the back of the Log, and checked them twice against the page, and then once more against the place in the dark behind his breastbone where they had been written first.

I think it came from him. Not from watching; I'd only watched him for one bout, and the first took three months. In the last exchange he threw me, and his hand stayed on my shoulder after the throw was finished, a second longer than it needed to. That's the only thing that doesn't fit anywhere else. It's one data point, and I've written that in the book where I'll have to look at it.

Lira knew first. I told her on Tuesday in the grey half before the light, and she read it twice and said she didn't know what it meant either, and gave me the bread.

I'm all right. I'm more than all right, most of the time. I lost and learned more than I've learned from most of the things I've won. I don't know what any of it is yet. I'm going to keep finding out.

At the carriers' hut at the bottom of the fish steps, the clerk with the inky fingers read the address out to the hut as he read every address, and weighed the letter on his little brass balance, and looked at Cael over it.

"Thinner than the last," he said.

"Torvin's," said the clerk, as he had said it every week since the autumn, as though it were a small private joke between the two of them, and hung it on the third hook along, under WEST.

Cael stood and looked at it. It was a single folded sheet, and it had in it two plain lines of figures copied from the dark, and in a week a man would sit down with it on a workshop step in Denvash and read it twice and not drink his tea. Cael had decided, at the kitchen table, that this was better than the other thing. He found, standing in the hut with the river going by outside and the barges knocking at the quay, that he had not changed his mind.

He went back up the steps one at a time, with his good hand on the rail.

[Steady, observant narration; let place, distance, and social position register]

The arm got better, slowly, the way arms did.

By Saturday he could close the left hand round a cup, though he could not yet lift the cup. By Sunday the swelling had gone down enough that he could see the shape of the bone again under the skin. The bruise had turned from black to a dark wet purple, and at its edges it had begun to go the colour of a pear left too long on a sill. The ribs caught at the top of every full breath, both sides, the left more than the right. The right hip, where the ground had come up, stiffened every night and loosened every morning on the long walk up the hill to the grey half, and he learned to leave early enough to let it.

On Monday he went down to the mender's.

The mender was at his bench with his loupe in and a clock on its back in front of him, and he did not look up when Cael came in under the four black-painted words on the doorframe. He did not look up for some time. It hurt a little to do it with the left. He did it with the left anyway, because he had been told to work it in cold water every morning and he thought that washers were very nearly the same thing.

Nobody said anything for the rest of the afternoon. At the end of it the mender counted the tins with his eyes, the way he always did, and nodded once over his clock, which meant Wednesday.

That was what he remembered about it afterward. Nothing had happened that morning to warn him. You are required to attend a senior evaluation, convened under the District Handbook, Part Six, at the post, Ardenmere, on the Thursday of this week, at the second hour after noon.

Under the closed-pending order of the fifty-fifth day, this evaluation discharges the senior authorization then applied for.

He read it twice, and then a third time, slowly, holding each word up against its neighbours, as he read everything he could not afford to get wrong. It did not change, and it did not say what would happen on Thursday at the second hour after noon, or what an assessor did, or what Part Six was. It said a time and a place and a name, and that was all it needed to say, because the time and the place and the name were the whole of it.

His hands were steady, which surprised him. He had thought for weeks that when it came he would feel it come, like the air leaning in Corvane's yard. Instead it had come against the salt crock on an ordinary Tuesday, between a bucket of cold water and a bowl of soup, and he felt mostly a kind of plain recognition, as you feel when a cart you have heard coming all morning finally turns the corner.

The six weeks had run out on the forty-second day, six weeks ago now. He had known it was coming, on every one of those days, and on most of them he had been too busy to look.

"I know you're not. That's not what I said." She stood up, under the slope of the ceiling, and he stood up too. "Go home. The widow's got a candle in her lap that she's going to light the minute your foot's off her bottom step, and she'll count to the top of it, and if you're still on the stair she'll tell the whole lane."

He went. On the fourth step, going down, he heard the door shut above him, and the key turn in it, and then, after a moment, the key turn back again, as though she had locked it from habit and then thought better of it, or worse.

[Steady, observant narration; let place, distance, and social position register]

Halden looked up from his table when Cael came down the three steps into the reading room, and looked at him for the length of a breath. Then he looked at the clock on the wall above the shelves, which said that it was very early indeed for anybody to want the law.

"Halden," said Halden.

"Part Six," said Cael.

Halden did not say anything for a moment. Then he got up from his table, slowly, as he had got up in the autumn, and walked down the long room to the left-hand shelves, and took down the thick district Handbook that Cael had read through twice in a day and most of a night. He did not bring it back to the long table. He turned it over in his hands and opened it from the back, and looked at what he found there, and came back along the room with it held open in both hands like a tray with something on it that might spill.

He set it down under the lamp.

The back of the book was a different paper. It was thicker and whiter and had been sewn in after the rest, and the pages had never been cut. They were still joined at the top and the outer edge, folded sheets, as they had come from the binder, so that you could look between them as into a row of little paper rooms and see that there was print inside, but not read it. At the head of the first sheet, upside down, it said PART SIX. THE SENIOR EVALUATION. RESERVED TO ASSESSORS.

"It's bound in with the district edition," said Halden. "Nobody's ever cut it." He took a paper knife from his own table, a thin bone thing worn yellow, and laid it beside the book. "Reserved to assessors means that an assessor is expected to know it. It doesn't mean anybody else may not. Anybody the registry has a number for may read anything in this room." He looked at the uncut pages. "Nobody has wanted to before."

"Thank you."

"I said I'd find you the next book." Halden went back to his table. Halfway there he stopped, and said over his shoulder, without turning round, "Begin at the beginning. Copy it from the first line. The people who start in the middle are always wrong about something."

So Cael began at the beginning.

He cut the pages one at a time, with the bone knife, carefully, slitting along the folds. The paper made a soft dry tearing sound in the quiet that seemed louder than it was. He read each page as it opened, and then he copied it into the front of the Log in his careful hand, all of it, every line, from Section 1: Definitions down. His left arm ached from holding the book flat, and he swapped hands, and it ached the other way.

It was dull, and it was long, and he understood very little of it on the first reading and a good deal more on the second. There were definitions, and who might ask for a senior evaluation, and how an assessor was to conduct one, and what happened when none of the rest applied. Section four was a long dry paragraph about practitioners whose classification could not be assessed by ordinary means, and a temporary category they could be entered under, and a facility they could be required to attend. He copied it line by line like all the rest, and thought, that's for people the Arbiter couldn't read, and went on to five.

By the time the light from the high windows had moved all the way across the long table and begun to go up the far wall, his hand had cramped twice and the Log had eleven more pages in it than it had had at dawn.

Halden came down the room at noon, when the reading room shut, to take the book back.

He looked at the cut pages, all of them slit now down their folds, lying open and loose, and then at Cael, and then at the Log.

"All of it?"

"From the first line."

Halden nodded slowly. He closed the book and held it for a moment with his hand flat on the cover, as if feeling whether anything inside had changed.

"Go home and read it again," he said. "Tonight. Slowly. You'll find something you didn't see here." He tucked the book under his arm. "People always do. It's why I tell them to copy it."

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

He read it again that night, at Torvin's kitchen table, after the lamps.

Torvin had said Lamps through the floorboards an hour ago. The range had been banked and was ticking as it cooled. Torvin's wife, going up, had looked at him sitting there with the Log open and a candle end in a saucer, and had not said anything, and had left the saucer. He had read the five sections through once, slowly, as Halden had told him to, and then again, more slowly. He had found nothing he had not found in the morning, and he had begun a third time.

Somewhere in the middle of the third reading, two hours before dawn, by a candle end gone down to a stub, section four stood up off the page.

It did not change. The words were the words he had copied in the reading room, every one. Where the primary classification of a practitioner cannot be assessed by ordinary means, the senior evaluator may enter the practitioner under a temporary non-standard category for the period of assessment. He had read it that morning and thought, that's for people the Arbiter couldn't read. He read it now and heard it in a different voice: in the voice of a woman who had read his objection three times with her lips moving, and had had weeks.

Cannot be assessed by ordinary means.

He had said that. He had handed Coss a sheet of paper that said exactly that, three months ago, at the desk that rocked. A standard evaluation could not assess his classification. That was the whole of his objection. That was the thing that had bought him six weeks.

And it was the first half of section four.

He sat very still at the kitchen table with the cold going through his shirt.

It was not fear, quite. It was the thing that came in the circle when a real opponent showed him what she meant to do, the cold clean alertness that sat under the ribs and made everything else very quiet. He had built the door himself, in the autumn, and walked through it, and been glad of it. Now he could see, from the other side, that it opened both ways. A careful assessor would only have to read his own objection back to him, and then turn the page.

Enter the practitioner under a temporary non-standard category. A practitioner so entered shall attend at a regional assessment facility within twenty-eight days, and remain there for the period of assessment.

Remain there. That meant not here. That meant a room in a building he had never seen, in a city two days west or further, for as long as somebody else decided an assessment took, and Lira and the grey half and the Cinder House and Torvin's and the mender's tins of washers all a long way off on the other side of it. It would all be done by procedure, correctly, with a stamp. Nobody would have to do anything a clerk could be ashamed of.

He made himself breathe, four and four, with the catch at the top.

Then he turned back three pages, to the beginning, because Halden had told him the people who started in the middle were always wrong about something, and because he did not yet know what else to do.

Section 1: Definitions.

He read them one at a time, with his finger under the line. Assessor. No. Senior evaluation. No. Primary classification: the classification returned by the practitioner's Arbiter at Kindling and entered in the registry, including any entry made in the Supplementary Register. He stopped. He read it again, and his finger did not move.

Then he read the next one.

Temporary non-standard category: the category under which a practitioner without primary classification is entered pending assessment.

He sat back.

The candle end guttered in its saucer and steadied. Somewhere upstairs the wheezing man began his long whistle at the top of every breath, and one of the brothers said something in his sleep about a rope.

Without primary classification.

The category was not for anybody whose classification could not be read. It was for people who did not have one. Section four gave an assessor the power to put a practitioner into the category, and section one, three pages earlier, said who could be in it. A boy whose Arbiter had returned nothing would be in it. A boy whose return had been lost, or never recorded, would be in it. And a boy whose Arbiter had taken eleven seconds and then returned a word, a real word, a word with four instances and a statute of its own in the Supplementary Register, and a brass plate that had lit eleven seconds late, had a primary classification. He had more of one than anybody in the district. It simply was not one the standard framework could use.

That was not the same as not having one. Section one said so, in the Compact's own words.

He did not let himself feel anything about it yet. He had learned that in the circle too. A plan that felt good at the mark was a plan you had not yet tested. He took a clean page at the front of the Log, and ruled it, and began to build the answer in four steps, as plainly as he could.

One. Section four lets the assessor put a practitioner into the temporary non-standard category when his classification can't be assessed by ordinary means. Mine can't. I said so myself.

Two. Section one, three pages before, says what that category is: it's for a practitioner without primary classification.

Three. Section one also says what a primary classification is: what the Arbiter returned, entered in the registry, including the Supplementary Register. Mine was entered there. Statute nineteen. Four instances. It resolved; the plate lit.

Four. So I have a primary classification. Section four gives her the power to put people in the category, and section one keeps me out of it. Not being assessable isn't the same as not being classified.

He read the four steps through. Then he read them from the bottom up, the fourth first, to see whether each one stood on the one below it or only leaned. They stood. He read them aloud under his breath, and they still stood.

Then he copied them clean onto the next page, without the crossings-out, in his best hand, short enough to say and not read. A thing said from memory across a desk sounded like knowledge, and a thing read from a page sounded like a hope.

When he looked up the window over the range had gone from black to grey, and Torvin's wife was standing at the foot of the stairs in her shawl, looking at him. He did not know how long she had been there.

She did not ask him anything. She went to the range and opened it and woke the fire, and put the oats on, and when they were done she put a bowl in front of him and stood over him with the wooden spoon until he had eaten all of it.

The clerk at the post's counter looked up at the clock on the wall behind him when Cael came in, and then down at Cael, and then at the bench.

She looked at him.

I have the power to enter you under the temporary category, and I'm inclined to use it, because it's the pathway the regulation provides for exactly this. You would come to regional. You'd be housed. You'd be assessed properly, by people who have instruments for it, over as long as it takes. It's not a punishment. It's the procedure." She folded her hands on the desk. "That's the case. He watched her wait.

He had watched a great many people stand on their marks and wait. Dessa waited like a wall; Corbin waited like a man reading a newspaper. This woman waited like somebody who had shut every door in a house, one after another, and was now standing in the hall listening to be sure that none of them would open. She had done it well. She had done it in order, with the words in the order the Handbook gave them, and she had not reached for the book once. If he had not sat at Torvin's kitchen table until the window went grey, he would have been sitting in the hall with her now, listening to the doors stay shut.

The classification returned by the practitioner's Arbiter at Kindling and entered in the registry, including any entry made in the Supplementary Register." He did not hurry. He had never once in his life been on the other side of a desk while somebody read. He did not like it much. "There's another thing," said Ilsev. "It isn't in the regulation, and I don't understand it, and I've thought for two days about whether to tell you. I've decided it's yours."

He sat very still.

"When I put your file into standard procedure at regional, to start this evaluation, it came back from the docket with a flag on it." She touched the corner of the face-down sheet with one finger, without turning it over. "A mark against the record. I didn't ask for it. I'd looked at the file the day before, when it was given to me, and the record was clean. The flag went on when I opened the procedure. Not before."

"What does it mean?"

"I don't know." She said it as flatly as she had said you're right. "I've looked for whose it is. Assessors keep the long registers, the ones a field agent never sees; I went through every one of them, and through the ones they point to. This doesn't come from any office I can find. Not mine. Not Coss's. Not any desk I've ever had a paper back from." She took the finger away from the sheet. "It might be nothing. It might be some old mark that goes on every file with a classification as rare as yours, that nobody ever bothered to write down anywhere I'd see it. I've thought of six things it might be that would be nothing at all."

She stopped, and he waited, because he could see that she had not finished.

"I don't believe any of the six. So I've put it in my report. A plain paragraph: that it's there, that I didn't request it, that I can't trace it, and that it went on when standard procedure began. I've drawn no conclusion from it, because I haven't got one to draw." She looked at him steadily. "Leaving it out would have made my report tidier and less true. I won't do that. And I thought that if I wouldn't do it to the regional office, I'd better not do it to you."

Cael did not say anything.

He was putting it where he put things. He could feel himself doing it: picking it up and weighing it, as he would have weighed a tell he had never met before, and setting it down beside the others. There was a sweep in the autumn that nobody had been able to account for. There was a man who had sat across a desk from him and said I don't know about it, and meant it, and would not be asked again. And now there was a mark on his record that had appeared on the morning somebody began to treat him like an ordinary case, and that a woman with more ways to look than Coss could not find the end of. He did not know what any of them were. He did not know whether they were one thing or three.

His hands had gone cold on his knees, and he left them there.

"Thank you for telling me."

Ilsev did not answer that. She stood up, and took her coat off the back of the chair, and put it on, and did up the buttons one at a time from the bottom, without hurrying, as if she were giving him the time it took to do them up.

When the last button was done she looked at him. "It isn't a gift. It's a fact about you, and facts about you are yours. You're owed the true thing, even when I can only give you the first half of the sentence."

She picked up the folder and the face-down sheet and put the sheet inside the folder without turning it over, and tucked the folder under her arm.

At the top of the stair she stopped and looked back at him.

"Mind the stair. It's narrower going down." She considered him a moment longer, with the plain attention that seemed to be the whole of her face. "Read the rest of the Handbook, Cael. All of it. Somebody should."

Then she went down the stair sideways, and he heard her say something to the clerk at the counter, and the street door stick and open and shut, and he was alone in the room over the fish steps with the desk that did not rock.

He sat there until he could feel his hands again. Then he went down.

Chapter 50 — A Talk Owing

[Restrained, watchful narration; keep the evaluation pressure close and human]

Lira was at the rail at the top of the fish steps where she had said she would be, with her arms folded on it and her face turned to the river, and she turned round when the door of the post stuck and opened and let him out.

She did not ask. She looked at him, the whole of him at once, and he watched her read it: that he was walking, and alone, and had no paper in his hand, and that there was something else in his face under the walking that she had not seen there before.

"It held," he said. "Legal review. Months."

She let her breath out. He saw her shoulders come down a finger's width, and then go up again, because she had seen the something else.

"And?"

"Walk with me."

He did not know, when he said it, where he was going. He knew only that he could not stand still at the top of the fish steps with the post at his back and say the rest of it, not yet, not with the door that stuck still swinging behind him. His legs knew where they were going before he did. They took him up away from the river and across the corner of the food market, past the bread woman's high cracked lantern and the cheese stall's dark one, and up the narrowing street toward the yards. It was not until he saw the black square of the Cinder House sign at the corner two streets below the lane that he understood.

It was Thursday, and there was a card.

Lira walked beside him the whole way and did not say a word. Once, at the corner of the market, she looked at him sideways as if she were about to, and he saw her pick the question up and look at it and put it down again beside her, as she had learned to do. He was grateful to her for that. He did not have the words in the right order yet, and he did not want to give them to her in the wrong one.

Vell was at her table in the shade of the back wall with her tea and her ledger and her pen laid across the page.

Cael went round the outside of the rope to the table, and stood in front of it, and waited for the exchange in the circle to finish, because you did not talk to Vell while there was an exchange in the circle.

The Force man put the Blade on his back. Vell said "End of the exchange," and then turned her head.

She looked at him, and at his left arm, which he was still holding a little away from his side, and at the bruise showing under his cuff, and at his face.

He had said them to Vell on a frozen Saturday three weeks ago, before Feryn, and to Dessa herself in the autumn, before the first time. "Then she can look at it on Saturday as well." Vell picked up her pen and looked at the circle, where the next pair were coming over the rope. "You're standing in my light."

He stepped out of it.

Lira took him up on the cooper's roof, because she said there were some things the yard should not hear, and she could see from his face that this was one of them.

They went up the ladder at the back of the shed and sat on the flat of the roof with their backs against the warm chimney. The spring had not got very far yet. He thought about that. He had thought it himself on the stool behind the partition, in other words. It was different to hear it said out loud on a roof by somebody who was not inside it.

He wrote to Hesk that night at the kitchen table, after the lamps.

He wrote it all. He had promised to, and he wanted to, which was not always the same thing. He wrote about Part Six and the bone knife and the uncut pages, because he thought Hesk would like the uncut pages more than anything else in the letter. He wrote section four out, and section one, and the four steps between them, plainly, the way he would have written out a load figure. He wrote you're right, twice, and legal review, and months. He wrote Coss at the window. He wrote the flag, exactly as Ilsev had given it to him, with nothing added and nothing taken away.

He wrote that he had a bout with Dessa on Sunday week, and that she had asked for it herself, and that his arm would be an arm by then.

Then he stopped, with the pen over the page.

There was a question he had been carrying since the roof. It had been sitting in him, under everything else, and it had not got any smaller. He did not know how to put it, and he had nobody else to put it to who would know more than he did, and he thought that if anybody in the world did, it might be a man who had worked in the Compact's own offices at twenty-two and left them.

He wrote it as plainly as he could.

I want to ask you something, and I don't need the answer quickly. People here know me now. Not what I am; most of them don't know that, and the ones who do haven't made much of it. But they know my face. The cook. Vell. The yard. The boys with the bets. Forty-one people stood in the sleet to see me lose. If whoever made that mark wanted me gone, would any of that matter? Or does it only feel like a wall, because I'm standing inside it, and from the other side it isn't one at all?

I don't know which. I think you might.

— Cael

He read it over twice by the candle end. Then he folded it and put it in the leather book to keep flat for the morning, and sat at the scrubbed table with the range ticking, and counted, as he did now, what he had not told Hesk.

There was nothing to count; he had told him everything there was. It was only that the everything had got larger.

At noon on Friday the carriers' clerk weighed it on the brass balance and looked at Cael over it.

"Yes."

"Torvin's," said the clerk, and hung it on the third hook.

He went to the Sunday card that week to watch, because there was nothing else he knew how to do with a week, and Dessa was not on it.

He had known she would not be. She fought when Vell put her down, and Vell had put her down for him, and Dessa had never in her life wasted a bout on a week she meant to spend getting ready. He took his hand off the stake.

He thought about it that night on the cot, and in the morning, coming up the hill in the dark with the bread, he gave her the list.

"I put my hand on the ground at my mark. Everybody knows that now. I go in on a tell, when I've found one; I always have. I count my breath, four and four, the way she does. I stand off for the first exchange and watch. I don't strike much." He gave her the bread. "That's all I can think of."

Lira tore the loaf and gave him half. She did not say anything. She went to her mark, and stood there in the grey half with her hands loose, and looked at him.

It was a small nod, very short, a dip of the chin no bigger than a sparrow taking a drink, and it was his. He knew it at once, the way you know your own handwriting on a page you do not remember writing. It was the nod he gave himself on his mark when the plan had come right and he was about to go. She had found it in the autumn, and done it at him then, and he had spent most of the winter trying to wear it away.

She looked at him steadily. "When you're tired it comes back. When you're hit, it comes back. He stood with the bread in his hand and did not eat it.

They worked on it all week.

It was not like the step, or the build, or anything he had learned in the grey half before. There was nothing to learn. There was only something to stop doing, and stopping was harder than doing, because the nod did not come from anywhere he could reach. It came out of the very place where he made up his mind; it was the outside of the inside of deciding. Every time he got ready to go in the box drill, his chin went down, a hair, and Lira said there and he had to begin again. By Wednesday he could keep it in when he was fresh, nine times in ten. By Wednesday afternoon, after the mender's and two hours of the box drill at full speed, he could keep it in three times in ten, and the other seven Lira said there, more and more quietly, until she stopped saying it and only touched her own chin.

"Eight days isn't a season," she said on Thursday, sitting on the low wall. "It didn't go in a season and it won't come out in eight days."

"Then what do I do?"

"I don't know." She gave him his half of the bread. "Go in knowing it's there. That's more than you had yesterday."

Hesk's letter came on Friday, against the salt crock.

It was the answer to the thin one, the one with the second notice in it, and it was thin too, which he took as a good sign before he had opened it. Hesk wrote long when he was frightened and could not do anything with it. He wrote short when he had decided.

Two, then. I read your letter on the step and at the bench and at the kitchen table, which makes three, and I'll stop there, because there's a level for the survey office on the bench that won't true itself.

I'll tell you what I felt first, since you'd ask. I was frightened for your arm before I was frightened for the other thing. That should tell you what I am before I'm anything else. Work it in cold water. Don't lift with it till it tells you you can.

The other thing I can't help you with, and I won't pretend to. I don't know what a hand can carry. I don't know what anything can carry, in this. I know you wrote "one data point" in your own book where you'd have to look at it, and I was prouder of those three words than of anything else in the letter, the notice included. Keep writing them. A man who writes "one" when he'd like to write "two" will be all right.

A man who beats you and then buys your supper is a man worth knowing. Keep his account open.
