In Denvash, a week behind, Hesk opened the timepiece.

It had come in on Thursday from a house on the canal, a merchant's carriage clock in a case of dark wood and brass, very fine, with a face painted with small blue flowers. It had come with a story. It had belonged, the merchant's man said, to three households in eleven years, and each of them had passed it on because it stopped. It stopped at no hour in particular and for no reason anybody could find, and started again the next day as if nothing had happened, and the last household had sent it to a woman who read cards before they would let it in the house again. The card woman had said it was unlucky. So the merchant, who had bought it cheap for that reason and was not a man who believed in cards, had sent it to the instrument-maker on Fen Street, to be told it was not.

Hesk had it open on the bench under the lamp with the back off, and the works lying in their brass frame like a small town seen from above.

He found it in a quarter of an hour. It was a single spring in the going train, the smallest one, seated a hair loose in its post, so that when the clock was jolted, or the room went cold, or nothing at all happened that anybody would ever notice, it slipped a tooth and the whole town stopped. It had been loose for eleven years. Three households and a card woman had told one another stories about it, and not one of them had ever taken the back off.

He sat looking at it. Then he reached behind him without looking for the drawer marked Springs, fine, and found the size he wanted by feel, as he found everything in that drawer. He did it with the left hand, because the right still had the long pink line across the palm where a coil from the next drawer down had gone into it in the autumn. He had never mentioned the hand in a letter. He did not think he would.

When the new spring was seated, he set the clock going, and listened to it.

The letter was on the end of the bench, where it had been for four weeks. It had come at the end of the second week of the spring, the one with the bone knife in it, and you're right, and Coss at the window, and a mark on a record that a careful woman could not trace. He had answered that letter in four lines within a day, because he had not been able to bear not answering it. He had not answered the question at the end of it. He had read the question every night since. He had answered the district letter, and said I'm close, and he had not been close. He had been sitting with the question as he sat with a figure that would not come out. It was a number he could not trace back to where it came from, and he would not sign it until he could.

If whoever made that mark wanted me gone, would any of that matter?

He looked at the clock with the small blue flowers on its face, going, and thought about how it had come to be on his bench at all. Then he saw that the answer was sitting in it, as plain as a spring once the back is off.

He thought about a file, thirty-two years ago, opened in a room he had stood in at twenty-two. He thought about how few people had ever known it was opened at all, and he stopped there. He stopped there as he always did, at the edge of it, with the old care, and did not go on. It was not his to go into tonight. Tonight was the boy's.

He took a sheet of paper from the shelf and uncapped the ink and wrote.

You asked me a question a month ago and I said I'd answer it when I had an answer I'd sign. I've had a clock on the bench this week that three families called cursed, and the curse was one loose spring the size of a fingernail paring. I'll tell you about it properly another time. But a thing that's known can't be put in a drawer without somebody asking where it went. A thing that's talked about gets brought to a bench, in the end, and somebody takes the back off. The quiet things are the ones that go out with the ashes.

He stopped and read it. It was nearly what he meant, and not quite. He sat with the pen over the paper while the clock went on beside him, steady, through a whole minute, two.

Then he wrote the rest of it.

Being seen is not the same as being safe. But it's not nothing.

Keep being known. Keep me told. I'm proud of you past anything I've the words for, and I'll say so properly when I've found them.

He read it twice. He did not read it a third time, because he was afraid that if he did he would start to change it, and it was right.

He folded it and sealed it and wrote on the front of it, in his square hand, ROOMS (the O leans), and the rest of the address, and propped it against the clock on the shelf over the bench, where he propped everything that had to go in the morning. It would go in the east bag at noon. It would be a week on the road. Whatever was happening in Ardenmere tonight, it had already happened by now. It would have happened a week ago by the time the boy broke the seal.

He sat a while longer in the lamplight, listening to the merchant's clock with the blue flowers on it, going, and not stopping, and not stopping.

[Building, spatially clear narration; earn the public confrontation and let its consequences land]

On Monday morning he stood in front of the board at the triangle and read what was not on it.

It was a good board, as boards went. It had been there longer than anybody could remember, a slab of old door nailed to the side of the cooper's shed where the three lanes met, and everything the district wanted the district to know went up on it sooner or later. There were rooms to let and a dog gone missing and a man in the river workshops who would mend a kettle while you waited. There was a notice about the gutter dispute between the cooper and the dyer, written by the dyer and corrected in charcoal by the cooper. And in the middle, where the light was best, there was Vell's card for Sunday, on the back of a bill for lamp oil, in her small square hand.

He knew every card she had put up since the autumn. He had read them all here, standing where he was standing now. For seven months the line under his bouts had said the same thing: unrated (vouched). It had said it under Renn, twice, and under Dessa, twice, and under Sarel and Talis and Corbin and the rest. When the yard had chalked a joke on the board after Corbin, it had been about Corbin putting his hand up, and not about the boy who had made him do it. The board knew him as a line in brackets.

He had never minded; he had wanted it that way, because in the autumn a line in brackets had been the safest thing a person could be.

He took the Log out of his coat and turned to the back, and stood at the board with it open on his forearm, and wrote down every person in Ardenmere who would ask where he had gone if he did not come back.

It did not take long. Lira. That one was first and needed nothing beside it. Torvin. Torvin's wife. Yeni. Sella. Doss. The house, all of it, even the wheezing man, perhaps, though only because Cael's cot would be empty and the wheezing man would have nobody to complain to about the draught. The old man. He would not ask anybody; he would stand in his gate and notice the lane was short of somebody, and that would be all. The mender. Halden. The boys, both of them, though they would ask each other and then argue about it. The bread woman. He had no name to write for her and wrote the bread woman. The fruit woman, the same. Vell, and then he looked at it and was not sure, and put a small mark beside it, as he did beside a tell he had seen only once.

Fourteen. Five of them without names that he knew.

He looked at the list. Then he thought about Coss's drawer.

The drawer for things that are finished. Coss had said it plainly, across a pie he had not eaten, as a kindness. A file closed on voluntary relocation was a file nobody opened again. It was not hidden, or burned; it only went into a drawer with a great many others, and the drawer was shut, and nobody ever had a reason to pull it out again. Nothing bad happened to a file like that. Nothing happened to it at all.

Fourteen people could be told a boy had gone home, and most of them would believe it, and the ones who did not would have nobody to ask.

He turned back a page to where he had written, two nights ago on the cot, that he did not know what he would do instead of leaving, and read it again. I'm going to find out the way I find out everything. He had found it out, he thought, standing at a board, by reading what was not on it.

Vell had a custom about her book. She had told it to him in the autumn, in his first week, when he had wanted to know why his name was not in it: a name went into Vell's book when the yard came to see it. It was no slight, she had said; it was what a book was for, since a fighter the yard did not come for was a fighter the yard would not miss. So she wrote him the way the yard knew him, in brackets, and waited.

Nobody had ever come to the Cinder House to see Cael. They had come to see Renn, or Dessa, or a Bronze in the sleet, and he had been the thing on the other side of the rope.

He shut the Log. Across the triangle the cooper was rolling a barrel out of his shed with his foot, very slowly, and the dyer was standing in her doorway with her arms folded, watching him do it.

Quiet made me easy to put away, he thought. So I'll stop being quiet.

He said it once more in his head, to see whether it held, and it did. Then he went up the lane toward the Cinder House, walking fast, before he could start finding all the reasons it would not.

She turned the ledger round to its own side again and wrote, at last, a single short line at the bottom of the page, and blotted it, and he could not read it upside down. "I'll send to Feryn. He's working the river towns this month, or he was a week ago. He'll know who's touring and who's worth a gate, and who'd rather stop than win." She looked up. "Now go and stand in somebody else's light."

He went back down the lane with what he had come for, and it should have felt like more than it did. The cold place under his ribs went down the hill with him, and he did not look at it.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Feryn came on Wednesday afternoon. He did not come to the Cinder House, or to Vell's table. He came to Torvin's, and when Cael came in from the mender's he found him in the yard, sitting on the low wall by the pump in his once-good coat, eating an apricot out of a paper and swinging one heel against the stones as if he lived there.

"Vell says you want to be loud."

"Yes."

"I came up on the barge this morning to find out why." Feryn finished the apricot and looked for somewhere to put the stone, and put it in his pocket. "Two days I've been thinking about it on a deck full of cabbages. You know what I thought first, when her note came? I thought, there it is. All winter that boy's been the most careful fighter I've ever stood across from, and he's finally found something stupid to do." Cael opened his mouth, and Feryn waved the apricot at him. "That was the barge talking. The barge is usually wrong. I've lost more money listening to barges than to bookmakers." He shifted along the wall to make room. "Sit down. Convince me."

Cael sat.

He told it as he would have told a bout, from the beginning, in order. He told it without Coss's name, but with everything else: a sweep through the market in the autumn that nobody could account for, a thin file, a mark on it that a careful woman from regional had found and could not trace. Then a man who had come to tell him, off the record, that there was a way out, if he took it quietly. A drawer for things that were finished. Fourteen names on the back page of a book, five of them without names.

Feryn listened. He did not interrupt, except twice, and both times with a question that went straight to a joint in the thing. Who told you about the drawer? Somebody who wanted you to have the choice. And: What does Vell get out of it? A full yard and a straight book. Cael answered both and went on, and watched Feryn turn each answer over and fit it in, as he had watched him turn over the third exchange at Amrit's.

When it was done Feryn sat with his elbows on his knees, looking at the pump.

"So you'd like to cost them something," he said at last. "That's a fighter's answer, anyway. Not a clerk's." He rubbed his jaw. "I've heard worse plans. I've made most of them, and I'm still here, which is more than the plans are." He was quiet a moment longer, and then he sat up. "All right. I know a name."

Cael waited.

"Darrow Innes." Feryn said it as though he were setting a weight down on the wall between them. "Bronze Rank 1. Iron Path. He's been doing this for money for eight years, which is longer than me, and he's good, and he's careful. I've never heard of him putting anybody in the healers' who didn't need to be put there." He looked at Cael sideways. "Do you know what Iron does?"

"I've watched two. A Bronze in my second week, and a Copper from Fenrow."

"Then you've watched it take." Feryn nodded slowly. "That's all Iron does, at the bottom of it. You hit it and it takes it, and it doesn't give it back. It goes in and goes somewhere and you never see it again. At Copper it's a thick hide. At Bronze it's a wall that's had eight years to learn where to put things." He turned the paper with the apricots in it round in his hands. "Darrow's touring. Down the river and back up it, the way I did, looking for gates with a name on them before his own evaluation in the autumn. He'll come for a marquee if it's a straight book and a full yard. He likes a straight book."

"Why him?"

"Because he won't kill you," said Feryn simply, "and he won't make it easy either, and either way you'll know something when it's over. And because if you beat him, it'll be said in five towns by the end of the month, and that's what you want." He looked at Cael. "Isn't it?"

"Yes."

Feryn put the paper of apricots down on the wall between them.

"I'll write to him tonight. He's two towns down, at a yard on the coal wharf, till the weekend." He stood, and brushed off his coat, and stood there a moment longer, looking down at Cael on the wall.

"You can ask," he said. "You've been wanting to since I sat down."

"Why are you doing it? You've got your own evaluation. You don't owe me anything."

Feryn did not answer quickly. He sat down again, which Cael had not expected, and looked at the pear tree in the corner, where the frost-browned flowers had all come down and the first small leaves had come out in their place.

"I did Bronze on my own," he said. "Nobody put a name across from mine that meant anything till I'd beaten every name in two circuits that didn't. I sat outside keepers' tables for the best part of two years at Copper, waiting to be worth somebody's afternoon. It took longer than it should have, and it cost more, and the people who could have made it shorter made it shorter for each other." He shrugged. "I always said that when I was somebody I wouldn't do that. Then I was somebody, and I'd forgotten." He picked up an apricot and looked at it. "And it's selfish as well, if you want the whole of it. I'd like to be there. I'd like to be able to say I was."

He put the apricot in his mouth and stood up for good this time.

"Tell Vell I've written," he said round it. "She'll want to know before I do."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He told Vell. He went up to the Cinder House straight away, while Feryn went off down the lane toward the river with his coat flapping, and found her at her table with the Wednesday card half written, and told her: Darrow Innes, Bronze Rank 1, Iron Path, a letter going down the river tonight.

Vell wrote the name on the corner of her blotter and looked at it.

"I've seen him once. Three summers ago, at Fenrow, against a Blade with a temper. He let the Blade wear the temper out on him for four exchanges, and then he put him down so gently the man thanked him." She tapped the name with her pen. "He doesn't spend anything he doesn't have to. You'd like him." She was quiet for a moment. "Yes. If he'll come, yes."

"Thank you."

"Thank me when he's come." She went back to the card, and then, still writing, in exactly the same voice: "Has the girl been told?"

It was nearly five o'clock. Lira was across the district at her sparring hour, and had been since two, and he had not seen her since the grey half that morning. In the grey half that morning he had done the box drill and the deflection and forty strokes at the post, and she had chalked a ring in the W column and written less beside it. And he had not said one word to her about Darrow Innes, or about Feryn on the barge, or about Monday, or about the board.

It was not that he had forgotten; he knew that was not it as soon as he went looking. He had carried it up the lane on Monday and back down again, and all through Tuesday at the post, and he had decided at every turn that he would tell her when there was something to tell, when it was real, when there was a name.

There had been a name for three hours.

"Tonight," he said.

Vell did not say anything. She looked at him over the card, and kept looking, until he understood that she had known the answer before she asked. Then she looked back down at what she was writing.

"Before the lamps. The widow's particular."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The fourth stair up to Lira's room talked. It had a creak in the middle that no amount of stepping to the side could get round, and she had told him once that she knew everybody in the house by how they managed it. When he came up that evening she had the door open before he reached the landing.

"You're early," she said. "And you went round the fourth on the left. You never go round it on the left." She stood in the doorway with her hair down and a shirt of hers half mended over one arm. "What's happened?"

"Can I come in?"

"Before the lamps." She stepped back. "Sit on the chair. Not the bed. The widow listens."

He sat on the chair. It was the only one, and it rocked. Lira sat down on the end of her bed with the shirt in her lap, and the evening light came in through the cracked pane she had mended with paper, the one that looked out toward Torvin's chimney, and lay across the boards between them.

He told her.

He told it as he had told Feryn, from the beginning: the board, the fourteen names, the drawer. Vell's table on Monday, and the three conditions. Feryn on the wall, a name, a letter going down the river tonight to a yard on a coal wharf: Darrow Innes, Bronze Rank 1, Iron Path.

She did not say anything while he talked. She sat with the shirt and the needle in her lap and did not sew, and she did not look at him; she looked at the floor between his boots. When he got to the letter going down the river, she put the needle into the shirt, very carefully, and left it there.

Then she looked up.

"You arranged this without asking me first."

"I was going to tell you tonight. Vell said—"

"That's telling." Her voice was quite level. It was the level of her voice at the barrel, which he had learned was the level she used when everything underneath it was not. "Telling's when it's done. Asking's when it isn't." She folded the shirt in half, and then in half again. "You went to Vell on Monday. You stood at the post with me on Tuesday, and this morning, and did forty strokes and let me chalk you a ring, and you'd already been to Vell. And then Feryn came up on a barge, and gave you a name, and you said yes to it, and it's in a letter." She put the folded shirt down beside her. "And now you've come up my stairs, round the fourth on the left, to tell me."

He opened his mouth, and shut it.

"Vell made it a condition. Didn't she. That I be told." It was not a question. "Told. She knew you, Cael. She's been keeping a book on you since the autumn, and she knew exactly what you'd do, and she made a rule about it, and you still went and did it."

"I hadn't signed anything."

He heard how it sounded as it came out. So did she. She did not answer it. She only looked at him, and waited, and he sat in the rocking chair and heard it go on sounding in the small room after it had stopped.

"Iron." She said it quietly. "An Iron Bronze. I stood at that barrel in the sleet and watched a Bronze put you on your back in the first exchange, before you'd seen anything at all. I watched you get up at eight. I watched you go into the fourth knowing you couldn't read it fast enough, because you'd decided you had to know. And I didn't say a word, because it was yours to decide, and you'd decided it with me. We'd sat on that roof and gone through it. Every piece." She was very still. "This one's bigger than Feryn. And I'm hearing it after the letter's gone."

He had a great many things he could have said. He could feel them lining up behind his teeth, all of them true: that he had been going to tell her; that it had moved faster than he had meant it to; that he had wanted a name before he brought her anything, so that she would have something real to look at; that he had kept Vell's condition to the letter. All of it was true, and all of it was the wrong size, and he knew, sitting there, that if he said any of it she would hear an excuse and be right to.

So he put all of it down, and said the thing underneath it.

"I didn't ask you because I was afraid you'd say no."

Lira did not move.

"And then I'd have had to listen to you. Because you'd have been right, or near enough, and I'd have known it. And I'd decided already, on Monday, at the board. I didn't want to have to undecide it." He made himself look at her. "So I did it in an order where you couldn't. I don't think I said that to myself. But that's what I did."

It was very quiet. Somewhere below them the widow was moving about in her shop, putting the shutters up.

"I've done it before. To Hesk. I kept five things from him for months, and told myself every week that I'd tell him when I understood them. I kept the step from you for three weeks. You made a rule about it, and I said it back to you, and I meant it." He looked at his hands. "It's the worst thing I do. I do it when I'm frightened of what somebody will say. And I did it to you, on the one thing that's yours as much as mine."

Lira gave him the look she gave a stance at the mark, the whole of it, from the feet up, before anything had moved.

"Right," she said at last.

She picked up the folded shirt, and put it down again on the other side of her.

"Tell me all of it, then. Properly. All the parts you didn't, because you thought I'd say no to them. What Feryn said about Iron. What Vell said about the crowd. What you're going to do about it, if you know, and what you don't know, if you don't." She drew her feet up onto the bed and sat with her arms round her knees. "If there's a piece you kept back because it'd frighten me, I want that piece first. I'd rather be worried and informed," she said, "than calm and useless."

So he told her all of it. It took a long time. He told her Feryn's first thought on the barge and Vell's not all of that is the kind of looking you want. He told her Feryn's two years outside the keepers' tables. He told her what Feryn had said about Iron taking things and not giving them back, and that he did not know what to do about that yet, not even slightly, and that it frightened him, and that he had not said so to Feryn or Vell. She asked questions, short ones, and each of them went to a joint, and by the end of it she was not looking at the floor any more. She was looking at the wall above his head, as she looked at nothing when she was adding.

"Iron. We'll have to find out what it does from the inside. I don't know anything about it. Nobody at the academy fought Iron against Wind girls; they thought we'd run away from it." She pressed her chin on her knees. "We will, as well. Some of the time."

"Then you're—"

"I'm in." She said it flatly. "I was always going to be in. That was never the question. You'd have known that, if you'd asked." She looked at him then, straight, and there was nothing level left in her voice. "But hear this, because I'm only going to say it once. I'm not angry any more. I've decided not to be, and I've done it. But it was given. You didn't earn it tonight, and you haven't paid it off by telling me now. It's just given." She held his eyes. "This forgiveness doesn't renew automatically. If you do it again, with something this size, I don't know what I'll do. I honestly don't. I only know it won't be this."

"I won't."

"Don't promise me. Show me." She unwound her arms from her knees. "In a month you can promise."

The light on the boards had gone orange and was going grey. She looked toward the window, toward Torvin's chimney beyond the paper mend, and he thought she was going to send him home. Instead she said, quite differently, almost to herself:

"You're more like him than you probably realize."

"Hesk?"

"He knew about you for years. He sat on it. He decided on his own what you could carry, and when, and you found out in a side room with a word on a plate." She turned the needle in the folded shirt. "And he'd have done this as well, I think. What you're doing. Gone and stood in the middle of the market, so nobody could ever say they hadn't seen him." She looked back at him. "Both halves. That's what I mean."

"Is it meant kindly?"

Lira considered it.

"Half of it," she said.

Down in the street somebody was lighting the first lamp, and the widow's voice came up the stairwell, not loud, saying a word that could have been anybody's name and was plainly meant for both of them. Lira stood up.

"Go home. Before she comes up. Grey half tomorrow, at first light. Not after it." She held the door. "And Cael."

He stopped on the landing.

"Go round the fourth on the right. Like you always do. I want to know it's you."

Chapter 55 — The Term

[Building, spatially clear narration; earn the public confrontation and let its consequences land]

Lira heard him go round the fourth stair on the right, and then she heard the street door, and then she sat on the end of her bed in the near dark and let herself shake.

It was not much, only her hands, mostly, and something in the backs of her knees. She sat and waited for it to finish, and it took longer than she would have liked. When it was done she lit the candle with the third match, because the first two broke, and sat looking at the flame.

She had not been lying. She had decided not to be angry and had done it, there in front of him, and that was the easy part; she had always been able to put anger down when she chose to, as you could put a stone down if you had picked it up yourself. What she could not put down was the thing that had been under the anger, which she had not let him see, and which had come up through the floor of her as soon as he was gone.

An Iron Bronze. Eight years for money.

She got up and went to the window and stood with her forehead nearly on the paper mend. Across the roofs Torvin's chimney was a black shape against a sky that still had some green in it. He would be in the yard by now, or on the stairs, going up past the brothers' door to the cot under Yeni's lamp. He would sit on the end of the cot and write it all down, Lira, told and the day, and something about the fourth stair, probably, because he wrote things down like that. And then he would write that it was the worst thing he did, because he had said so to her face and he would not let himself say a thing out loud that he had not also put in the book.

She thought about the sleet.

She had stood at the barrel with her arms folded on the top of the rope, as she always stood, and watched a man in a good coat stroll about the circle with his hands half open. Then the air had come down out of nowhere on top of Cael and folded his guard flat and put him on his back before he had seen anything at all. She had not moved; her arms had stayed folded on the rope, and she had stood there and counted with Vell, under her breath, because counting was something to do with her mouth, and at six he had rolled over, and at eight he had stood up, and she had not moved.

Afterwards he had said she looked calm, and she had let him say it.

She had not been calm. She had been doing the thing she had learned at the academy, in the examination hall, on the morning she skipped the middle of the deflection in front of three examiners and a slate. She had done it clean, and better than the form; she had known it was better while she was doing it, and she had seen in their faces that they knew it too, and that it did not matter. She had stood still in the middle of the floor while they wrote, with her hands at her sides and her face giving them nothing at all. Then she had walked out of the hall, very straight, and down the back stairs where the coal went up, and sat on the third step from the bottom in the dark, and come apart there, quietly, where nobody could see it but the coal.

She had come apart afterwards, and nobody had ever known, and for years she had been rather proud of that.

At the barrel in the sleet she had done the same thing, only without the stairs, and it had nearly not worked. That was what she had been carrying round since the winter without looking at it. At the fourth exchange, when Feryn came in fast and put his hand where Cael was going and turned him over, she had been halfway through the rope before she knew it, with her hands on it and her weight already going. Then Vell had called it, and she had stopped, and nobody had seen. But she knew.

And this one was bigger.

She turned away from the window and sat down on the rocking chair he had sat on, which was still warm, and put her elbows on her knees.

She could stand back. That was the first thing she made herself look at, because it was the thing that had been sitting in the corner of the room since he said Darrow Innes, waiting to be looked at. She could coach him from the post in the grey half, and do it well, and build him the best two weeks anybody had ever built for a Copper. Then, on the day, she could stand somewhere further off than the barrel, by the gate, say, with the girls from the wall, where she would not have her hands on the rope or count under her breath with Vell. Nobody would think less of her. Most of the people who trained fighters in this district did not stand at the rope at all; they stood at the back, or went to the eel stalls and waited to be told.

She looked at it honestly, all of it, the way he would have wanted her to, and the way she would have made him.

Then she put it down.

She would not be any use by the gate. She knew how he fought now better than anyone in the district, better than Vell, perhaps, though Vell would never have allowed it. She knew where his hips went square when he was tired and where his left foot turned out on the back corner, and what his ears did when he was going to say gone and did not want to. She knew that he nodded before he moved, and that Dessa had read it, and that a Bronze who had been doing this for eight years would read it sooner. And she knew that the touch to her chin from the barrel had told him about the nod in Dessa's third exchange, and that he had seen it and believed it in the middle of a fight. Nobody by the gate could do that, and nobody but her.

So she was in. She had said it to him and it had been true when she said it, and now she said it to herself in her own room with nobody listening, and it was still true.

That left the other thing, the one the stairs had been for.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

She took the tin out of her pocket.

It was a flat tin that had once had throat sweets in it, with a picture of a lady in a hat on the lid, worn nearly off. She had carried it since the autumn and counted it on this bed perhaps a hundred times, and three weeks ago she had counted it, and there was enough in it for a cart. Fenrow, or further. She had sat on the low wall at the Cinder House and told him so, and then told him she had put it back in her pocket, and she had meant that too.

She opened it and counted it again now, by the candle, out of habit, and it was the same as it had been; it did not know anything had happened.

During, she thought, I'll be at the barrel. She would be where she always was, with her arms on the rope and her face giving away nothing at all, and she would watch him and tell him what she saw, with her chin and her fingers and once, perhaps, with his name. She would not come through the rope, and she would not count under her breath with Vell. She would coach him, all of her, from the first exchange to the last, and she would not let one bit of her be anything else while he was in there, because he would look at her, and he had to see a coach.

And after—

She sat with that, because it was harder than the first part. The first part she had done before, at the academy and in the sleet. The second part she had never done; she had always gone down the back stairs.

She looked at the cracked pane, and the paper over it, and Torvin's chimney gone black now beyond it, and said it out loud, quietly, to see what it sounded like in the room.

"During, I coach," said Lira. She heard her own voice go flat and steady on it, the barrel voice, and was glad. Then, more slowly: "After, I get to be a person."

It sounded strange, like something said by somebody who was not her. She said it again, and the second time it sounded a little more like her, and the third time she found that she meant it. After the call, whatever the call was, she would not go down any stairs. She would let it come up wherever she was standing, in front of whoever was there, him included. If it was fear he would see it, and if it was the other thing he would see that. She had spent years being the girl who came apart only where nobody could see, and she had been proud of it, and she thought now, sitting on a warm chair in the dark, that it had been a kind of lie. It was not a large one, but he had told her the truth about himself tonight, the worst of it, out loud in this room, and she did not see why she should keep a smaller one about herself.

That was a term. She had set it, and she would keep it, and nobody but her would ever know it had been set.

She pinched the candle out.

In the dark she thought about Iron, of which she knew nothing except that it took a blow and did not give it back; she had seen a Copper Iron from Fenrow take a long right from Dessa on the forearms and not even look at it. Power was no good against a thing whose whole Path was taking power in. You could not hit through it; you would break your hands trying, and he had good hands, and they were the only ones he had.

So not power. She lay down on the bed in her clothes and looked at the ceiling and added.

Power went in and went somewhere; everybody said so. It goes in and goes somewhere, and you never see it again. Very well. If you could not hit through a thing, you could perhaps hit it in the same place, again and again, before it had finished putting the last one away. She had a strike like that herself, one strike, short and straight from the hip, that she had spent two weeks at the post on when she was new to the district. Nothing about it was meant to hurt anybody; it was meant to arrive in the same place every time. She had taught it to him in the autumn, and he had liked it, because it was the one strike he owned.

Precision that piles up, she thought. Not one that ends things. One that adds.

It was her way, the way she had always wanted to do everything and had never been let: one small true thing, the same small true thing, until it added up to more than anybody had thought it could. Nobody at the academy had ever let her finish adding anything.

She was asleep before she had finished adding this. She woke before it was light with the sum still there, and went down through the widow's shop with her boots in her hand and out into the little yard behind it, where the widow kept her barrels of tallow and her broken things. The old straw tick was where it had been since the autumn, rolled and tied against the wall under a sack, too lumpy to sleep on and too good, the widow said, to burn.

The widow was up, as she always was, standing at her back door in her shawl with a cup, watching the sky. She looked at Lira, and at the tick, and at Lira again.

"I'll give you a mark for it," said Lira.

"It's not worth a mark."

"Then give me change."

The widow considered this, and gave her change, out of her apron, in coppers. Lira took the mark out of the tin to pay for it, and stood holding the open tin in the grey light with one coin fewer in it. It was the first thing she had ever bought out of it. She had saved it for a door, and then for a cart, and the first thing it had paid for was a lumpy straw mattress to tie round a post.

She shut the lid, and put the tin back in her pocket. Then she put the tick on her shoulder and went up through the lanes with it, at first light, toward the Cinder House.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

When Cael came into the yard the post in the grey half was fat.

Lira had wrapped it from the height of his knee to the height of his head in an old straw tick, folded double, and tied it round and round with a rope that had seen better days on a barge. The grey canvas with the chalk columns on it was hanging from a nail on the wall behind, where it would be safe. She was standing beside the post with her sleeves rolled and the chalk in her hand, and the look on her face was the barrel look, and he understood that the last evening was finished with, and that she would not mention it, and that he should not either.

"Hit it," she said.

He hit it. It went whuff, softly, and took his fist in up to the knuckles, and gave nothing back.

"Again."

He hit it again. Whuff. There was no mark. There was no sound worth calling a sound, and nothing jarred up his arm, and when he took his fist away the straw swelled back slowly into the shape it had been, as if he had never touched it.

"That's what it's like. Or that's what I think it's like. I asked Doss this morning at your yard door, coming in off his watch, and he said near enough, only it's worse, because the post doesn't look at you." She came round the post and stood beside him. "You can't hurt it. You can't knock it down. It won't tell you when you've done well. You'll hit it a thousand times and at the end it'll look the same as it does now." She held out her hand, palm up. "Give me your fist."

He gave it to her, and she rubbed the chalk across his knuckles, hard, until they were white, and let go.

"Five," she said. "The same place. As fast as you can make them true. Not as hard. As true."

He put five into the straw at the height of a man's lowest rib, fast, and felt each one go in and come back. When he stepped away there were five small white marks on the ticking where his knuckles had kissed it, and they were spread across the width of his whole hand and a little more.

"That's a man's side." She was looking at them. "All of it. That's not a place."

"They were all on the rib."

"They were all on his ribs, if he's got ribs the size of a door." She brushed the marks off with the flat of her hand. "Again."

He did it again, and again. She stood at his shoulder and watched his wrist, not his fist. After the fourth time she took his wrist in her hand and turned it a few degrees, so that the first two knuckles came in square instead of the last two. After the sixth she told him he was pulling the strike back before it had finished going in, to get the next one out faster, and that every one of them was arriving a little short because of it. After the ninth she said nothing at all and only watched.

"Every one of those wanted to be the one that counted," she said at last.

"Isn't that the idea?"

"Not here." She tapped the post. "Not one of them counts. The first doesn't, and the second doesn't, and the fifth doesn't. Throw him a strike that has to count by itself, and he'll take it, and put it wherever he puts things, and stand there, and you'll have spent it." She put her finger on the straw at the height of a lowest rib, on one small place. "Forget the strike. What you want is somewhere on him that hasn't finished healing yet. Then you put the next one in it before it has. Then the next."

"That's backward from everything I've done since the autumn," he said. "I've spent all winter making every one I throw worth throwing."

"Then do it backward." She chalked his knuckles again. "You're good at learning things twice."

He thought, while he hit, about a fight he had watched in his second week in Ardenmere, from the rope, with Lira beside him and the notebook on his knee. A Bronze Iron against a Stone woman with grey at her temples. It had gone seven exchanges, and the thing he had written down about the Iron man was that he struck short and hard, with no reach at all, and that everything he hit, he seemed to hit in exactly the same place.

He stopped with his fist half drawn back.

"They do it," he said. "Iron. That's what they do themselves."

Lira looked at him.

"The Bronze in my second week. Against the Stone woman. He hit her in the same place every time. I wrote it down. I didn't know why." He looked at the five white marks, which were a little closer together this time, nearly inside a palm. "Maybe that's how they think. Because it's how their own bodies work. Things pile up in one place."

"Then he'll know what you're doing." She said it slowly. "When you start doing it."

"Yes."

"And you'll have to do it anyway."

"Yes."

She looked at him for a moment, with her head on one side, and then she nodded, short, and he saw something go across her face that he had not seen there since before Feryn. It was gone before he could name it.

"That," she said, "is the first useful thing either of us has said about Iron." She chalked his fist. "Five. Same place. True."

By the end of the third morning the five white marks would fit under two of her fingers, and by the end of the fifth they were coming closer together still. They had also begun, though neither of them said so, to arrive faster than the straw could swell back between them.

Doss came down into the kitchen at the hour he always came down, an hour before his watch, to eat what Torvin's wife had left for him under a cloth. He found Cael at the table with the Log open and a candle, and sat down across from him with his bad knee out straight under the bench, and ate without talking.

"The girl asked me about Iron," he said at last.

"She told me."

"I told her what I could. She didn't write any of it down. She just listened, with her head on one side, like a hen." Doss broke his bread. "You'll want it as well, I suppose."

"If you'll tell it again."

Doss was quiet. He was a big slow man with a flat face that had been hit a great many times, and when he was thinking his scarred knuckles went still on the table.

"Twice," he said. "At Bronze. One season and a half, I was Bronze in her book. Two of those were Iron men. Different men. Same thing." He looked at the candle. "You hit a Shield, it shines. You know you've hit it. You hit Stone, you feel the grit go flat; you know. Force shoves you after. Ember, you get the heat in your face. Something comes back. Every Path I ever hit, something came back off it and told me I'd been there." He put his bread down. "Iron, nothing. You put your best into it, and it goes in, and that's all. Like dropping a stone down a well and never hearing it land."

"And then?"

"And then you do it again. And again. And somewhere in the third exchange you start to think you never threw it. That's the bit nobody tells you." Doss looked at his own hands on the table. "You stop believing your hands. They tell you they've landed, and you can feel they've landed, and the man in front of you is stood there like he's waiting for a cart. So you start to think your hands are lying. And once you think that, you're done. You start holding back, to save them. Or you start swinging wild, to make them prove it." He picked up his bread again. "Either way he's got you, and he's not done a thing."

Cael wrote it down. Doss: nothing comes back. You stop believing your hands. Then you're done.

"Was there anything," he said, "that he did after? After you'd landed a good one?"

Doss chewed, and swallowed.

"He'd wait," he said at last. "The second one would. After a big one. Not long. You'd think he was being polite." He shrugged. "I thought he was being polite. I was fifty-one fights in and I thought an Iron Bronze was being polite to me." He looked at Cael, and there was something nearly like a smile at the corner of the flat mouth. "Write that down as well. Write down that I was a fool."

Cael wrote down He'd wait. After a big one. He did not write down the other part.

He was still turning it over the next morning, coming down from the old man's gate, when he passed the woman who kept the chalk board at the bottom of the lane of yards. She was sitting on her stool beside it in the sun, as she always was, with her slate of prices and a tin cup of something hot. He had walked past her perhaps three hundred times since the autumn. She had grey at her temples and a way of sitting very square on the stool with both feet flat, and it was only now, with he'd wait in his head, that he looked at her properly and knew her.

He stopped.

"You fought the Iron man," he said. "In the autumn. At the Cinder House. My second week. Seven exchanges, and you put your hand up."

She looked at him over the cup.

"I did," she said. "You're the circuit boy from Torvin's. The one who watches feet." She drank. "I heard you've got an Iron coming."

"Bronze. From down the river."

"Bronze." She set the cup on the edge of the board, between Tuesday and a quarter-mark the hour. "Well. He hit me in the same place every time. You'll have seen that, if you were watching."

"I wrote it down."

"I counted after. In the evening, from the marks." She touched her own side, low, under the arm, where her coat lay against it. "Eleven. All in a place you could have covered with a cup." She looked up the lane, toward the old man's gate, and back. "And every time I got one in on him, a real one, he'd stand there a moment before he came on again. Not long. Like a man who's carried a full bucket across a yard and wants to set it down before he picks up the next." She shrugged. "I thought I was hurting him, at first. I wasn't. He was only putting it somewhere."

"Where?"

"If I knew that," she said, "I'd have won."

He thanked her, and she went back to her slate. When he was halfway down the lane she called after him, not loudly, without turning round on the stool:

"He'll let you hit him. The first while. Don't let that fool you into thinking he's slow."

He wrote it down at the bottom of the lane, against the wall, standing up. Chalk-board woman (the Stone woman, week two): he'd stand a moment after a good one. Setting a bucket down. Putting it somewhere. Then, under it, because two people had told him the same thing without knowing each other: Doss said it too. He'd wait.

He looked at it. Two was not three, and it was not a pattern yet, so he drew a small ring round it and left it open.

Darrow Innes said yes on the Sunday.

The answer came up the river in Feryn's hand, on the back of a carter's slip, and Feryn brought it to the Cinder House himself, after the card, and put it on Vell's table without a word. He'll come. Sunday fortnight. Straight book, full gate, her rules, her call. Says to tell the keeper he saw her at Fenrow and he'll take her word over a magistrate's.

It went until somebody put a hand up, or could not go on, or she called it. Once he was over the rope, nobody stopped it but her; what happened inside was his to carry, and nobody was making him do it.

Cael watched them go.

"I gave them the lists," said Vell, to her ledger. "I'm told it's quicker."

He had written to Hesk on the night of the fourth stair, all of it, by the bead of Yeni's lamp, and posted it in the west bag at noon the next day: Darrow Innes and the board and the fourteen names, Vell's three things and the one he had kept only to the letter, and Lira's room, and what he had said in it, which had been harder to write down than to say. He took it out to the low wall by the pump. The pear tree had finished with its flowers; the last of them lay brown in the corner of the yard where Torvin's wife had swept them, and the tree had put out small green leaves in their place, all at once, as if it had changed its mind about something.

He read that twice. It was the plainest sentence in the letter, and it did not promise him anything; Hesk never promised him things he could not put his name under, and he had not done it here. He tried them both together on the Tuesday night, in Torvin's yard, facing the trough.

He had not meant to. It was not in the plan, since nothing borrowed was in the plan, and he and Lira had settled that on the first morning of the straw post without either of them having to say it. But it had been sitting in him since Feryn's wall like a question at the end of a page: there were two of them now, side by side in the dark behind his breastbone, the leaning one and the heavy one, and he had only ever picked up one at a time.

So he stood with his back to the house and the moon on the whitewash, and went in.

He found the Wind first, as he always did, and held it, the readiness, the tilt, which was slow coming but came a little, the ground going short under him by a finger's width. Then, without letting go of it, he reached past it for the other one.

The Wind went out of his hands as soon as he reached. It did not fade; it was simply gone, the way a thought goes when somebody says your name. He stood there with nothing.

He tried again. This time he went for the heavy one first, and began to gather it, the long breath, the middle going still and thick; he could see it start in his shadow on the wall. Then, half through the breath, he reached back for the Wind, and the gathering broke. It did not go forward, or anywhere; it only came apart in the middle of him, like a stack of bricks with the bottom one pulled, and went nowhere at all, and the water in the trough lay flat and still with the moon in it and did not so much as shiver.

His arms went heavy anyway. That was the worst of it. He had got nothing, and the wet sand came into both arms from the shoulder down all the same, as if he had.

He sat on the low wall for most of an hour with his hands in his lap and thought about it.

One at a time, then, and slowly. The Wind came when it liked, and when he asked it came late and small; the other needed a whole breath, and showed in his middle like a stone in a sack, and cost him his arms. And the two of them would not sit in his hands at the same time, because reaching for one let go of the other. He could not do it, and he was not sure there was any it to do.

In the morning in the grey half he told Lira, who listened with the chalk in her hand and then went to the canvas hanging on its nail on the wall, where the post's columns had gone to keep them safe from the straw. On the Wednesday before the bout, at first light, Coss was standing at the gate in the wall of the Cinder House yard.

Cael saw him from the straw post and did not know him for a moment, because he had never once thought of Coss in this yard, where Coss had never come. In the autumn he had walked every lane of the district and asked nothing about the yards, and in the spring he had sat at a pie stall in his Sunday coat. He had not once come up the lane to the place where the boy actually fought.

He was here now, in the brown coat, and the brown coat was creased all down one side as if he had slept in it on a bench. He had not shaved. He stood in the gate with one hand on the post of it and looked at the yard as if it were somewhere he had read about and had not expected to be so small: the groove, the rope on its stakes, the barrel, Vell's empty table in the shade of the back wall. Then he looked at Cael, at the straw post, and at the chalk on Cael's knuckles.

Lira had seen him too. She looked at Coss, and then at Cael, and without a word she took the chalk and went down to the far end of the grey half and began going through her own corners alone, where she could see everything and hear nothing.

Cael went across the yard to the gate.

"I came on the night mail," said Coss. His voice was hoarse. "From regional. I've two days without pay, and I've spent one of them on a cart, and I'll spend the other going back on the noon one." He looked past Cael at the post. "Is that what you do?"

"Some of it."

Coss nodded slowly. Then, as if he had decided to stop putting it off, he took a folded paper out of his inside pocket and held it out.

It was a district return. Cael had seen the form at the post, at the clerk's counter: a long sheet that went to regional every week, with boundaries and permits and pigs. Halfway down it, in the clerk's careful hand, under Public notices posted in the district, somebody had copied Vell's card word for word. LAST BOUT, SUNDAY FORTNIGHT. DARROW INNES (Bronze 1, Iron Path) against unrated (vouched). Somebody else had drawn a single neat line under it in red.

"Your post's clerk copies every board in the district into his return. He always has. It's in the form. Nobody's read that column in twenty years." He took the paper back and folded it. "Somebody read this one. My section head put it on my desk on Monday, with that line under it, and went away. He didn't say anything. Last time he said a view. This time he didn't say anything at all."

He put the paper away.

"That's what I came to tell you. That nobody's saying anything. You don't know these people, and I don't either, not really, but I know the floor I work on. When it stops talking, it's because somebody's been told it needn't." He looked at Cael. "You've made it loud. Loud gets answered. I don't know what the answer is. I don't know who'd give it. I only know there's a desk somewhere that's read this, and I can't see it from mine."

"Then don't do it." Coss's voice cracked on it, and he stopped, and started again, lower. "Not like this. Pull out. Say it's the ribs. Say anything you like. Nobody in this world ever blamed a boy for a sprain. Vell would take it. The Iron man would take it; he's touring, there's a gate every Saturday on that river." He put his hand flat on the gatepost, hard, as he had put his hands flat on the table either side of a pie. "Go back to being a line in brackets for a season. Let legal sit. Let them forget."

Cael looked at him.

He had never seen Coss like this, though he had seen him level at a desk with a stamp, and careful in a reading room, and very still over a pie he had not eaten. He had never seen him not know what to do with his hands.

"I was quiet all autumn," Cael said. "I did everything you'd have told me to." He held Coss's eyes. "It didn't keep the sweep out of the market, or the mark off my file, or you off that cart."

Coss did not answer.

"Somebody else wants me gone. Not you. Lira worked that out on a roof the day you came, and I think she's right, and I think you think so too. Somebody I've never met has decided I'd be better somewhere small, and they don't need a reason anybody can read. I can't out-quiet that." He looked at the creased brown coat, and the hand on the gatepost. "I've tried. I was better at it than anybody. It's the one thing they've already got."

Coss stood there with his hand on the post of the gate.

Then he took his hand away, and looked at it, as if he had not known it was there. He sat down on the end of the trestle bench just inside the gate, the one the girls from the wall used when there was nobody fighting, and put his elbows on his knees.

"I've a daughter," he said.

Cael did not say anything.

"She'll be fourteen at midsummer. She does her lessons at the kitchen table with her tongue between her teeth." Coss looked at the dirt between his boots. "When I go out on a file she asks me at the door whether this one's going to be interesting, and I tell her they never are. I told her that in the autumn, about yours." He was quiet a moment. "I haven't told her anything since. There's nothing in it I could tell a child."

He turned his hat round in his hands.

"I sit and watch her do her sums, and I think about your file. Thin, and odd, and walking off its road in three places. And I think, if it were hers, what would I want?" He shook his head slowly. "I don't know. What I'd want her to do, I couldn't tell you. I know what I'd want done for her. I'd want somebody to come and say it to her face, whatever they had, in their own coat. Not across a desk." He looked up. "That's all this is. It's no use to you. I know it's no use."

"It's some use."

Coss looked at him a moment longer. Then he stood up, slowly, a man who had been on a cart all night, and put his hat on.

"Then don't do it by halves. If you're going to be loud, don't stop at loud enough." He looked once more round the yard, at the post and the straw and the groove and Lira going through her corners at the far end without once looking their way. "I'll not come again before Sunday. I can't. I've no days left."

He went out through the gate. Cael watched him go down the lane in the grey light, in the creased coat, without looking back this time, toward the river and the noon cart.

Lira came back up the grey half when he was out of sight.

"He's frightened for you."

"Yes."

"Good." She held out the chalk. "Somebody up there ought to be."

That night, at the very back of the Log, below the fourteen names, he wrote: Coss has a daughter. Fourteen at midsummer. He came on the night mail on his own days to tell me nobody was saying anything. He sat looking at it. Then he wrote one more line under it, and did not know quite why: He asked me what he'd want if it were her. I think he was asking himself, and he came all this way to do it out loud.

Chapter 57 — The Crossing

Somebody had been at the board at the triangle in the night.

Vell's card was still in the middle of it, where the light was best, on the back of its lamp-oil bill. LAST BOUT, SUNDAY FORTNIGHT. DARROW INNES (Bronze 1, Iron Path) against unrated (vouched). But under it, on the bare grey wood of the old door, somebody had written in charcoal, in large uneven capitals that sloped downhill toward the cooper's shed, HESK-WARD. Somebody else had underlined it twice. A third person, in chalk, had added 13 TO 1 beside it, and a fourth had crossed that out and written SHAME.

Cael stood and looked at it on the way up, at noon, with Lira beside him and his wraps over her arm.

"Red Cap," said Lira. "He can't do a W. Look at it."

The W was two Vs that had not quite met. Cael looked at it. In seven months the board had known him as a line in brackets, and now it had his name on it, spelt by a boy who could not do a W, in a hand that would wash off in the first rain.

"Come on," said Lira. "You're not fighting the board either."
