He sat with it a long time.

Recorded. Whatever kept that book had seen what the yard saw, and that was all it had to say. Vell had at least said so entered, and said his name, and written down how; this one wrote less than Vell, and did not even say who had won. It made him want to laugh, sitting there, and his ribs were very clear that he was not to.

He took the Log out of his coat and opened it on his knee.

The front went first, as always, and went down easily, because it was his and he had built every piece of it on the straw. Seventeenth. Darrow Innes, Bronze Rank 1, Iron Path. Won, fourth exchange, called, by incapacity. Each exchange in a line. The crossing, with the empty line filled in at last: Ruling: it held. Low left, rib to hip. One man; one afternoon. Doss's thing, and what he had done about it: believed his hands. The nod, read in two exchanges, and Lira's chin. Feryn's hand, put where the exchange would end, borrowed and used. What won it: Lira's way. Say it plainly. Ten in one place, and not one of them meant to count. The costs: the forearm, the right side, the ribs, a week, the edges, going. The arms full of sand in the middle of a bout, which had never happened, and which Lira was owed a long talk about.

Then he turned the book over to the back.

Seventh instance. Darrow, third exchange. The step. Not asked. Everybody saw.

Eighth instance. Darrow, fourth exchange.

He sat with the pencil over the page.

He tried to draw it first, as Corvane had taught him to draw a thing he could not say, with a stick figure and a long arm coming at it and two marks in its chest; but the two marks were wrong, because they were two and it had not been two, and he struck it through. Then he tried words. The Wind took me round and then — and struck that, because there had been no then in it anywhere. I picked up both — and struck that, because he had not picked up anything. He had reached for one and found himself holding a basket with two handles, and the reaching and the finding were in the one room in himself that he had never been able to see into, so that he could no more write down how to do it again than he could have written down how he had grown an inch since the autumn.

So in the end he wrote the only sentence that would stand up on the page. It did not explain anything; he wrote it the way you drive a stake in at the edge of a marsh, not to say what is out there in the reeds, but to say where the dry ground stops.

They're not separate things I switch between. They're one thing with parts I haven't found all of yet.

Chapter 59 — By Name

[Building, spatially clear narration; earn the public confrontation and let its consequences land]

In the morning the edges of the room were edges again.

He lay on the cot and tested it before he moved anything else. He looked at the window, and then quickly at the shelf, and the shelf was where he had sent his eyes and arrived there with them, not after; he did it twice more to be sure, and then he tried to sit up, and found out what the ribs thought about mornings.

Yeni was already gone, her blanket folded into its square, and the wheezing man was asleep with his mouth open. Somebody had put a cup of water on the floor by the cot, where he could reach it without bending, and had turned Yeni's lamp, which was out, toward the wall, so that the first light from the window would not come off its brass into his eyes. He drank the water with both hands, and his arms answered him slowly and sorely, like men called to work on a holiday, but they answered.

It took him a quarter of an hour to dress, and he went down the stairs one at a time, holding the rail and breathing like the man of ninety Lira had promised, and came into the kitchen.

Torvin's wife was at the range. She looked round at him once, all of him, from his feet to his face and back, as Darrow had looked at him from across the circle, and turned back to the pot without a word. When he had got himself down onto the bench she put a bowl of oats in front of him with real milk on them and an egg broken into the middle, still soft. Then, in front of the bowl, she put a bun.

"It's not from me. It's from her."

Sella was at the end of the table in her boots, eating bread with great dignity. She did not look up.

"That's five. Five buns I've lost on you since the autumn. She keeps count. I'd lost count. She hadn't." She turned a page of somebody's old newspaper that she was not reading. "I'll bet against you again, you know. Next time. I've told everybody."

"I know."

"Somebody in this house has to be on the other side." Sella looked at him at last, over the paper, at the way he was sitting with his right arm held against himself. "You look terrible."

"Thank you."

"It's a compliment. On you it's a compliment." She went back to the paper.

Doss came in from his watch while Cael was eating. He stood in the doorway in his big coat with his bad knee and his flat face and looked at Cael, and then came and sat down across from him and took the cloth off his own plate.

"I heard." Doss ate a little. "I heard you believed your hands."

"Yes."

Doss nodded slowly, chewing. Then, without looking up from the plate, he put his scarred right hand flat on the table, palm down, beside Cael's bowl, for a moment. Then he took it away and went on eating.

Lira came to the kitchen door at the hour of the grey half and did not come in.

"You're not training. Don't ask. You're coming up to sit on the bench and watch me teach the wall girls to fall over, and then you're going to Vell's table, because she's sent the pie boy for you twice already this morning and he's getting cross."

So he went up to the Cinder House at the pace of a cart with a bad wheel, with Lira beside him going at the same pace without once mentioning it, and sat on the bench in the grey half while she taught four girls from the wall how to fall in the soft corner by the drain. The straw post stood in its corner with its rope round it. Somebody had already had a go at it; there was a fist-shaped hollow in the straw at the height of a small boy's shoulder.

"Red Cap." Lira had followed his eyes. "Before it was light. He's been telling everybody he knows where the place is."

Feryn came while the girls were falling. He came through the gate with his bag over his shoulder, which he had not had before, and his once-good coat buttoned to the throat, and stood in front of the bench looking down at Cael's way of sitting.

"He's gone. Darrow. On the first barge down, before the light. I walked him to the steps." He shifted his bag. "He asked me to tell you a thing."

Cael waited.

"He said he'll be back up this river in the autumn, for his evaluation, and when he comes, he'll want to know." Feryn's mouth went up at one corner. "He said he's not in a hurry. He said you shouldn't hurry either. He said that more than once, as if he thought you might."

"He's right."

"He's usually right. It's the most tiresome thing about him." Feryn looked at the straw post, and the hollow in it, and back. "And I'm off myself, on the noon barge. There's a yard on the salt flats that's been asking for me since the winter, and I've been up and down this river three weeks, coughing on people." He hitched the bag again. "The coat's not done. The tailor says Thursday. Grey, with a collar. I'll not see it till the autumn." He looked down at his frayed cuffs, and at Cael. "You'll have to send it after me."

"Where?"

"Somewhere. I'm always somewhere. Vell will know." He looked at Cael a moment longer, and the cough and the jokes went out of him, as they sometimes did. "My account's still open. You know that."

"I know."

"Good." He turned to go, and turned back. "You did a thing yesterday I'll be thinking about for a year. I'd like to say I knew. I didn't know. I thought you'd lose well." He grinned. "I'll say I knew anyway, in a few towns. Don't contradict me."

He went out through the gate in the wall. The girls by the drain watched him go, and one of them fell over without meaning to, and Lira told her that counted. Then Lira jerked her head toward the back wall, and he got up.

Vell was at her table in the shade of the back wall, with her tea and her ledger and her pen laid across the page. The pie boy had stopped being cross. He stood at the end of the table and watched Cael come across the yard toward it with the look of somebody who has been told to fetch a thing and is relieved to see it arriving.

There was nothing in the circle. It was a Monday.

"Sit down."

He had never once sat at her table. Nobody did; you stood in front of it. But there was a stool, and she pushed it out with her foot, and he sat down on it with his arm held against his side.

She did not say anything about the bout. She drank her tea, and put the cup down, and turned the ledger round on the table so that it faced him, and put one finger at the top of a line and took it away.

He read it.

Cael Hesk-ward, assessed-Copper, def. Darrow Innes (Bronze R1, Iron Path)

After it there was the rest: the exchange, the call, the yard. But it was the first part he read, and he read it several times. His name was at the beginning of the line, in her small square hand, where in seven months there had only ever been a pair of brackets.

"The yard came."

"Yes."

"I've a custom about that." She drank. "So it's in."

He sat looking at it, and thought about the back page of the Log, with fourteen names and five of them missing, and about the board at the triangle, and a W that did not meet.

"Do you know what that's for? That line?"

"So that people would notice."

"People noticed yesterday. People notice everything; they forget it by Thursday." She put her finger on the line again. "This is for Thursday. And next year. If you stop coming to my table, there are three hundred people who'll want to know why, and some of them will come and ask me. I'll open this and show them that line, and tell them I don't know where you've gone. And they'll go and ask somebody else. And then somebody else." She closed the ledger, gently. "That's all a book's for. It doesn't keep anybody safe. It keeps them asked about."

He did not say anything.

"Thank you."

"I didn't do anything. I wrote down what happened." She looked at him over her cup with her flat, thorough look. "I'm not going to ask you what it was. You'd say you didn't know, and I'd believe you, and then we'd both have wasted a morning."

"I don't know."

"I know you don't. I watched you not know it, from four paces." She put the cup down. "Go home. Lie down. Come back when the girl lets you, not before, and not on a Sunday. I'll not card you this month. You've nothing left to prove to anybody this month except your ribs." She picked up her pen. "You're in my light."

He got up off her stool, which took some time, and went. At the gate he looked back, and she was writing something in the back of the book, at the pages nobody read.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

In the afternoon he went down to the market, because Lira said he could walk if he walked slowly, and the boys found him at the bottom of the market steps.

They came at him from two directions at once, Red Cap from the east lanes and the other from the river, and they both stopped dead about six feet away and looked at him and then at each other, as if to agree on who was going to speak, and failed.

"Hesk-ward," they both said, together.

Then they stood there, appalled, and turned and began to argue in fierce low voices about who had said it first, and whose idea it had been to say it at all, and Cael went on past them up the steps. Halfway up he heard Red Cap say, quite loudly, that they had agreed, and the other say that agreeing wasn't the same as doing it at the same time like a pair of geese. It went on all the way to the top.

The bread woman was at her stall under her high cracked lantern with her chin up. When she saw him coming she reached down under the counter, not into the basket where she kept the loaves from underneath, but further, to a cloth bundle on the shelf below it. She took out of it a small round loaf with a dark top, the one she kept back every morning, the one he had seen her eat herself at noon a hundred times, and put it in his hands.

He reached for his coin.

"Don't you dare."

"I'd like to know your name. You told me once. There were barrels."

She looked at him with her chin up. Then she laughed, short and loud, so that the fruit woman at the next stall looked round.

"You had your chance. Go and eat that before it's cold."

He went, and ate half of it on the low wall by the pump at Torvin's, slowly, because chewing turned out to involve the ribs, and he thought it was the best bread he had ever eaten, and he knew he would never find out her name now, and he did not mind.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The letter was against the salt crock when he came in at dusk.

He knew the hand from the door, but not the date until he picked it up and counted, standing in the kitchen with it in his hand. It had been written on the Sunday before last, after Hesk had sat three days with the letter from the night of the fourth stair, and it had gone into the east bag the best part of a week before Darrow Innes came into the yard. Hesk had not known how any of it would go, and he did not know now. The bout was a day old, and Hesk would not know for a week.

He took it out to the low wall by the pump and broke the seal in the last of the light.

Cael,

I've had yours three days, and I've written this four times, and burned three. I'll tell you why, and then I'll say the thing.

You told me what you mean to do on Sunday fortnight, and who against, and why. I've read it till the folds have gone soft. I'm frightened, and I won't pretend I'm not, because you've never once in your letters pretended not to be, and I'd be ashamed to do less. By the time this reaches you it'll be over, one way or the other, and I'll be sitting here not knowing which. I find I can bear that better than I'd have thought. I'll tell you why.

It's the last part of your letter. Where you told me what you did to the girl, and what she said, and that you'd done it to me as well, all winter, five times over, and to her before. You wrote it down plainly, in ink, and posted it to the one person who'd have forgiven you for leaving it out.

You tell me she says you're more like me than you know. She's right, and kinder about it than I'd have been. I kept a thing from you for years because I'd decided I was the one to carry it. I never once wrote you a letter that said: here is the part where I did it wrong. You've written me one at fourteen.

I said I'd say it properly when I'd found the words. I thought they'd be about the fight. They aren't. I don't know how the fight went. I know how you went into it: loud, and told, and with her beside you because you'd asked her, even if you asked her late. That's the thing I'm proud of. It would be the same thing whichever way Sunday went, so I can say it now, before I know, and not have to take any of it back.

I'm proud of you. There. That's it said properly, in ink, where I can't get at it again with a pen.

Write and tell me how it went. Then write and tell me what you had for your supper after, because I'll want that as well.

— H.

He read it twice, and then sat on the wall with it on his knee for a long time, with the pear leaves going dark over his head and the house behind him starting its evening noises, the brothers arguing on the stairs and Torvin's wife's spoon against the pot.

Where I can't get at it again with a pen.

That was Hesk all over, who would not send a thing until it was right and, once it was right, would not let himself near it again in case he spoiled it. He had found the words, and they were not the ones he had gone looking for, and he had said so.

He thought about writing back tonight, and telling him the fourth exchange as near as he could, which was not very near, and the crossing, and the straw post, and the bucket and the gate, and what he had had for supper after, which had been nothing, because he had been asleep, and then an egg in the morning, and a bun that Sella had lost.

He folded the letter along its own folds and put it in the front of the Log, inside the cover, on top of the other two. You're describing a home. It's not nothing. I'm proud of you. The three of them lay together there, a little thicker each time, and the cover did not quite close over them any more.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On the Tuesday, two days after the bout, he saw the stranger in the market.

He had gone down for apricots, because the fruit woman had sent word by Red Cap that she had some, and because walking was supposed to be good for the ribs if he did not do too much of it. It was an ordinary afternoon, the market half full, the slow kind of afternoon after a busy morning, with the stallholders sitting down on their crates and talking across the rows. He had bought the apricots and was standing by the fruit woman's stall eating one, not thinking about anything, which he had been learning to do, when he felt himself being looked at.

He knew the feeling; he had felt it from a mark a hundred times, the moment before a bout when you know the person across the circle has stopped looking at the yard and started looking at you. He did not turn toward it. He went on eating the apricot, and turned the rest of himself a little, as if to look at the knife-grinder's wheel, and let his eyes go where the feeling came from.

Across the market, at the end of the second row, there was a person standing still.

That was all, at first. In a market everybody moves: people walk, and stop, and bend over a stall, and straighten, and walk on; even the ones standing still are moving, shifting their baskets, looking for somebody. This one was not doing any of that. They stood by the end of the knife-grinder's bench, a little back from it, in plain clothes the colour of the market, with nothing in their hands, and they were not looking at the stalls, or at the grinder, or at the people going past.

They were looking at him.

Not at his arm held against his side, or at the bruise he knew showed at the edge of his collar, or at the boy who had beaten a Bronze. They were looking at him, the way Corvane had looked at Feryn's shirt: at the place where the thing was, not at the things on top of it.

He held very still and made himself catalogue it as he would have catalogued an opening stance, without spending anything, without turning his whole self toward it and giving away that he had seen.

Not Compact; he was as sure of that as he had been of anything. He had stood across a desk from Coss and across a table from Ilsev, and both of them carried their work about with them like a case: a hurry with edges, a stamp, a person above them who would want to see what they had done. There was no case here, no pin, no little black book with a strap, and nobody anywhere behind this person who was going to read a report. There was only the looking.

And it was patient, which was the thing he would try to write that night and not manage. It was patient the way the old man in his gate was patient, and not at all like him: the old man was patient because he had nowhere he needed to be. This was patient the way a person is who has been somewhere a long time already and expects to be there a good while yet. It did not feel like a look that had started this afternoon. It felt like the first one he had been allowed to see.

He did not know how long it lasted. Not long; exactly as long, he thought afterward, as it took him to understand that he was being looked at and that he was being let know it.

Then the person turned, without any hurry, and walked into the market, and the market closed behind them as water closes, and they were gone. He watched the place where they had been, and there was nothing there but the knife-grinder, bent over his wheel, and the sparks.

He did not go after them.

His ribs would not have let him, but it was not his ribs. He had felt, in the length of that look, that it had been timed: that whoever it was had decided when he would see them and when he would stop, as Darrow had decided when the first exchange was over. A person who did that would not be found by a boy with a broken rib pushing through a market; they would be found only if they wished it. Going after them would have cost him everything he had left, and bought him nothing but proof that he had been allowed to look.

Spend nothing you don't have to.

He finished the apricot and thanked the fruit woman, who looked at his face and did not ask him anything, and walked back up through the lanes to Torvin's at the pace the ribs allowed. He went through the kitchen and out to the yard and sat down on the low wall by the pump, under the pear tree.

He sat there without taking out the Log, turning it over: the stillness, the plain clothes, the no-case, the look that had been allowed. He turned it over as he had turned over every opponent he had ever had to read, from every side, looking for the joint in it.

He did not find one. He was still sitting there when the light began to go, and Yeni came to the kitchen door with her sewing, and looked at him, and went back in.

Chapter 60 — The Message

[Building, spatially clear narration; earn the public confrontation and let its consequences land]

Lira came in through the kitchen at dusk with flour on her sleeve, because Yeni had found her at the widow's back door helping carry sacks, and had said four words to her, and Lira had put the sack down where she stood.

She came across Torvin's yard and sat down on the low wall beside him, on the left, without a word, and tore the end off a loaf she had in her bag and held it out, and he took it. They sat under the pear tree with the light going and ate the bread, and she waited.

"There was somebody in the market," he said at last.

He told it from the beginning, as she liked it, without saying what it meant: the apricots, the feeling from the mark, the knife-grinder's bench. A person standing still where everybody moves, with no case, no pin, no book. The look, and how long it lasted, and how it seemed to have been timed, and how they had turned and the market had shut behind them.

Lira did not interrupt, and when he had finished she sat with her chin on her fist and looked at the trough.

"Not Compact. You're sure."

"As sure as I am of anything I've only seen once." He turned the bread over. "Coss carries his work about with him. So did Ilsev. You can see it on them, a sort of hurry with edges, and somebody behind them waiting for a report. Even the man with the pin in the autumn had it, and all he did was walk through a market." He shook his head. "This one had nothing behind them at all. They weren't going to tell anybody what they'd seen. They'd come to see it for themselves."

"That's not better."

"No."

"Is it worse?"

He thought about it honestly.

"I don't know. It's other. It's not the thing I've been afraid of since the autumn. It's a different thing, standing next to it." He looked at the bread in his hand. "And it came after. Two days after. Not in the autumn, when nobody knew my face. Not on Sunday, in the crowd, where it would have been easiest to stand and look. After. When there was a line in Vell's book and my name on the board in Red Cap's writing."

Lira was quiet.

"I made myself loud for one kind of looking. I thought about who else might hear; I said it to you on the steps. But I thought about it the way you think about rain on a day you've already decided to go out." He set the bread down on the wall. "Whoever that was, Coss's drawer may be nothing to them. I could have lit a lamp on Sunday for somebody who was never looking in drawers."

"Or," said Lira, "they'd found you already, and Sunday only made them decide to let you see."

He looked at her.

"You said it felt like the first look you'd been allowed. Not the first look." She shrugged. "I don't know either. I'm only adding. It comes out both ways."

They sat on while the brothers argued on the stairs inside about a shirt, and the wheezing man's window stood open, and somewhere toward the river a dog was asking the lane its one question.

"Can I say a thing, and you not argue with it till I've finished?"

"Yes."

"You saw this at the third hour after noon." She did not look at him. "Yeni says you came in at the fourth and sat on this wall, and didn't move. She came and got me at the end of the sixth. Not you. Yeni." She let that sit. "Two hours, Cael. On a wall. Turning it over on your own till you'd made your mind up what it was, so that you'd have something tidy to bring me."

He opened his mouth, and shut it.

"I'm not angry. That's the other thing, the one with Vell, and that's paid, and this isn't that. This is smaller. But it's the same shape." She turned her head at last. "You don't have to have it worked out before you come and get me. You don't have to have anything worked out. You keep forgetting there's two of us. You can bring me a thing in pieces and we can sit on a wall and look at the pieces together. That's what I'm for. It's half of what I'm for."

"What's the other half?"

"Telling you you're doing it again." She almost smiled. "You're carrying all of it by yourself because you think that's what being careful means. It isn't. Being careful is not doing it alone."

He sat with that, and tested it against two hours on a wall, and against the fourth stair, and against five letters to Hesk with five things left out of them, and it held each time.

"I'll try."

"I know you will. And I'll check." She bumped his knee with hers. "You know I check."

"I know you check."

"Good." She stood up, and dusted the flour off her sleeve, which only spread it. "Eat that. You'll not think any better about strangers on an empty stomach, and you'll not think at all with ribs like that if you don't sleep." She held her hand down to him, on the good side, and he came up off the wall the old man's way, one piece on the next, and she watched him do it and said nothing about it at all.

At the kitchen door she stopped.

"Whoever it is, they looked at both of us on Sunday. I was at the barrel. They'll have seen me too." She considered it. "So it's not yours to carry. Not even half."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Coss opened the district return on the Wednesday afternoon, three days after, at his desk at regional, with the window behind him going grey.

He had not meant to read it. Nobody read the district returns, which came in every week in a canvas sack and stood a month in a rack by the door before they went down to the cellars, counted and never opened. But the Ardenmere return had been put on his desk on Monday of last week with a line under it in red, and since then he had gone to the rack himself for the next one before the clerk could tie it up.

It was in the clerk's careful hand, as always: boundaries, permits, a dispute about a gutter referred back to the parties, and under Public notices posted in the district, the card from the Cinder House board, copied word for word as the form required, and then, because the clerk was a careful man and the form said all matter posted, the chalk that somebody had written underneath it:

HESK-WARD. FOURTH. VELL'S CALL.

Coss read it twice, and then put his thumb to the bridge of his nose and sat with his eyes shut.

He had come back on the noon cart from Ardenmere a week ago with his days all spent and a creased coat and a cold. He had told himself all the way back, through two nights of carters' benches, that he had done what he could, and that it had been nothing, and that the boy would do what the boy had decided. At his desk on the Friday he had not been able to keep from thinking about the date on the card, and at home on the Sunday he had not been able to eat his dinner until the evening had gone far enough that it must be over, so that his daughter had asked him whether he was ill.

It was over, and he had not known how until now: a chalk line in a clerk's copy of a district board, three days late, sent in a canvas sack.

He opened his eyes and drew the file across the desk to make the entry, as he had made ten thousand entries, with the line already in his head: Subject remains in the district. No compliance action taken. Legal review pending. Public notice (district return, this week) of a circuit result; no compliance bearing. He uncapped his pen.

He opened the cover, and stopped.

There was a slip pinned inside it.

It was on the heavy grey paper they used on the floors above his, with a printed head along the top, a narrow band of small type and a row of numbers, and he knew the head. He had seen it twice before in eleven years, across the room, on other agents' desks, and both times the agent had closed the file very quickly and looked at nobody for the rest of the afternoon. He had never once seen it on a file of his own.

Below the head there was a code that was not in his register and had no prefix he knew at all, not even the regional one the autumn's sweep had carried. Under the code there was no office, no initials, no reason and no instruction. There was a date.

The date was Monday. The day after.

He sat looking at it.

He was very careful with himself about what it was, because he did not know. In the ordinary way a slip with that head meant that somebody above his floor, and above his section head's, wanted to know when the file moved; who, or why, it did not say. Whether it had anything to do with the mark Ilsev had found in the spring, he could not tell, though this one could at least be traced as far as a floor he had never been allowed to stand on. Whether it had anything to do with a chalk line in a clerk's copy of a board, or a Bronze lying down on raked dirt in front of three hundred people, or nothing at all, he could not tell either. A thing could be dated the day after another thing without being caused by it; he had told a great many people that, over the years, when they had come to him with two dates and a story.

He only knew that it was another place where the file had walked off its road, which made four, and that he could still see the footprints going away into the snow, more of them now and all going the same way, and still could not see who was walking.

The procedure allowed him to send a query upward. He took the form out of his drawer and laid it beside the file, and thought about his last query, the one about the sweep, which had come back in the spring pouch with a single word on it in a hand he did not know. Noted. He thought about putting his own name at the bottom of a question about this slip, and whether a man who did that might find, a month on, a slip of grey paper pinned inside his own file in the room at the end of the corridor. He did not think it likely, and he was not a man who called things likely without evidence. But sitting there with the form in front of him, he could not quite say it was not.

He had a daughter of fourteen at midsummer who did her sums at the kitchen table with her tongue between her teeth.

He put the form back in the drawer.

Then he closed the file without making the entry. He did not write subject remains, or legal review pending, or public notice of a circuit result, or anything at all. The pen lay on the desk beside it with its cap off, and the ink dried on the nib.

He took out his working log.

He had kept it for eleven years, in his own hand, in plain black books bought with his own money and shelved at home one after another. Nobody had ever asked him to keep it, or read it, and in it he had written every file he had opened and every file he had closed, and why, and what he had seen. He had written in it on the night of the sweep that the sweep was not standard, and on the night of the boy's objection that the objection was correct. He had written the Noted in it, and copied the word exactly, and the date it came. He had never once opened a file and not written down that he had.

He opened the log to the day's page and looked at it for a long time, and then closed it again, with nothing written, and put it in his inside pocket and buttoned his coat over it.

It was the first page he had ever left empty on purpose, and he did not like it. He sat at his desk in the grey light from the window and did not like it at all, with his hand flat on the closed file, and he understood that he had just done the first thing in his working life that he could not have written down and then stood behind.

He did not know who he was keeping it from, and that was the part he would lie awake with: whether it was from them, whoever they were, or from himself, or from a boy on a cot two days east who had asked him across a pie whether he knew what a flag was, and had watched him not move. He had told the boy the truth then; he had not known anything about a flag. He did now. He knew exactly as much as a slip of grey paper and a printed head and a date could tell a man, which was almost nothing, and was more than he had known on any day before this one.

At the end of the day he put the file back in the drawer for things under review, and locked the drawer, and took the key home with him, which was not the procedure either.

His daughter was at the kitchen table with her lessons when he came in. She looked up at him with her pencil in her teeth.

"Was anything interesting?"

He hung up his coat, with the log still buttoned inside it, and stood a moment with his hand on the coat.

"Somebody I know won something."

"Who?"

"Nobody you know." He sat down across from her, and drew her slate toward him, and looked at her sums. "You've carried the seven wrong."

She looked, and saw it, and rubbed it out, and did it again with her tongue between her teeth. He sat and watched her do it, and did not think about anything else for nearly a quarter of an hour, which was the longest he had managed in a month.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He wrote to Hesk on the Wednesday night, by the bead of Yeni's lamp, with the Log on his knee for a desk and his arm held against his side.

He told him the fourth exchange as near as he could, which was not near, and the crossing and the straw post and the bucket and the gate, the nod and Feryn's hand, the yard door and the chair, and that Vell had his name at the start of a line. He told him about supper: that there had been none, because he had been asleep, and then an egg, and a bun that Sella had lost on him, and the bread woman's own loaf, which she had kept back for herself every morning for seven months and given away to him, and he did not know her name. He did not tell him about the stranger in the market. Then he sat a while, and he did tell him, in four plain lines at the end, because he had promised to tell the next thing as it came and he had already been told off once this week for sitting on a wall.

Then he turned the Log over to the back.

He read the line he had written on Sunday night, at the bottom of the eighth instance, under the struck-through drawings: the fence at the edge of the marsh.

It did not belong there, he saw now; it was not about one bout or one half second. It was about all of it, every instance and both notices and whatever the next one was, and it ought to be somewhere he would see it every time he turned the book over, as Hesk's letters were somewhere he saw them every time he opened it. So he turned to the inside of the back cover, where there was nothing yet but the board's grain, and copied it there, slowly, in his best hand.

They're not separate things I switch between. They're one thing with parts I haven't found all of yet.

The front of the book had three letters in it now, and the back had a fence. He looked at the two ends of the book.

Then he turned to the last written page, under the eighth instance, and wrote the thing he had been turning over since the knife-grinder's bench. He had turned it over on the wall, and again with Lira, and all through the next day. It was short enough that it had to be right.

Someone else wants me gone. I used to think that meant the Compact. I'm starting to think Coss doesn't know who he was talking about either.

He read it back once, and did not change it.

Then he closed the Log, with its letters in the front and its fence in the back, and put it on the shelf beside Hesk's leather book, and lay down very carefully on his left side, which was the side that let him, and was asleep before Yeni had finished turning down the lamp.

In the morning he went up to the grey half, because Lira had said he could sit on the bench if he did nothing but sit.

The east wall's shadow lay long across the yard, as it did every morning, so that the Cinder House was split down the middle, a grey half and a bright half, with the groove going through both. The straw post stood in the corner of the grey half with Red Cap's fist still printed in it. Lira had taken the grey canvas off its nail on the wall and hung it back on the post, over the straw, where it had been all winter. The columns were on it in her chalk: the gone column, ruled off at forty, and the falls, and the long W with its strokes and rings and its small cost words, same, less, less, same, and the shorter P, with its four rings that said trough, and one stroke with no ring that said both. nothing. arms anyway.

He sat on the bench with his arm against his side and watched her.

She stood in front of the canvas with the chalk. Then, at the top of a clean stretch of grey beside the P, she wrote a W, and beside it a P, and drew a short line between the two of them, joining them. Under that she made one stroke, and put a ring round it, because it had come. Beside the ring, in her smallest letters, she wrote ribs. Then, after a moment, arms. Then, after a longer moment, she wrote one more word, and stood back so that he could read it from the bench.

Sunday.

She looked at it a while, with her head on one side.

"There. Now it's on the post."

She put the chalk in her pocket and came and sat down on the bench beside him, on the good side, and they watched the girls from the wall come in through the gate in a row, yawning, for their coin's worth of falling over. The sun had come up somewhere behind the east wall. The shadow had begun to shrink back across the dirt toward it, as it did, a little at a time.

When it reached the bench, Lira got up and moved them both along it, to the next bench, and sat down again, and said nothing about it. When it reached that one, she moved them again. She kept them in the grey half for as long as there was any grey half left.
